Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Problem with chromatographic column was identified in test Related substances. Column 
efficiency was not confirmed. So, laboratory used the similar column but with greater length.
Related substances test also caused problems during NDA process but have another issue - 
bad resolution between peaks and system non-stability - HA (MoH) asked to include 
additional solution and time for column equation. MoH used their own column for this 
analysis so we suppose that probably the issue was related to the concrete column. Turku 
answered that the method was validated and no need to change it, MoH accepted this 
explanation. Facing with the problem with this method again we need to initiate additional 
evaluation and find the reason for such method errors to avoid quality issues in future. Bayer 
provided Roszdravnadzor with a new column according to ND so, no any old/incorrect 
column took place in this case.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 ( CTD section):
Bayer Oy is using the following columns in the related substances analysis of Kyleena IUS:
for LC impurity test 1 Merck's column Purospher STAR RP-18 endcapped 125 mm x 3 mm x 
3µm, Merck Hibar 1.50413 is used,
and for LC impurity test 2 Waters's column Spherisorb ODS-2, PSS839999, is used.
With these columns the required efficiency requirements from the method validation have 
been met in the analysis.

Currently, however, Waters does not produce this Spherisorb column any more. Therefore, 
Bayer Oy is currently using as a substitute a column manufactured by VDS Optilab:
VDS Optilab; Spherisorb-ODS 125mm x3mm x 3um, cat.no. SPD20G030125. With the 
Optilab column the efficiency requirements of the analytical method have also been met.
According to Bayer Oy's opinion it is better to use columns with the dimensions mentioned in 
the Test Procedure of Kyleena IUS, though the column manufacturer would be different, 
rather than a column with a greater length for example.

In some cases, when performing HPLC analyses it may be difficult to achieve all the 
efficiency requirements of the analytical method with a column having correct dimensions 
and stationary phase. Achievement of these requirements can vary with each new column 
even if they are from the same manufacturer. At Bayer Oy the procedure is such that the 
column is changed until the requirements specified in the Test Procedure are met with a 
column used. Only columns with which these requirements are met are used for actual 
analysis.
keywords: HPLC-method; chromatograms; related substances; system suitability test; analytical method validation

PRODUCTION METHOD (brief description)
Premix: Cellulose microcrystalline, crospovidone, and lactose monohydrate are mixed in a fluid-bed granulator.
Granulation liquid: Hypromellose 5 cP and sodium laurilsulfate are dissolved in purified water. Micronized BAY 63-2521 is then suspended in this solution forming a granulation liquid.
Granulation process: The premix is granulated with the granulation liquid in a fluid-bed granulator and dried. The dried granules are sieved.
Final blend: In a suitable device, e.g. drum mixer, the granulate and the sieved magnesium stearate are combined and mixed to form the final blend.
Tabletting: The blend is compressed into tablets.
Film-Coating: Hypromellose 3 cP, hydroxypropylcellulose and propylene glycol are subsequently solved in initially heated water which cools down during the solving procedure. The color pigments titan dioxide and ferric oxide yellow/red are suspended in that solution afterwards. The resulting homogeneous coating suspension is sieved and is sprayed on the tablets in a suitable coating device, e.g. a pan coater.
Granulation and Compression: Cellulose microcrystalline, lactose monohydrate and crospovidone are mixed (premix).
The granulation liquid is prepared from riociguat micronized, sodium laurilsulfate, hypromellose 5 cP and purified water in bulk to granulate the premix.
The dry mixture is granulated in a fluidized bed granulator with the granulating liquid. The granulate is dried and sieved and then the lubricant magnesium stearate is added to form a ready to press mixture.
The ready-to-press mixture is compressed to tablets on a tablet press.
Film-coating: The compounds propylene glycol, titanium dioxide, (ferric oxide yellow, ferric oxide red) hydroxypropylcellulose and hypromellose 3 cP are suspended in a container to form the coating suspension. In a coating pan, the coating suspension is sprayed through nozzles onto the tablets.

The only changes in the formulation since the Bioavailability studies were carried out are regarding the Film-coating color, as it is referred in the pharmaceutical development document P.2.2.01.

Throughout the whole clinical development, the tablet composition and manufacturing principles were not changed with only one exception regarding the color of the film coat. Whereas tablets used in clinical studies phase I and phase II were coated in red (titanium dioxide and ferric oxide red as pigment), in clinical phase III studies the color was changed to pale orange (titanium dioxide, ferric oxide yellow and ferric oxide red as pigment) due to blinding of the studies. The basic composition, the total amount of color pigments (0.83 mg/tablet) and total amount of film coat (2.5 mg/tablet) were not been changed.

The proposed commercial products are of the same core composition as the clinical phase III formulations. The changes introduced by modifying the film-coating, had no influence on dissolution results. As expected, there is only a very small influence of the film-coat, which is usually dissolved in aqueous media within few minutes, as it is referred in the Method Development – Dissolution P.5.3.21.

3.2.P.5.1 The colour of the solution may be “colourless” at release and stability. According to the batch analysis data and stability data, the solution never was colourless. In light of the specification change of the colour to “red”, please reconsider the solution being colourless.

Answer/Response:
It is Bayer’s proposal to continue to include “colourless” to the description of the Vitrakvi Oral Solution.
It is the approach of Bayer to add this description to all pale liquid, water-containing solutions. This is due to the fact, that most liquids are marketed in coloured containers, like for example the brown glass bottles used for Vitrakvi Oral Solution.
In this combination Bayer has experienced that pale coloured solutions are judged as colourless, by observing the content through the coloured container.
This applies in particular to the pale yellowish solution of Vitrakvi.
Based on this experience, Bayer includes “colourless” in the description of the Vitrakvi Oral Solution.

Person (QP) of the releasing site is ultimately responsible for the quality of the drug product:
[…] “There may be several sites involved in the various stages of manufacture, importation, 
testing and storage of a batch before it undergoes certification. Regardless of how many sites 
are involved, the QP performing certification of the finished product must ensure that all 
necessary steps have been completed under accepted pharmaceutical quality systems to assure 
compliance of the batch with GMP, the MA and any other legal obligations in the Member 
State where certification is taking place.” […]
Therefore, regarding certification of the quality of the drug product, the batch releasing site is 
the most relevant site.

guidelines

Question/Consideration: As mentioned in the Briefing Book, the reconstituted and diluted solution is considered a supersaturated solution, what is the solubility of Aliqopa in NaCl? In S.1.3.01#012739046-02, the solubility in Citric acid is 6.2 ∙ 10-1 mg/ml, is that the same solubility in NaCl?
Answer/Response:
As can be seen from document S.1.3.01, solubility of copanlisib dihydrochloride is highly pH dependent. The pH value of the citrate buffer (pH 5) for which the solubility is quoted above is about the same as that of the reconstituted and diluted NaCl solution (pH 4.7-5.3). The solubility of 6.2 ∙ 10-1 mg/ml is given for copanlisib dihydrochloride and corresponds to a solubility for copanlisib of 5.4 ∙ 10-1 mg/ml. It is therefore less than the concentration of the reconstituted and diluted solution, which has a copanlisib concentration of 5.8 ∙ 10-1 mg/ml. However, solubilities in the citrate buffer and the reconstituted and diluted lyophilizate are not strictly comparable.
Although the reconstituted solution is oversaturated, no precipitation of the API takes place under the prescribed handling conditions and the solution is kinetically stabilized.

Source: S.1.3.01-02 General Information - General Properties / Copanlisib dihydrochloride drug substance (#012739046; unchanged)
keywords: General Properties; stability data DS; solubility; stability data; Drug Product

Question/Consideration: What is the concentration of “supersaturated solution”?
Answer/Response: The reconstituted solution contains 15 mg/ml of copanlisib. The reconstituted and diluted solution has a copanlisib concentration of 0.58 mg/ml. All copanlisib solutions with a copanlisib content > 5.4 ∙ 10-1 mg/ml are considered supersaturated.
keywords: Drug Product; concentration; stability data; Shelf Life; assay

Question/Consideration: According to S.1.3.01, API is very slightly soluble in Buffer (citrate) pH 5, it seems that it is also very slightly soluble in DP (reconstituted and diluted NaCl solution, pH 4.7-5.3). How does Bayer test the solubility in DP and how to determine the solution is “supersaturated solution” ?
Answer/Response:
Solubility of copanlisib in the drug product is not routinely tested. As explained in Bayer’s answer to Question 1, for copanlisib dihydrochloride, the solubility of 6.2 ∙ 10-1 mg/ml is given, this corresponds to a solubility for copanlisib of 5.4 ∙ 10-1 mg/ml.
In the reconstituted solution, copanlisib concentration is 15 mg / mL, copanlisib content in the reconstituted and diluted solution is 5.8 ∙ 10-1 mg/ml. Thus, both solutions, the ´reconstituted solution´ as well as the final solution administered to the patient are supersaturated solutions.
Nevertheless, precipitation of API could not be observed when different holding time scenarios were tested for reconstitution and dilution in accordance with the patient information which allows 24 hours storage at 2°C to 8°C. As described in the Briefing Book, section 7.1., the tested storage scenarios had not effect on the copanlisib content in the diluted solution, and copanlisib content in the reconstituted and diluted solution was shown to comply with the expected values. Precipitates of crystalline copanlisib were not observed.
keywords: Drug Product; stability testing; holding time; stability data; in-process control

Question/Consideration: In Briefing Book, 4.3 Analysis for elemental impurities for the drug product. “In addition, no silicon oil residues could be detected using 1H-NMR”. In 4.4 Identification of turbidity causing species via filtration. “No crystalline copanlisib has been microscopically identified on the gold filter via SEM (scanning electron microscopy)”. Answer/Response:
Potential presence of silicon oil residues in lyophilizate samples of Aliqopa affected by the OOS was investigated using 1H-NMR by the external QC lab Currenta. Unfortunately, the test report only contains a summary of the data but not the raw data including the chromatogram. Raw data will need to be ordered separately.

During the investigation to identify potential residues causing the turbidity of the solution, the prepared solution was passed via a gold coated filter plate of polycarbonate with laser punched pores of 0.8 µm. Subsequently, an investigation based on visual microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was conducted.
No reliable evidence of presence of crystalline copanlisib could be confirmed.

Reference 1: Microscopic picture of the filter plate after passing a turbid sample

Reference 2 (for comparison only): Microscopic picture of filter plate after passing solution of drug substance that contains crystalline traces discolorations

In order to verify the origin of the small discolorations on the filter plate (see Reference 1), a SEM investigation was conducted. This method provides a high degree of detectability especially for small objects.

Extremely small amounts of residues might be assumed. These findings are confirmed by showing a lower contrast in the SEM-picture than the laser-punched pores in the filter plate.

Within this investigation, no reliable identification of foreign objects nor copanlisib could be confirmed.

Reference 3: SEM picture of filter plate from Reference 1

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Please provide all available data (analytical results), updated specifications (Moxifloxacin-NO) 
if >10% AI, and, if available, an action plan (CAPA) to minimize contamination for Avalox 
Solution for infusion, 400 mg per 250 ml and Avalox Film-coated Tables, 400mg.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 :
Executive Summary
Bayer reports updated confirmatory testing results for Moxifloxacin 400 mg Tablet and 
Moxifloxacin IV solution 400 mg:
• Based on validated methods (limit tests), five out of six nitrosamines (1-
Nitrosopyrrolopiperidine, 6-Nitrosopyrrolopiperidine, NN-Dinitrosopyrrolopiperidine, 
NDEA, NMBA) were found to be consistently below 10% of the AI or the risk level 
of 1:100,000, thus concluding the nitrosamine activities with Step 2. 
• Updated Moxifloxacin-NO results originate from a new validated quantitative test 
method:
o Moxifloxacin solution for infusion 400mg/250ml (iv): previously shared test
result and the risk assessments from last year are supported (22-September-
2022). 
o Moxifloxacin 400mg film-coated tablets: variability in results for
Moxifloxacin-NO is detected; the results are partially above the proposed AIL 
and an interim limit is being defined for Moxifloxacin-NO.  
• The benefit-risk assessment for both products remains positive.  
No field actions are pursued. 
• Mitigation measures to reduce the Moxifloxacin-NO content are under investigation.  
• An in vivo mutagenicity study is pursued to establish a product specific acceptable 
intake limit. In the interim, routine testing of Moxifloxacin-NO is being established 
for Moxifloxacin tablets via an internal specification.

On 22-September-2022, we submitted the required Step 2 preliminary results about 
nitrosamine impurities in Moxifloxacin IV solution 400 mg and Moxifloxacin film-coated 
tablets, 400 mg. Please note that the preliminary results from 2022 were generated by a semi-
quantitative limit test method only.
Since then, a fully quantitative method was developed and validated for Moxifloxacin-NO, 
and the confirmatory testing for Moxifloxacin IV solution 400 mg and Moxifloxacin 400 mg 
tablets has been completed.

Testing Results
Fully validated analytical methods have been used to determine the amount of six N-nitroso 
impurities in Moxifloxacin IV solution 400 mg and Moxifloxacin 400 mg tablets. An 
investigation report with detailed information on confirmatory testing results for 
Moxifloxacin Hydrochloride and Moxifloxacin Hydrochloride for Parenteral Use, 
Moxifloxacin 400 mg tablets and Moxifloxacin IV Solution 400 mg is attached. This 
investigation report includes:
- Confirmatory Testing Results (incl. description of test methods and validation 
summaries)
- Investigation Report and Root-Cause-Analysis
- Mitigation Measures -Proposals
  o Continue root cause investigation to reduce Moxifloxacin-NO contents
  o Commitment to execute in-vivo mutagenicity study
  o Routine testing of tablets for Moxifloxacin-NO (via internal specification)
- Toxicological Risk Assessment Benefit-Risk Assessment
- Toxicological evaluation
- A clinical benefit-risk statement

In the following the relevant information from the confirmatory testing is presented for both 
formulations.

Moxifloxacin IV solution 400 mg
Previously generated and communicated data were supplemented with the recent 
confirmatory testing completed with the new quantitative method:
Nitrosamine Impurity / Results Confirmatory Testing [ppb] / Results Confirmatory Testing [ng/day], rounded / # of tested batches / Evaluation based on proposed Acceptable Intake Limit (3250ppb = 1300ng/day)
- Moxifloxacin-NO: 0-418 ppb; 0-167 ng/day; 7 batches; < 30% AIL
- 1N-Nitrosopyrrolopiperidine: < 25 (LOQ); < 10 ng/day; 10 batches; < 10% AIL
- 6N-Nitrosopyrrolopiperidine: < 100 (LOQ); < 40 ng/day; 3 batches; < 10% AIL
- NN-Dinitrosopyrrolopiperidine: < 40 (LOD); < 16 ng/day; 3 batches; < 10% AIL
- NDEA (API tested only): < 5; < 2 ng/day; 6 API batches; < 10% AI (26.5 ng/day)
- NMBA (API tested only): < 20; < 8 ng/day; 6 API batches; < 10% AI (96.0 ng/day)

Conclusions / Next Steps for Moxifloxacin IV solution 400 mg
• The previous risk assessment for Moxifloxacin IV solution 400 mg is supported: The 
benefit-risk ratio remains unchanged.
• Confirmatory Testing will be extended to cover further batches from the recently 
introduced manufacturer Fresenius-Kabi, Italy.
• Following pertinent regulatory guidance, competent authorities will be informed about 
mitigation measures to reduce the amount of Moxifloxacin-NO once developed.

Moxifloxacin 400 mg Tablets
Updated confirmatory test results obtained with the quantitative method showed a high 
variability for Moxifloxacin-NO values with batches exceeding the Acceptable Intake (AI) of 
1300 ng/day proposed based on a read-across to N-Nitrosopiperidine last year. In order to 
reflect the medical need of the product, and justified by the very short duration of treatment, 
the toxicological evaluation, and the benefit-risk assessment, an Interim Limit of 3900 ng/day 
was defined for Moxifloxacin-NO. All other nitrosated impurities tested were found in very 
low values:
Results Confirmatory Testing [ppb] / Results Confirmatory Testing [ng/day], rounded / # of tested batches / Evaluation based on proposed Acceptable Intake Limit (3250ppb = 1300ng/day) and Moxi-NO Interim Limit (9750 ppb = 3900 ng/day)
- Moxifloxacin-NO: 407-8599 ppb; 163-3440 ng/day; 23 batches; < Moxi-NO Interim Limit
- 1N-Nitrosopyrrolopiperidine: < 25 (LOQ); < 10 ng/day; 31 batches; < 10% AIL
- 6N-Nitrosopyrrolopiperidine: < 40 (LOD); < 16 ng/day; 15 batches; < 10% AIL
- NN-Dinitrosopyrrolopiperidine: < 100 (LOQ); < 40 ng/day; 15 batches; < 10% AIL
- NDEA (API tested only): < 5; < 2 ng/day; 5 API batches; < 10% AI (26.5 ng/day)
- NMBA (API tested only): < 20; < 8 ng/day; 5 API batches; < 10% AI (96.0 ng/day)

Root cause evaluation:
- The root cause for the variability of Moxifloxacin-NO values is not known yet. The 
investigations are pursued with priority.

Risk assessment:
- Moxifloxacin-NO is not a new impurity. There are no data present in the PV 
database that would indicate a reasonable possibility for causal relationship between 
the formation of malignancies and moxifloxacin treatment.
- Moxifloxacin products address indications with a high medical need; Moxifloxacin is 
listed in WHO essential medicines list for the treatment of multi-drug resistant 
tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and Y. Pestis.
- The longest recommended treatment duration in an approved indication is 21 days.
- In summary, the benefit-risk assessment for the product remains positive.
- Bayer does not see a need for a field corrective action.

Toxicological evaluation:
- Moxifloxacin-NO is a large molecule compared to NO-piperidine (read-across 
compound of proposed AIL) and therefore, steric hindrance can be expected, thus 
limiting the interaction with DNA and, consequently, the induction of mutations. 
Applying mutagenicity and carcinogenic potency like NO-piperidine represents a 
worst-case assumption.
- The introduction of an Interim Limit of 9750 ppb = 3900 ng/day for Moxifloxacin-NO 
is justified.
- Additionally, an in vivo mutagenicity assay with Moxifloxacin-NO is already planned 
(data expected Q3 2024).

Future production and steps to mitigate the issue
- Production materials and conditions from different sites are currently analyzed to 
obtain hints for critical parameters, which could reduce the Moxifloxacin-NO 
variability and content during production.
- Introduction of an Interim Limit (see above) for Moxifloxacin-NO in Moxifloxacin 
400 mg tablets.
- The analytical method for Moxifloxacin-NO will be implemented as routine test 
method for release testing via internal specification.
• Moxifloxacin drug product batches will be tested for Moxifloxacin-NO and 
released against the interim limit of 9750 ppb = 3900 ng/day. The interim limit is 
justified due to the medical need of the product, the short treatment duration, the 
toxicological evaluation, and the confirmed positive benefit-risk assessment of the 
product.
• This procedure will be applied on an interim basis until the results of the in vivo 
mutagenicity study become available (see Toxicology perspective above) and/or

in vivo mutagenicity study become available and/or mitigation measures to reduce 
the amount of Moxifloxacin-NO are ready to be implemented. The observed 
results for Moxifloxacin 400mg film-coated tablets comply to the defined interim 
limit.
Due to the still ongoing investigations into production improvements and the 
availability of results from the toxicological study (in vivo mutagenicity assay), Bayer 
asks for an extension of the Step 3 timeline until Dec. 2024, for both Avalox Solution 
for infusion, 400 mg per 250 ml and Avalox Film-coated Tables, 400mg (please refer 
to Request for Step 3 timeline prolongation letter).

Bayer Weimar has a cleaning Validation concept (see SOP REGS-DE09-SOP-002609 
“Regelung 
zur 
Validierung 
von 
Reinigungsprozessen 
für 
Herstellequipment 
(Reinigungsvalidierung)” formerly REGS-DE09-LD-000067) which conducts the validation 
activities at a determined lead substance (i.e. worst-case active pharmaceutical ingredient 
[API]).
Based on the requirements of the above mentioned SOP and the data documented in the 
supplement REGS-DE09-SUP-002319 “Reinigungsvalidierungsrelevante Daten der 
Wirkstoffe / Produkte des SC Weimar” a ranking among all APIs being potentially in contact 
with the all manufacturing equipment surfaces is made. With this ranking the lead substance 
is determined. In chapter 6 of the supplement the ranking of API and the determination of the 
lead substances is defined (see translated copy of chapter 6 see below).
[table content omitted in source text formatting]
According to this matrix, the highest SCORE of 15 results for levonorgestrel, gestodene and 
ethinylestradiol. Because of this equality of points, the lead substance is determined by 
determining the lead substance candidate with the lowest nominal water solubility [mL / g]. 

Determination of the lead substance: Levonorgestrel

According to chapter 6.4.1 “Lead substance” of REGS-DE09-SOP-002609 applies the 
following rule.
The active ingredient with the highest total score is referred to as the lead substance (see 
chapter 6 of supplement REGS-DE09-SUP-002319). The lead substance represents the worst-
case scenario for carrying out the cleaning validation for the SC Weimar. If the cleaning 
validation is passed using the lead substance, it is assumed that all other APIs with a lower 
total score can be cleaned off better.

Due to the production portfolio it is possible, that the manufacturing on specific equipment 
will not use / include products with the determined lead substance Levonorgestrel. In that 
case, based on the equipment-specific API-portfolio the API with the highest total score of the 
equipment-specific subset of APIs is to be used as the equipment-specific lead substance for 
the cleaning validation activity (base is the ranking list in chapter 6 of supplement REGS-
DE09-SUP-002319).
The analysis and selection of the equipment-specific lead substance from the equipment-
specific subset of APIs is conducted during the compilation of validation plan.

Chapter 6.5.5.2 of the SOP “REGS-DE09-SOP-002609” defines the residual API limits.
Compliance with the MACO (Maximum Allowable (Acceptable/Allowed) Carryover) for the 
entirety of all product-contacting equipment surfaces with active ingredient contact in SC 
Weimar is ensured by summarizing all active ingredient residues of the valid cleaning 
validation reports. For this purpose and regardless of the API the determined highest 
proportion of the active ingredient residue for each production step is calculated. The highest 
proportions per production step are added API-specifically in order to consider the different 
pharmacological properties. Chapter 8 of the supplement “REGS-DE09-SUP-002319” 
calculates and lists the most stringent API residual limit not to be exceeded. Therefore the 
determination of the lead substance is associated with a predefined API residual limit of 
the entirety of all product-contacting equipment surfaces. A calculation within each validation 
plan is therefore not necessary.
SOPs mentioned in the repose are attached for your references.

Regarding the selection of the equipment for the cleaning validation we performed a risk 
analysis to check if the Cleaning holding times can be transferred to similar equipment. 
Therefore, a grouping for the equipment in the formulation department was done (please see 
REGS-DE09-ATT-000644, 2021_03_Bewertung_CHT_von_Hautanlagen 
und_Nebenequipment_RV_F-RA-266.01). As WSG 300 and WSG 120 are basically similar 
equipment (category granulation, Fluid-bed-granulators) we can transfer the CHT from WSG 
120 to WSG 300. Several technical parameter were taken into consideration. Besides that we 
have monitoring in place which needs to be performed for every equipment regularly. The 
same applies to P3100.
To elaborate more on this. Every Equipment needs to fulfill the acceptance criteria within a 
hold time of one month with no additional cleaning required during this period. The cleaning 
validation performed on WSG 120 confirms that the cleaning methods applied produce the 
expected results. Any contamination from the active ingredient, cleaning agents or 
microbiological impurities that remains after cleaning will be below the set limits.
Based on the CHT reports on the cleaning of primary systems, it was investigated whether the 
primary system used at the supply center Weimar are comparable and, if so, whether any can 
be grouped together.
We filed several system groups (granulation, tabletting, coating). Within those groups any 
system can be used as a benchmark against which to check CHT given the comparable risk of 
contamination. The current 30-day CHT thus continues to apply to sealed equipment without 
restrictions.

Question/Consideration: Regarding the preparation of standard solutions (= Reference solution R2) for some lots in the Identificationt (3) (= Identification of EE and LNG (HPLC 4)), "Different from the AAF (= TRD P.5.2.901) regarding the weighing/dilution procedure record, but the final concentration of the standard solution is the same" that was added on raw data submittedas an explanation. Please show weighing/dilution procedure record in the batch concerned. And explain the difference between raw data and AAF regarding the preparation procedure of the standard solution. In addition, please show the present operation manual, etc., explain how to prepare the standard solution at this time and in the future, and explain the appropriateness of the contents of AAF. For other test items, confirm and explain whether there are any procedures that differ from those described in AAF.
Answer/Response:
The weighing and dilution operations for the preparation of standard solutions in the Identification (3) (= Identifaction of EE and LNG (HPLC 4)) are explained using Tablet A (=Triquilar 6) (Batch No.: WEM5RC), Tablet B (= Triquilar 5) (Batch No.: WER3WL) and Tablet C (= triquilar 10) (Batch No.: WEM51G) from the submitted conformity investigation documents 4 ~ 6 as examples (Figure 1 ~ Figure 3).
In M3.2.P.5.2.1 ~ 3 (= TRD P.5.2.901#007009152-01, P.5.2.901#007008886-01 and P.5.2.901#007011695-01) ((hereinafter referred to as M3.2.P.5.2), the final concentration, and the specified preparation procedure as a example, are described regarding the standard solution (R2) (= Reference solution R2). Hence, in the conformity investigation documents, the final concentaration of the standard solution (R2) was the same, but the weighing and dilution operations are different from M3.2.P.5.2. In addition, the AAF included an example of the preparation procedure in M3.2.P.5.2, which caused discrepancies with the conformity investigation documents. For the other test items [Identification (1) (= Identification of EE and LNG (HPTLC)) and Dissolution (= Dissolution of EE and LNG (HPLC 3))], the procedure for Identification (1) was the same as that described in AAF (Figure 4 ~ Figure 6), but the procedure for Dissolution (= Dissolution of EE and LNG (HPLC 3)) was different in the preparation of solution (B) (Table 7~ Table 9 and Figure 7 ~ Figure 9).
Although the final concentrations are the same and there is no risk that differences in preparation procedures will affect the analysis results.
Given the description in M3.2.P.5.2 and the current status of the conformity investigation documents, we abelieve that it is appropriate to describe the preparation procedure of standard solutions in the AAF in terms of concentration, rather than describing specific weighing and dilution procedures at present and in the future.
Based on the above, we have decided to describe the test items for which preparation procedure are exemplified in M3.2.P.5.2 (Identification (1), (2) and (3), Dissolution and Assay) in the AAF in terms of concentration, and the AAF will be changed as follows.

P.5.2.901-01 / Test Procedure / Ethinylestradiol + Levonorgestrel sugar-coated tablet 30 μg + 50 μg (TRIQUILAR 6) (P.5.2.901#007009152; unchanged)
P.5.2.901-01 / Test Procedure / Ethinylestradiol + Levonorgestrel sugar-coated tablet 30 μg + 125 μg (TRIQUILAR 10) (P.5.2.901#007011695; unchanged)

Question/Consideration: Regarding Identification (2) (= Identification of LNG (HPLC 1)) for Triquilar 10, the preparation method for the standard solution (= Reference Solution R) is different from that described in the CTD and AAF (= TRD P.5.2.901_007011695_01). Please explain the reason for the difference and whether it is necessary to modify the CTD and AAF (TRD P.5.2.901).
Answer/Response:
As a result of rechecking the preparation procedure (concentration) of the standard solution (= Reference solution R) in Identification (2) (= Identification of LNG (HPLC 1)) for Tablet C (= Triquilar 10), it was found that the contents of the conformity investigation document differed from those described in the CTD and the AAF (Table 10). The reason for the discrepancy was due to a typing error when creating the local operating procedure “Laborvorschrift” in German (Figure 10, old version) from M3.2.P.5.2.3 (= TRD P.5.2.901#007011695-01) in English (Attachment 1). As shown in the Figure 11, there is no change in the peak shape and the retention time in the standard solutions with different concentrations. Therefore, it was judged that there is no effect on the test result, "the difference in retention time between the main peak of the sample solution and the first peak eluted in the standard solution is within 2%", of the identification using standard solutions with different concentrations. Note that the latest local operating procedures have been properly corrected for a typing error (Figure 10, new version).
Since the preparation procedure of the standard solution described in M3.2.P.5.2.3 (= P.5.2.901#007011695-01) is correct, there is no modification to the CTD. In addition, for the AAF, instead of describing the specific weighing and dilution operations as indicated in the response to Inquiry 20221026-Q-01-2, we will revise the concentration description.

Source:  P.5.2.901-01 / Test Procedure / Ethinylestradiol + Levonorgestrel sugar-coated tablet 30 μg + 125 μg (TRIQUILAR 10) (P.5.2.901#007011695; unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
HA Request 1:
• Request to provide the storage condition and shelf-life of constituted solution (after 
dilution)
Answer/Response:
In the past (March 2021) such request to include information about the storage condition and shelf-life of the constituted solution had been received within another label update procedure. Bayer evaluated this topic and came to the conclusion that the current CCDS and VN local label already provide information regarding the reconstituted solution in section Instructions for use/handling: “The ready-to-use infusion solution must be freshly prepared each day in order to guarantee the sterility.” As confirmed by the responsible CMC-Manager at that time, no further data regarding the reconstituted solution are available.

After receipt of the current deficiency letter, the situation for the reconstituted solution has been evaluated again. However, no new information or stability studies are available.

No in-use stability studies were planned or conducted for Ilomedin considering the following:
As per the EMA Note for guidance on in-use stability testing of human Medicinal products, the purpose of in-use stability testing is to establish - where applicable - a period of time during which a multidose product can be used whilst retaining quality within an accepted specification once the container is opened.
Ilomedin 20 is a unit dose product and justification for not providing the in-use stability is as below:
• The product is supplied in a single unit container i.e., ampoules.
• After the dilution the drug product is administered at once, not in multiple intervals.
• The final product is packed in glass ampoules that are subjected to heat sterilization as per compendial requirements, the one-time opening/reconstitution/dilution excludes the risk of microbial contamination.
• Lastly, according to EMA Note for guidance on maximum shelf-life for sterile products for human use after first opening or following reconstitution, it is difficult to predict all the possible conditions under which the product will be opened, diluted, reconstituted and stored, etc., the user is responsible for maintaining the quality of the product that is administered to the patient. To assist the user, relevant information is provided in the User Information texts, such as the SPC, Package Insert, and labels.
Bayer CCDS and VN local label show the current state of knowledge for the reconstituted solution:
“The constituted solution of Ilomedin is ready to use after dilution and this needs to be freshly prepared each day to maintain sterility.”

The above instructions imply that there is no need to define shelf life since it is already stated to prepare freshly each day.

If not used immediately, in-use storage times and conditions are the responsibility of the user.

Thus Bayer concludes that with specific product properties, detailed instructions for use/handing and deep experience in prescribing this product worldwide, Bayer believes that information related to re-constituted solution is adequate and appropriate as presented in the current VN local label. It is sufficient to ensure the safety and efficiency of the product.
keywords: Shelf Life; Storage Condition; In-use stability; stability testing; Sterilization

doc_name: VV-RFI-002166 - Response to non-CMC questions - 1st LoQ
Question/Consideration: Question 2 – Efficacy endpoints as per treatment interval
Answer/Response:
As the European Medicines Agency (EMA) requested additional data, the Applicant provides in Section 7 and below 2-year data from a snapshot of PULSAR (appr. 80% of all participants completed Week 96 data collection) and PHOTON (100% of all participants completed Week 96 data collection). The same dataset is presented herein to MFDS.

HD aflibercept dosed every 12 weeks (HDq12) or every 16 weeks (HDq16) maintained non-inferior efficacy through Week 96 compared to 2 mg aflibercept, consistent with the results demonstrated at Week 48 and Week 60 with respect to improvement in BCVA in patients with nAMD or DME. Based on Week 96 results available to date, no safety signals and no new ADRs were identified for PHOTON and PULSAR (see Section 7).

Patients in PULSAR and PHOTON randomized to HDq12 and HDq16 were planned to be treated with Eylea high dose (Aflibercept 8mg) every 12 and 16 weeks, respectively, after 3 monthly injections. Starting at Week 16, if patients met the Dose Regimen Modification (DRM) criteria for shortening described in the clinical study protocols, the treatment interval was shortened by 4 weeks. Starting at Week 52, if patients met the DRM criteria for extension described in the clinical study protocols, the treatment interval was extended in 4-week increments. That means, patients who maintained stable visual and anatomical outcomes were promoted to longer treatment intervals in a step-wise fashion (to a maximum of 24 weeks) and patients who did not show stable visual and anatomical outcomes were step-wise shortened (to a minimum of 8 weeks).

Therefore, during the course of the first two years treatment intervals could be shortened and extended several times. The course of the treatment intervals is displayed in Figure 1 to Figure 4 where each row represents one patient. Thus, a patient might have been on different treatment intervals at different timepoints which is why it is not feasible to provide an analysis of change in BCVA per treatment interval, e.g. q8, q12, q16 and q20.

However, the outcomes with regards to BCVA are shown per randomization to the 2q8 arm with fixed 8 week treatment intervals and to the HDq12 and the HDq16 arm with variable treatment intervals possible as stated above (Section 7.4.2.1 for PULSAR and Section 7.4.3.1 for PHOTON). In addition, the applicant provides below the results for patients on HDq12 and HDq16 who required shortening of the assigned treatment interval and the results for patients who could be extended to q20.

PULSAR: Patients shortened to q8, maintained at q12/q16
Table 5 (Section 7) presents the proportion of PULSAR Week 96 completers who maintained their assigned dosing intervals through Week 96, as well as those whose intervals were shortened or extended through Week 96 (exploratory endpoints). The vast majority of patients in the HD groups had their last treatment interval of ≥ 12 weeks (85.3% in HDq12 and 88.8% in HDq16) and ≥ 16 weeks (60.2% in HDq12 and 78.1% in HDq16). Therefore, it can be concluded that the vast majority of patients maintained their visual and anatomical outcomes on intervals of 12 and 16 weeks or even longer. Only a minority of patients required shorter intervals of 8 weeks (n = 40 and n = 65, in the HDq16 shortened to q8 and HDq12 shortened to q8 subgroups respectively).
BCVA changes from baseline at Week 48 are summarized in Table 1 for several subgroups defined by the treatment regimen.

PULSAR: Patients extended to q20
Furthermore, through Week 96, up to 47% of HD patients extended their treatment interval to q20 or longer intervals. A total of 185 patients completed at least one q20 interval before Week 96. The patients who continued on q20 or longer intervals had similar efficacy profiles than the other groups (See Section 7.4.2). For example, the mean change in BCVA at Week 96 in patients randomized to HDq16 who extended their treatment interval to q20 and who completed two q20 intervals was 9.6 letters (LOCF, full analysis set).

PHOTON: Patients shortened to q8, maintained at q12/q16
Table 7 (Section 7) presents the proportion of PHOTON Week 96 completers who maintained their assigned dosing intervals through Week 96, as well as those whose intervals were shortened or extended through Week 96 (exploratory endpoints). The vast majority of patients in the HD groups had last intended treatment intervals of ≥ 12 weeks (91.8% in HDq12 and 95.0% in HDq16) and ≥ 16 weeks (64.1% in HDq12 and 87.8% in HDq16). Therefore, it can be concluded that the vast majority of patients maintained their visual and anatomical outcomes on intervals of 12 and 16 weeks or even longer. Only a minority of patients required shorter intervals of 8 weeks (n= 6 and n = 27, in the HDq16 shortened to q8 and HDq12 shortened to q8 subgroups respectively).
BCVA changes from baseline at Week 48 are summarized in Table 2 for several subgroups defined by the treatment regimen.

PHOTON: Patients extended to q20
Furthermore, at Week 96, 44.3% of patients of HD patients extended their treatment interval to q20 or longer intervals. A total of 133 patients completed at least one q20 interval before Week 96. The patients who continued on q20 or longer intervals had similar efficacy profiles as the other groups (see Section 7.4.3). For example, the mean change in BCVA at Week 96 in patients randomized to HDq16 who extended their treatment interval to q20 and who completed two q20 intervals was 9.0 letters (LOCF, full analysis set),

Discussion:
Although per protocol patients were randomized to 2q8, HDq12 or HDq16, further adjustment of treatment intervals in the HD groups was driven by the DRM criteria for shortening (from Week 16) and extension (from Week 52) as stated above. These criteria selected for shorter intervals patients who showed worse visual and anatomical outcomes, and selected for longer intervals those who showed good visual and anatomical outcomes. Consequently, patients who were assigned to shorter intervals (i.e. q8) were per definition required to have worse outcomes than their overall group, while those on longer intervals (i.e. q20) were required to have better outcomes. The subgroup analysis for PULSAR is in line with these assumptions.

In both studies, a high proportion of patients in the HD groups extended their treatment intervals to q20 or longer. However, the extension to q20 was only possible for patients who showed stable visual and anatomical outcomes at q16 based on the pre-defined criteria. This stepwise treatment extension is fully in line with treatment regimens used in real-world clinical practice like treat & extend (T& E). This ensures that the optimal, individual treatment interval is gradually determined without putting the patient at risk of disease progression or recurrence.

While this approach has the clear advantage that it is directly applicable to clinical practice, it also introduces a selection bias if visual acuity results for subgroups who met the shortening or extension criteria are analyzed. As the extension was only possible for patients who showed stable visual and anatomical outcomes, the q20 subgroups contain patients that rather responded well and with that there is also a tendency towards higher visual acuity gains in these subgroups. The same holds true for patients shortened. As these patients met the shortening criteria, which included a loss of visual acuity, also a lower gain of BCVA could be expected in these subgroups. In essence, these outcomes are a consequence of the criteria used to select the patients for each subgroup.

The results from PHOTON for patients who shortened their treatment intervals were drawn from small subgroups of only n = 6, n = 11 and n = 27 in the HDq16 shortened to q8, HDq16 shortened to q12 and the HDq12 shortened to q8 subgroups, respectively. Although here the patients assigned to shorter intervals show a higher mean BCVA gain, these outcomes are based on small sample sizes and need to be interpreted with caution; no conclusions can be drawn from this small sample. The patients assigned to q20 constituted a larger proportion and had good outcomes.

In PULSAR, the sample size per subgroup was higher with n = 40, n = 33 and n = 65, in the HDq16 shortened to q8, HDq16 shortened to q12 and the HDq12 shortened to q8 subgroups respectively but still any observed tendency should be interpreted with caution.

Is it well established that there are differences in the treatment responses across patients. Therefore, in clinical practice, individualized treatment regimens, such as T&E, have been established in recent years as the preferred approach for managing chronic ocular conditions requiring IVT anti-VEGF therapy.

Consequently, the proposed HD aflibercept dosage recommendation (similar to the approved Eylea 2 mg Product Information) clearly guides the treating physician to adjust the intervals based on the individual patient´s visual and anatomical outcomes, i.e. to shorten or extend treatment intervals as needed.

doc_name: VV-RFI-002166 - Response to non-CMC questions - 1st LoQ
Question/Consideration: Question 3 – Justification of non-inferior margin for a ≥ 2-step improvement in DRSS
Answer/Response:
With regards to the PHOTON study, it was designed primarily to evaluate the effects of aflibercept 8 mg in the treatment of DME and therefore did not aim to include DRSS-focused selection criteria. In PHOTON, the “Proportion of Participants with a ≥ 2-Step Improvement in DRSS Score at Week 48” was selected as a key secondary endpoint. This evaluation of DRSS was included in the context of the fact that aflibercept 2 mg is in the US approved not only for the treatment of DME, but also, following the results of the PANORAMA study (Brown et al, 2021), for the treatment of DR. Therefore, evaluating the effects of aflibercept 8 mg was considered relevant for the US territory. The Applicant would like to emphasize that the current label proposal for aflibercept 8 mg in Korea does not contain the indication DR.

The non-inferiority margin for a ≥ 2-step improvement in DRSS is justified from the Applicant’s perspective as it was discussed with the US FDA (see below) and as the data from PHOTON finally lead to approval of aflibercept 8 mg for the indication diabetic retinopathy (DR) in the US. Noteworthy, the agency preferred a 10% margin.

Meeting minutes: Type-B, Pre-BLA Meeting September 26, 2022, from 12:00-1:00 pm (Eastern)
Does the Agency agree that the Sponsor may include, in the BLA application, a request for indication of diabetic retinopathy (with or without DME) for the IAI 8 mg BLA, supported by the pre-specified secondary endpoint of proportion of patients with ≥ 2-step improvement in DRSS in the PHOTON study?
Agency Response: The pre-specified secondary endpoint of ≥2 step improvement in DRSS for the indication of DR in PHOTON study is acceptable for filing. Whether this study also supports the indication of DR in addition to the DME indication would be a review issue. For the secondary endpoint of the proportion of subjects who achieve ≥2-step improvement in DRSS from baseline at Week 48, you propose a noninferiority (NI) margin of 15%. A NI margin of 15% is not acceptable. We recommend that a NI margin of 10% be used to establish noninferiority. Please note that, based on your hierarchical testing strategy in the PHOTON study, this endpoint will be tested only if noninferiority of HDq12 to 2q8 followed by noninferiority of HDq16 to 2q8 in the primary efficacy endpoint of the mean change in BCVA from baseline at Week 48 are established.
Meeting Discussion: The Agency clarified that the proposed secondary endpoint of a ≥ 2-step improvement in DRSS in the PHOTON study is likely to be acceptable for BLA filing for the indication of DR. Approvability would be a review issue.

With regards to the clinical study results of the PHOTON study, the HDq12 treatment arm was non-inferior to 2q8 with respect to this endpoint (adjusted difference 1.98%, 95% CI -6.61, 10.57). However, this could not be shown for the HDq16 group (adjusted difference -7.52%, 95% CI -16.88, 1.84) (Module 5.3.5.1, PHOTON W48 CSR R-14239, Table 14.2.2.1). The non-inferiority margin was prespecified at 15%, however HDq12 would also have met a 10% NI margin. Based on the provided results aflibercept 8 mg (Eylea HD) was approved in the US for the indication DR (also for DME and nAMD).

doc_name: VV-RFI-002166 - Response to non-CMC questions - 1st LoQ
Question/Consideration: Question 4 – Efficacy with the 16w interval in DME
Answer/Response:
As detailed below, all treatment arms in PHOTON achieved similar functional benefits. Differences in anatomical endpoints were mostly associated with injection timing and did not translate into clinically meaningful differences in quality of life or visual acuity.

The PHOTON study was designed primarily to evaluate the effects of aflibercept 8 mg in the treatment of DME, while the evaluation of effects on DR was secondary. The eligibility criteria of the PHOTON study therefore aimed to include an informative population in terms of DME assessment, which does not equate the one selected for DRSS assessment. Studies aiming to evaluate primarily proportions of 2-step improvement in DRSS select patients with high baseline DRSS levels, usually moderately severe to severe NPDR (47 to 53), to be able to detect such an improvement. In PHOTON, this was not required, given the primary objective of the study was to evaluate the effects of aflibercept 8 mg in the treatment of DME. Also, there were sizeable proportions of patients with mild to moderate NPDR for whom 2-step improvements were unlikely or impossible.

Despite the limitations in study design, the evaluation of DRSS was included in the context of the fact that aflibercept 2 mg is in the US approved not only for the treatment of DME, but also for the treatment of DR. Therefore, evaluating the effects of aflibercept 8 mg was considered relevant for the US territory. The key secondary endpoint of the proportion of participants with a ≥ 2-step improvement in DRSS score at Week 48 was pre-specified to potentially support an indication of aflibercept 8 mg for treatment of DR in the US. This endpoint was tested with a non-inferiority margin of 15% which was met by the HDq12 arm (adjusted difference 1.98%, 95% CI -6.61, 10.57) but not by the HDq16 arm (adjusted difference -7.52%, 95% CI -16.88, 1.84) (Module 5.3.5.1, PHOTON W48 CSR R-14239, Table 14.2.2.1). All groups had a substantial positive effect, and the results show some degree of variability. Furthermore, considering that the primary endpoint showed that BCVA improvement as a direct effect of DME treatment was non-inferior for HDq12 and HDq16 compared to 2q8, it is concluded that the effect on DRSS stage improvement does not correlate with the effect on DME, and improvements in DRSS are not a prerequisite for vision improvements in DME.

The proportions of participants who gained ≥ 15 letters in BCVA from baseline to Week 48 and to Week 60 was 18.7% and 21.5% in the HDq12 arm, 16.6% and 16.0% in the HDq16 arm, compared to 23.0% and 26.1% in the 2q8 arm. In order to better reflect the current characteristics of the relevant patient population, the PHOTON study allowed enrollment of patients with baseline BCVA letter score up to 78 letters, in contrast to the VIVID and VISTA studies conducted for approval of aflibercept 2 mg for treatment of DME where the upper limit was 73 letters. Taking into consideration that a BCVA letter score ≥ 84 letters corresponds to a Snellen equivalent of 20/20 or better, or a decimal score ≥ 1.0, it is concluded that there is a ceiling effect limiting the proportion of participants who will achieve BCVA gains ≥ 15 letters. The proportion of participants with baseline BCVA higher than 73 letters was 18% in the HDq12 arm, 14.1% in the HDq16 arm and 12.0% in the 2q8 arm, providing further room for participants in this group to achieve BCVA gains ≥ 15 letters.

In the descriptive analysis by visit, the proportions of participants with BCVA gains ≥ 15 letters after 3 initial monthly doses, at Week 12, are 13.8%, 12.3% and 16.4% for HDq12, HDq16 and 2q8 respectively, showing the impact of baseline differences in this descriptive endpoint already during the initial monthly treatment phase. These proportions increase until Week 48 for the HDq12 and HDq16 arms and remain stable from Week 48 to Week 60, showing the appropriateness of the HD regimens in maintaining vision gains.

The proportion of participants who achieved ≥ 69 letters in BCVA at Week 48 and at Week 60 was 65.3% and 64.7% in the HDq12 arm, 62.6% and 62.0% in the HDq16 arm, compared to 63.0% and 60.6% in the 2q8 arm. The similarity of these values provides further support to the appropriateness of the HD regimens in achieving and maintaining a highly functioning visual acuity level. Structural variables measured by optical coherence tomography (OCT) such as presence of fluid and changes in central subfield thickness also show positive effects in all arms.

The proportions of participants without fluid (no intraretinal fluid (IRF) and no subretinal fluid (SRF) at the foveal center (as assessed by the central reading center) at Week 48 and Week 60 was 58.5% and 61.8% in the HDq12 arm, 43.8% and 58.0% in the HDq16 arm, compared with 54.5% and 68.5% in the 2q8 arm, respectively.

The LS mean change from baseline in CRT at Week 48 and Week 60 was -176.77 and -181.95 in the HDq12 arm, -148.84 and -166.26 in the HDq16 arm, compared with -164.85 and -194.16 in the 2q8 group, respectively. The CRT values at Week 48 and Week 60 show overlap between treatment arms, and changes at any visit depend mostly on the timing of the most recent injection.

The structural parameters measured by fluorescein angiography (FA) included presence of leakage and change in area of leakage. The proportions of participants without leakage in FA were low in all arms. At Week 48 and Week 60 the proportions were 7.6% and 7.9% in the HDq12 arm, 0.7% and 2.0% in the HDq16 arm, compared with 2.5% and 4.3% in the 2q8 arm, respectively. The change in area of leakage from baseline to Week 48 and to Week 60 was -13.9 and -13.9 in the HDq12 arm, -9.4 and -12.0 in the HDq16 arm, compared with -9.2 and -14.4 in the 2q8 arm, respectively. Similarly to the variables measured by OCT, the FA variables also showed overlap between groups across timepoints and a relation to the timing of the most recent injection.

The NEI-VFQ-25 total score also showed a small positive LS mean change from baseline to Week 48, of 4.06 in the HDq12 arm and 2.94 in the HDq16 arm compared with 2.82 in the 2q8 arm, respectively. There were no substantial changes to Week 60, and no clinically meaningful differences between the different treatment arms.

Finally, the Applicant provides long term data (Section 7) with this response. The results through Week 96 with regards to change in BCVA, were consistent with the non-inferiority demonstrated at Week 48 and Week 60 for aflibercept 8 mg administered every 12 or 16 weeks compared to aflibercept 2 mg . Solely based on the Week 60 data, a trend towards lower numerical BCVA gains in PHOTON might be considered with an estimated difference in LS-means changes from baseline between HDq16 and 2q8 at Week 48 of -1.44 and at Week 60 of -1.76 letters (non-inferiority demonstrated at both timepoints, p-values of one-sided test for non-inferiority at a margin of 4 letters 0.0031 and 0.0122 at Week 48 and Week 60 respectively). At Week 96, the estimated LS-means difference between HDq16 and 2q8 was again less pronounced with -1.11 letters (nominal p-value of one-sided test for non-inferiority at a margin of 4 letters 0.0044) (Table 3). These fluctuations suggest that the observed minor numerical differences are natural variability and do not indicate true clinically relevant differences between the ability of these different regimens in maintaining visual outcomes.

Overall, the Applicant therefore concludes, that the minor tendencies towards lower numerical BCVA gains in the HD aflibercept groups compared to 2q8 are not clinically relevant and are considered natural variability. All treatment arms achieved similar functional benefits. Differences in structural endpoints were mostly associated with injection timing and did not translate into clinically relevant differences in quality of life or visual acuity.

Source(s) mentioned in the response: Module 5.3.5.1, PHOTON W48 CSR R-14239, Table 14.2.2.1; Table 3; Module 5.3.5.1, PHOTON W60 CSR R 14238, W48 Table 14.2.1.1 and W60 Table 14.2.1.1a; Module 5.3.5.1, PHOTON TLF EMA CHMP Day-120 W96 CSR_key, Table 14.2.1.1b.

Question/Consideration: Question 1 – Description of shortening and extending cycle of treatment interval
Answer/Response:
The Applicant proposes to amend section “Dosage and Administration” as follows. The previous guidance to adjust the treatment interval is split up into a more detailed description how and under which circumstances the interval can be extended to up to every 5 months. Similarly, a more detailed guidance is proposed for inclusion under which circumstances shortening of the treatment interval should be considered. The Italic underlined text shows additions, while text crossed out shows deletions.

Dosage and Administration
[…]
EYLEA 8 mg treatment is initiated with 1 injection per month for 3 consecutive doses. Injection intervals may then be extended up to every 16 weeks. The treatment interval may be adjusted based on the physician’s judgement of visual and/or anatomic outcomes.
Subsequently, the treatment interval may be further extended up to every 5 months, such as with a treat and extend dosing regimen, while maintaining stable visual and/or anatomic outcomes (see sections 14.3 “Clinical efficacy and safety”) adjusted based on the physician’s judgement of visual and/or anatomic outcomes up to every 5 months. There are limited data for treatment intervals longer than 5 months.
If visual and/or anatomic outcomes deteriorate, the treatment interval should be shortened accordingly based on the physician’s discretion. EYLEA 8 mg with treatment intervals of 1 month for more than 3 consecutive doses has not been studied (see section “14. Information for Experts of Precautions for use”).
[…]

The Applicant proposes to supplement this more detailed guidance by a cross-reference to Section 14.3 “Clinical efficacy and safety”, where more details can be found how interval extension and shortening was done in the clinical trials. The Italic underlined text shows additions.

3) Clinical efficacy and safety
(1) Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration (nAMD)
[…]
Beginning at week 16, per study protocol patients randomized to the 8Q12- and 8Q16-groups could move to a more frequent dosing regimen based on visual and anatomic outcomes. Per study protocol the interval was to be shortened if both of the following criteria were met:
1. >5 letters loss in BCVA from week 12, and
2. >25 microns increase in central retinal thickness (CRT) from week 12 or new foveal hemorrhage or new foveal neovascularization.
Regardless of whether patient intervals were maintained or shortened in year 1, per study protocol all patients in the 8Q12- and 8Q16-groups were eligible for interval extension (by 4 weeks increments), beginning at week 52, if the following criteria were met:
1. <5 letters loss in BCVA from week 12, and
2. no fluid in the central subfield on OCT, and
3. no new onset of foveal hemorrhage or foveal neovascularization.
For patients who did not meet the criteria for shortening or extension of the interval, the dosing interval was maintained.
[…]
(2) Diabetic macular edema (DME)
[…]
Beginning at week 16, per study protocol patients randomized to the 8Q12- and 8Q16-groups could move to a more frequent dosing regimen based on visual and anatomic outcomes. Per study protocol the interval was to be shortened if both of the following criteria were met:
1. >10 letter loss in BCVA from week 12 in association with persistent or worsening DME, and
2. >50 microns increase in CRT from week 12.
Regardless of whether patient intervals were maintained or shortened in year 1, per study protocol all patients in the 8Q12- and 8Q16 groups were eligible for interval extension (by 4 weeks increments), beginning at week 52, if the following criteria were met:
1. <5 letter loss in BCVA from week 12, and
2. CRT <300 microns on SD OCT (or <320 microns if measured including RPE).
For patients who did not meet the criteria for shortening or extension of the interval, the dosing interval was maintained.
[…]

Question/Consideration: Question 1 - Arterial thromboembolic events
Answer/Response:
The Applicant acknowledges the comment and proposes to add the information below in Section ‘2. Carefully administer to the following patients’ and in section ‘4. General precautions’.

2. Carefully administer to the following patients
[…]
3) Arterial thromboembolic events (ATE)
Arterial thromboembolic events (ATEs) are adverse events potentially related to systemic VEGF inhibition.

4. General precautions
Arterial thromboembolic events (ATEs) are adverse events potentially related to systemic VEGF inhibition. There is a theoretical risk of ATEs following intravitreal use of VEGF inhibitors.
A low incidence rate of arterial thromboembolic events was observed in the EYLEA 8 mg clinical studies in patients with nAMD and DME. Across indications no notable difference between the groups treated with 8 mg aflibercept and the comparator groups treated with 2 mg aflibercept were observed.
ATEs, as defined by Antiplatelet Trialists' Collaboration (APTC) criteria, include nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or vascular death (including deaths of unknown cause).
There are limited data on safety in the treatment of patients with nAMD or DME with a history of stroke or transient ischemic attacks or myocardial infarction within the last 6 months. Caution should be exercised when treating such patients.
There was a low incidence of reported APTC ATEs in nAMD studies (PULSAR) from baseline through week 60 was 0.4% (3 out of 673) in the combined group of patients treated with EYLEA 8 mg compared with 2.4% (8 out of 336) in patients treated with EYLEA 2 mg.
There was a low incidence of reported APTC ATEs in the DME study (PHOTON) from baseline to week 60 was 4.5% (22 out of 491) in the combined group of patients treated with EYLEA 8 mg compared with 3.6% (6 out of 167) in patients treated with EYLEA 2 mg.

doc_name: VV-RFI-002166 - Response to non-CMC questions - 1st LoQ
Question/Consideration: Question 2 – Major efficacy endpoints
Answer/Response:
The Applicant’s opinion is that the following functional and clinical evaluations should remain in Section 14.3 “Clinical efficacy and safety” of the Korean PI as they resemble relevant information from the PULSAR and PHOTON results, supporting the primary outcomes.

a) Proportion of participants achieving an ETDRS letter score of at least 69 (approximate 20/40 Snellen equivalent) at Week 48 and Week 60
b) Proportion of participants gaining at least 15 letters in BCVA from baseline at Week 48 and Week 60
c) Proportion of participants losing at least 15 letters in BCVA from baseline at Week 48 and Week 60

The threshold of 69 ETDRS letters represents an important visual functional level for driving ability and other daily living activities. The proportion of patients with 15 letters gain or loss has been the standard and established primary endpoints for the registration of anti-VEGF compounds and represents a key threshold for the evaluation of the functional effectiveness on the treatment in patients with nAMD and DME (Brown 2016).

The below clinical endpoints are relevant information to guide ophthalmologists in their clinical practice, providing the necessary confidence to physician in adapting the therapeutic pattern of nAMD and DME patients according to the PULSAR and PHOTON results and label with the potential to decrease the treatment burden.

d) Patients maintained with q16 treatment interval through Week 48 and Week 60
e) Patients maintained with ≥ q12 treatment interval through Week 48 and Week 60
f) Patients maintained with ≥ q12 treatment interval through Week 48 and Week 60 for the pooled HD aflibercept groups.

The mean number of active injections in the PHOTON study population through Week 96 was 12.9, 8.6 and 7.5 in the 2q8, HDq12 and HDq16 treatment groups, respectively (Module 5.3.5.1, PHOTON W96, Table 14.1.4.1b). For the 869 completers at the 96-week time point in the PULSAR study, the mean number of active injections was 12.8, 9.7 and 8.2 in the 2q8, HDq12 and HDq16 treatment groups, respectively (Module 5.3.5.1, PULSAR W96, Table 14.1.4/2). After the introduction of anti-VEGF injections for the treatment of retinal diseases, the classic monthly or bi-monthly (fixed) dosing of the intravitreal injections of anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) has been proven efficacious and safe in clinical trials (Schmidt-Erfurth 2014; Schmidt-Erfurth 2017). For effective retinal disease management, it is important to understand patient treatment preferences and to what extent patient’s trade-off convenience factors, such as frequency of clinic visits and injections, with therapeutic benefits and medical costs. While efficacy is still the driver for receiving IVT treatment, concerns on treatment costs and preferences in less frequency of clinic visits makes the number of injections an important factor to progress the treatment of retinal diseases (Ozdemir 2022; Gale 2017).

As highlighted above, the Applicant’s opinion is to provide the most relevant endpoints in this section. Also, in our answer to question 3 we clarified that the PHOTON study was designed primarily to evaluate the effects of aflibercept 8 mg in the treatment of DME. The “Proportion of Participants with a ≥ 2-Step Improvement in DRSS Score at Week 48” was selected as a key secondary endpoint because aflibercept 2 mg is in the US approved not only for the treatment of DME (Diabetic Macular Edema), but also, for the treatment of DR (Diabetic Retinopathy), while in Korea DR is not an approved indication in addition to DME. Therefore, evaluating the effects of aflibercept 8 mg on DRSS was considered relevant for the US territory but not for Korea. Consequently, the applicant suggests not to include the “Proportion of Participants with a ≥ 2-Step Improvement in DRSS Score” in this section as it is not relevant for the physicians in Korea.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1.1
1) Relevant regulation: paragraph 1-2-B-3 of article 7
Reasons for request: insufficient data on verification of virus removal of drug substance
Supplementation request: data on verification of virus removal for the drug substance manufacturer (Raheen Ireland)
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1.1 (3.2.S.2.6; 3.2.A.2):
Virus removal studies for aflibercept were performed in qualified small-scale models which are representative of the PA9 Raheen manufacturing site. The study reports are included in CTD Section A.2.03.
At-scale manufacturing site-specific virus removal verification studies are not performed, as it would require introduction of viruses into a GMP-approved facility.
Small-scale studies were performed, and they were determined to be fully representative of both the Rensselaer and Raheen manufacturing processes. During the DSI technology transfer from PA5 Rensselaer to PA9 Raheen, a gap assessment was performed and the identified gaps were assessed and mitigation strategies were employed. The assessment concluded that the non-identical hardware and manufacturing equipment at PA9 Raheen and in PA5 Rensselaer were functionally equivalent, see CTD section S.2.6.01. The only two gaps with potential impact to viral clearance were the control mechanism of the virus filter inlet pressure, and the bed height variability due to different chromatography column packing, that may lead to differences in linear velocity and column protein load. There was no change to the production process itself or process parameters, which are the same at both sites.
The equipment difference of the virus filter inlet pressure control mechanism was mitigated through control optimizations and both systems maintain robust operation below the defined pressure maximum. Furthermore, the parameter is classified as a CPP (Critical Process Parameter) and is closely controlled and monitored through review of the data historian as part of the Master Batch Record in PA9 Raheen and within the in-process monitoring program.
The impact of bed height variability on column protein load was mitigated by changing the manufacturing documentation to use the actual bed height for column loading calculations. The potential minor linear velocity variability was further assessed by Regeneron based on platform data and published literature, and concluded to not have any significant impact on viral clearance. The amount of buffers going through the columns is not impacted by the bed height variability as these buffer amounts are controlled by the equipment and calculated per actual column volume (CV).
The changes implemented to mitigate both gaps had no impact on the validity of the small scale models. Therefore the viral clearance data in CTD section A.2.03 is valid for both the Rensselaer PA5 and Raheen PA9 DSI manufacturing sites.

Question/Consideration:
Question 4
Identification: Please add the preparation of sample solutions without reference substances to the registration specification (JX specification).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4:
HPTLC is used for identification of the used APIs in Progynova 1mg (estradiol valerate). The identification is done by comparing the spots on the HPTLC plate. Different compounds move up the plate by different speeds, based on the different attraction between the substances, the mobile phase and the stationary phase. Therefore, different compounds can be separated and this separation is used for identification. In the present case, the standard method of comigration is used. On the TLC plate is applied (a) the reference substance, whose identity we know and (b) the substance/tablet to be examined mixed with a defined content of reference substance. Solutions of (a) and (b) are applied and developed on a common TLC plate. A comparison of the retention behavior of the observed spots is made. We expect a congruent behavior of all observed spots, since they should be the same substances. So we expect a spot for (a) and the same for (b). In (b), the manually added reference standard should behave congruently with the substance contained in the tablet, if it is the same substance. The method of comigration is used to be able to exclude any differences or external influences on the development of the TLC plate. This has the advantage that the substance under investigation is tested against both an external (a) and internal standard (b).

According to the release (P.5.1.01#020135106) and shelf life specification (P.5.1.02#020135107) the identity testing of estradiol valerate (EV) in “Estradiol valerate sugar-coated tablet 1.0 mg (PROGYNOVA)”, using HPLC, is carried out with the help of the validated coelution method for HPLC to show “spot homogeneity for the drug substance”.

The identity testing of estradiol valerate (HPLC3) using the coelution method is described in detail in the test procedure (P.5.2.01#020135571).

Three solutions S, R2 and SR are to be prepared. The sample solution S contains a sample with the to be identified substance. The reference solution R2 contains the proposed drug substance EV. The sample solution SR is a 1:1 mixture of the sample solution S and the reference solution R2. During the identity test the sample solution S is only prepared to produce the sample solution SR.

The validated HPLC coluetion method is a state-of-the-art method for the identity testing of drug substances in drug products. Herein a sample solution SR is injected into the chromatographic system which contains the substance to be identified and a reference solution of the proposed drug substance (in this case Estradiol valerate).

If the to be identified substance is not the same as the drug substance in the reference solution (in this case estradiol valerate) two spots would be visible in the chromatogram of the SR solution (= mixture of sample solution and reference solution). If only one spot is visible in the chromatogram of the mixture and the spot is matching in terms of spot shape to the spot of the purposed drug substance in the chromatogram of the pure reference solution R2, spot homogeneity is given and the identity is confirmed.

The advantage of the coelution method over other methods, e.g. retention time comparison, is the insensitivity of the method to the influence of the matrix of the drug product or minor changes of the chromatographic conditions during testing e.g. pressure deviations.

Dissolution: Provide a comparison study of multiple self-made batches for the in vitro dissolution behavior before and after the production site change, using 50 rpm, including dissolution curves and similarity comparisons.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 6:
Additional comparative dissolution data was recorded using a stirring speed of 50 rpm. Due to the poor solubility of the drug substance estradiol valerate, two approaches were included in the comparative study. First one batch from each production site was tested (n=12) in the dissolution medium water without SDS addition.
Secondly, three batches from each production site were tested in water + 0.3% SDS at 50 rpm.

In Figure 1, the obtained dissolution profiles in water (without SDS) are illustrated.
Figure 1: Overlay of the dissolution profiles in water (without SDS)
Time points [min] 15 / 20 / 30 / 45 / 60 / 75
Delpharm batch 952A mean: 0 / 1 / 1 / 2 / 3 / 4; c.v.: n/a / 45.2 / 49.2 / 25.7 / 20.7 / 18.5
Weimar batch WEW76G mean: 0 / 1 / 1 / 2 / 3 / 3; c.v.: n/a / 28.9 / 62.2 / 37.7 / 20.1 / 25.9
The dissolution profiles are visual similar. The data confirms the poor drug substance solubility, as only 3-4% are dissolved after a time of 75 minutes. Based on the high coefficients of variation, the f2-calculation was performed formally only, using the last three time points with the lowest variation of the individual values. The f2-value of 97 confirms the similarity of the dissolution profiles in water without SDS at 50 rpm.

Additionally, three individual batches of both production sites were tested in the dissolution medium water + 0.3% SDS, in order to operate under sink conditions, which is required according to USP <1092> and Ph. Eur. 5.17.1. Furthermore these dissolution profiles fulfill the evaluation criteria of the Chinese “Guidelines for CMC Change Study of Marketed Chemical Drugs (Trial)” and EMA Guideline on the Investigation of Bioequivalence CPMP/EWP/QWP/1401/98 Rev. 1 in order to calculate the f2-values.

The results are shown in Figure 2.
Figure 2: Overlay of the dissolution profiles in water + 0.3% SDS
Time points [min] 15 / 20 / 30 / 45 / 60 / 75
Production site Delpharm
952A mean: 21 / 59 / 70 / 85 / 89 / 90; c.v.: 25.1 / 9.6 / 7.7 / 5.3 / 4.6 / 4.3
957A mean: 17 / 58 / 70 / 83 / 88 / 89; c.v.: 27.3 / 8.9 / 6.5 / 4.2 / 4.0 / 3.7
960A mean: 18 / 56 / 67 / 83 / 87 / 89; c.v.: 31.5 / 8.9 / 6.5 / 5.2 / 5.0 / 5.1
Production site Weimar
WEW76G mean: 18 / 58 / 68 / 84 / 88 / 90; c.v.: 26.7 / 10.3 / 8.1 / 6.3 / 7.4 / 5.0
WEW76H mean: 18 / 58 / 69 / 85 / 89 / 91; c.v.: 23.2 / 7.8 / 5.9 / 4.6 / 5.0 / 4.8
WEW95E mean: 14 / 50 / 62 / 78 / 83 / 85; c.v.: 37.8 / 15.8 / 12.6 / 8.5 / 7.6 / 7.0
It can be seen, that all batches show a similar and continuous dissolution behavior, reaching the plateau of 80-100%.
The dissolution data of the three time points 30, 45 und 60 min fulfill all evaluation criteria of the above mentioned guidelines, and were used for the f2-calculation:

f2-Values
Batch No. 952A vs WEW76G: 88; vs WEW76H: 97; vs WEW95E: 57
Batch No. 957A vs WEW76G: 89; vs WEW76H: 88; vs WEW95E: 60
Batch No. 960A vs WEW76G: 92; vs WEW76H: 83; vs WEW95E: 66

With f2-values between 57 and 97, the similarity of the dissolution profiles of all combinations of all batches could be confirmed in the dissolution medium water + 0.3% SDS.
It can be concluded, that all available data using a stirring speed of 50 rpm confirms the product equivalence based on the dissolution profile comparison & f2-evaluation in both dissolution media: water without surfactant and water with SDS.
