The method is proven to be specific and the criteria set for linearity are met.  
For Linearity, nine solutions were prepared, the concentrations of which correspond to 
0.04 %, 0.4 %, 4.1 %, 21 %, 41 %, 58 %, 82 %, 99 % and 124 % of the theoretical 
rivaroxaban concentration in the tablets test solution (0.24 mg/mL). Each solution was 
injected twice.
From the obtained peak areas the calibration line was determined by linear regression, 
please see Table 2 in the T.02.47.
The results obtained show that all requirements are fulfilled. The calibration curve is 
linear in the investigated range of 0.04 % to 124 % relative to theoretical rivaroxaban 
concentration in the test solution (0.24 mg/mL). Thus linearity of the analytical procedure is 
verified.

Accuracy/Recovery rate was verified for both test parameters: Assay and Impurities.  
For Assay, three solutions were prepared by adding suitable quantities of drug substance 
stock solution to a placebo mixture in order to obtain rivaroxaban concentrations which 
correspond to approx. 70 %, 100 % and 130 %, based on the theoretical concentration of 
rivaroxaban in the test solution (0.24 mg/mL). Each solution was injected three times and was 
analyzed as directed in the Test procedure (T.02.02). The results were compared to the results 
from corresponding solutions without placebo and the recovery rates were calculated.
The results for Accuracy / Recovery Rate (Assay) are shown in Table 3 in the T.02.47. 
The requirements for the criterion "Accuracy" are fulfilled if the confidence interval (99 %) of 
the mean includes the 100.0 % value or if the complete confidence interval is between 99 and 
101 %. The results obtained show that the confidence interval of the mean includes the 100.0 
% value. Thus accuracy of the analytical procedure is verified.

For Impurities, the impurity Oxaphthalimid was used as surrogate because no degradation 
products are specified for Rivaroxaban coated tablet 15 mg. The sample solutions were obtained
by adding suitable quantities of Oxaphthalimid stock solutions to samples prepared according 
to the Test Procedure (T.02.02) at 3 different concentration levels (about 0.05 %, 0.20 %, and 
0.24 % based on the theoretical concentration of rivaroxaban in the test solution of 0.20 
mg/mL). Each concentration level was prepared three times from independent stock solutions.
The results were compared to the results from corresponding solutions of Oxaphthalimid 
reference standard and the recovery rates were calculated.
The test data obtained for accuracy of impurities/degradation products are shown in Table 
4 in the T.02.47.
Accuracy is considered given if the mean recovery for each individual concentration level 
does not differ by more than 4 times the respective variation coefficient of the method from the 
theoretical value (100 %) and the mean value of all recoveries does not differ by more than 2 
times the variation coefficient of the method from the theoretical value (100 %). Alternatively, 
the requirements for the criterion "accuracy" are fulfilled if the confidence interval (99 %) of 
the mean includes the 100.0 % value or is within 80 – 120 %.
All acceptance criteria for accuracy described above were fulfilled including the alternative 
acceptance criteria. Thus, the accuracy of the analytical procedure is verified for impurities and 
degradation products because all recovery rates are within the range 80 and 120 %.

Precision of the instrument and method as well as intermediate precision were verified for 
both test parameters: Assay and Impurities.
For Assay, the precision of the instrument was checked by repeated analysis of a 
rivaroxaban solution. The control solution (83 % level) was prepared as directed in the Test 
Procedure (T.02.02). The solution was injected six times in succession, and the coefficient of 
variation of the detector signals obtained was calculated.
The results for Precision of the Instrument (Assay) are shown in Table 6 in the T.02.47.
The requirements for "Precision of the instrument" are fulfilled if the coefficient of 
variation is  1.5 %. The obtained result of the coefficient of variation is 0.3 %, thus precision 
of the instrument is verified.
For the precision of the method, six samples were prepared according the Test Procedure 
(T.02.02) with concentrations of active ingredient corresponding to approx. 100 % based on 
the theoretical concentration of active ingredient in the test solution (0.24 mg/mL). The 
coefficient of variation of the six test solutions was calculated.
The results for Precision of the Method (Assay) are shown in Table 10 in the T.02.47. 
The requirements for "Precision of the method" are fulfilled, if the coefficient of variation 
for each concentration level is ≤ 3.0 %. Based on the results obtained, the requirements are 
fulfilled. Thus, precision of the method for the analytical procedure is verified.

For Impurities, the criteria for “precision of the instrument” are fulfilled, if the 
coefficients of variation are ≤ 15.0 % for any level.
Because no degradation products are specified, the impurity Oxaphthalimid was used as 
surrogate. The sample solutions were obtained by adding suitable quantities of Oxaphthalimid
solutions to samples prepared according to the Test Procedure (T.02.02) at 3 different 
concentration levels (about 0.05 %, 0.20 %, and 0.24 % based on the theoretical concentration 
of rivaroxaban in the test solution of 0.20 mg/mL). A single test solution was prepared for each 
concentration level and injected six times respectively. The test solutions were injected six 
times one after another, and the coefficients of variation of the detector signals obtained were 
calculated for each concentration level.
The test data obtained for precision of the instrument for impurities/degradation products at 
each level are shown in Table 7, Table 8 and Table 9 in the T.02.47.  
The obtained results demonstrate the requirements to be fulfilled. Thus, precision of the 
instrument for impurities/degradation products is verified.

The criteria for "precision of the method" are fulfilled, if the coefficient of variation is ≤ 
15.0 % for any level.
Because no degradation products are specified the impurity Oxaphthalimid was used as 
surrogate. The sample solutions were obtained by adding suitable quantities of Oxaphthalimid 
solutions to samples prepared according to the Test Procedure (T.02.02) at 3 different 
concentration levels (about 0.05 %, 0.20 %, and 0.24 % based on the theoretical concentration 
of rivaroxaban in the test solution of 0.20 mg/mL). Six test solutions were prepared for each 
concentration level and each test solution was injected once. The test solutions were injected 
once one after another, and the coefficients of variation of the detector signals obtained were 
calculated for each concentration level.
The test data obtained for precision of the method for impurities/degradation products at 
each level are presented in the Table 11, Table 12 and Table 13 in the T.02.47.
The obtained results demonstrate the requirements to be fulfilled. Thus, precision of the 
method for impurities/degradation products is verified.

For the test of the intermediate precision, six samples were prepared with concentrations 
of active ingredient corresponding to 100 %, based on the theoretical concentration of active 
ingredient in the test solution (= 0.24 mg/mL), independently by two analysts (A and B) on five 
different days using different equipment. The mean assay and the coefficient of variation of 
each sequence were calculated.
The results for Intermediate Precision are presented in Table 14 in the T.02.47. 
The requirements for "Intermediate Precision" are fulfilled, if the coefficient of variation 
for each sequence is ≤ 3.0 %. The obtained results demonstrate the requirements to be fulfilled. 
Thus intermediate precision of the analytical procedure is verified.

Question/Consideration: Describe local test method with exact amount of EMC virus added to plate, in units of TCID50/mL.
Answer/Response:
Bayer confirms that the local test procedure for the CPE Potency test is in line with the global 
method described in the TRD P.5.02.60-03.

The exact amount of EMC virus added to the plate, in units of TCID50/mL cannot be fixed 
since the value is variable from virus bank to virus bank and depends on the overall viral titer 
determined for the virus bank at the time of qualification. Qualification of a new virus working 
bank follows a defined titration protocol laid out in an underlying test instruction and SOP.
Briefly, the procedure is as follows:
- 
For each newly derived virus bank or sample with unknown titer, the virus titer is 
determined first.
- 
For this, the sample or virus bank lot will be serially diluted (e.g. 1:10, 1:2 dilution series) 
and the titer of infectious particles in units of TCID50/ml will be calculated.
- 
Typically, the titer of a new virus working bank in units of TCID50/ml ranges between 107
to 108 .
- 
The calculated TCID50/ml varies between different virus banks. Therefore, no fixed value 
can be defined for TCID50/ml.
- 
In a subsequent step, each new virus bank will be qualified and specifically titrated for the 
A549 CPE bioassay.
- 
For this, a dilution series of different EMC virus concentrations derived from a virus bank 
lot (e.g. 1:25, 1:50, 1:75, 1:100) will be used in the CPE bioassay.
- 
In order to determine the optimal number of infectious viral particles and thus the acceptable 
dilution of the new virus working bank to be used in the CPE bioassay, all criteria of the 
system suitability test need to be fulfilled (see further details below).
- 
The system suitability test (SST) criteria for the A549 CPE bioassay are defined and strictly 
controlled. The applied SST criteria are described in  P.5.02.60-03 (please refer to section 
5.D of the document).

- 
Briefly, defined SST criteria for the A549 CPE bioassay are:
o OD Difference
o Curve adjustment
o Ratio of upper asymptotic
o Ratio of steepness
o Ratio of pharmacological effect
o CV% test report

- 
All virus concentrations (dilutions), which meet the requirements of the SST are suitable 
for use in the A549 CPE bioassay and can thus be used for the potency test.
- 
Due to the fact that the virus titer of different virus banks can vary, also the final dilution 
suitable for the CPE bioassay can vary between different virus banks.
- 
In the instance of more than one virus dilution, which meets the acceptance criteria of the 
SST, only one dilution is defined and consistently used for the CPE bioassay.
- 
In addition, as part of the qualification protocol, the mean bioactivity values of the samples 
prepared with the current and the new virus bank are compared with each other.
- 
The mean bioactivity values should not differ more than ±2 to 3 SD from data generated 
with the new and previously used virus bank (according to a defined trending chart).
In summary, a fixed value for TCID50/mL cannot be defined as the viral titer varies between 
different virus banks. Despite this, a fixed value for TCID50/ml is not required, as each new 
virus bank will be qualified and titrated directly using the A549 CPE bioassay. The CPE 
bioassay is tightly controlled by defined SST acceptance criteria, which will determine the 
virus-bank specific dilution to be suitable for the A549 CPE bioassay. Suitable virus dilutions 
can vary between different virus banks, but will all meet the defined SST acceptance criteria of 
the CPE bioassay test.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
After comparing the current CEP with the proposed one, we understand that the variation 
must be presented as type IB because it includes the following that is not contemplated in the 
current one: Risk management summary for elemental impurities and Particle size by laser 
diffraction.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
Please be informed that the variation is intended to add a new manufacturing site (Newchem) 
with CEP for the API, not to replace. This is covered by the proposed variation B.III.1.a) 3, 
and all conditions and documents are fulfilled, so we would like to maintain the category 
Type IAin instead of changing to type IB.

The CEPs should not be compared since they are independent documents related to each site 
and they do not reflect all the information.

The line 24 “Risk management summary for elemental impurities” is not mentioned in Bayer 
CEP because this information is not mandatory to be included, and at the time Bayer 
requested the CEP (2005) the ICH guidelines did not require this information. Indeed, Bayer 
has covered the assessment for this information and the limits to ICH Q3D impurities are met 
under section S.3.2.05 “Risk assessment on elemental impurities”.

Related to lines 25 to 29, particle size distribution, please be aware that this information is not 
mandatory to be included in the CEP and it is decided by the MAH. The Particle Size 
Distribution, Test Procedure and Validation of the test are explained in the S.4 section 
(S.4.1.01 specifications, S.4.2.01 Test, S.4.3 validation).

The Cyproterone Acetate material provided by Newchem to Bayer complies with the Bayer 
specifications, including Particle Size Distribution. There is no change and the same quality, 
safety and efficacy is maintained.

In summary, the CEPs should not be compared, but even if so, impurities and particle size 
distribution are information not mandatory to be mentioned in the CEP, and there is a quality 
agreement in which Newchem will provide the API with the same Bayer specifications, so the 
impurities and particle size distribution will be maintained.

Comparison of Bayers test procedure with monograph of the Indian Pharmacopeia
The impurities and related substances are tested on the Sorafenib tosylate micronized drug 
substance.

(T.03.03#000223156-04). More specifically, the table on page 13 of this document provides a

impurities:

• CTF-aniline
• PAPE-Isopropyl carbamate
• PAPE-urea
• Deschloro compound
• CTF-Ethylcarbamate
• 2-Cl-3-TF-compound
• CTF-urea.

The monograph of the Indian Pharmacopeia requires testing of three specified impurities:
Sorafenib Impurity A
Sorafenib Impurity B
Sorafenib Impurity C

these impurities correspond to the following impurities listed in Bayers test procedure:

Sorafenib Impurity C corresponds to CTF-urea

prior to the implementation of the monograph of the Indian Pharmacopeia based on the 
process knowledge and purity profile that results from Bayers manufacturing process of 
Sorafenib tosylate micronized drug substance.

determination of related substances with regard to Bayers submitted test procedure.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
You were asked to confirm that the integrity test has been validated for the container/closure system 
and that positive and negative controls were used during testing. You state the validity of the detection 
method of the microbial ingress test was demonstrated via a growth promotion test performed after the 
completion of the ingress test. One bottle was used for growth promotion from each of the 11 
containers containing the submersion fluid. Further, you state the positive controls were not subjected 
to the immersion test; however, they were inoculated with the test organism Pseudomonas aeruginosa 
and incubated.
Answer/Response:
This is not acceptable. The inoculation of a test unit shows that the media can support the 
growth of the challenge organism. This type of control is a fertility control. A positive control for 
use in a container closure integrity test is used to show that breaches, should they occur, would 
be picked up by the test method used. A positive control test unit has defects intentionally made 
in the closure system to demonstrate that the test method is able to detect a defect. Validation 
data results should include details of the study performed, details of positive and negative 
controls used, and limits of detection i.e., the sensitivity of the method. It is also expected that 
results would be provided for evaluation.

Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.2.4/3.2.P.7):
In relation to this request, Bayer have re-reviewed the TGA requirement regarding the sterile 
injectable products and the evidence required to support the registration (Reference: Appendix A – 
Specific mandatory requirements dated 21-Feb-2018 from the Mandatory Requirements for an 
effective application). The document states on page 25 that for 3.2.P.7 “For sterile injectable drug 
products, the following must be provided”; point 2 states “for containers closed by other means (i.e. 
vials, syringes), information on container closure integrity tests such as dye penetration or microbial 
ingress tests”.
Document P.2.4.910#004464526 was previously submitted to the TGA as part of the Ultravist 370 
8x500mL bottle application in 2019 (Submission ID: PM-2019-03020-1-2; Report D20-190411) as a 
suitable microbial ingress study and this was accepted by the evaluator at the time to meet the TGA 
requirement (see Fig. 1). As such, a similar assumption was made on this precedent that this study 
would also support this application to the TGA for Gadovist 65mL/100mL bottles (and the study is 
suitable for both container types due to the study design).
Additionally, we note that an ingress test was inadvertently not submitted to the TGA as part of the 
responses to questions previously raised and we hereby submit this to demonstrate that the Container 
Closure Integrity is maintained. Please refer to document P.2.4.901#004451179. Both these studies 
meet the TGA requirement to demonstrate container closure integrity testing.
As per the previous responses, Bayer confirm that validation was performed, however the TGA 
requirements does not make specific reference to the requirement that the validation results are 
required to be provided for evaluation. Previous recent applications to the TGA for similar container
types did not require the Sponsor to provide such data (Submission IDs: PM-2019-03020-1-2 for 
Ultravist and PM-2020-06591-1-2 for Dotagraf).

Fig. 1 – summary of evaluation comments from submission ID: PM-2019-03020-1-2; 
Report D20-190411

system

Question/Consideration: R.2.01_022981471_02, page 8 of 38, Table 1-1: regarding the difference in batch size, it is explained that "Interaction of the solution with surfaces and potentially batch size dependent effects are discussed separately.” Please explain specifically the interaction of the solution with surfaces and potential batch size dependent effects.
Answer/Response:
The purpose of the process development is - amongst others - to investigate the potential interactions of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL DP with the single use material. Another point to be investigated is the potential effect of the different batch sizes on the DP.
For the potential interactions of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL DP, a leachable sample of the vial filling process was collected to study the potential process equipment related leachables released possibly from single use material in contact with the Aflibercept solution.

All single use process components were evaluated regarding their leachable risk, and categorized as low, medium and high-risk components. Extractable data of the defined single use components were applied in the risk assessment together with the process conditions and contact surface areas of components. Conclusion of the leachable risk assessment was that due to medium and high-risk components, safety of vial filling line single use components should be confirmed by studying process equipment related leachable compounds.

Formulated drug substance was used as a matrix blank, which had no contact with any of the vial filling process single use components. Then the same formulated drug substance was filled into vials during the engineering run of the development process. The leachable sample for the vial filling process was taken at the end of filling line to maximize the contact with the single use components and to include all process components to the study. Sample and matrix blank were analyzed with headspace-gas chromatography – mass spectrometry (HS-GC-MS) for volatile compounds, with GC-MS for semi-volatiles, with liquid chromatography – MS (LC-MS) for non-volatiles, and with inductively coupled MS (ICP-MS) for extractable elements.

Analytical evaluation threshold (AET) for the process leachable study was defined by applying the safety concern threshold (SCT)/threshold of toxicological concern (TTC) of 1.5 µg/d for potentially genotoxic and mutagenic impurities in lifelong treatment.1 The recommended therapeutic dose of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL is 70 µL per eye administered as an intravitreal injection. In a worst case, both eyes are treated, resulting in a maximum dose of 140 µL (70 µL per eye) per treatment day, which is taken from two different vials. The PQRI recommends applying an analytical uncertainty factor (UF) of 2, but ISO 10993-18 recommends an UF of 4 and 10 for (HS-)GC-MS and LC--MS analyses, respectively, when calculating the AET for a leachable study.2 Accordingly, to maximize patient safety, the AET for this study was calculated using the higher UF values, and the AET for HS- and GC-MS analyses was 2.5 µg/mL and for LC-MS analyses 1.0 µg/mL.

Only potential process leachable compound was detected with the HS-GC-MS technique. 2-propanol (CAS 67-63-0) was present also in the matrix blank, but the amount was more than 3 times higher in the process leachable sample. The amount of 2-propanol was 29.5 µg/treatment i.e. if both eyes were treated. 2-propanol is a typical solvent often released from plastic components. According to ICH Q3C(R9) 2-propanol is a Class 3 solvent with low toxic potential, for which it is considered that amounts of 50 mg per day or less are acceptable without justification. The amount of 29.5 µg 2-propanol per bilateral treatment with aflibercept 8 mg is more than 1600-fold lower than the permitted daily intake (PDE) value of 50 mg for 2-propanol and thus regarded as safe.

No other process equipment related organic leachable compounds were detected when data evaluation was started from 0.3 µg/mL, 8 and 3 times below the AET values for HS- and GC-MS, and LC-MS techniques, respectively. All elemental impurities were in ng/dose and ng/treatment level, which were approximately 1000-times less than the safety concern threshold of 1.5 µg/d. The highest result was obtained for Si, which was 35.6 ng/treatment.

Single use plastic containing process components did not release any process equipment related leachable compounds or elemental impurities of concern. The vial filling process at the STE-1 facility was shown to be safe and suitable for the intended use of filling vials with Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL.

Other contributing factors like mixing speed and shear stress were investigated in small scale studies during earlier process development and have only negligible effects. These findings will be verified during the PPQ runs.
The main effect of the different batch sizes is the potential difference in process equipment related leachables, which however will not be of concern within the range of batch sizes.
Source: R.2.01-02 Comparability Protocol / Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial for intravitreous injection (Bayer AG, Berlin, STE-1) (#0022981471; unchanged)

Question/Consideration: If the extractables data have been obtained, please explain specifically the study.
Answer/Response:
The container closure system used for the drug product Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial for intravitreous injection consists of a vial, a stopper and a flip cap. The flip cap has no contact with the drug product. The stopper is made of butyl rubber and is coated with fluoropolymer. Analytical evaluation threshold (AET) for the extractable study was defined by applying the safety concern threshold (SCT)/threshold of toxicological concern (TTC) of 1.5 µg/d for potentially genotoxic and mutagenic impurities in lifelong treatment.3 An analytical uncertainty factor of 2 was applied for defining the final AET, which was 0.15 µg/mL for all prepared extracts corresponding to 0.75 µg/stopper.
Extractable study samples were prepared with pH 5 adjusted phosphate buffer, 50% 2-propanol and for volatile extractable compounds thermal extraction was executed with the stopper as is. Sample extracts were analyzed with headspace-gas chromatography – mass spectrometry (HS-GC-MS) for volatile compounds, with GC-MS for semi-volatiles, with liquid chromatography – MS (LC-MS) for non-volatiles, and with inductively coupled -MS (ICP-MS) for extractable elements. Extraction conditions and analytical techniques are summarized in Table 1.

No organic extractable compounds exceeding the AET of the study were detected in pH 5 phosphate buffer, which can be considered to represent the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in contrast to the worst-case conditions in thermal extraction or when extracting the stopper with 50% 2-propanol (Table 2). In the 50% 2-propanol extract, extractable compounds were detected in GC-MS and LC-MS analyses. Extractable elements were detected in pH 5 phosphate buffer and 50% 2-propanol extracts, but only the amount of Zn (7.08 µg/stopper) exceeded the AET and SCT of 1.5 µg/day for potentially genotoxic and mutagenic impurities in lifelong treatment of the study. Zn is an essential element for humans and belongs to elements which do not have a specified permitted daily exposure limit according to the ICH Q3D guideline for elemental impurities4. Administration of 4.2 µg Zn per day in the case of bilateral treatment with Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL5 is negligible in comparison to the daily average requirements of Zn of 6.2 to 10.2 mg/day for women with a reference weight of 58.5 kg and from 7.5 to 12.7 mg/day for men with a reference weight of 68.1 kg (EFSA Panel on Nutrition, Novel Foods and Food Allergens, Scientific Opinion on Dietary Reference Values for zinc, EFSA Journal 2014;12(10):3844). Thus, the extracted amount of Zinc is considered safe.
Under the harsh extraction conditions of the stopper with 50% 2-propanol the following compounds exceeded the AET and SCT of 1.5 µg/day: rubber oligomer of the type C21H40 (CAS 2512216-71-4) was detected with 17.89 µg/stopper in the GC-MS analysis and the fatty acids stearic acid (CAS 57-11-4) and palmitic acid were found in the GC-MS as well as in the LC-MS analysis with maximum amounts of 10.09 µg/stopper for stearic acid and 3.83 µg/stopper for palmitic acid both in the LC-MS analysis. For rubber oligomers of type C21H40 no toxicological or literature data are available. According to a presentation from Nelsons Labs. on Rubber Oligomers of 2019, which was held by Dr. Piet Christiaens, Scientific Director of Nelson Labs Europe, at the SVP Symposium on March 31, 2022, and which is available on the internet (https://www.nelsonlabs.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/2022-03-31_5_Presentation-Piet-Christiaens_Rubber-Oligomers.pdf), C21H40 oligomers are considered as cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbon compounds with one double bond, for which the Structure Activity Relationship reveals no immediate concern. Based on these data it is concluded that C21H40 oligomers are of low toxicological concern. The detected amount of 17.89 µg/stopper translates into a dose of 9.5 µg for bilateral treatment with Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL6. Based on the fact that Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL is not administered daily, but with intervals of initially 1 month for the first 3 doses, which may then be extended up to every 4 months and subsequently up to every 5 months, the small amount of 9.5 µg/bilateral administration for this compound which was extracted under worst case conditions with 50% 2-propanol is considered to be uncritical. Since no rubber oligomers have been identified after extraction of the stopper in pH 5 phosphate buffer, which resembles the composition of Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL more closely, rubber oligomers are also not expected after extraction of the stopper with Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL. The small amount of rubber oligomers of type C21H40 identified in the harsh 50% 2-propanol extraction of the vial stopper are thus not considered to be of toxicological concern.
In contrast to the rubber oligomers, the toxicity of fatty acids is well known. The European Food Safety Authority EFSA in their 2017 “Re-evaluation of fatty acids (E 570) as a food additive” (EFSA Journal 2017;15(5):4785) concluded that the fatty acids including palmitic (C16) and stearic acid (C18) did not raise a concern for genotoxicity and are of low acute toxicity. With respect to repeat-dose toxicity the toxicity database was limited, however, no adverse effects were observed in subchronic toxicity studies with up to 10% in the diet (equivalent to 9000 mg lauric acid (C12)/kg body weight per day). The panel noted that with the contribution of fatty acids as food additives (E 570) with on average 1% of the overall exposure to saturated fatty acids from all dietary sources (food additive and regular diet) of 400 – 1000 mg/kg body weight per day in adults there was no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels. These data indicate that the small amounts of palmitic and stearic acid detected after the harsh extraction of the vial stopper with 50% 2-propanol, which translate into maximal doses of 2.07 or 5.48 µg/bilateral administration of Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL, are toxicologically irrelevant.
The extractable study data will be used for designing a leachable simulation study for the vial stopper. The leachable simulation study, in which samples are prepared using the drug product, will produce a more realistic estimate about the formation of possible leachable compounds during the shelf-life of the drug product.

Question/Consideration: Please explain the details of the leachable simulation study.
Answer/Response:
Vials filled during the engineering runs at the filling line STE-1 are closed with rubber stoppers. The leachable simulation study is executed to forecast formation of potential leachable compounds during the leachable stability study.
Leachable simulation samples are prepared by incubating vials 72 ± 2 h at 25 ± 2 °C stopper downwards to maximize the contact between stopper and drug solution. The normal storage conditions for the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial are 2 – 8 °C. In contrast to that, the sample incubation conditions accelerate the leachable formation. After incubation samples are analyzed with headspace-gas chromatography – mass spectrometry (HS-GC-MS) for volatile compounds, with GC-MS for semi-volatiles, with liquid chromatography – MS (LC-MS) for non-volatiles, and with inductively coupled MS (ICP-MS) for extractable elements. Potential leachable compounds are reported by applying the analytical evaluation threshold (AET) defined from safety concern threshold (SCT)/threshold of toxicological concern (TTC) of 1.5 µg/d for potentially genotoxic and mutagenic impurities in lifelong treatment.9 An analytical uncertainty factor of 2 in minimum will be applied for defining the final AET. The filling volume of the vial is 0.263 mL, and one vial is used for the treatment of one eye, but in the worst case both eyes are treated. Therefore, SCT of 1.5 µg/d is for two stoppers, and total administered volume is 0.140 mL. Thus, AET will be 1.5 µg/2 doses/d*0.070 mL/dose = 10.71 µg/mL. Final analytical uncertainty factors will be defined in the study protocol.
Final confirmation of the potential leachable compounds is obtained in the leachable stability study initiated after the PPQ runs. The first timepoint, T0, for the leachable stability study will be in August 2024, after which 3 months will be required for reporting the results. Planned timepoints for the leachable stability study are T0, T6, T12, T24, and T36 months.

Question/Consideration: It is explained that release testing, stability testing, and extended characterization will be evaluated in the comparability study of the additional manufacturing process (R.2.01_022981471_02, page 26 of 38, Table 6-1). For each test, please explain the criterion to be "comparable" for each test item.
Answer/Response:
The data evaluation and acceptance criteria for the comparability study, described in section 7 of R.2.01_022981471_02 (page 34 – 37), is explained with further supporting information below.

Release testing:
The STE-1 validation batches need to comply with the release specification acceptance criteria described in Table 4-6, which are more stringent as compared to the approved shelf-life specification acceptance criteria (CTD section 3.2.P.5.1) for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL drug product in vial.
In addition, as described in section 7.1 of R.2.01_022981471_02, the applicant will calculate quantitative comparability limits for purity and potency tests (see Table 7-1) based on batch release results of historical vial batches and the three Catalent vial comparator batches. At the time of filing R.2.01_022981471_02, the number of available historical vial batches was not considered as sufficiently larger than the data set used to calculate the release specification acceptance criteria. Therefore, the applicant proposed to include batch release results of subsequently manufactured commercial vial batches, including the three vial comparator batches. Note that the exact comparability limits can still not be provided within this response document, since the batch release testing of the three vial comparator batches was not yet performed. However, the total number of batches, which will be used for the calculation is now fixed and described within an internal document (n=24 batches). Since the statistical methodology that will be applied for the calculation (95% confidence/ 99% coverage tolerance intervals) is also fixed, there is no room for interpretation of the comparability limits once those will be calculated. In case those limits should turn out to be wider than the release specification acceptance criteria, which is not expected, then the release specification acceptance criteria will be equal to the comparability limits.

Stability testing:
For the evaluation of stability results the applicant kindly refers to section 7.2 of R.2.01_022981471_02. Tables 7-2, 7-3 and 7-4 describe those analytical methods, which test quality attributes that are known to undergo notable change under the respective stability condition and therefore reflect the degradation pathways of the Aflibercept molecule. The results from each storage condition will undergo a thorough evaluation. First, the results of STE-1 PPQ and Catalent comparator batches will be compared graphically for the last available time-point via overlays of raw data where applicable (chromatograms for purity by SE-UPLC, electropherograms for purity by non-reduced and reduced CE-SDS as well as charge variant analysis by iCIEF, not applicable for isoaspartate content). In this way it will be ensured that there are no new or missing peaks in the raw data and thus degradation is comparable between STE-1 and Catalent.
Second, a quantitative comparison of stability results will be performed for the abovementioned quality attributes listed in tables 7-2, 7-3 and 7-4. Here the evaluation will be performed differently for 2 - 8 °C results on the one hand and for 25 °C and 37 °C results on the other hand. The reason for this differentiation is that only the release and 3 months stability results will be available at 2 - 8 °C at the time of filing for each of the quality attributes listed in Table 7-2, while results from several data points will be available at 25 °C and 37 °C for the quality attributes listed in Table 7-3 and 7-4, respectively.
The two data points at 2 – 8 °C (release and 3 months) per quality attribute are not sufficient to compare the rate of degradation (slopes of the regression lines per quality attribute) via statistical methodology. Therefore, the 3 months results of the STE-1 PPQ batches at 2 – 8 °C will be compared to the 3 months results of historical vial batches and of the three Catalent vial comparator batches in a tabular manner (in total n=12 batches for comparison) via descriptive statistics first (note that release results are compared independently already as described above). The comparison of 3 months results via descriptive statistics means that if the results of the STE-1 PPQ batches will be within the minimum/ maximum range of the 12 other batches or if they are better, then they will be considered as comparable. Note that n=12 is a limited data set for this type of comparison. Therefore, in case the STE-1 PPQ results will be worse than the results of the 12 other batches, 95% confidence/ 99% coverage tolerance intervals will be calculated on the results of the n=12 batches. If the results of the STE-1 PPQ batches will be within the tolerance interval of the respective quality attribute, they will be considered as comparable.
The 25 °C and 37 °C stability results of the quality attributes described in Table 7-3 and 7-4, respectively, will be evaluated as described in detail in section 7.2.2. The rates of degradation (slopes of regression lines) at these elevated temperatures will be compared between STE-1 PPQ and Catalent comparator batches via the statistical methodology analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). The respective acceptance criteria are provided in section 7.2.2 of R.2.01_022981471_02.

Extended characterization:
For the evaluation of extended characterization results the applicant kindly refers to section 7.3 of R.2.01_022981471_02. Please note that the analytical methods applied for extended characterization testing are considered to provide additional supporting information on top of the results derived from analytical methods used for routine release and stability testing. Since extended characterization methods are not routinely applied for testing of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL drug product, quantitative acceptance criteria cannot be defined for the comparability exercise. This is however not considered to be required, because the routine analytical methods already provide a thorough control over drug product quality and potential changes (please see section 6.3 of R.2.01_022981471_02) and are associated with quantitative acceptance criteria during batch release and stability testing. The purpose of extended characterization testing instead is to generate data and thereby supporting information from orthogonal analytical methods as described in section and 6.3 and 6.5 of R.2.01_022981471_02. This type of data will primarily be evaluated in a qualitative manner as described in section 7.3 for each analytical method, including respective acceptance criteria. Numerical results obtained from the peptide mapping method will additionally be compared between the three STE-1 PPQ and the three Catalent comparator batches. However, due to this small data set, the results will not be evaluated statistically, but need to be similar between each other only. The term “similar” was derived from ICH Q5E. Please note however that the respective results will be provided during submission as part of CTD section 3.2.R.2 to ensure full transparency to PMDA regarding the data sets used to derive the applicants´ conclusions on comparability.
Source: R.2.01-02 Comparability Protocol / Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial for intravitreous injection (Bayer AG, Berlin, STE-1) (#0022981471; unchanged)

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( CTD section): 3.2.P.2.2, 3.2.P.5.3
Please find attached the updated technical documents P.2.2.02-02 which include the primary data (chromatograms of samples and reference standards, Certificates of Analysis of reference standards used in dissolution test) for dissolution profiles results for one exemplarily batch for each strength (KM600S9 for the 10 mg tablets and KM600S0 for the 20 mg tablets). The applicant is satisfied that these data are sufficient to verify the dissolution data provided for all requested batch data.
Sodium laurilsulfate acts as a wetting agent in the drug product manufacturing process. It plays no role in the disintegration or dissolution of the tablet. The amount present per tablet (<1 mg) is not expected to have a significant impact on the dissolution behavior at pH 4.5.
As explained in technical document P.5.3.21, the dissolution medium must provide “sink conditions”. This condition means that the solubility of the drug substance in the dissolution medium is at least 3-fold higher than the concentration at 100% dissolution. For example, if a 20 mg tablet results in a concentration of 22 µg/mL in the medium (900 mL), the solubility of finerenone micronized drug substance must be ≥ 66 µg/mL in that medium. A lower solubility (< 3-fold) can result in slow or incomplete dissolution, while higher solubility (>> 3-fold) can result in very rapid dissolution and a loss of discriminatory power of the dissolution test.
Finerenone requires only a modest increase in solubility, with the aid of a surfactant, at pH 4.5 to achieve the right “sink” conditions. Sodium laurilsulfate, even at 0.1%, strongly enhances solubility, but Tween-20 only moderately. Therefore, Tween-20 (at 0.1%) is a better choice of solubility enhancer for finerenone than sodium laurilsulfate. The medium consisting of actetate buffer pH 4.5 + 0.1% Tween-20 could be shown to be discriminatory. It is unlikely that acetate buffer with sodium laurilsulfate (0.1% or less) would be yield to same result.

roztwór do wstrzykiwań, 768,86 mg/ml
MA nr: R/2270

based on Article. 13b section 3 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 1234/2008 of 24
November 2008 regarding the examination of changes to the conditions of marketing
authorizations marketing for medicinal products for human and veterinary use medicinal
products (Dz. Urz. EU L 334, 12/12/2008, p. 7, as amended) inform about the negative
opinion regarding the reported changes for the reasons described below:
As part of the application in question, a variation IB No. B.I.b.1 z) was also submitted with
scope of introduction to the dossier (to Module 3.2.S.4.1 - specification of the active
substance applicable to the manufacturer of the medicinal product) non-routine testing of the
microbiological purity parameter with the frequency: Conduct the test on every 20th batch or
at least once a year. However, non-routine inspection of the microbiological purity parameter
is not applicable in the substance specification of active substance used in a sterile
parenterally administered medicinal product, because routine inspection of the above
parameter in this case is necessary in order to minimize the microbiological load in the
ingredients of the medicinal product before its sterilization (in accordance with the Guideline
on the sterilization of the medicinal product, active substance, excipient and primary
container, EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015: The levels of bacterial endotoxins in the
finished product can be impacted by the bioburden and bacterial endotoxins in the
components (i.e. active substance, excipients and containers), and by microbiological
contaminants introduced during manufacture. To ensure an acceptable level of bacterial
endotoxins in the finished product, the level of microbiological contaminants of the
components should be minimal). Moreover, inhibitory properties of the active substance on
the increase of microbiological contamination were not demonstrated.
Taking the above into account, non-routine testing of the microbiological purity parameter in
the specification of the active substance used in the sterile medicinal product administered
parenterally, cannot be accepted and the above-mentioned non-routine frequency removed
from the proposed registration dossier.
Therefore, an appropriately amended application and registration documentation should be
submitted in the above-mentioned scope (i.e. corrected Modules: 3.2.S.4.1, 3.2.S.4.4,
3.2.S.4.5).

Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
In accordance with ICH guidance Q6A non-routine testing of microbial purity is acceptable in
case the conditions defined in the guidance are fulfilled. For our drug substance iopromide we
followed ICH Q6A, decision tree #6 “Microbiological Quality Attributes of Drug Substance
and Excipients” that allows skip testing for microbial purity testing if the test results of
monitoring for microorganisms are consistently below acceptance criteria levels.
As for our drug substance iopromide all test results from the regular monitoring of the
manufacturing process for potential microbiological contamination and the yearly stability
program evaluating the batches during storage demonstrate that no microbiological
contamination is observed and that the results are consistently far below the acceptance
criteria, we introduced skip testing. For reference, we would like to amend document
S.4.4.11-01 `Additional Batch-Related Information` which presents corresponding data for
more than 200 batches tested during the years 2021 and 2022.
Please find the detailed justification for the frequency of testing the parameter `microbial
purity` in accordance with ICH Q6A in document S.4.5.01-01 `Justification of Specification
and Skip Testing`. Besides the limits, therein, also skip testing on a risk-based approach is
discussed in very detail and considered justified based on respective supporting data presented
in documents S.4.4.11-01 `Additional Batch-Related Information`. Due to its physical
properties, e.g. solid state, low water content, the drug substance iopromide is considered to
not support microbial growth.
Moreover, the data presented in report P.2.5.01-01 `Pharmaceutical Development -
Microbiological Attributes` present a microbial test set-up for the drug product which can be
considered worst-case conditions with respect to the water content compared to iopromide
drug substance. After an experimental period of 24 - 30 hours, only two out of eight test
microorganisms showed slight growths in the drug product solution. Thus, it can be stated that
the drug substance iopromide does not explicitly exhibit inhibitory properties on microbial
growth. But, the substance itself as a dry powder is not capable of supporting microbial
growth in the sense of ICH Q6 A decision tree #6.
The drug product is an aqueous solution with a water content of approx. 50 % (depending on
the formulation) whereas the drug substance only contains max. 1.5 % water. The factor that
is most important for the possibility of microbial growth is the water activity of a substance
(aw). Optimum growth conditions are found at an aw value of > 0.9, whereas specific bacteria
are able to grow at aw values down to 0.6. Wheat flour with a water content of typically
around 10 % can be seen as a comparable substance to iopromide drug substance. Wheat flour
at 20 °C has an aw value of approx. 0.2. In analogy, the drug substance iopromide with a water
content of max. 1.5 % will have an aw value of safely below 0.6, so that it can be concluded
that the drug substance is not capable of supporting microbial growth or viability in the sense
of ICH Q6A decision tree #6.
Introduction of microbial purity testing on drug substance level can therefore be regarded as
precautionary measure to safely control the bioburden introduced into the drug products
formulation. In addition, the drug substance manufacturing process involves steps that are
capable of reducing microorganisms possible present (see S.4.5.01-04) and the monitoring
microorganism levels are consistently far below the acceptance criteria (S.4.4.11-01).
Therefore, testing on a skip-lot basis is considered acceptable according to ICH Q6A decision
tree #6. Skip-lot testing is not in contradiction to the principles laid down in
EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015 as far as the conditions of ICH Q6A decision tree #6
are fulfilled.
Considering the above the drug substance iopromide is regarded adequately controlled
according to the specification provided with S.4.1.01-06. Corresponding batch data are
provided in S.4.4.01-01.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Process validation (3.2.S.2.5)
3.1 
A contamination was found on two batches during process validation. Please explain 
what correction measures were made, please clarify if correction procedures were 
tested and proved beyond validation batches.
3.2

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.S.2.5; 3.2.R):
3.1
Microbial recoveries were observed in the second and third validation batches (8337600003 
& 8337600004).  A second set of three consecutive validation lots was successfully produced 
without any recoveries directly after implementation of the corrective actions.
Since the six validation batches, and the implementation of the corrective measures, an 
additional 48 commercial batches of aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL have been produced in 
Process Area 2 expansion (PA2X) for Bayer by Regeneron. Since the initial contamination 
during the validation batches and implementation of corrective actions, no microbial 
recoveries have been found in any of the batches. All in-process controls were observed to be 
below the action limit and all release specification acceptance criteria were met.
The three corrective measures implemented in response to the microbial recoveries were 
briefly summarized in CTD section S.2.5.01-02 and are further described here below.

Corrective Action 1
Update of internal procedure to provide clear instruction on the order single use manifolds 
should be removed and installed from the ultrafiltration/diafiltration (UF/DF) skid to limit 
exposure of the tangential flow filtration (TFF) filters.
Additional guidance to change gloves and spray gloves with isopropyl alcohol prior to 
installation of new manifolds was implemented in the internal procedure.

Corrective Action 2
Replacement of reusable parts with single-use material, where appropriate.

Corrective Action 3
Reduction of the number of Pellicon 3 TFF filter cassettes and update of the applicable Single 
Use UF/DF methods, manufacturing record, and internal forms to scale flowrates to maintain 
flux across the TFF membranes and revise hold up volumes throughout the manufacturing 
record

3.2.
The procedure and results for the validation for shipment conditions of the finished product 
are included in the submitted CTD Section R.5.02-01.

Question/Consideration:
Question 4
Characterization of structure and properties (3.2.S.3.1)
Please clarify if glycosylation affects on the biological activity and how it is affecting.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4 (3.2.S.3.1):
Two separate studies were performed to evaluate the potential impact of glycosylation on the 
biological activity of aflibercept in terms of (1) sialic acid content and (2) glycan occupancy.
Each aflibercept molecule contains up to 10 N-linked glycosylation sites which possess 
structural heterogeneity with respect to the level of terminal sialic acid present on each 
complex bi-antennary glycan. Furthermore, sialic acid content and Z number (average sialic 
acid content per glycan) are key quality attributes that are evaluated at release of each 
manufactured aflibercept drug substance intermediate (DSI) lot. For reference, fully sialylated 
aflibercept theoretically contains 20 sialic acid moieties with a Z number of 2.0; however, 
batch release results indicate that typical DSI lots are not fully sialylated (Z numbers ranging 
from 0.9 to 1.1).
In the first study, the impact of sialic acid content on the biological activity of aflibercept was 
evaluated. Aflibercept DSI was fractionated over an anion exchange (Q) column to generate 
fractions exhibiting differential sialic acid content based on the negatively-charged nature of 
the sialic acid moiety. These fractions were evaluated for binding to VEGF ligand and 
potency by bioassay (Table 1). The aflibercept samples evaluated in this study exhibited 
between 4.6 and 11.5 total sialic acid moieties.
All samples with differential sialic acid content exhibited comparable bioassay activity (83-
103%) and binding (85-116%). These values are consistent with the historical range for 
bioassay activity (78 – 129%) and binding (88 – 112%) for aflibercept DSI and demonstrates 
that differences in sialic acid content does not have a significant impact on potency (Table 1).

In a second study, hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) was used to fractionate 
aflibercept, resulting in enrichment of aflibercept samples containing different levels of 
glycan occupancy (Figure 1). Intact mass analysis confirmed that Fractions 3, 4, and 5 were 
enriched for 10, 9, and 8 N-linked glycans, respectively (Figure 1).
The HIC-fractionated samples were further assessed for impact on potency and binding 
(Table 2). Based on these results, the level of glycan occupancy does not have a significant 
impact on the potency or target binding of aflibercept.
Source:  S.3.1.01-01 Structure Elucidation and other Characteristics/Aflibercept
solution 114.3 mg/mL (#022985354; new)
keywords: Elucidation of Structure and other Characteristics; General Properties; assay; spectra for impurity iso-B; Characterisation of Impurities

Question/Consideration:
Question 5
Impurities (3.2.S.3.2)
Please clarify if the charge variation species affect on the biological activity, please elaborate.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 5 (3.2.S.3.1):
To investigate the impact of charge heterogeneity on potency, a charge variant enrichment 
study was performed. An aflibercept DSI lot was subjected to a preparative cation exchange 
column, yielding three fractions (enriched Regions 1-3), which were preferentially enriched 
for iCIEF Region 1 (acidic), Region 2 (main), and Region 3 (basic) variants, respectively 
(Table 3, Figure 2). Additional extended characterization of these fractions suggested that the 
charge heterogeneity inherent to aflibercept is heavily influenced by sialic acid content.
The potency of each enriched charge variant fraction was assessed using a cell-based bioassay 
(Table 3). Each enriched charge variant fraction exhibited bioassay activity between 86-120%, 
comparable to the unfractionated DSI sample (87%). From this assessment, it was concluded 
that charge heterogeneity, arising from post-translational modifications, does not have a 
significant effect on the biological activity of aflibercept.

solution 114.3 mg/mL (#022985354; new)

substance intermediate (DSI), Formulated drug substance (FDS) and drug product (DP) based

The submitted justification of specification for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in CTD 
section S.4.5.01-01 for Potency mentioned “FDS acceptance criteria are aligned with the 
established DSI acceptance criteria, as potency is not changed by the FDS processing step”.

The justification of DSI specification is the same for aflibercept drug substance (DS) for

The method is proven to be specific and the criteria set for linearity are met.  
For Linearity, nine solutions were prepared, the concentrations of which correspond to 
0.05 %, 0.5 %, 5.0 %, 25 %, 50 %, 70 %, 100 %, 120 % and 150 % of the theoretical 
rivaroxaban concentration in the tablets test solution (0.20 mg/mL). Each solution was 
injected twice.
From the obtained peak areas the calibration line was determined by linear regression, 
please see Table 2 in the T.02.47.
The results obtained show that all requirements are fulfilled. The calibration curve is 
linear in the investigated range of 0.05 % to 150 % relative to theoretical rivaroxaban 
concentration in the test solution (0.20 mg/mL). Thus linearity of the analytical procedure is 
verified.

Accuracy/Recovery rate was verified for both test parameters: Assay and Impurities.  
For Assay, three solutions were prepared by adding suitable quantities of drug substance 
stock solution to a placebo mixture in order to obtain rivaroxaban concentrations which 
correspond to approx. 70 %, 100 % and 130 %, based on the theoretical concentration of 
rivaroxaban in the test solution (0.20 mg/mL). Each solution was injected three times and was 
analyzed as directed in Test Procedure (T.02.02). The results were compared to the results from 
corresponding solutions without placebo and the recovery rates were calculated.
The results for Accuracy / Recovery Rate (Assay) are shown in Table 3 in the T.02.47. 
The requirements for the criterion "Accuracy" are fulfilled if the confidence interval (99 %) of 
the mean includes the 100.0 % value or if the complete confidence interval is between 99 and 
101 %. The results obtained show that the confidence interval of the mean includes the 100.0 
% value. Thus accuracy of the analytical procedure is verified.

For Impurities, the impurity Oxaphthalimid was used as surrogate because no degradation 
products are specified for Rivaroxaban coated tablet 20 mg. The sample solutions were obtained
by adding suitable quantities of Oxaphthalimid stock solutions to samples prepared according 
to the Test Procedure (T.02.02) at 3 different concentration levels (about 0.05 %, 0.20 %, and 
0.24 % based on the theoretical concentration of rivaroxaban in the test solution of 0.20 
mg/mL). Each concentration level was prepared three times from independent stock solutions.
The results were compared to the results from corresponding solutions of Oxaphthalimid 
reference standard and the recovery rates were calculated.
The test data obtained for accuracy of impurities/degradation products are shown in Table 
4 in the T.02.47.
Accuracy is considered given if the mean recovery for each individual concentration level 
does not differ by more than 4 times the respective variation coefficient of the method from the 
theoretical value (100 %) and the mean value of all recoveries does not differ by more than 2 
times the variation coefficient of the method from the theoretical value (100 %). Alternatively, 
the requirements for the criterion "accuracy" are fulfilled if the confidence interval (99 %) of 
the mean includes the 100.0 % value or is within 80 – 120 %.
All acceptance criteria for accuracy described above were fulfilled including the alternative 
acceptance criteria. Thus, the accuracy of the analytical procedure is verified for impurities and 
degradation products.

Precision of the instrument and method as well as intermediate precision were verified for 
both test parameters: Assay and Impurities.
For Assay, the precision of the instrument was checked by repeated analysis of a 
rivaroxaban solution. The control solution (100 % level based on the theoretical concentration 
in the test solution 0.20 mg/mL)) was prepared as directed in the Test Procedure (T.02.02). The 
solution was injected six times in succession, and the coefficient of variation of the detector 
signals obtained was calculated.
The results for Precision of the Instrument (Assay) are shown in Table 6 in the T.02.47.
The requirements for "Precision of the instrument" are fulfilled if the coefficient of 
variation is ≤ 1.5 %. The obtained result of the coefficient of variation is 0.3 %, thus precision 
of the instrument is verified.
For the precision of the method, six samples were prepared according the Test Procedure 
(T.02.02) with concentrations of active ingredient corresponding to approx. 100 % based on 
the theoretical concentration of active ingredient in the test solution (0.20 mg/mL). The 
coefficient of variation of the six test solutions was calculated.
The results for Precision of the Method (Assay) are shown in Table 10 in the T.02.47. 
The requirements for "Precision of the method" are fulfilled, if the coefficient of variation 
for each concentration level is ≤ 3.0 %. Based on the results obtained, the requirements are 
fulfilled. Thus, precision of the method for the analytical procedure is verified.

For Impurities, the criteria for “precision of the instrument” are fulfilled, if the 
coefficients of variation are ≤ 15.0 % for any level.
Because no degradation products are specified, the impurity Oxaphthalimid was used as 
surrogate. The sample solutions were obtained by adding suitable quantities of Oxaphthalimid 
solutions to samples prepared according to the Test Procedure (T.02.02) at 3 different 
concentration levels (about 0.05 %, 0.20 %, and 0.24 % based on the theoretical concentration 
of rivaroxaban in the test solution of 0.20 mg/mL). A single test solution was prepared for each 
concentration level and injected six times respectively. The test solutions were injected six 
times one after another, and the coefficients of variation of the detector signals obtained were 
calculated for each concentration level. The test data obtained for precision of the instrument 
for impurities/degradation products at each level are shown in Table 7, Table 8 and Table 9 in 
the T.02.47.  
The obtained results demonstrate the requirements are fulfilled. Thus, precision of the 
instrument for impurities/degradation products is verified.
The criteria for "precision of the method" are fulfilled, if the coefficient of variation is ≤ 
15.0 % for any level.
Because no degradation products are specified the impurity Oxaphthalimid was used as 
surrogate. The sample solutions were obtained by adding suitable quantities of Oxaphthalimid 
solutions to samples prepared according to the Test Procedure (T.02.02) at 3 different 
concentration levels (about 0.05 %, 0.20 %, and 0.24 % based on the theoretical concentration 
of rivaroxaban in the test solution of 0.20 mg/mL). Six test solutions were prepared for each 
concentration level and each test solution was injected once. The test solutions were injected 
once one after another, and the coefficients of variation of the detector signals obtained were 
calculated for each concentration level.
The test data obtained for precision of the method for impurities/degradation products at 
each level are presented in the Table 11, Table 12 and Table 13 in the T.02.47.
The obtained results demonstrate the requirements are fulfilled. Thus, precision of the 
method for impurities/degradation products is verified.

For the test of the intermediate precision, six samples were prepared with concentrations 
of active ingredient corresponding to 100 %, based on the theoretical concentration of active 
ingredient in the test solution (0.20 mg/mL), independently by two analysts (A and B) on five 
different days using different equipment. The mean assay and the coefficient of variation of 
each sequence were calculated.
The results for Intermediate Precision are presented in Table 14 in the T.02.47. 
The requirements for "Intermediate Precision" are fulfilled, if the coefficient of variation 
for each sequence is ≤ 3.0 %. The obtained results demonstrate the requirements are fulfilled. 
Thus intermediate precision of the analytical procedure is verified.

Question/Consideration:
Question 5-2
Explain the synthetic route of the starting material and all impurities that may potentially be 
introduced from the synthetic route. Then, explain the impurity removal efficiency in each 
step based on data.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 5-2 ( Module 3: S.2.3 ):
Pyridine-2-carboxylic acid is synthesized by hydrolysis of 2-Cyano pyridine.
2-Cyano-pyridine may be contaminated with 3-cyano-pyridine, 4-cyano-pyridine and  
2-methyl pyridine.

3-Cyano-pyridine

2-Methyl pyridine

The main product of the hydrolysis step is Pyridine-2-carboxylic acid. Possible impurities in 
Pyridine-2-carboxylic acid are therefore Pyridine-3-carboxylic acid, Pyridine-4-carboxylic 
acid. and the non-reactive impurity in the raw material 2-methyl pyridine.

carboxylic acid

Therefore, the specification of Pyridin-2-carboxyloic acid includes specification limits for 
Pyridine-3-carboxylic acid, Pyridine-4-carboxylic acid and 2-Methylpyridine.
Fate and origin of the above-mentioned possible by-products are controlled by the 
specification of the starting material Pyridin-2-carboxyloic acid.
In addition, the by-products are controlled in the stage of intermediate Picolinamide 
phenylether.
In detail, the specified impurities of Picolinamide phenylether are: 4-Aminophenol , 4-
Chloropicolinate methylamide, Formyl-PAPE, Picolinamide diphenyl ether, 
Chloropicolinamide phenyl ether and APOX-dipicoline methylamide.
None of the impurities specified in the intermediate Picolinamide phenylether contain a 
pyridine related structural element originating from the impurities Pyridine-3-carboxylic acid 
and 2-Methylpyridine.
4-Chloropicolinic acid methylamide, Formyl-PAPE, Picolinamide diphenylether, Chloro 
picoline amide phenylether and APOX-dipicoline methylamide contain a pyridine related 
structural element originating from the impurities Pyridine-4-carboxylic acid. Thus they are 
considered reaction by-products originating from the impurity Pyridine-4-carboxylic acid.
Fate of potential impurities of pyridine-2-carboxylic acid in the manufacturing process of 
intermediate Picolinamide phenylether is understood. The control strategy is justified by the 
compliance with criteria specified for  pyridine-2-carboxylic acid and Picolinamide 
phenylether.

Question/Consideration:
Question 6
For each step, explain why the step was or was not classified as a critical step, and identify all 
critical control parameters for each of the critical steps.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 6 ( Module 3, S.2.2 ):
In the manufacturing process of API, the basic structure of the API is formed in Step 1, Step 2 
and Step 3. The related substances generated in these steps cannot be removed in Step 4 and 
later. Therefore, Steps 1 to 3 are set as critical step to control the reactions and the generation 
of related substances. As shown in the response to Question 7, based on 
validation/manufacturing experience, the process parameters of Steps 1 to 3 (except pH of 
Step 1) are considered to be non-critical, however each step can be appropriately controlled 
by the parameters set in the steps. In order to control the manufacturing process and to 
guarantee the quality of intermediates, the intermediates obtained in Steps 1 to 3 are handled 
as critical intermediates, and API in compliance with the specifications can be manufactured 
by conforming to the testing and acceptance criteria specified for each critical intermediate.

Question/Consideration:
Question 18
For each step, explain why the step was or was not classified as a critical step, and identify all 
critical control parameters for each of the critical steps.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 18 ( Module 3: P.3.3):
For the manufacturing process of Nexavar Tablets, granulating and tableting process are 
designated as critical steps because the processes impact potentially to DP quality (water 
content, disintegration, dissolution and dose uniformity). DP quality can be controlled by 
setting in-process control in each process.
In addition, the drying needs a close control. This is why the IPC acceptance criteria for loss 
on drying are tightly limited (0,3-0,7 %). This parameter is routinely monitored via IPC 
testing. Granulation is therefore classified as a critical process step.
In the tableting process, target weight is specified as a critical matter. Also tablet weight and 
disintegration are specified as IPC tests to ensure that assay/uniformity and dissolution are not 
negatively affected. IPC testing is performed during routine production. Tableting is therefore 
classified as a critical process step.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1 (3.2.P.8)
There is a consistent trend that the TYMC reaches the limit at the end of shelf life (36 months) 
when stored at 30°C/75% RH for products manufactured at the new site (Site Bitterfeld), while 
this observation is not made at the original Site Leverkusen. Please provide justification.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.8):
The stability of production scale batches of Rivaroxaban coated tablets 10 mg, 15 and 20 mg 
manufactured at Bayer Bitterfeld GmbH, Bitterfeld-Wolfen, Germany was investigated during 
the shelf life of 36 months. The results are available in the technical registration documents 
T.04.02. An evaluation of the results is presented in the technical registration documents 
T.04.15. 
 
The measurements at T0 and T36 do not differ in the method or execution, nor are they based 
on changes in the Ph.Eur.  
For the calculation of results, when no colonies could be detected, the calculation was 
adjusted. "<50 CFU/g" for TAMC and TYMC at the time of T0 was correctly determined 
using the calculation valid at that time and does not need adjustment. 
"<100 CFU/g" is the result when no colonies are found after the change ("<100 CFU/g" 
would be the T0 result, if re-calculated). 
 
The reported microbial count on the analysis certificate corresponds to the reporting threshold 
of the method, as with the result of no colonies, the method is limited to stating <100 cfu/g in 
terms of accuracy. This is considered sufficient to meet the specification limits. 
Consequently, there is no trend towards the end of the shelf life.
Source: T.04.02-05 Stability Data / Rivaroxaban coated tablet 10 mg (Site Bitterfeld)
(T.04.02_015394974, updated)

To 1)
With regard to the pH 3.5 Acetate Buffer
The submitted test procedure S.4.2.01 describes the pre-treatment method, i.e. the preparation

Dissolve 25.0 g of ammonium acetate in 25 mL of water and add 38.0 mL of 6 N hydrochloric

3.5, dilute with water to 100 mL, and mix.

is described in the USP<231> as following:
Dissolve 25.0 g of ammonium acetate in 25 mL of water, and add 38.0 mL of 6 N

Question/Consideration: For Table 3–10 of “P.8.3.01_022972870_08 Stability Data.pdf”, please justify the out of specification for Purity by SE-UPLC (Main peak) at month 6 and the omission of test for isoaspartate and sterility.
Answer/Response:
The out of specification results in the accelerated stability study are within expectation since the product is known to undergo degradation when exposed to elevated temperatures for longer periods of time (here 25 °C). This is shown primarily by an increase in isoaspartate content and aggregates determined by SE-UPLC, while main peak purity determined by SE-UPLC accordingly decreases. Another major degradation pathway at accelerated storage conditions is fragmentation as determined by reduced and non-reduced CE-SDS (see also CTD section P.8.1.01-05).
Therefore, the storage conditions of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial for intravitreous injection are defined as 2 °C to 8 °C as shown in P.8.1.02-02.
Additionally, the total time that the product is exposed to temperatures above 8 °C (time out of refrigeration, TOR) during the manufacturing process is monitored and limited to account for the temperature sensitivity of the product, please refer to P.3.4.01-02.
Sterility was not tested in accelerated stability studies as the purpose of these studies was to investigate the degradation behavior of the product at this storage condition as described above. Sterility was, however, part of the test panel for the long-term stability studies and was tested at the end of shelf-life.
Isoaspartate was tested in accelerated stability studies and the results are included in the updated CTD section P.8.3.01-10 provided with this response.
In addition, CTD sections P.8.1.01-05 and P.8.3.01-10 were updated with 24 months data for long-term studies for batches 8345600001, 8345600002 and 8345600003.

Question/Consideration: Please justify the necessity of this amount of overfill.
Answer/Response:
During process development a hold-up volume (HUV) study was performed to determine the fill volume to ensure the injectable dose of 70 µL also considering the HUV of the vial, syringe, and needle components, and a priming volume experienced during drug product (DP) administration.
The major goals of the study were to demonstrate that at a fill volume of 263 μL, an injectable volume of at least 70 μL will be reliably achieved while minimizing the potential of extracting a second dose volume of 70 μL.
Study results demonstrated that a minimum fill volume of 238 μL produced a mean injectable volume of at least 70 μL. The target fill volume was therefore set at 263 μL, with a lower action limit of 238 μL (-10% of target volume) based on historical knowledge of fill variability at the manufacturing site and was validated during DP process performance qualification.
Source: P.2.4.01-01 Pharmaceutical Development - Container Closure System / Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial for intravitreous injection (#022972832; unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Only the results of the identity test and the assay of the drug products before and after the 
change of gadoxetate sodium reference materials are presented, but in the purity test (2) related 
substances, it is also used for system suitability.
Since the amount of individual related substances and total related substances has increased in 
gadoxetate sodium reference material after the change in the preparation method compared with 
before the change, take the following measures.
1) Explain why related substances increase in sodium gadoxetate reference material after
changing the preparation method. 
2) Consider whether or not it is necessary to explain with specific data whether this effect
also affects the analytical method of related substances in the drug product. 
3) Based on the above, explain again the Justification of loosening the specification of
related substances of gadoxetate sodium reference material after changing the 
preparation method.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (CTD section):
1)
As a result of the manufacturer change for Gd-EOB-DTPA reference standard the complete 
process of manufacturing could not be performed from one party and consequently before 
freeze-drying an evaporation step needed to be added to the process in order to perform the 
lyophilization by a third party as indicated in the documentation provided.
Because the evaporation of water at the rotavap is conducted at 40°C and the drying process at 
50°C in a fresh air drying cabinet, this is the most likely reason why, the amount of related 
substances has increased in comparison with the previous batch. The added step in the 
preparation is not evaluated as a significant change in the preparation method.

2)
The analytical method for the determination of related substances and decomposition products 
in Sodium Gadoxetate solution 0.25 mol/L for parenteral use (PRIMOVIST) is a HPLC 100% 
area method. The amount of the impurities is determined based on a relation of the individual 
impurity peaks to the sum of all evaluated peaks of the sample. The Gd-EOB-DTPA reference 
standard is used to confirm the system suitability (system performance: resolution). Thus, the 
amount of the impurities in the reference standard has no impact on the testing results of related 
substances and decomposition products in drug product.

3)
As shown in 1) and 2) of this inquiry, the change in the preparation method does not affect the 
test results of the drug product and therefore it is appropriate to loosen the specification values 
for related substances in Gd-EOB-DTPA reference standard based on the actual values after the 
change.

Question 6
Gather the information on the elucidation of the structure and other characteristics with results 
and supports applied in at least one batch in order to corroborate the application of this

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 6 ( CTD section):

The BAY 81-8973 glycoprotein is synthesized as a single chain 330-kD precursor with a 
domain structure of A1-A2-B-A3-C1-C2 subunits. Proteolytic processing at the B-A3 
(between Arg 1648 and Glu 1649) junction yields A1-A2-B heavy chain and A3-C1-C2 light 
chains to form a large heterodimeric structure linked by a divalent cation bridge.  Multiple 
N-linked and O-linked glycans are present on the structure, predominantly within the 
B-domain.  The A1 and A3C1C2 domains each have two occupied N-linked sites.  
Additionally, there are six occupied tyrosine sulfation sites and one with minimal occupancy.
The structural characterization of BAY 81-8973 Drug Substance (DS) lots was performed 
employing the following methods:  size exclusion chromatography (SEC), sodium dodecyl
sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE), liquid chromatography (LC) 
techniques combined with tryptic and thrombin enzymatic digestions, and mass spectrometry 
(MS).  In addition to testing each clinical and conformance DS lot against the BAY 81-8973 
Product Reference Standard (STD 0090 RM2), the currently licensed rFVIII-FS product, was 
analyzed in parallel, per previous agency requests.  The rFVIII-FS lot chosen for the 
comparison was the lot used in the BAY 81-8973 pre-clinical studies. The tests include 
routine release tests (as noted in Table Error! No text of specified style in document.–1) and 
extended characterization assays.

The data obtained for structure elucidation show that the molecule has the expected profiles 
for protein size distribution, protein backbone sequence and mass.  The expected disulfide 
bonds have been confirmed in each lot.  These attributes are shown to be comparable to those
for the rFVIII-FS product.  The aggregate levels are shown to be lower in the BAY 81-8973 
product relative to rFVIII-FS, primarily due to the removal of plasma proteins.
Characterization of the N-linked and O-linked glycans released from the molecule has shown 
consistency of structures present between clinical and conformance lots, the Product 
Reference Standard and rFVIII-FS.  The BAY 81-8973 clinical and conformance lots have 
been shown to have increased levels of the highly branched tri-and tetra-antennary sialylated 
species relative to rFVIII-FS. Since glycan sialylation can affect the clearance of the molecule 
in the body, this attribute is tested as part of release specifications.
Glycan extended characterization has also shown that levels of alpha-galactose and NGNA on 
each clinical and conformance Drug Substance (DS) lot were always below 1%.  These 
alpha-galactose levels are below the values generally observed for rFVIII-FS.
As expected from characterization of rFVIII-FS, BAY 81-8973 clinical, conformance and 
reference standard lots have been confirmed to have six highly occupied tyrosine sulfation 
sites at residues 346 in the A1 domain, 718, 719, and 723 in the A2 domain and at 1664 and 
1680 in the light chain.  A residue at Tyrosine 395 has been shown to have very low 
occupancy.  High occupancy at this site was not expected from review of other FVIII 
products.
In addition to looking for the expected post translational modifications (PTMs), the tryptic 
digest MS spectra of BAY 81-8973 clinical and conformance lots were also interrogated for 
further modifications that commonly occur on proteins such as oxidation, deamidation and 
glycation.  Low levels of oxidation have been confirmed to be consistent on specific 
methionine residues for each lot.  Deamidation was observed consistently at very low levels 
(~1%) on five residues.  Glycation was not observed to have occurred in any lots.
