Question/Consideration:
Question 10
The dev part, the manufacturer refers to a Kogenate product. Given that this product is not 
marketed in Tunisia, this part must be provided in detail
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 10 (Module 3: P.2.2, P.2.3):
We hereby confirm Kogenate was approved in 2009 by the HA in Tunisia. The development 
objective for Kovaltry (BAY 81-8973) was to create the successor to the Kogenate product.
Drug Product has the same formula strengths, protein concentration, formulation, 
container/closure, and fill sizes. Therefore, the strategy for BAY 81-8973 Drug Product process 
development was to evaluate the rFVIII-FS platform Drug Product manufacturing process and 
to demonstrate that the same process in the same facilities, using the same utilities, equipment, 
and process flow would be suitable for manufacture of BAY 81-8973 Drug Product. (P.2.3.01)
The BAY 81-8973 formulation is a platform formulation from Kogenate (rFVIII-FS), and has 
been used for BAY 81-8973 in the development studies, commercial-scale preclinical and 
clinical batches, and conformance batches. Data from BAY 81-8973 development studies and 
clinical manufacturing experience demonstrated satisfactory stability results. Therefore, no 
changes were made to the Drug Product formulation between development, clinical studies, and 
commercial conformance lots. Based on acceptable stability data using the rFVIII-FS 
formulation for BAY 81-8973, the identical formulation will be used for BAY 81-8973 Drug 
Product commercial manufacturing. Extended characterization was carried out to further 
investigate the physicochemical and biological properties of the BAY-81-8973 molecule. 
Characterization of clinical and conformance Drug Product (DP) lots was carried out alongside 
the BAY 81-8973 Product Reference Standard (STD 0090 RM2), as well as a licensed rFVIII-
FS lot to identify any differences or similarities in the proteins, per earlier agency request to 
compare molecules. The rFVIII-FS lot chosen for the comparison was the lot used in the BAY 
81-8973 pre-clinical studies (27N1190). Results obtained by physicochemical analyses for each 
clinical and conformance DP lot using intrinsic fluorescence, far UV circular dichroism and 
differential scanning calorimetry show all lots to have equivalent conformational structure and 
thermal stability. It is also concluded that results are comparable to those obtained for the 
licensed rFVIII-FS product. With respect to biochemical characterization of the molecule, the 
results of the thrombin and FXa activation studies and FIXa and vWF binding studies indicate 
functional activity of the rFVIII product, with profiles and results that are consistent with the 
structure of the rFVIII molecule. All clinical and conformance DP lots have comparable results 
to the Product Reference Standard and the licensed rFVIII-FS lot.

Question/Consideration:
Question 13
The protocol as well as the validation report of the manufacturing process and the sterilizing 
filtration of the finished product must be provided
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 13 (Module 3: S.2.5 and P.3.5):
The BAY 81-8973 DP manufacturing process includes the Final Bulk Formulation, Filling,
Freeze-Drying, and Vial Capping processes. The evaluation of the process validation was based
on manufacturing process parameters and in-process controls. Each validation batch was tested
for compliance with the specification.
During manufacturing of DP, QA released conformance Drug Substance material was used for
the BAY 81-8973 DP conformance batches. A matrix approach was used, which included
manufacturing DP using Drug Substance batches derived from early, middle, and late stages of
the cell culture. This approach confirmed acceptable performance throughout cell culture age
on the Final Bulk Formulation, Filling, Freeze-Drying, and capping process. Refer to S.2.5.01
for the conformance scheme.
Furthermore, BAY 81-8973 DP conformance batches were manufactured using the same
process in the same sterile filling facility utilized for manufacturing the clinical BAY 81-8973
DP batches that used the same primary container closure intended for commercial application.
All relevant cell culture, purification, formulation, filling, and freeze-drying process parameters
remained unchanged. Therefore, data from clinical production and conformance runs is fully
representative of the commercial process.
A bracketing approach was used for the stability studies of the BAY 81-8973 DP dosage
strengths between 250 IU and 1000 IU per vial for those strengths manufactured with the
2.5 mL fill size, and 3 lots of each of the 5 mL fill size products, i.e., 2000 IU and 3000 IU.
When clinical batches are combined with the conformance batches, at least three (3) batches
were produced for each formula strength, except for the 500 IU formula strength, which was
bracketed between the 250 IU and 1000 IU formula strengths.
The Process Parameters, were well controlled and all critical quality attributes were consistently

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Regarding to the renewal request for Gadovist 1.0 mmol/ml injectable solution in PFS submitted under no. 271C/18.03.2022, we are requesting to confirm that presented formulation contains the same active substance (gadobutrol monohydrate) with the one declared in the file on which the Authorization was based – MA 10460/2017/01-02-03. We are mentioning that, although in Annex 4 of MA is mentioned Gadobutrol as INN, the scientific data transmitted with at the time under letter no. 5861/10.06.2008 in the authorization file makes reference to 2 crystalline forms, both of them monohydrated I and II. In the same time, the quality specification of the active substance mentions water content as maximum 7%, limit which is within the one from EU.Ph Monograph for gadobutrol monohydrate. We are mentioning the fact that active substance manufacturer (Bayer AG, Germany) has an approved CEP R0-CEP 2017-275-Rev 02, and in renewal file is mentioned the fact that quality reference of active substance is EU.Ph Monograph for gadobutrol monohydrate (04/2021:2735).
In the same time quantity of Gadobutrol monohydrate (mg) will be declared as “equivalent of XXX mg gadobutrol”.
This request is available for medicine Gadovist 1.0 mmol/ml injectable solution (MA: 10724/2018/01-02-03-04-05-06-07).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.3.2):
We would like to provide the following information in response to your query regarding the drug substance:
1. Gadobutrol as Monohydrate:
We hereby confirm that the final active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) for our product is Gadobutrol Monohydrate. The standard manufacturing process may yield Monohydrate I, Monohydrate II, or a mixture of both. These two crystalline forms are equivalent in terms of their characterization, including solubility and stability.
Below, we provide details of the manufacturing process and the distinction between the production of Gadobutrol and Gadobutrol Monohydrate:
Manufacturing Process for Gadobutrol
• Synthesis of the Ligand: Cyclen (1,4,7,10-tetraazacyclododecane) is reacted with specific reagents to synthesize the desired ligand.
• Complexation with Gadolinium: The ligand is complexed with gadolinium oxide (Gd₂O₃) to form crude gadobutrol.
• Purification: The crude gadobutrol is purified using ion exchange chromatography and other purification techniques to achieve high purity.
Manufacturing Process for Gadobutrol Monohydrate
In addition to the steps outlined above, an additional crystallization step ensures the formation of Gadobutrol Monohydrate:
• Crystallization: After complexation and purification, the solution is concentrated, and ethanol is added to achieve a specific water content.
• Controlled Crystallization: The mixture is heated under reflux and then cooled to crystallize Gadobutrol Monohydrate. This step ensures the product contains the correct amount of water to form the monohydrate.
We confirm that the final API complies with the above process. The crystallization step involving ethanol and water is performed, and water content is thoroughly tested to ensure the monohydrate form. The limit of Water content are inline to Ph.Eur Monograph.
2. No Monitoring or Control of Solid-State Form:
Given the equivalency in the properties of Monohydrate I and II, there is no requirement to monitor or control the specific solid-state form. Consequently, the ratio of the crystalline forms in the drug substance, even when a mixture is present, has not been evaluated.
3. Interchangeable Use of Terminology:
The names Gadobutrol and Gadobutrol Monohydrate are used interchangeably in documentation and product descriptions.
4. Molecular Mass:
The relative molecular mass for Gadobutrol Monohydrate, it is 622.730 (equivalent to Gadobutrol is 604.720)
Please find the declaration Confirmation of Final API as Gadobutrol Monohydrate
Also please note that potency correction factor is applied during the API weighing step of the Gadovist manufacturing process to ensure that the physically weighed amount corresponds precisely to the effective amount of Gadobutrol.
The potency is a batch-specific value that accounts for factors such as water content, ensuring the correct assay of Gadobutrol. This correction is critical to maintaining consistent and accurate dosing.
During the release testing process, the parameter “Assay of Gadobutrol” is tested for every batch by Quality Control. The results must comply with the range specified in the release specifications to confirm the product's quality and potency.

Source:  Gadobutrol solid state form-Confirmation of Final API as Gadobutrol Monohydrate
Statement on Gadobutrol Weighing

List of SFDA Questions to be sent to the MAH: Module 1.1  A justification letter to include

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):

Background and scope of these changes is related to the Letter of Recommendation from 
EMA to Bayer AG.  As per the letter of recommendation issued within procedure number 
EMEA/H/C/004054/0000 at the time of the Jivi CHMP Opinion for the Marketing 
Authorization, Bayer AG committed to re-evaluate the specification limits proposed for Drug 
Substance (DS) and Drug Product (DP) after 30 batches have been manufactured and to 
continue the development and implementation of a process specific HCP assay.  
The first re-evaluation took place for the specification parameters Osmolality, Specific 
Activity and Total Protein and related changes were submitted for DS and DP for strengths 
500 - 3000 IU, which have been approved under Procedure No. 
EMEA/H/C/004054/II/0019/G. 
 
With this variation package we are presenting the re-evaluation of the other, remaining 
specification parameters for DS and DP and the new process specific HCP method and related 
specifications. Consequently, we would also like to introduce changes that are related to 
method improvements in the same variation package.

Description of the changes in this variation submission: 
Updated release and stability specifications for DS and Drug Product (DP) for Potency, High 
Molecular Weight (HMW), Low Molecular Weight (LMW), Purity, Glycine, Histidine and 
Calcium are being proposed. For content specific attributes (total protein, specific activity, 
and osmolality), specifications were not recalculated for the 250 IU dosage strength. There 
have been no commercial batches produced of the 250 IU strength since the initial product 
licensure and thus no new data to consider. Existing specifications are maintained for the 250 
IU dosage strength. Excipient specifications have been adjusted for all dosage strengths as 
they are independent of protein concentration. Additionally, the test methods SEC-HPLC and 
RP-HPLC for the determination of Purity are adjusted to include some of the Impurity region 
as a product variant and redefine some of the LMW region as belonging to the main product 
peak.  The new limits are based on redefinition of the test methods for Purity and LMW. No
methodology change: integration change only.  The specifications pertaining to the size 
exclusion and reverse phase HPLC (HMW, LMW, Purity and LC/HC ratio) have been 
recalculated for all dosage strengths due to changes in the assay integration.  
A new process specific Host Cell Protein (HCP) Immunoassay is proposed for replacement of 
the current method used for HCP determination which is not process-specific. Related 
updated specification limits are proposed for implementation in testing DS- Q Eluate. 
Additionally, the HCP as a process performance attribute for the Membrane Adsorption 
Eluate-Formulated (MAEF) process step is proposed for removal. 
An optimized test method of Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) for determination of Sodium 
and Calcium is proposed. The optimized method will replace the current method used for 
testing Drug Substance (DS) and Drug Product (DP). 
 
Changes in the acceptance criteria for peak ratios and revised peak calculations are proposed 
to optimize the Tryptic Digest Peptide Map (peptide map) method. 
Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate-Poly-Acrylamide Gel Electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) Silver Stain 
Method is proposed for replacement of the Reverse Phase HPLC method for identity testing 
of DP. 
 
Clinical Control CTL 2117 RM2 and its system suitability criteria will be replaced by 
Conformance Control CTL 2131 RM1 and its system suitability for Reverse Phase HPLC 
Methods for DS and DP considering that the clinical stability program for all Jivi clinical 
product ended in December 2020.  As such, clinical control CTL 2117 RM2 is no longer 
needed. Additionally, reference standard STD 0218 RM1 is being introduced for use in RP-
HPLC (2.5 µm) and peptide map assay. Reference standard is introduced using the 
limits/conditions as detailed in the approved qualification protocol.


• 
REC 18510: DP - Implement SDS-PAGE Silver Stain Drug Product Identity testing for Jivi 
Packaged Final Containers

REC 30534: DS and DP - Implementation of new release and stability specifications for DS and 
DP for Potency, High Molecular Weight (HMW), Low Molecular Weight (LMW), Purity, LC/HC, 
Glycine, Histidine, Sodium and Calcium as well as redefinition of test methods for Purity and 
LMW

and Calcium in DS method and related changes in DP method 
• 
REC 30577: Implement a revision to the acceptance criteria for Tryptic Peptide Map Analysis

Justification for grouping: 
It is justified based on Regulation 1234/2008, Annex III.2 because the same specification 
parameters and HCP method are being modified based on the same underlying evaluation and 
commitment, so that the variations are consequential. The justification for grouping of the 
other method changes is that these method changes are interrelated to the committed 
specification assessment and resulting changes too.

ensure the reference aligns with the originator FPS, which also specifies the limit as 8.3

Answer/Response:

Please note that the formula in the dossier reads as follows:
ELC can be calculated as
ELC=K/M= 5.0/0.3=16.7 EU/mL
based on the formula stated in EP 5.1.10:

✓ EP Monograph 5.1.10.:

5.0/0.6 = 8.3 IU/ml .
Kindly see enclosed the mentioned references.

iii) Referring to the calculation for release in the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
The analysis of this particular batch was performed in a sequence with multiple other batches.
The documentation of used standard and reference substances were filed in QAO 23006829
and was referenced in the raw data. Furthermore, the preparation of used reagent solutions is
documented in additional logbooks with specific IDs as they are used within a broader time
frame for several analyzes.
The raw data of the UV instrument are not transferrable to another system. Thus the
absorbance results are transferred manually by the operator to the raw data sheets and are
checked in the system by the supervisor. For this specific request, we added a screenshot of
the system (please refer to chapter 2.1 in document P.5.4.11_02).
As it is shown in the test procedure P.5.2.901_004451110_03 (K268E150) the 2.00 mL of the
reference solution is added with 18.0 mL water in a 25 mL flask (1:10 dilution ratio). This is
because during test conduction different reagents (hydrochloric acid, sodium nitrite solution,
amidosulfonic acid solution and naphthylethylenediamine dihydrochloride solution) are
added.
These single steps are not noted in detail, which complies with the rules of good laboratory
practice (GLP). The calculation of the amine result with the absorbance results is performed
manually with a calculator in a doer-checker-principle. No further raw data for this
calculation exist.

Question/Consideration:
Question 9
The specifications for the following tests are missing: water content. Attach analytical 
methodology.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 9 (CTD section P.5.6):
The test parameters resistance to crushing and water content were investigated during 
pharmaceutical development. Water content was found to increase when tablets are stored
without humidity control (25 °C/80 % RH in open containers). The increase in water content 
was accompanied by a decrease in tablets hardness. High temperatures (60 °C and 80 °C) 
decreased the water content which was also accompanied by a reduction in tablet hardness. 
However, the values observed for hardness during long-term stability testing remain 
sufficiently high to allow for tablet handling and shipping. The increased water content of the 
tablets did not affect the formation of degradation products or the dissolution behavior of the 
tablets as demonstrated in stress tests and long term stability studies. It is concluded that the 
test parameters “resistance to crushing” and “water content” are not indicative of product 
quality. They are therefore not included in the specification.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
P.2 Pharmaceutical Development
The MAH should provide more details on the lab scale study for the freeze-drying process; 
how the study was conducted, the equipment used, and further, the number and nature of 
samples included in the study should be described. The lab scale data is presented in Figure 
1-1, 1-2 and 1-3. However, the data used for the figures (raw data points) should also be 
provided, preferable in tables. Further, the MAH should justify the feasibility of the lab scale 
study as model for the manufacturing scale freeze-drying process, including a comparison of 
the set-point process parameters. An overall conclusion on the confirmation of the freeze-
drying cycles and set points and the applicability to the commercial manufacturing process 
should also be provided. The dossier should be updated accordingly.
Answer/Response:
A feasibility lab scale study for using the commercial platform 5 mL lyophilization process to 
manufacture 4000 IU Damoctocog Alfa Pegol Drug Product was performed. The 4000 IU 
Damoctocog Alfa Pegol lyophilizate vials were prepared by filling diluted drug substance into 
Glass type I vial/Stopper bromobutyl gray type I, partially stoppered and then lyophilized 
with the 5 mL commercial lyophilization process in a lab scale freeze drier. The 2000 IU 
Damoctocog Alfa Pegol Drug Product lyophilizate vials were also prepared using the same 
vial/stopper/equipment but using the commercial 2.5 mL lyophilization process as a control, 
since 4000 IU and 2000 IU have the same nominal concentration after reconstitution (IU/mL). 
Freeze drier setpoints, segment durations and ramp rates for the lab scale freeze drier were the 
same as that for both 5 mL and 2.5 mL commercial processes, where Table 1 summarizes the 
5 mL lyophilization parameters at lab and commercial scale.
After lyophilization, the vials were manually capped with flip-off caps and stored in a stability 
chamber at 40°C for a four-month stability study.  The duration of 4 months is to perform a 
feasibility assessment of the 5 mL lyophilization process for the manufacturing of 4000 IU 
Damoctocog Alfa Pegol rather than demonstrating formal stability. At each pre-determined 
time point of four months, vials were sampled and verified for headspace vacuum using a 
head space pressure analyzer. Samples were then analyzed for potency and HMW/LMW of 
lyophilized 4000 IU drug product vials and compared with 2000 IU lyophilized drug product 
vials as a control to understand the performance of the 5 mL lyophilization process. The 
number of samples for each analytical test, raw data and timepoint are shown in Table 2 and 
Table 3.

Set point (shelf temperature, pressure), ramp rates and segment durations for both the lab 
scale and commercial scale processes were identical (Table 1), thus the applicability of the lab 
scale study is relevant for the 5 mL commercial manufacturing processes.

Source TRD: P.2.3.60_022985496_02 Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process 
- Freeze Drying - amended

Question/Consideration:
Question 7
For the 5.0 mL diluent PFS a nominal overfill of 0.15 mL and 0.1 mL is proposed for SCB 
and Vetter, respectively. The MAH justifies the 0.15 mL overfill at SCB by stating that the 
overfill ensures that a volume of 5.0 mL of reconstituted product is delivered to the patient. 
Considering the previously performed retention volume study including both PFS from Vetter 
and SCB (SCB section P.2.6) in combination with the delivery systems, the 0.15 mL/0.1 mL 
overfill for the 5.0 mL PFS is not found fully justified. The MAH should reconsider the overfill 
and/or provide further justification that the 0.15 mL/0.1 mL overfill will ensures that a volume 
of 5.0 mL of reconstituted product is delivered to the patient during infusion in the clinical 
setup. The dossier should be updated as appropriate.
Answer/Response:
The diluent prefilled syringe used for the reconstitution of Factor VIII requires an overfill to 
compensate for transfer loss.

Based on retention volume studies in section 3 of P.2.6.01_022985338_01 with a maximum 
retention volume of 0.25 mL for either Vetter or Berlin, combination of overfill contained in 
the Drug Product vials, the sWFI overfill in either Vetter or SCB prefilled syringes, and 
approximately 0.2 g of the lyophilized solids in the Drug Product vials, ensures that adequate 
amount of reconstituted rFVIII product is delivered to the patient.
For the 5.0 mL diluent PFS a nominal overfill of 0.15 mL and 0.1 mL is proposed for SCB 
and Vetter, respectively in P.2.2.01_004384890_02 and P.2.2.01#009151807_02.
For the 5 mL fill size, the target fill weight of final formulation bulk in the vial is 5.25 g 
(equivalent to 5.2 mL) for rFVIII Drug Product.  A nominal overfills of 0.1 mL of diluent in 
the Vetter prefilled syringe assures the combined volume of reconstituted product in the 
product vial is greater than 5.2 mL (resulting from 5.1 g of diluent and approximately 0.2 g of 
lyophilized solids) and an extractable volume of 5.0 mL. Similarly, a nominal overfill of 
0.15 mL of diluent in the SCB prefilled syringe assures the combined volume of reconstituted 
product in the product vial is greater than 5.2 mL (resulting from 5.15 g of diluent and 
approximately 0.2 g of lyophilized solids) and an extractable volume of 5.0 mL.
Furthermore, the overfill volumes for Vetter and SCB prefilled syringes used for licensed 
Kovaltry 5 mL products are the same for the 4000 IU Jivi. There are no changes to the 
physical properties of the 4000 IU since the formulation composition is the same as the 
Kovaltry 5 mL licensed product.

Question/Consideration: The stability data were obtained from batches of 60 capsules packaged in a 120ml HDPE bottle. Please confirm whether the container closure system for the registered pack size is also a 120ml HDPE bottle. Please also provide justification for using the stability data of 60 capsules per 120ml bottle to support the shelf life of the registered pack size of 56 capsules per bottle.
Answer/Response: For the commercial 56 capsule count presentation, the headspace in the bottle is slightly increased compared to bottles filled with 60 capsules. A higher amount of oxygen is consequently included in the closed bottle. For the 100 mg formulation, which uses size 0 capsule shells, the impact on changed headspace is 2.7 mL for a difference of four capsules in fill amount (0.68 mL is the volume of one size 0 capsule). With regard to variability of available headspace, the 75 cc bottle is specified to a nominal volume of 87 mL ± 4 mL. This variability is due to the blow molding manufacturing process of the bottle. Compared to the variability of the bottle volume, the variability in headspace between bottles filled with 56 capsules and bottles filled with 60 capsules is even lower and therefore regarded as negligible. For the 120 cc bottle, the variability in nominal volume of the bottle will be even higher than for the 75 cc bottle (for the 25 mg capsule, filled in size 2 capsules). As the packaging material itself remained unchanged and therefore having the same water and air permeability, no impact stemming from the different capsule count is expected.
keywords: Container closure system; Shelf Life; Stability data

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
The "residue of ignition" parameter in the concentrated hydrochloric acid specifications 
presented in the application annexes of interest (c, ç, g, i, a) can be tested separately if 
requested in accordance with the EP 2.4.14 monograph and EP 11.0 concentrated 
hydrochloric acid monograph, as stated in your cover letter of interest (a). However, one of 
the parameters that should be tested within the scope of EP 11.0 concentrated hydrochloric 
acid monograph is "Residue on evaporation" with a max limit of 0.01%. Provided that the 
change is made only to fully comply with the pharmacopoeia, the "Residue on evaporation" 
test parameter must be included in the requested concentrated hydrochloric acid 
specifications.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
Bayer apologizes and wants to clarify that the intention of our variation was to register the test 
items “Free chlorine” and “Sulfate” according to Ph. Eur. and to delete the test item “Iron” of 
our specification for “Hydrochloric acid”.
With regard to "Residue on evaporation", the test item “Residue on ignition” is considered at 
least equivalent or even better compared to Ph. Eur. Monograph test item “Residue on 
evaporation” and our proposed limit of max. 5 ppm is much tighter than the Ph. Eur. 
Monograph limit of max. 0.01 % (corresponding to 100 ppm).
Bayer also wants to point out the following acc. to general notices of Ph. Eur. chapter 1.1.2.2: 
“An article is of Ph. Eur. quality if it complies with all of the requirements stated in the 
monograph. This does not imply that a manufacturer must perform all of the tests described in 
a monograph when assessing compliance with the Ph. Eur. before release. The manufacturer 
may obtain assurance that an article is of Ph. Eur. quality on the basis of its design, together 
with its control strategy and data derived, for example, from validation studies of the 
manufacturing process.”
Therefore Bayer concludes that the test item “Residue on ignition” is suitable to substitute the 
test item “Residue on evaporation”.

As a result of a review of the control strategy, the

robust transition analysis method.

Currently, column lift-off volume (LOV) is used for
Protein A, Cation Exchange, Anion Exchange,
Hydrophobic Interaction and Size Exclusion
chromatography steps as an indication of
chromatography performance and to signal
potential deterioration of a given column.

The manufacturer proposes to delete the LOV IPC

Gaussian Height Equivalent of a Theoretical Plate

conductivity transition.

column deterioration. It has demonstrated superior
robustness as a column monitoring technique

excursions when compared to the current LOV
monitoring approach. TA in combination with
chromatogram review will be used outside of the
IPC program as part of a holistic strategy to monitor

cells to seed the 10,000 L production bioreactor. This quality attribute is categorized as a general
(non-critical) attribute since it is used to monitor operational consistency and, historically, has not
had a direct impact on the product quality when maintained within normal operating ranges.

Transfer of cells for the 20 L cell bag and for the 50 L, 500 L, and 3,000 L bioreactors is VCD-
driven whereas the transfer of cells, to subsequent steps, for shake flask and the 2 L cell bag is time-
driven. Therefore, the expansion of permissible VCD limit for shake flask initial VCD does not
impact the transfer determinations for the cells.

Historical review of aflibercept drug substance production data showed that any variability seen in
the early seed expansion unit operations does not persist into the production bioreactor (10,000 L),
as the cell density is able to recover to levels that are in alignment with historical experience at the
production bioreactor step.

Additionally, there are other IPCs in-place that ensure consistent cell growth and expansion.
These include, but are not limited to, the initial VCD, final VCD and final viability of the 2 L and
20 L cell bags along with the respective IPCs of the 50 L, 500 L, and 3,000 L expansion
bioreactors.

The evaluation confirmed that the process will continue to operate within the established
process time limits which are well within the validated LIVCA Limit (839 hr:57min –
1068 hr:59min), therefore there is not a risk of experiencing population doublings beyond those
proven with the LIVCA lot or a risk to the genetic stability of the cell culture as a result of the
proposed updates to expansion times.

Therefore, with these controls in place, the Sponsor concluded that it is acceptable to modify
the initial VCD for cell thaw as this change shows no impact to cell culture performance and
product quality.

The currently approved limit was established based on guidance, practices, and data available
at the time to be able to detect any variability outside historical experience. The reassessment of the
shake flask initial VCD GQA is based on the approach defined in S.2.4.01 in section “On-Going
Process Monitoring and Improvements in IPC Limits: As additional experience and data are gained
during commercial manufacturing, the proposed IPCs and their action limits will be re-evaluated.”

Considering the low risk of the proposed change, formal validation runs were not performed.
Data have been collected from multiple commercial lots produced within the expanded viable cell
density (VCD) range (0.27 – 0.68 x 106). Data for eight commercial lots are provided in this
response and demonstrate that there is no downstream impact to the process.
Trending charts have been provided in Annex 1 at the end of this document for in-process
controls (IPCs) and lot release data.
keywords: in-process control; controls of critical steps and intermediates; risk assessment; batch data; stability testing

2. Justification for the proposed drug substance Appearance test deletion please clarify the

Visible particulates testing is not required according to guidance for intermediate stages of a
parenteral or intraocular protein formulation (DSI, DS and FB). Also, in line with ICH Q6B
“Specifications: Test Procedures and Acceptance Criteria for Biotechnological/Biological
Products”, only the physical state (e.g., solid, liquid) and color testing is required for drug
substance. Additionally, tests specified in United States Pharmacopoeia (USP) <790>
“Visible Particulates in Injections” and European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur.) 2.9.20
“Particulate contamination - visible particles” are specific for Drug Product (DP) only.

The Aflibercept manufacturing process at Regeneron is well established and supported
with long-standing historical manufacturing and quality control (QC) experiences to
control and minimize the presence of particles during processing. Every lot of DSI,
DS and/or FB, if stored, is filtered through 0.2 µm filter into mixing bag and dispensed
into sterile biotainers. The dispensing of the material occurs in a classified area which
is monitored through environmental monitoring program, in accordance with internal
procedures. All produced lots are sampled and tested for bioburden and turbidity as a
part of release testing. Turbidity testing is performed to ensure product/process
consistency, and that the material is clear. This testing provides detection of
proteinaceous instability and/or potential large quantity particle loads introduced
beyond the characterized levels.

Visible particles in the final DP are minimized and their presence is controlled. During
DP manufacture (filling), the FB solution undergoes a double filtration as part of the
aseptic manufacturing process. The test item “visible particulates” is and will remain a
release criterion for DP final release and stability specification. In addition, 100%
Visual Inspection of DP containers for visible particles according to Pharmacopeia is

Question 1.1.3.1:  
Exclude the first criterion, as exceeding the specified range of optical densities may indicate 
either improperly prepared solutions, an out-of-specification result, or an unsuitable standard 
sample and does not allow conclusions to be drawn about the suitability of the system.
Answer/Response:
Response 1.1.3.1: 
Exceeding the linear range of the method gives an indication that the validated range of the 
method is not met for a specific measurement (for various reasons) and as such no 
conclusions with regard to the content of the sample measured can be taken, as the signal 
obtained is not linear to the analyte anymore. Therefore, it is important to ensure that the 
linear range of the analysis is met, otherwise no valid results will be obtained as per the 
method validation. It is highly recommended to keep this criterion as a measure to guarantee 
that all measured values are generated within the frame of the validated method and do not 
exceed the validated range of this absorbance method.
keywords: validation parameter linearity; analytical method validation; Validation of Analytical procedures; test method

Question/Consideration:

Eliminate the use of a standard sample and associated manipulations, since the essence of the 
system suitability test is actually the evaluation of the relative standard deviation of the 
optical densities (which can be performed on the test solution), and the calculation of the 
result does not require the use of a standard.

Response 1.1.4:
It is correct that calculation of the result for the sample does not require the use of a standard. 
The use of a qualified reference material (i.e. the reference standard or standard sample) to 
confirm that all equipment used is working properly and all necessary liquid handling steps 
have been executed as per the procedure. An expected result obtained for the standard, which 
is a qualified material stored at conditions preventing change over time, confirms the 
functionality of all used equipment and appropriateness of all standard handling steps under 
the actual conditions of use. If an unexpected result is obtained for the reference standard, it

test the suitability of the system, where instead of the stock solution with a concentration of 
2.5 mg/mL use a diluted solution with a concentration of 0.025 mg/mL (which after dilution 
with reducing buffer solution will be 1% (0.005 mg/mL) of 0.5 mg/mL);
Answer/Response:
Response 1.3.6.5.1: 
The Applicant proposes a system sensitivity criterion based on the IgG standard. Monoclonal 
IgG is the established system suitability standard for the method and supports the existing 
criteria. The same system sensitivity solution and resulting sensitivity criterion was already 
established for the approved 40mg/mL strength.
During method validation, the LOQ (0.005 mg/mL) was determined through the analysis of 
the signal/ noise (S/N) of the main peak of a monoclonal IgG system suitability standard 
under non-reduced conditions.  The monoclonal IgG system suitability standard was chosen 
since the main peak of IgG standard has better resolution than aflibercept sample under 
electrophoresis, which makes the S/N evaluation more accurate. Also, the migration time of 
the main peak of IgG standard is similar to the typical size variants observed for aflibercept. 
The LOQ is the lowest amount of analyte in a sample that can be determined with acceptable 
precision and accuracy under the stated experimental conditions. As experimental conditions 
(i.e., instrument parameters) are not changing in between reduced and non-reduced assay 
conditions, and as the purpose of the sensitivity standard is to ensure system performance, it is 
only necessary to evaluate under the one condition. Hence, the monoclonal IgG system 
suitability standard was analyzed by CE-SDS under non-reduced conditions. The single intact 
main peak generated from the dilution of the standard was used to ascertain the LOQ of the 
assay method and S/N ratio for main peak of IgG sample was analyzed by Empower 3 
software.
It is therefore proposed to add a sensitivity standard and system suitability criterion based on 
the validated LOQ for the diluted monoclonal IgG standard under non-reduced CE-SDS 
conditions.

concentration of 0.01 mg/ml under non-reducing conditions.

Non-reduced monoclonal IgG control for sensitivity assessment (0.01 mg/mL):

Monoclonal IgG solution for sensitivity assessment (0.05 mg/mL) with 160 μL of 
Dilution Buffer (Non-Reducing) for a final concentration of 0.01 mg/mL. 
Record all dilutions.

Note: Sensitivity assessment, including preparation of non-reduced monoclonal IgG solution 
for sensitivity assessment, is included in the ND in accordance with requirements of the EAEU 
regulatory authorities; it is not presented in the original documentation of the company, and it 
is not performed by the manufacturer during routine analysis.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1.10.3.3.  
Assessment of asymmetry factor of reference peaks 5(M1), 17(M2), 25(M3/SS), 37(M4), 
47(M5). Establish an appropriate validated requirement to account for pronounced peak 
asymmetry under selected chromatographic separation conditions (e.g., "no more than 3").
Answer/Response:
Response 1.10.3.3: 
In accordance with ICH guidelines, identification tests are specifically designed to verify the 
identity of an analyte within a sample. In the context of peptide mapping, this verification is 
accomplished through the visual comparison of the test article chromatogram with the 
reference standard and example chromatograms. The primary aim is to ensure that all of the 
47 peaks are distinct and align accurately with those in the reference standard, which confirms 
the identity of the analyte. While assessing the asymmetry factor of reference peaks such as 
5(M1), 17(M2), 25(M3/SS), 37(M4), and 47(M5) can be important in quantitative analyses to 
ensure precision and accuracy, it is less relevant in qualitative methods like peptide mapping. 
As such, even if peak asymmetry is observed, it should not impact the ability to unequivocally 
identify the analyte. Therefore, establishing strict requirements for peak asymmetry, such as 
the suggested "no more than 3," is not considered necessary in the context of qualitative 
identification methods, as the qualitative nature of peptide mapping inherently accommodates 
variations in peak shape without compromising the identification. The same method with the 
same set of suitability criteria was established and approved for the 40 mg/mL strength in 
compliance with the Russian Pharmacopoeia
keywords: identity test in DP specification; analytical method validation; Compendial Method; Chromatogram

Question/Consideration:
Question 1.10.3.4.  
Assessment of the sensitivity of the chromatographic system by calculating the actual value of 
the limit of quantification expressed as a percentage of the total area of all peaks of peptide 
fragments in the chromatogram of the standard solution. It is reasonable to perform such 
calculation for one of the reference peaks (for example, peak 5(M1)) by the formula LOQ = 
(S×10)/(s/n), where s/n is the value of the signal-to-noise ratio calculated for the selected 
reference peak, S is relative peak area (in %) calculated from the total area of all peaks of 
peptide fragments in the chromatogram;
Answer/Response:
Response 1.10.3.4: 
Peptide mapping is used as an identity test and not a quantitation test, therefore signal-to-
noise ratio for the marker peaks is not obtained during method validation. The qualitative 
comparison between the test article chromatogram, the reference standard chromatogram, and 
the example chromatograms, in addition to the quantitative comparisons between the marker 
peaks, is sufficient to determine test article and system suitability, resulting in the correct 
validation of identity.
Moreover, the method states that the reference standard chromatograms must be similar to 
one another in terms of relative retention time and overall elution pattern, specifically peak 
retention time, peak shape and peak height. Furthermore, the comparison between reference 
standard chromatograms is not limited to 5 marker peaks, as all of the 47 peaks must be 
evaluated. Since this is an identification method, and the comparison is performed by visual 
assessment, an estimation of LOQ is not recommended by EAEU Ph. GPM 2.1.2.39 "Peptide 
Mapping".
keywords: LOD/LOQ; LoQ; identity test in DP specification; Chromatogram; Validation of Analytical procedures

Question/Consideration:
Question 1.10.3.5.  
Alternatively, the sensitivity of the chromatographic system can be assessed by calculating the 
signal-to-noise ratio for one of the reference peaks with a validated requirement for the 
resulting value corresponding to a typical value of the relative area of the selected peak 
relative to the total peak area of the peptide fragments in the chromatogram. For example, for 
a reference peak with a typical relative area value of about 1% (of the total peak area), set the 
requirement for the calculated signal-to-noise ratio as "at least 20", which would correspond 
to an LOQ of 0.5%.
Answer/Response:
Response 1.10.3.5: 
In response to the question regarding the necessity of assessing sensitivity in a 
chromatographic system for peptide mapping, it is important to note that peptide mapping is 
primarily used as a qualitative identity assay rather than a quantitative one. This means that 
the focus is on identifying the presence of specific peptide fragments rather than measuring 
their concentration. Consequently, there is no requirement to calculate the signal-to-noise 
ratio for marker peaks during method validation, as would be necessary in a quantitative 
assay. The identity of the test article is confirmed through a qualitative comparison of the 
chromatogram with reference standards and example chromatograms, ensuring that the 
relative retention time, peak shape, and peak height are consistent. This visual assessment of 
the chromatograms, which includes evaluating all 47 peaks rather than just a subset, is 
sufficient to establish the identity of the sample. Therefore, the Applicant proposes that 
estimating the limit of quantitation (LOQ) is not applicable or recommended, as per the 
guidelines set by EAEU Ph. GPM 2.1.2.39 "Peptide Mapping". The method relies on the 
qualitative similarity in the elution pattern and retention times across chromatograms, 
ensuring system suitability and correct identity validation without the need for sensitivity 
assessment.
keywords: LOD/LOQ; LoQ; identity test in DP specification; Chromatogram; analytical method validation

Question/Consideration:
Question 1.10.4.1:  
Set a validated value for the disregard limit (significance threshold) of the peaks, e.g. "0.5%" 
(a threshold value of the relative peak area (calculated, relative to the total area of all peptide 
peaks in the chromatogram) below which the corresponding peak is not taken into account).
Answer/Response:
Response 1.10.4.1: 
In the context of peptide mapping, which is a qualitative method used for identity 
confirmation, setting a disregard limit for peaks based on their relative area, such as "0.5%", 
is not typically necessary. The primary goal of peptide mapping is to ensure that the test 
article's chromatogram is qualitatively similar to that of the reference standard and example 
chromatograms, focusing on the presence and alignment of specific marker peaks rather than 
their quantitative measurement. As such, the significance of minor peaks below a certain 
threshold does not impact the qualitative assessment of identity. The disregard limit is more 
relevant in quantitative analyses where precise quantitation of impurities or minor 
components is necessary. In qualitative methods like peptide mapping, the emphasis is on the 
overall pattern and alignment of peaks, ensuring that key identity peaks are consistent with the 
reference standard, rather than on the detailed quantitation of every peak. Therefore, the 
Applicant proposes that applying a disregard limit is not applicable or required for the visual 
identity confirmation in peptide mapping.
keywords: identity test in DP specification; Chromatogram; related substances; analytical method validation

The method procedure states that the chromatograms of the test sample that are digested at the

those of the reference standard in terms of retention time and elution profile, including aspects 
such as peak retention time, shape, and height. The comparison of chromatograms is not 
restricted to the five marker peaks and, and all 47 peaks must be visually assessed. Since this 
is an identification method relying on visual assessment, and since emphasis should be placed 
on the overall elution pattern between the reference standard and the test article 
chromatograms, setting a disregard limit for additional or missing peaks is not recommended.
keywords: identity test in DP specification; Chromatogram; Reference Standards or Materials; analytical procedures

Answer/Response:

API is light sensitive.
As per ICH guidelines “Note for Guidance on The Photostability Testing of New Active

studies.

and transportation.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
The observation is reiterated regarding: FINISHED PRODUCT – Provide Analytical 
methodology containing the description of the radionuclide purity test. What was provided 
corresponds to the active ingredient, not the finished product. Justify.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.4, P.5):
Based on the drug substance production process, the precursors of radium-223; thorium-227 
(half-life = 18.7 days) and actinium-227 (half-life = 21.8 years) are potential radionuclidic 
impurities in the drug substance solution. Given their half-lives, these radionuclides, if 
present, would be carried forward from the drug substance solution to the drug product and 
remain in the drug product during the entire shelf life. On this basis, the radionuclidic purity 
with respect to thorium-227 and actinium-227 is tested on drug substance level only as further 
outlined and justified in the following:
Due to the use of dedicated production facilities and disposable production equipment, as well 
as storage of the drug substance solution in a closed container within the production facility, 
new radionuclidic impurities cannot appear in the drug product. The drug product 
manufacturing steps involve dilution of the drug substance solution with the pre-mixed 
excipient solution, filtering, filling and autoclaving. Thus it is evaluated as justified to carry 
forward the results for radionuclidic purity from the drug substance to the drug product. For 
further details please refer to the corresponding `Justification of Specification` documents for 
the drug substance (S.4.5.01-09) and drug product (P.5.6.01-01). Analysis of radionuclidic 
purity is performed by gamma spectroscopy using an HPGe detector for quantification of 
gamma ray emission and is described in the `Test Procedure` of the drug substance (S.4.02-
01).

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Whilst it is accepted that some parameters of the finished product specification are not stability- indicating, the shelf-life specification must include all parameters which the product would be expected to comply with, if tested. The shelf-life specification in section 3.2.P.5.1 must therefore retain the test for sterility. Alternatively, a single finished product specification covering both release and shelf-life could be provided, with footnotes added as to which parameters are tested on stability batches. It is expected that confirmation of sterility is at least confirmed on stability batches at end of shelf-life, so section 3.2.P.8.2 should be revised accordingly.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.P.5.1section):
In case of the Sterility test, Bayer Oy states that according to the Questions & Answers in EMA web pages (Quality of medicines questions and answers: Part 2 / Stability - Endotoxin testing and sterility testing at the end of shelf-life), EMA is stating:
“Sterility testing should be performed at least at the end of shelf life but it can be replaced by testing of the container closure integrity.”
Therefore Bayer Oy does not include Sterility test in the Shelf-life Specification of Mirena, but substitutes this test with the two proposed Container closure integrity tests: Strip 180º test and Bubble test.
Naturally sterility test is performed for the product at release. During shelf-life sterility is verified by the container closure integrity test, as accepted also by EMA. This approach is approved by FDA as well.

When a process parameter is described as a target followed by a range proposed in parentheses, that range should be identified as a Proven Acceptable Ranges (PAR), e.g., 40 °C (PAR: 30 – 50 °C), instead of 40 °C (30 – 50 °C). Alternatively, to minimize changes that would be needed, a statement can be added at the beginning of S.2.2 to say that ranges reported in parentheses are considered Proven Acceptable Ranges (PARs).

You are requested to provide revised copies for the description of the commercial manufacturing process in m3.2.S.2.2, identify all the PARs in m3.2.S.2.2, and address the following discrepancies.

a) Step 1 - Bis-TFM-pyridyl amide intermediate (7476):
i. The following PARs were not located in Step 1 of m3.2.S.2.2:
For acid chloride formation as per Table 4-1 – m3.2.S.2.6:
• Amount of toluene: 80 – 120%;
• Amount of dimethylformamide (DMF): 90 – 110%;
• Amount of thionyl chloride: 90 – 110%.
For amide formation as per Table 4-2 – m3.2.S.2.6:

• Amount of toluene: 75 – 125%;
• Amount of pyridine: 90 – 110%, based on the used amount of 7475.

iii. The seed for crystallization in Step 1 is “Bis-TFM-pyridyl amide intermediate (7476)”. You are requested to confirm whether the seed is from one of the intermediate 7476 lots previously synthesized and tested complying with the Bis-TFM-pyridyl amide intermediate (7476) specification provided in m3.2.S.2.4. If different specification applies, please provide.

b) Step 2 - Methyl-bis-TFM-pyridyl amide intermediate (7477):
i. The following PARs were not located in Step 2 of m3.2.S.2.2:

For isolation of 7477 as per Table 4-8 – m3.2.S.2.6:

Please specify the type of water content method in the process description.

You are requested to confirm whether the seed is from one of the intermediate 7485 lots previously synthesized and tested complying with the Elinzanetant dihydrochloride isopropanol solvate intermediate (7485) specification provided in m3.2.S.2.4. • Isopropanol crystallization range: experiments used ±12% (0.15–0.19 kg/kg); M3.2.S.2.6.01 was too narrow and will be corrected to 88–112% as in M3.2.S.2.2.

These two ICH Q3C Class 1 residual solvents are not controlled in downstream intermediate(s) or the final drug substance. You are requested to discuss the justification of the proposed specification for dichloromethane with the supporting fate/purge data.
Answer/Response:
Bayer states dichloromethane is controlled in intermediate 7477 with a limit of max. 600 ppm and batch data show levels below 60 ppm (LoQ) (M3.2.S.2.4.01 and M3.2.S.2.4.05).

Assuming worst-case 600 ppm dichloromethane in 7477 and DCM specification limit of 0.030% (300 ppm) for 1,1-dichloroethene and 1,2-dichloroethane, Bayer calculates residue in 7477 of 0.18 ppm for each class 1 solvent:
600 ppm × 0.030% / 100% = 0.18 ppm.
This is below ICH Q3C limits (8 ppm and 5 ppm).

Bayer also performed purge factor calculations for steps 3–5 with an overall predicted purge factor of 10^7, supporting further depletion toward the final drug substance. Table 1 provides predicted purge factors per operation across steps 3–5.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
The specification for pre-sterile filtration bioburden should be ≤ 10 CFU/100 mL (TAMC).
Answer/Response:
For Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vials, the applicant considers the applied comprehensive
microbiological control strategy including a pre-sterile filtration testing volume of two times 50 mL
the quality of the product. A similar bioburden control strategy is applied for Aflibercept solution
114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringes (PFS) and was accepted by EMA with procedure
EMEA/H/C/002392/IB/0091/G based on scientific justifications that are also applicable to the vial
and as presented in the following.
The total testing volume for pre-sterile filtration bioburden at Bayer AG, Berlin (BAG) is 100 mL of
Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL, which is divided into two times 50 mL: 50 mL are used for
testing of TAMC (Total Aerobic Microbial Count) and another 50 mL for testing of TYMC (Total
Yeasts and Molds Count) according to the membrane filtration procedures as described in Ph.Eur.
monograph 2.6.12. For each test a limit of ≤ 5 CFU/50 mL is set as also reflected in CTD sections
P.2.3.01-04, P.3.3.01-01 and P.3.4.01-01.
Using different incubation media and incubation temperatures for TAMC and TYMC enables
optimized growth conditions for bacteria, yeasts and molds and hence improves the likelihood of
detecting any bioburden. If molds or yeasts grow under the TAMC incubation conditions, their
counts are included in the TAMC reporting, and if bacteria grow under the TYMC incubation
conditions, their counts are included in TYMC reporting, respectively.
The manufacturing process of the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL vial presentation at BAG was
developed and validated with an in-process control limit of two times ≤ 5 CFU/50 mL for TAMC and
TYMC each. The pre-sterile filtration bioburden method has been verified at BAG ahead of process
validation according to the requirements in Ph.Eur. monograph 2.6.12 for testing TAMC and TYMC
in two times of 50 mL volume.
In contrast, the manufacturing process of the vial at the currently approved manufacturing site
Catalent Indiana, LLC, Bloomington, US (Catalent) has been developed and validated with an in-
process control limit of ≤ 10 CFU/100 mL (total viable count). The bioburden method suitability
test was successfully demonstrated per Ph.Eur. 2.6.12 with a volume of 100 mL. Since process
validation and initial method verification were performed at Catalent using 100 mL, the same
volume is used during routine manufacturing at that site, applying an acceptance criterion of ≤ 10
CFU/100 mL for pre-filtration bioburden.
The sampling volume approach used at BAG for the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial is
supported by the following considerations.
A statistical model to determine a suitable test volume for prefiltration bioburden is outlined in the
PDA publication “A risk-based Approach to Setting Sterile Filtration bioburden Limits” (Yang H:PDA
J Pharm Sci Technol:2013:67:601-609). The publication considers the microbial retention capacity
of the sterilizing filter in relation to the batch volume and the filter surface area as well as the risk
factors associated with bioburden testing [A) risk for false negative bioburden testing results and
B) risk of breakthrough of ≥ 1 CFU through the sterile filter].
Transferring these calculations to the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL vial process at BAG by
considering a microbiological retention rate of > 107 CFU/cm², a filter size of 800 cm2 as well as a
risk A) of  ≤ 0.1% (probability of passing a batch with bioburden exceeding the acceptance limit)
and a risk B) of factor 10-5 (filter penetration of < 1 in 100,000 batches), a maximum batch
volume of 46 L is acceptable in a very conservative scenario by sampling 30 mL with an acceptance
limit of 3 CFU/30 mL. That means with a pre-sterile bioburden limit of 3 CFU/30 mL only 1 batch
out of 100,000 batches would have a theoretical risk of bioburden breakthrough.
As the actual batch volume for the manufacturing process applied at BAG is with 5.2 – 21.5 kg
(corresponding to 4.9 – 20.3 L) lower, the validated filter retention capacity is significantly higher
with > 6 × 107 CFU/cm² and the sampling volume is with two times 50 mL notably larger than in
the calculation, the probability of a bioburden breakthrough is even further decreased.
BAG two filtration steps are performed: a bioburden reduction filtration and the sterile filtration.
For the bioburden reduction filtration, the same sterile grade filter is applied assuring the same
microbiological retention capacity during bioburden reduction filtration and a very low bioburden
load prior inline sterile filtration. The bioburden reduction filtration is employed as a precaution
only. The unfiltered bulk solution has already a low bioburden, as the bulk solution is provided
bioburden controlled.
Apart from this, the pre-sterile filtration bioburden testing is only one piece in the integral process
control strategy which also includes further measures applied by BAG to control the microbiological
quality of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL vial as summarized below:
 
Formulated Drug Substance (FDS) utilized in the manufacturing process is microbiologically
controlled with a release specification limit of ≤ 1 CFU/10 mL as presented in CTD section
S.4.1.01-01.
 
The sterile filtration and filling process is conducted by trained operators under aseptic
conditions compliant to recent cGMP guidelines. Sterile filtration is conducted in a Grade C
environment. Aseptic filling of vials is performed in a Grade A isolator environment under
LAF surrounded by a Grade C environment involving equipment which is single use.
 
The sterilizing filter was validated in a worst-case approach. A retention capacity of at least
6.0 × 107 bacteria per cm2 filter was proven for Brevundimonas diminuta (as described in
CTD section A.1.03-01) which is exceeding the requirements as per
EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/BWP/850374/2015 (retention capacity 107 bacteria per cm2 filter).
 
During the manufacture of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL vial two filtration steps are
performed with the same microbiological retention capacity.
 
For both filtrations, pre-filtration bioburden is controlled by testing with a total testing
volume of 100 mL (two times 50 mL of the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL each for
TAMC and TYMC with a limit ≤ 5 CFU/50 mL each).
 
The manufacturing hold times are controlled and minimized between processing steps.
Refrigerated storage of process intermediates further reduces the risk of microbial growth
in the course of the manufacturing process.
 
Release samples are tested for sterility as critical quality attribute indicative for microbial
contamination.
The aforementioned procedures efficiently mitigate risks of bioburden preload or contamination
during processing as acknowledged by the pharmaceutical industry (Bechtold-Peters K:Eur J Pharm
Biopharm:2024:198:114151, “Risk-based approach to setting sterile filtration microbial bioburden
limits – Focus on biotech-derived products”), and as also supported by the applicant’s experience in
the manufacture of Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL presentations. Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL in
vials and PFS, which are using the same kind of control strategy, demonstrated no concern with
regards to sterility since marketing of the product in 2012. In particular, the experience with
Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL presentations underlines the suitability of the IPC in controlling the
manufacturing process when being embedded in a holistic approach to control microbiological
quality.
In summary, the bioburden testing method compliant with Ph.Eur. 2.6.12, with a sampling volume
of two times 50 mL and an acceptance criterion of ≤ 5 CFU/50 mL for TAMC and TYMC each,
sufficiently ensures detection requirements for in-process testing as part of the overall product
control strategy. The IPC is embedded in a set of further control measures to ensure
packaging materials are tightly controlled. The applicant is convinced that the collective measures
which are implemented to control microbiological quality, as validated, are adequate to assure
sterility and quality of the finished product.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
A) In the FDS process validation of Regeneron Ireland,
- Justification of acceptance criteria of protein concentration in UF/DF process

B) Hold time data of Intermediate performed by Regeneron Ireland (microbial and physicochemical stability data per process)
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.S.2.5):
A) In the FDS process validation of Regeneron Ireland,
- Justification of acceptance criteria of protein concentration in UF/DF process
During manufacturing process development, the acceptable manufacturing range for the target final concentrated pool (FCP) protein concentration was established based on development and characterization studies, and historical manufacturing experience. A high protein concentration in the FCP would be diluted through the sucrose adjustment and formulation unit operations to acceptable levels. A low protein concentration at the FCP stage could cause over-dilution during formulation, potentially leading to a formulated drug substance (FDS) that is below the specified range. The established range for commercial manufacturing (165-184 g/L) is considered a non-critical process condition to be met during routine manufacture to ensure process consistency.
Typically in Biotech processes, the final concentrated pool after ultrafiltration/diafiltration, is set clearly higher than the actual minimal needed concentration.

In addition to the target FCP protein concentration, the lower limit for the FCP protein concentration was then set and classified as a critical quality attribute (CQA).
The CQA (≥ 128.8 g/L) is the minimum FCP protein concentration necessary to ensure that the material produced will have a concentration that is compatible with further product dilution and formulation steps. Additional details are provided in Error! Reference source not found. below.
Following the ultrafiltration/diafiltration (UF/DF) unit operation, during the formulation step, there is a dilution due to the addition of the sucrose buffer, excipient buffer and dilution buffer. The acceptance criteria (≥ 128.8 g/L) was established as the minimal concentration needed at the FCP stage to ensure that the FDS will be within the final release specifications (103 - 126 g/L) after the addition of the three buffers.

B) TMP limit and result of UF/DF process in all batches
Please see below for the UF/DF feed flow rate and transmembrane pressure results and limits.
The excursions below the allowable transmembrane pressure (TMP) and feed flow rate limits of lot 8337700061 were attributed to restarting the primary concentration phase following an unintentional hold1 in the method, which had no impact to validation as there was not an increase in high molecular weight formation for batch lot 8337700061. (see S.2.5.01_022985518_01 point 2.1.4. Concentration and Diafiltration Process Step Performance).
1 During processing an operator inadvertently stepped on the floor scale, triggering a high weight alarm and a temporary system hold.

B) Hold time data of Intermediate performed by Regeneron Ireland (microbial and physicochemical stability data per process)
In S.2.5.01_022985518_01 section 3 Validation of Extended Hold Times, reference is made for the chemical and microbial testing to the original process validation performed at the sending unit (Regeneron, USA, process area PA2X). While chemical stability is equipment and solution dependent, and microbial stability is equipment dependent, both chemical and microbial stability are site independent. The same hold bags and a closed system is used. A point-by-point justification for referring to PA2X hold time validation is given in Table 3-2.
Supplemental hold time validation at PA12 was performed only for UF/DF hold time (see section 3.1. Microbial Hold). Although the UF/DF in-process pool bags are also identical between Regeneron, USA PA2X and Regeneron, Ireland PA12, the microbial hold was validated in PA12 during PPQ to extend the hold time for manufacturing flexibility.
Therefore please also refer to the document previously submitted for the process validation in the sending unit PA2X, S.2.5.01#022972866_02 section 4 Validation of Extended Hold Times.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
- Justification of specification by assessing release test of Vial and PFS
- MFI analysis result and consideration of PFS
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (3.2.S.4.5; 3.2.P.2.2; 3.2.P.2.4; 3.2.P.5.6; 3.2.R.2):
Justification of specification by assessing release test of Vial and PFS
The statistical methodology typically used by the applicant for the calculation of batch release comparability limits are 95% confidence/ 99% coverage tolerance intervals (TIs). This methodology was not applied here, because the same methodology was used for the calculation of the vial batch release specification acceptance criteria using almost the same set of historical vial batches that was available for the comparability exercise between drug product (DP) in vial and DP in PFS. For the calculation of specification acceptance criteria for DP in vial please refer to CTD section S.4.5.01-01 and P.5.6.01-01.
For the comparability exercise between DP in vial and DP in PFS only three further vial batches, i.e. the three vial comparator batches, were available. Therefore, the minimum/ maximum range of the available vial batches was used as a benchmark for the comparability exercise, which is a more stringent approach compared to 95% confidence/ 99% coverage tolerance intervals. The 95% confidence/ 99% TIs are provided in the Table 2 together with the statistics as reported in CTD section R.2.02-02. Note that for SE-UPLC a decimal place was added to the statistics. All TIs are wider than the respective minimum/ maximum range. Comparing the results of the PFS against the historical vial min and max values is therefore considered justified for assessing the comparability between PFS and vial.

MFI analysis result and consideration of PFS
As the glass syringe barrel is lubricated with silicone oil to ensure the movement of plunger stoppers and as the syringe tips are manufactured under the employment of tungsten format parts, the impact on the quality of the drug product was thoroughly assessed for both components.
In a first study, silicone oil and tungsten were spiked to Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL to analyze the stability of the product using a Design of Experience approach. Spiking concentrations corresponded to 10%, 100%, and 200% of the specified maximum silicone oil content of the syringe, respectively the specified maximum tungsten content of the syringe. Comprehensive results are presented in the CTD section P.2.2.10-02. Overall, no meaningful changes were observed in physical appearance, clarity, color, pH, protein concentration and protein integrity over the course of 24 months storage at 5 °C. Further, no meaningful increases in subvisible particulates measured by microscopy were observed. Overall, all acceptance limits were met.
The data confirmed the compatibility of the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL formulation with potential residues of free silicone oil and tungsten and confirmed the compatibility of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL with the container closure system (see CTD section P.2.2.10-02).
In a second study, the overall risk of a potential silicone (oil) leaching into the drug product solution was analyzed. Syringes of technical batches filled at Vetter were subjected to different stresses that were applied either under lab conditions or at commercial scale equipment.
The stressed syringes were analyzed regarding the potential silicone oil transfer using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) and flow imaging microscopy (MFI). The MFI software was applying a filter to dedicatedly count for silicone oil droplets/particles.
Samples measured by MFI and ICP-OES were subjected to pressure changes (to simulate potential stopper movement during air transport as well as during the outer surface sterilization process) and intensive shaking using a vortex device. Overall, as presented in Table 3 and Table 4 no increase of silicone oil particles and free silicone oil compared to the unstressed control was observed.
Independent of the tested scenarios and analytical methods, all data for the technical batches fall in the range of expected method and sample variability.
Further, extractable studies were performed with primary packaging components including the syringe barrel. Extraction was performed with water and 50% ethanol. Analysis was performed with LC-MS, GC-MS and HC-GC-MS. Thereby, in none of the extractable solvents silicone containing organic compounds exceeding the safety concern threshold of 1.5 ug/day were detected (see CTD section P.2.4.06-01).
The extractable results are further confirmed in the leachable stability study of three Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL PPQ finally packaged batches. Results after storage of 12 months are available, no silicone containing organic leachable compounds have been detected in concentrations above the reporting threshold of 1.0 µg/mL of AFL 114.3 mg/mL solution (CTD section P.2.4.07-01). The study is continued up to the end of 24 months shelf life.
Overall, the studies performed do not indicate a product quality risk with regards to silicone and tungsten particles and confirmed the compatibility of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL with the container closure system.

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.P.2.4; 3.2.P.2.6; 3.2.P.8.3):
3.1)
Detailed results of the extractable study are provided and leachable study data including study design, storage conditions and results were included in the respective CTD sections P.2.4.06-01 and P.2.4.07-01, respectively.

3.2)
The applicant would like to describe the difference between the evaluated in-use stability time of 6 hours at 25°C (for the PFS as prepared for dosing) and the 24 h at 25°C reserved for Health Care Professionals (HCP´s) handling of the unopened blister of Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe (PFS).
The proposed label of Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL in PFS includes the following statement: “Prior to usage, the unopened blister pack of EYLEA 8 mg may be stored at room temperature (25 °C / 77°F) for up to 24 hours”. The applicant would like to point out that 24 hours described in this statement does not refer to the compatibility (“in-use stability”) study described in CTD section P.2.6.01-01.
Whereas the proposed label statement refers to the unopened blister with intact sterile barrier and is based on the assessment of the overall time out of refrigeration (TOR) described in section P.8.3.11-04. In this dedicated study the maximum TOR for Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL in PFS was assessed as part of the overall process validation. The total TOR for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL drug product (DP) in PFS covers the end-to-end manufacturing time consisting of filling, labeling, assembly, blistering, sterilization and packaging as well as the time for distribution and delivery of the finished goods to the patient. For Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL in PFS, the overall TOR is defined and controlled, and the maximum TOR includes 24 h reserved for HCP´s handling to allow storage of the unopened blister prior to usage at room temperature. For this study, currently, all available 24 months stability results are within the shelf-life specification. Very few data points were pending at the time of finalization of this response document.
Furthermore, as the results of the analytical comparability program demonstrate that the PFS manufacturing process (sterilized PFS were used) yields Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL drug product that is analytically comparable to the drug product manufactured in vial, the generated vial data should provide sufficient confidence that also for PFS storage at 25°C for 24 h is supported.
The overall data supports the claim that the unopened blister can be stored at room temperature for up to 24 hours.
On the other hand, the applicant provided data proving the compatibility of the drug product solution with the injection needle. This dedicated “in-use stability” study is described in CTD section P.2.6.01-01. After exposure to the maximum TOR following the concept described in P.8.3.11-04 PFS were taken out of blister, needles were attached, PFS were primed and held primed (prior the injection step) for up to 6 hours at 25°C. Subsequently, the DP was analyzed. The data confirm that there was no quality impairment due to the contact of the DP with the inner lumen of the injection needle for up to 6 hours at 25 °C and that the product is stable in a primed syringe stage. This study was intended to confirm the compatibility with the administration configuration prior to application. The data was obtained to increase the knowledge of the drug product and it is not foreseen to define a specific in-use stability time.

Bayer Response to Question 4 (3.2.P.3.5; 3.2.P.8.3):
Functional performance has successfully been tested as part of ongoing real-time stability studies for a duration of 24 months to date. Results are provided in the CTD section P.8.3.11-02. All acceptance criteria were met for the functional performance tests during long term storage.
Functional performance is evaluated as an in-process control within the overall control strategy. This testing has been conducted during the DP process validation and will continue to be upheld throughout commercial manufacturing.
Functional performance testing is conducted in accordance with ISO 2859-1 Sampling procedures for inspection by attributes — Part 1: Sampling schemes indexed by acceptance quality limit (AQL) for lot-by-lot inspection“, which provides a sampling plan and procedure for the acceptance of batches based on the inspection of a sample set. This standard outlines the methodology for determining whether a batch of product meets specified quality requirements without providing specific actual results or values.
The evaluation process under ISO 2859-1 involves the testing of a representative sample size from a manufacturing batch and the assessment against predetermined acceptance criteria. The acceptance or rejection of manufacturing batches is based on the number of samples found in the batch specific sample set that are conforming or nonconforming with the acceptance criteria. The test results are reported as “pass” or “complies” as shown in P.3.5.01-01.

Question/Consideration:
Question 5
A) Assessment data on effects of exposure to refrigeration and room temperature of drug product on Endotoxin test result (Low Endotoxin Recovery)
B) Justification of specification of Particulate Matter Content
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 5:
A)
Endotoxin test results after exposure to refrigeration and room temperature are available for the formulated drug substance (FDS) and are provided in CTD section S.4.3.01-02. The results show no impact to endotoxin recovery for FDS when held at refrigerated conditions or at room temperature.
The FDS has the same composition as the drug product solution and resultantly, it can be assumed that also for the drug product testing low endotoxin recovery does not occur.
To confirm the absence of LER, a dedicated study was conducted at the manufacturing and testing site at Vetter Pharma. The results met the predefined requirements and are provided in the final study report.

B)
Specification acceptance criteria for Subvisible Particulate Matter Content are integral part of Ph. Eur. chapter 2.9.19. The sub-chapter “ Method 2. Microscopic particle count test” states under Evaluation “Test 2.B – Solutions for infusion or solutions for injection supplied in containers with a nominal content of less than 100 mL: The preparation complies with the test if the average number of particles present in the units tested does not exceed 3000 per container equal to or greater than 10 µm and does not exceed 300 per container equal to or greater than 25 µm”. The submitted and more stringent specification acceptance criteria of ≤ 200 particles/mL for ≥ 10 µm particles and ≤ 20 particles/mL for ≥ 25 µm particles were harmonized with the specification acceptance criteria approved and in place for Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL in prefilled syringe. These proposed limits already constitute a significant tightening versus the limits allowed per Ph. Eur. for parental solutions, considering also that Ph. Eur. limits refer to particles allowed per container and the proposed limits refer to particles/mL. Based on the target fill volume of 0.184 mL/PFS the currently proposed acceptance criteria in particles/mL equate to ~37 particles/container for ≥ 10 µm particles and ~4 particles/container for ≥ 25 µm particles, and thus constitute a tightening by a factor of ~81 when compared to acceptance criteria per container stated in Ph. Eur. chapter 2.9.19.
Moreover, for particulate matter content the currently available data set for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL is considered as too limited to derive tighter specification limits. Subvisible particulate matter results are known to not be normally distributed and it is thus difficult to predict the range of future results. The applicant therefore considers the proposed limits of ≤ 200 particles/mL for ≥ 10 µm particles and ≤ 20 particles/mL for ≥ 25 µm particles as justified.

Variations number 4 and 5:
In principle, the replacement of an IPC with reference to a process parameter is an example of 
enhanced pharmaceutical development. No development of the manufacturing process could 
be found in the submitted documentation, and this was not discussed in the Quality overall 
summary.
Normally, demonstration that an IPC can be replaced by a controlled (set of) process 
parameter is provided in section 3.2.P.2.3. Development data should be presented to justify
