Question/Consideration:
Question 39
Description of procedures to guarantee cold chain: The firm has submitted the stability data. 
Query: The firm has to submit the Description of procedures to guarantee cold chain
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 39 (Module 3: R.5):
BAY 81-8973 lyophilisate Drug Product (DP) is transported via expedited truck and air from 
Bayer Berkeley, CA to international distribution centers within the Asia Pacific region using 
pallet-sized thermally-insulated passive shipping systems (referred to as “shipping systems”) 
that are designed to maintain product integrity and control temperature. They were qualified 
and are continuously temperature monitored to ensure temperature control during transport.
Temperature recording devices are placed at several locations on the pallet/payload to monitor 
and record the product temperature throughout the shipment duration. Upon the shipment’s 
arrival at the distribution center, the temperature data is reviewed to determine product 
acceptance.
Shipping studies, including physical, thermal and live shipment testing, were performed on MPs 
and the shipping systems to establish the suitability of the shipping process. Physical testing 
was performed to ensure the packaging design adequately protects the product from damage 
during shipment. Thermal testing was performed to ensure the passive shipping systems 
maintain product temperature within an acceptable range throughout transport duration.  Based 
on the physical, thermal, and live shipment qualification results the shipping processes, 
shipping systems and product packaging support shipments of BAY 81-8973 lyophilisate to 
international distribution centers within the Asia Pacific region.

Question/Consideration: An explanation should be provided for the specification limit value being 1.0% for any individual impurity, while the total impurity limit in the finished product specifications is 1.0%,
Answer/Response:
The acceptance limit for single impurity is based on the limit specified in ICH guideline Q3B(R2) “Impurities in new drug products” for a drug product with maximum daily dose below 1 mg. The acceptance limit for the sum of all impurities is based on the USP monograph on Levonorgestrel.
Ph. Eur. has published a compendial HPLC purity method for Levonorgestrel (LNG) drug substance, which is in use for LNG drug substance quality control (QC) at Bayer. The same Ph. Eur. purity method has been validated for use in Mirena IUS also.
The synthesis impurities that are not potential degradation products are controlled in LNG release testing and are therefore omitted from the drug product specifications. The potential known and unidentified LNG degradation products above ≥ 0.1% reporting threshold are included in the test results.
The current limit for the Sum of impurities is tightened from 2.0 % to 1.0 %, and at the same time the limit for the Individual impurity is added into the Mirena specification. Hence, this is a new requirement for the product. According to opinion of Bayer Oy the proposed impurity limits are appropriate and well justified.

Question/Consideration: Presentation of relevant regulations and scientific sources regarding the possibility of applying 'Container Closure Integrity' tests instead of sterility test, depending on the class and risk level of the medical device
Answer/Response:
The maintenance of the sterile barrier integrity, and hence the sterility throughout the shelf life is demonstrated during stability testing by testing the integrity of the primary package. The integrity of the package is tested with bubble test and the seal strength of the package with strip test.
The substitution of Sterility test with Container closure integrity tests during the shelf-life is in accordance with the guidelines or principles of both FDA and EMA:
In Questions & Answers of EMA web pages (Quality of medicines questions and answers: Part 2 / Stability - Endotoxin testing and sterility testing at the end of shelf-life) the following is stated:
“Sterility is part of the shelf-life specification.
Sterility testing should be performed at least at the end of Shelf-life, but it can be replaced by testing of the container closure integrity. Depending on the nature of the container, intermittent integrity testing might be envisaged, independent of whether the sterility testing is replaced or not.”
https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory-overview/research-development/scientific-guidelines/quality-medicines-qa-introduction/quality-medicines-questions-answers-part-2
This approach is approved by FDA as well in Guidance document “Container and Closure System Integrity Testing in Lieu of Sterility Testing as a Component of the Stability Protocol for Sterile Products”.
FDA guideline states for example the following:
“Alternatives to sterility testing as part of the stability protocol, such as replacing the sterility test with container and closure system integrity testing, might include any properly validated physical or chemical container and closure system integrity test (e.g., bubble tests, pressure/vacuum decay, dye penetration tests or seal force tests, etc.). Such tests may be more useful than sterility testing in demonstrating the potential for product contamination over the product’s shelf life or dating period.”
Source: P.5.1.02_07 Shelf Life Specification / Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#022984914; unchanged) [Annex-2]
P.5.6.01_02 Justification of Specification / Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#008081237; unchanged) [Annex-3]

keywords: Container closure system; Sterility Testing; Shelf Life ＆ Storage Condition; stability commitment; Risk Asessment

Question/Consideration: Submission of the risk assessment report for the application of 'Container Closure Integrity' tests instead of sterility test,
Answer/Response:
The proposed approach is in accordance with the relevant Health Authority Guidelines (EMA & FDA). Therefore, according to Bayer Oy’s opinion there is no need to additionally perform any risk assessments concerning the sterility test substitution for the testing during the Shelf-life.
For example, the FDA Guideline states the following for container closure integrity tests:
“Because of the limitations of sterility tests, they are not recommended as a component of a stability program for confirming the continued sterility throughout a product's shelf life or dating period. Alternative methods may be more reliable in confirming the integrity of the container and closure system as a component of the stability protocol for sterile products.
Sterility tests may be subject to potential interference due to adventitious microbial contamination introduced at the time of testing, resulting in false positive readings.”
An intact package is a pre-requisite for maintaining the sterility of the product. Therefore, testing of the integrity of the package and verifying it by performance of the Container closure integrity tests justifies reliably whether the package is sterile or not.
In the proposed Specifications container closure Integrity is part of the Shelf-life specification only, they are reported in Stability data (P.8.3.02) for the same batches.

Question/Consideration: Presentation of scientific justification and sources for the selection of the finished product active substance identification specification,
Answer/Response:
Bayer Oy proposes two different identification methods for Levonorgetsrel drug substance in the Mirena intrauterine delivery system.
Of the two proposed methods the infrared identification applying ATR (attenuated total reflectance) technique is a specific method by which the drug substance will be identified based on the characteristic IR spectrum of Levonorgestrel. The IR-method is developed particularly for identification in which the IR-spectrum is recorded from the inner surface of the drug reservoir and characteristic bands indicating LNG are used for identification.
In addition, Levonorgestrel drug substance is identified in the liquid chromatographic (LC) assay test with UV detection. The LC-method is developed for controlling of the assay of the drug substance. It provides a conventional way for identification by comparison of retention times obtained from sample and standard.
This approach of using two different identification methods, of which the other is a specific method for identifying Levonorgestrel, is in accordance with the EMA guideline (EMA CPMP/ICH/367/96; NOTE FOR GUIDANCE / SPECIFICATIONS: TEST PROCEDURES AND ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA FOR NEW DRUG SUBSTANCES AND NEW DRUG PRODUCTS: CHEMICAL SUBSTANCES), which is stating the following:
“Identification solely by a single chromatographic retention time, for example, is not regarded as being specific. However, the use of two chromatographic procedures, where the separation is based on different principles, or combination of tests into a single procedure, such as HPLC/UV diode array is generally acceptable. On the other hand, Identity tests should be specific for the drug substance, e.g., infrared spectroscopy.”

Levonorgestrel drug substance is known to be very stable. This is true also for the drug product Mirena manufactured using the stable drug substance levonorgestrel. Vast amount of batch data (over 1500 batches of Mirena manufactured during the last 20 years) as well as data from numerous stability studies have proven that levonorgestrel drug substance in Mirena is stable. It can be stated based on the numerous stability studies performed on Mirena that only negligible degradation occurs during the shelf-life. The sum of Degradation products remains near the zero level during the whole shelf-life of Mirena.

Question/Consideration: Submission of impurity limit calculations performed in accordance with ICH guideline Q3B (R2) and Levonorgestrel USP monograph,
Answer/Response:
The test procedure for impurities in Mirena IUS has been revised to include only levonorgestrel (LNG) related degradation products, not any more synthesis related impurities as the current test. This approach is in line with the EMA guideline CPMP/ICH/2738/99 (ICH Q3B). The guideline states: “impurities present in the drug substance need not be monitored or specified in the drug product specifications unless they are also degradation products”.
This proposed new impurity test is removed from Release Specifications, i.e. it will be included in the shelf life testing only. To support the change, the acceptance limit for the sum of the degradation products is tightened from NMT 2.0% to NMT 1.0%. The potential known and unidentified LNG degradation products above 0.1% reporting threshold are included in the test results.
Levonorgestrel is inherently stable. The long history of Mirena IUS has verified that LNG remains virtually unchanged in the product manufacture, and during the shelf-life. This is demonstrated by comparing results of five MIRENA IUS drug product stability batches with the results for corresponding drug substance batches (P.5.6.01_03). The results for drug substance batches in accordance with the Ph. Eur. method indicate actual low amount of the degradation products for Mirena IUS as the synthesis related impurities need not to be included in the results. This is shown to be true for the drug product batches listed, as the maximum result for the Sum of degradation products is only 0.1 %.
The daily dose released from a Mirena IUS is ca. 20 μg. According to the EMA guideline CPMP/ICH/2738/99 the identification threshold for impurities in a drug product with a maximum daily dose of 1 mg is 1.0% or 5 μg Total Daily Intake (TDI), whichever is lower. The potential known and unidentified LNG degradation products above 0.1% reporting threshold are included in the specifications of Mirena. Calculated as daily intake an impurity at 0.1 % level in Mirena provides a daily intake of 0.02 μg only. The level of possible unspecified degradation products in Mirena are therefore far below the identification threshold of 5 μg TDI. Even the sum of all degradation products calculated as daily intake (1.0 % of 20 μg daily dose) is ca. 0.2 μg (TDI) only.
Based on the arguments above the proposed limits for the impurity test are well justified.

Question/Consideration: Submission of the justification and evaluation report regarding the “Identification” and “Uniformity of dosage units” specifications proposed to be removed from the finished product Shelf-life specifications are not critical for the shelf life of the product,
Answer/Response:
Identification: The drug substance added into the drug product is identified at release, and naturally the identity/drug substance can’t change after the batch manufacture. The levonorgestrel drug substance identified at release remains as levonorgestrel during the whole shelf-life of the product. Therefore, identity test during Shelf-life can be seen as redundant.
Uniformity of content test parameter will be deleted from Shelf Life Specification because it is adequate to report only "Assay of system" test result in stability studies.
It will suffice to perform the Uniformity of dosage units test at release for Mirena. Levonorgestrel drug substance is very stable and only negligible degradation may occur at a level not to affect the actual assay of Mirena (Assay of system). Uniformity does not alter after the batch release and therefore deletion of this parameter from the Shelf-life Specification is justified. By determining the Assay of System, and the low level of possible Degradation products, during the Shelf-life the quality of Mirena can be adequately controlled.
WHO Stability guideline from year 2018 mentions the need for testing of stability-indicating attributes during the Shelf-life of finished drug product: [Annex-12]
https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/Q1F_Stability_Guideline_WHO_2018.pdf
“Stability studies should include testing of stability-indicating attributes of the finished pharmaceutical product, i.e. those that are susceptible to change during storage and are likely to influence quality, safety and/or efficacy.”
Neither Identification test nor the Uniformity test is stability indicating, therefore their omission from the Shelf-life specification is stated to be justified.

Question/Consideration: Submission of justifications for the change in the sample preparation procedure in the sterility test method.
Answer/Response:
The Sterility test does not change in any way, only the sample preparation procedure is simplified. Sterility test is performed as direct inoculation in accordance with Ph. Eur. 2.6.1/USP <71>.
-
The risk for laboratory contamination associated with the cutting phase will be omitted.
-
The procedure is similar to insertion into patient: the IUS is used intact.
-
USP <71>, Medical devices states with regard to the sterility testing: Articles can be immersed intact or disassembled into the test media.
-
The change does not affect the validated status of the method as removing the cutting phase does not affect the sample’s antimicrobial properties in the culture media. Thus, microbial growth due to possible non-sterility of the sample can be detected as well as in the current method with sample cutting.
-
The risk for detecting less growth after the change is very small, as due to the handling and the heat treatments during the manufacturing steps before assembly, the most probable location for microbial contamination is on the outer surfaces of the IUS.
-
The risk for viable contamination within the product after sterilization is negligible based on following:
 o materials do not support microbial growth.
 o bioburden level of Mirena IUS is generally very low
 o The results for Mirena IUS sterility test from several years have fulfilled the specifications apart from one case where a laboratory contamination was suspected.
 o manufacturing of the components, assembly and primary packaging of Mirena IUS take place in cleanliness class C.
 o product is exposed to heat during the manufacture, as both drug core, and the tubing are heated in post-curing oven at 150°C for 4 hours.
 o no water is used in the manufacturing of the product or its components, which limits the possibility of microbial contamination.
 o primary contact surfaces in the production are disinfected.
 o ethylene oxide has high diffusivity and permeability and thus penetrates the material easily. This ensures the sterility of the product in its entirety.
The change in the sample handling procedure of Mirena intrauterine delivery system is justified and it does not jeopardize the validity of the test results of the updated Sterility test procedure.

Question/Consideration: Presentation of the justifications and risk assessments for the removal of the in-process control parameters “Concentration of Levonorgestrel” and “Homogeneity” and the in-process control method “Levonorgestrel quantification”,
Answer/Response:
There is no actual change in the manufacturing process of Mirena in connection of the deletion of mass homogeneity IPC, mixing process itself remains unchanged. Furthermore, the IPCs, Concentration of levonorgestrel and Homogeneity, can’t be considered as two separate IPC tests, as they are both obtained and calculated from exactly the same blend analysis.
Bayer has manufactured Mirena batches for 30 years already and hence the mixing process is well established, and therefore proven to produce homogenous levonorgestrel-elastomer mixtures. In order to support the IPC deletion the actual mixing time (at least 40 minutes) applied on the product over the years was added and specified as an IPC to substitute the homogeneity test. Therefore, the proposed IPCs are only adapting to the actual conditions of the manufacturing process.
A process validation report P.3.5.01_02 in which the mixing time of min. 40 minutes has been observed and reported is provided to the competent Health Authority for review. In this validation study homogenous mixtures were achieved with the mixing time of 40 minutes.
As a further assurance of the continuously homogenous mixtures achieved in the mixing step of Mirena data on recent 283 batches (manufactured between 03.01.2024 and 31.01.2025) of Mirena is provided. The data refers to average results of 4 IPC samples collected from these 283 batches, which means that the data in graphs and histograms is based on 1132 blend samples in total.
The requirement for the average levonorgestrel concentration is 48 – 52 %, and the RSD of 4 determinations must be ≤ 2 %. The average results of 283 batches fall between 47.9 and 50.8 %, with the average of all determinations as 49.4 %. Average of the calculated RSD values is 0.4 %. maximum observed RSD has been 1.6 %.
The data provided reliably verifies that mixing process of Mirena results into a homogenous mixture when mixed for 40 minutes. Therefore, Bayer considers deletion of the homogeneity IPC justified.

Question/Consideration: Presentation of scientific justifications for determining the in-process control limits of “Final mixing time” and “Length of hormone core”,
Answer/Response:
Final mixing time min. 40 minutes has been successfully used to validate the mixing process. Mixing for both shorter and longer times as 40 minutes has been studied for Mirena. Mixing for less 20 minutes provides already homogenous mixtures. It was also found out that mixing for more than 60 minutes does not improve the homogeneity anymore. Therefore, the mixing time of (at least) 40 minutes has been chosen as the adequate mixing time to be used for mixing levonorgestrel-elastomer mixture of Mirena (please see the data in response to question 14). Mixing performed for 40 minutes is long enough to overcome possible variations in the materials and/or mixing process to ensure homogeneity for all batches without exceptions.

The nominal length of the hormone core of Mirena is 19.5 mm. The weight of this piece is ca. 104 – 105 mg, which contains ca. 52 mg of levonorgestrel (lng), as the proportion of lng in the mixture is 50 %. The nominal levonorgestrel assay of Mirena is 52 mg, requirement limits for the Assay are 47 – 57 mg.
The IPC limits for the length of the hormone core in the assembly process are 19.0 – 20.0 mm. The correct length of the core piece is ensured by 100 % camera control at the assembly step. The IPC range for the length (19.0 – 20.0 mm) corresponds with weight range of 98 – 111 mg. With the specified length limits the levonorgestrel amount in an IUS will be between 49 and ~55 mg. This levonorgestrel amount in IUS fulfils the assay requirement for the lng content in one Mirena IUS clearly. Hence, utilization of the defined IPC tests for the assembly process ensures correct amount of drug substance in Mirena for the whole use period.

- deletion of small batch size not in production anymore
- deletion of manual assembly process not in use
- deletion of ETO2 sterilizer at Bayer Oy not in use anymore
- deletion of smaller 16 pallet sterilization line at Sterigenics not in use
- deletion of APET primary packaging material not in use

An updated process validation report P.3.5.01_02 in which the mixing time of min. 40 minutes has been observed and reported is provided to the competent Health Authority for review. The assembly of the batches has been performed with the mechanical process in this process validation, and the batches have been sterilized in ETO3 chamber, as the batches were manufactured in 2023. Question/Consideration: Please provide a specific explanation for the appropriateness of including the spray rate of the API granulation liquid (0.90 kg per minute) and the inlet air temperature (85° C) in the Step 2 (granulation process) as minor change notification items, for example by showing data (proven acceptable ranges) that examine the effect of parameter fluctuations on the quality of the formulation.
Answer/Response:
The manufacturing process development included a comprehensive design of experiments (DoE) in laboratory scale and commercial scale (manufacturing site: Bayer AG, Leverkusen). The DoE study in commercial scale was performed on the three process parameters - spray rate, spray pressure and product temperature and the impact on the quality attributes of the granules and tablet cores was thoroughly investigated. All granule batches could be compressed to tablets complying with the specification. Consequently, the final process risk analysis indicated a reduced risk associated with the granulation parameters (please refer also to information in the technical document P.2.3.01_022872031_02).
On that basis, the process parameter ranges were established for the manufacturing site in Leverkusen (please refer also to information in the technical documents P.3.3.01_022822890_01 and P.3.3.01_022822891_01).
For the implementation of the manufacturing process at the new manufacturing site Delpharm, Milano, appropriate process parameters needed to be defined based on the prior knowledge gained during the development phase according to the equipment used at the manufacturing site Delpharm, Milano. Regarding the spray rate in the granulation process, the proven acceptable range at production scale was 1.4 to 1.8 kg per minute for the manufacturing site Bayer AG, Leverkusen corresponding to a range of 12.5% relative to the setpoint of 1.6 kg per minute. The proven acceptable range for the manufacturing site Delpharm, Milano was derived accordingly from the setpoint of 0.9 kg per minute, resulting in a proven acceptable range of 0.80 to 1.0 kg per minute.
Regarding temperature control, the manufacturing site Bayer AG, Leverkusen controls by product temperature (set value: 34°C), however, since the equipment used at manufacturing site Delpharm, Milano does not have the functionality to keep product temperature constant, Delpharm controls by inlet air temperature (set value: 85°C) instead. In Leverkusen a comprehensive design of experiments was conducted which also included the variation of the product temperature. As described above all granule batches could be successfully compressed into tablets and there was no impact on any critical quality attribute. Hence, it was concluded that the criticality of the process parameters in fluid bed granulation is low (please refer to P.2.3.01_022872031_02). Fundamentally, both parameters - product temperature and inlet air temperature - contribute to the same physical quantity, in this case the thermodynamic energy input. Therefore, for the implementation of the manufacturing process at manufacturing site Delpharm, Milano, a systematic investigation including variation of the inlet air temperature was not considered as necessary, because its impact on the critical quality attributes was deemed low based on the prior knowledge gathered during process development and establishment at manufacturing site Bayer AG, Leverkusen. Furthermore, for the granulation process, the quality of the granules is controlled by loss on drying (1-3 %) as in-process control, and this is applicable for both manufacturing sites Bayer AG, Leverkusen and Delpharm, Milano. Consequently, the applicant considers a change of the inlet air temperature as minor notification matter.
Ultimately, the appropriateness of these parameters was demonstrated in a manufacturing process validation (please refer also to process validation report P.3.5.01_022982751_01). All manufactured batches (three per dose) met the pre-defined acceptance criteria which included the drug product specifications, in-process controls and additional testing such as blend uniformity testing and content uniformity testing.
The addition of magnesium stearate occurs during the post-blending step (i.e. preparation of the ready-to-press-mixture). A sieve is used to eliminate potential aggregates of the raw material before addition. According to the initial risk analysis, no post-blending parameter was found to impact the Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs) of the tablet (please refer also to information in the technical document P.2.3.01_022872031_02). Therefore, a change in screen size will not impact any CQA of the drug product. This was successfully demonstrated within the aforementioned manufacturing process validation at the manufacturing site Delpharm, Milano where a sieve size of 1.0 mm was utilized. The process parameters for the manufacturing process at the manufacturing site Delpharm Milano were defined accordingly (please refer also to information in the technical documents P.3.3.01_022982208_01 and P.3.3.01_022982185_01).
In summary, the comprehensive process development and subsequent manufacturing process validation have demonstrated that the defined process parameters, including the spray rate, inlet air temperature, and screen size for magnesium stearate, do not adversely impact the critical quality attributes of the final drug product. Therefore, these parameters are appropriately classified as minor changes.

Source: P.2.3.01_022872031 v02 Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process/ Finerenone coated tablet (unchanged)
P.3.3.01_022822890 v01 Manufacturing Process and Process Controls/ Finerenone coated tablet 10 mg (unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Section 1.0.4 [In-use Stability Report]
Please provide cycling studies/stress test if applicable under “in-use stability report” to support the statement of “Prior to usage, the unopened blister may be stored outside the refrigerator below 25 °C for up to 24 hours.” in the proposed SmPC (p19).
Answer/Response:
The proposed label statement “Prior to usage, the unopened blister may be stored outside the refrigerator below 25 °C for up to 24 hours.” is based on the assessment of the overall time out of refrigeration (TOR) assessment described in section P.8.3.11-03. In this dedicated study the maximum TOR for Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL in PFS was assessed as part of the overall process validation. The total TOR for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL drug product (DP) in PFS covers the end-to-end manufacturing time consisting of filling, labeling, assembly, blistering, sterilization and packaging as well as the time for distribution and delivery of the finished goods to the patient. For Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL in PFS, the overall TOR is defined and controlled, and the maximum TOR includes 24 h reserved for health care professionals handling to allow storage of the unopened blister prior to usage at room temperature. For this study, currently, 18 months stability data are available and all results are within shelf-life specification. The study will be continued until the end of shelf-life. Based on the currently available data no trend towards out of specification is seen and the data suggest that the specification will be met also at the end of the intended shelf life of 24 months.
Furthermore, as the results of the analytical comparability program demonstrate that the PFS manufacturing process (sterilized PFS were used) yields Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL drug product that is analytically comparable to the drug product manufactured in vial, the generated vial data should provide sufficient confidence that also for PFS storage at 25°C for 24 h is supported.
The overall data supports the claim that the unopened blister can be stored at room temperature for up to 24 hours.
Additionally, the applicant commits to provide the 24 months long-term stability data once they are available.

Bayer Response to Question 1 (CTD section P.5.2):
The identification tests “Identity A (Ph.Eur.) and Identity B (Ph.Eur.) are introduced as additional parameter to specification for Rivaroxaban tablets as required by the Ph.Eur. Monograph. These test parameters are already met with the former test “Identity (HPLC)” of current applied Bayer specification and test procedure for Rivaroxaban coated tablets. Test “Identity A (Ph.Eur)” is confirmed by the UV spectrum of the main peak in the HPLC chromatograms of the reference standard and the test item. The test “Identity B (Ph.Eur.)”is met by defining both main peak retention time and size in the HPLC chromatograms of the reference standard and the test item
According to Ph.Eur monograph, all impurity peaks (by-products and degradants) at or above reporting threshold are determined compared to current in-house method where only degradant peaks are analyzed. The acceptance criteria of max. 0.2% applies to test “any unspecified impurity (Ph.Eur.)” as well as set for current determination of unspecified degradation product. The specification for total impurities according to Ph.Eur. is set at max. 0.3% compared to current specification for sum of degradants of max. 0.5%.

Question/Consideration:
Other Observations - Question 3
It is necessary to describe in the cover letter the methodology for conducting the 
microbiological purity test and provide data confirming the suitability of this technique.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Other Observations - Question 3:
The “Microbial purity” test is included in both T-02.28 - Release Specification and T.02.01 - 
Shelf-life Specification along with the acceptance criteria and the used method, which is 
included in the technical document T.02.02- Test Procedure. Compendial references are made 
to Eur/USP/Ph. Jap. (harmonized method).
The following additional explanatory information regarding  the test method “Microbial 
purity” used for Rivaroxaban coated tablets (2.5 mg, 10 mg, 15 mg and 20 mg) will be 
provided in the updated version of the normative document:
Reduce sample mechanically before weighing. Prepare a test solution by suspending 10 g of 
product in 100 mL buffered sodium chloride-peptone solution. From this dilution, transfer 10 
mL in another 100 mL buffered sodium chloride-peptone solution, resulting in a final dilution 
of 1:100 (solution 2).
TAMC: Plate 2 x 1 ml solution 2 with casein soya bean digest agar
TYMC: Plate 2 x 1 ml solution 2 with Sabouraud-dextrose agar
Incubate according to Ph. Eur./USP/JP:
TAMC: Incubate 3 – 5 days at 30 – 35°C
TYMC: Incubate 5 – 7 days at 20 – 25°C
For the test for the absence of Escherichia coli, suspend 10 g of the product in 100 mL 
buffered sodium chloride-peptone solution (solution 1). 10 ml of solution 1 is used to 
inoculate 100 mL Casein soya bean digest broth (solution 2) for preincubation at 30-35 °C 
for 18-24 h. After incubation transfer 1 ml of solution 2 to 100 ml MacConkey Broth and 
incubate 18 - 72 h at 30 – 35°C.
The suitability of the counting method was demonstrated in the presence of the product 
according to the harmonized method Ph. Eur./USP/JP. Validation studies have been 
performed with all four dosage strengths. See document Validation of Test for Microbial 
Purity with TRD code T.02.34-02 from dossier section 3.2.P.5 which provides additional 
details about the microbial enumeration test.

Question/Consideration: Attach a monograph of the reference pharmacopoeias as support and justification for the elimination of the essays mentioned in your note.
Answer/Response:
The Japanese Pharmacopoeia (JP) 18th edition has introduced updates under General Notice No. 34 regarding the control of elemental impurities. This update aligns with ICH Q3D (R1) guidelines for elemental impurity risk assessment and control in pharmaceutical products. According to General Notice No. 34: 
• JP drug products are expected to comply with elemental impurity controls as described in the general test sections of the pharmacopoeia. 
• When drug products are controlled according to these guidelines, it is not necessary to perform routine testing for elemental impurities (e.g., heavy metals and arsenic) in drug substances, excipients, or drug product monographs. 
Therefore, the need for separate tests for arsenic and heavy metals in the drug substance specification has been eliminated as long as compliance with elemental impurity requirements is demonstrated. In line with ICH Q3D (R1) guidelines, a comprehensive risk assessment for elemental impurities has been conducted for the drug product. The results confirm that all elemental impurity levels, in limits when evaluated in the context of the drug product’s intended use and patient safety. The proposed change aligns with regulatory guidelines and practices, ensuring harmonization across markets while maintaining the highest standards of safety and efficacy for the drug product. 
General note No.34 in the Japanese Pharmacopoeia 18th Edition (JP18) is enclosed in the response.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Today we just received email from our health authority, requesting for us to fill in a self-
evaluation form for the change below, and the deadline of response is by the end of today.
Considering the urgent timeline, we create and initiate a RFI binder in BRAVE, and we need 
your support for the item 10 in the form.
To better answer the question#10, would you please let us know:
• What was the change type in USA for REC 31893, 32972 and 32565? Such as which 
is Type IB (moderate change), annual report (minor change), etc;
• According to the regulation guideline, how do we classify these types (rational) based 
on risk assessment?
• Overall what our submission plan was and the corresponsive considerations?
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
REC32565: In US, according to Changes to an Approved NDA or ANDA（Guidance for 
Industry）Page #11，“D. Minor Changes (Annual Report), 3. A move to a different 
manufacturing site for the manufacture or processing of drug substance intermediates other 
than the final intermediate”，adding new manufacturing site of starting materials and 
intermediates of drug substance is generally considered as minor change (annual 
report).   Based on internal risk assessment this could be a moderate change (Change Being 
Effected in 30 Days, i.e. CBE-30), according to internal implementation policy in Bayer, we 
need to wait for 6 months before implementing a CBE-30 change. Considering a faster 
implementation, we decided to submit supplemental application (Prior Approval Supplement, 
i.e. PAS), which we can received the approval after approx.. 4months and then implement. 
Bayer upgraded this change to major change is not due to risk issue, it is about the faster 
implementation. In addition, according to EU variation guideline LexUriServ.do，Variation 
category B.1.a.1. can be found on p. 25 of 84 of the pdf. In general, B.I.a.1.a) is the closest 
variation type, but some new manufacturer is not part of the same pharmaceutical group as the 
already approved manufacturer. This is why we could not use Type IAIN (minor change) but 
had to upgrade the variation to Type IB unforeseen (moderate change), please find the 
enclosed EU approval letter for details.

REC32972 and REC31893: As for adding new manufacturing sites for other starting materials 
of drug substance and updating of DARO-IV manufacturing process description, according to 
Changes to an Approved NDA or ANDA (Guidance for Industry) as above,  in US it is 
generally considered as Annual report (minor change), due to combination of dispatched
documents in Bayer, REC31893 has been combined in the REC32565 for submission. 
Furthermore, in EU, according to LexUriServ.do, the new manufacturer is not part of the 
same pharmaceutical group as the already approved manufacturer, it has been classified and 
submitted as Type IB (moderate change), please find the enclosed EU approval letter for 
details.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
3.2.P.3.4 Control of critical steps
1. Data to support the replacement of the concentration and homogeneity measurements by 
the final mixing time of 40 minutes should be provided. In addition, a maximum mixing time 
should be defined and justified, based on manufacturer’s experience.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.3.4):
There is no actual change in the manufacturing process of Mirena in connection of the 
deletion of mass homogeneity IPC. The mixing process remains unchanged, only the 
homogeneity IPC test is proposed to be removed from the validated mixing process.
Bayer has manufactured Mirena batches for 30 years already and hence the mixing process is 
well established, and therefore proven to produce homogenous levonorgestrel-elastomer 
mixtures. In order to support the IPC deletion the actual mixing time (at least 40 minutes) 
applied on the product over the years was added and specified as an IPC to substitute the 
homogeneity test. Therefore, the proposed IPCs are only adapting to the actual conditions of 
the manufacturing process.
An updated process validation report P.3.5.01_02 in which the mixing time of min. 40 
minutes has been observed and reported is provided to the competent Health Authority for 
review. In this validation study homogenous mixtures were achieved with the mixing time of 
40 minutes.
Bayer Oy has performed mixing time study for Mirena regarding the mixing phase. 3 different 
final mixing times (20, 40 and 60 minutes) were tested. The mixture was homogenous already 
after mixing of 20 minutes. The situation did not alter significantly neither after mixing of 40 
minutes nor after mixing of 60 minutes. The average assay of 10 homogeneity samples was 
near to 50 % in all occasions, also RSD of the samples did not alter significantly.
Results of the mixing time test:

Based on the mixing study and the overall long experience regarding the mixing step, it can 
be justified that mixing time of 40 minutes produces reproducibly and reliably homogenous 
mixtures for Mirena. Therefore, when using only the 40 minutes mixing time no maximum 
mixing time needs to be defined in the manufacturing batch record.

As a further assurance of the continuously homogenous mixtures achieved in the mixing step 
of Mirena data on recent 283 batches (manufactured between 03.01.2024 and 31.01.2025) of 
Mirena is provided. The data refers to average results of 4 IPC samples collected from these 
283 batches, which means that the data in graphs and histograms is based on 1132 blend 
samples in total.
The requirement for the average levonorgestrel concentration is 48 – 52 %, and the RSD of 4 
determinations must be ≤ 2 %. The average results of 283 batches fall between 47.9 and 50.8 
%, with the average of all determinations as 49.4 %. Average of the calculated RSD values is 
0.4 %. maximum observed RSD has been 1.6 %.
The data provided reliably verifies that mixing process of Mirena results into a homogenous 
mixture when mixed for 40 minutes. Therefore, Bayer considers deletion of the homogeneity 
IPC justified.

system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#IQMS-401680; new)
The test procedure for impurities in Mirena IUS has been revised to include only 
levonorgestrel (LNG) related degradation products, not any more synthesis related impurities 
as the current test. This approach is in line with the EMA guideline CPMP/ICH/2738/99 (ICH

or specified in the drug product specifications unless they are also degradation products”.
This proposed new impurity test is removed from Release Specifications, i.e. it will be 
included in the shelf life testing only. To support the change, the acceptance limit for the sum 
of the degradation products is tightened from NMT 2.0% to NMT 1.0%. The potential known 
and unidentified LNG degradation products above 0.1% reporting threshold are included in 
the test results.
Levonorgestrel is inherently stable. The long history of Mirena IUS has verified that LNG 
remains virtually unchanged in the product manufacture, and during the shelf-life. This is 
demonstrated by comparing results of five MIRENA IUS drug product stability batches with 
the results for corresponding drug substance batches (P.5.6.01_03). The results for drug 
substance batches in accordance with the Ph. Eur. method indicate actual low amount of 
degradation products for Mirena IUS as the synthesis related impurities need not to be 
included in the results. This is shown to be true for the drug product batches listed, as the 
maximum result for the Sum of degradation products is only 0.1 %.
The daily dose released from a Mirena IUS is ca. 20 μg. According to the EMA guideline 
CPMP/ICH/2738/99 the identification threshold for impurities in a drug product with a 
maximum daily dose of 1 mg is 1.0% or 5 μg Total Daily Intake (TDI), whichever is lower. 
The potential known and unidentified LNG degradation products above 0.1% reporting 
threshold are included in the specifications of Mirena. Calculated as daily intake an impurity 
at 0.1 % level in Mirena provides a daily intake of 0.02 μg only. The level of possible 
unspecified degradation products in Mirena are therefore far below the identification 
threshold of 5 μg TDI. Even the sum of all degradation products calculated as daily intake 
(1.0 % of 20 μg daily dose) is ca. 0.2 μg (TDI) only.
Based on the above arguments the proposed limits for the impurity test are well justified.

Question/Consideration:
Question 9
9. Release rate: Considering the long-term use of the drug product that releases levonorgestrel 
at a mean rate of 13-20 μg/24h for 8 years, the ranges +/- 10% and 15% at levels 2 and 3 of 
the release rate test seem rather wide and are supported neither by the batch results nor by the 
clinical batches.

As shown in the summary of the results presented for 42 batches in table 2-10, the standard 
deviation is between 1.5 and 2.2 and all batches comply at level 1. The current specifications 
present only one level acceptance criteria for the average (18-26 μg/d) and the individual 
values (17-29 μg/d), and the applicant assumes that the results at day 8 with the new test are 
similar to the results at day 15 with the current test. The proposed limits are wider than the 
current ones and a non-compliant batch to the current specifications at day 15 might comply 
with the level 2 or level 3 of the proposed specifications at day 8. Therefore, to maintain 
similarity between the testing points linked to the clinical performance, i.e. the current day 15 
release rate and the proposed day 8 release rate, the applicant is asked to reduce the range at 
day 8 for level 2 and level 3 to a range representative of the presented results and 
representative of the day 15 results.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 9 (3.2.P.5.1):
Bayer recognizes the release rate acceptance limits proposed for the new method can be 
considered wider than the current method limits for the day 15. Therefore, the day 8 Level 2 
and 3 ranges are revised, as requested, and in addition more scientific data is provided to 
justify the ranges. Bayer sees that the revised specification is justified since the addition of 
sampling points and the level testing procedure increases significantly the overall control of 
the manufactured batches. 
The current and the new methods are statistically compared in the P.5.3.21 and P.5.6.01 to 
proof the day 8 of the new method ensures the intended release rate profile similarly as the 
day 15 in the current method. This justifies that the batch data can be used to set the 
specification and the link to the clinical performance has remained. In addition, it should be 
noted that the new method increases the sampling points, i.e., it brings two new test points, 
and they also have 3-level testing procedure. The discriminatory power studies presented in
the P.5.3.21 show that some result of a defected IUS are outliers of the day 2 and 5 proposed 
limits but would fulfill the current specification for day 15. This is strong evidence for the 
quality control power of the new 3-point method.  
P.5.3.21 demonstrates the potential of the release method for the long-term release profile 
determination. Three MIRENA batches were tested up to eight years (2920 days) and a 
regression curve can be used to calculate the relationship between in vitro release rate and 
time. The provided graphs demonstrate that over a period of eight years the three batches 
release Levonorgestrel at the same rate, and the residual content of LNG is greater than 25% 
at eight years ensuring a continual decreasing dissolution profile over time. 
At the day 8 range of ±5% is set for Level 2 (16.5 -27.4 µg/day) and range of ±8% is set for 
Level 3 (16.0 -28.2 µg/day). The ranges correspond to the current method day 15 range for 
individuals (17-29 µg/day). The new ranges required a slight shift down from the current 
range based on the batch data. The 3-level testing procedure having the increasing sample size 
(n=6-12-24) and slightly opening limits increases the overall quality control power. The Level 
1 sample size corresponds the current method sample size but the Level 1 range for the 
individuals, 17.3 - 26.1 µg/day, is significantly tighter than the current range for individuals.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
In the supplementary application of JYHB2200228, it is stated that the chloride content in the DP is indirectly controlled by the osmolality test of the DS solution. Please explain how to control the chloride content of this product after deleting the osmolality test in the DS specification.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (S.4, P.5):
The chloride content of the finished drug product originates from the premixed buffer solution “sodium citrate solution 20 mmol/L in sodium chloride 0.11 M with calcium chloride”（which contributes to approximately 98 % of the drug substance solution in terms of volume，540 mL ÷ 549.3 mL = 98%）, and the premixed buffer solution “sodium citrate solution 28 mmol/L in sodium chloride 0.11 M”（which is used for dilution to drug product target radioactivity concentration）。

The composition and specification of the two premixed solutions are described in S.2.3.02-03 “Raw Material – Specification“ and respective P.4.1.02-01 “Excipients – Specification” and summarized below.

Table 1:  Composition and specification of sodium citrate solution 20 mmol/L in sodium chloride 0.11 M with calcium chloride

Table 2: Composition and specification of sodium citrate solution 28 mmol/L in sodium chloride 0.11 M

Identity test for chloride and test for osmolality are part of both specifications of premixed buffer solutions. Since more than 98% of the drug substance solution comes from sodium citrate solution 20 mmol/L in sodium chloride 0.11 M with calcium chloride, the osmolality of the drug substance solution can be indirectly reflected by the osmolality of this premixed buffer solution.
Due to the addition of sodium chloride as an isotonic agent in the premixed buffer solution, the osmolality is a direct evaluation parameter of the isotonic effect. The chloride content of drug product can still be controlled by the osmolality testing results of the two premixed buffer solutions and the drug product. Moreover, the results of the statistical evaluation of more than 220 drug product batches including overall control strategy applied for the drug product supports this justification for the deletion of chloride.

The correlation between citrate input amount in the drug substance preparation process, citrate content in the drug substance, citrate input amount in the drug product production, and citrate content in the finished drug product is further detailed below and is consistent at 7.2.mg/mL across all the before mentioned steps/products：
（1）Citrate input amount in the drug substance preparation process and the final concentration：

The total citrate input amount in the drug substance is 0.01545 mol，the final concentration is 7.2 mg/mL.

= 7.2 g/L
= 7.2 mg/mL

The composition of the drug substance solution is presented in Table 3:. Hydrochloric acid is a small ingredient of this citrate buffer, and a typical concentration is given in Table 3:.

(3) Citrate input amount in the drug product production and final concentration:
The drug product is manufactured by dilution of the radium-223 drug substance solution with the premixed excipient solution sodium citrate solution 28 mmol/L in sodium chloride 0.11 M, to achieve the target radioactivity concentration. For example, take 540 mL of Radium 223 chloride drug substance solution (containing citrate concentration of 7.2 mg/mL) and 2360 mL of premixed buffer solution 2 (containing citrate concentration of 7.2 mg/mL ), to make 2900 mL of drug product solution (containing citrate concentration of 7.2 mg/mL).

(4) Citrate content in the finished drug product is the same as for the drug substance:
The drug product solution composition in a 10 mL vial is summarized in Table 4.

2. Relationship between the hydrochloric acid content and citrate content in the finished product, the storage time and pH change
Hydrochloric acid is a small ingredient of sodium citrate solution 28 mmol/L in sodium chloride 0.11 M and its content is not monitored as a process parameter. Therefore, no monitoring data for hydrochloric acid content is available. The amount of hydrochloric acid in the drug product is very low and varies based on the drug product dilution to target radioactive concentration (please refer to Table 4 above). pH is a stability indicating parameter. For individual drug product data regarding the parameters citrate content and pH over storage time please refer to P.8.3-Stability Data.
Within the context of the variation submitted for the deletion of obsolete testing parameters (e.g. citrate) from the drug substance specification a more detailed analyses on citrate content vs. pH and other interdependencies has been conducted as presented in the following:

3. Suitability of the linear relationship between citrate content and pH change based on research data such as process control data, quality data and stability data.
The two current drug substance specification parameters citrate and pH have been found to change as a function of storage time and increased radioactivity. To investigate the correlation between pH and citrate during drug substance storage, stability data were investigated by statistical analysis. The two responses, citrate and pH, were correlated to three independent variables by multiple regression analysis. The variables were site of manufacture (Agilera and Cardinal Health (CAH) in US), radioactive concentration at day 0 (5.9 – 12.2 MBq/mL) and storage time (0-7 days).
Release and stability data from 12 drug substance batches presented in Table 5 were used to investigate the correlation between pH and citrate.

Analysis of variance provides information about the significance of tested variables that are correlated to a response. The effects of the independent variables were quite similar for pH and for citrate. The storage time (0-7 days) was found to have a clear significant effect while the assay radium-223 at day 0 was found to have borderline significant. The similarity between effects on citrate and pH (inversed effect due to citrate decrease and pH increase during storage) suggests that the change in these two parameters may originate from the same underlying mechanism, i.e. radiolysis. The site of manufacturing was not found to have a significant effect on any of the two responses. A linear regression of citrate on pH showed highly significant correlation between the two parameters (p = 7.9 x 10-7).
The linear correlation between pH and citrate is presented in Figure 1. The variation observed around the regression line is influenced by the citrate measurements given as integer values.

In conclusion, the citrate concentration in drug substance, premixed buffer solution (28 mmol/L sodium citrate/0.11 M NaCl solution) and drug product was always consistent at 28 mmol/L (or 7.2 mg/ml). The citrate content has a significant correlation with pH, and the citrate content in drug substance can be indirectly reflected by the monitoring results of pH in drug substance, pH and citrate in premixed buffer and drug product. Deletion of citrate from drug substance specification will not increase the quality risk of the drug product.

Question/Consideration:
Question 4
Nitrate is introduced by the process, and this test is deleted in this application; it is stated that it can be controlled by the DS process. Please clearly state the specific control measures for subsequent commercial production.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4 (S.2, S.4):
At the time of international initial product registration, nitrate was included as a retrospective monitoring test in the drug substance release specification. Since then, data from the commercial scale was collected over more than 12 years. In addition to historical retrospective data collection for Xofigo and the thorough process knowledge gained, a statistical evaluation was performed as detailed in document S.4.5.01-04. The evident result from this evaluation proves a well-controlled manufacturing process indicated by steady and very low nitrate levels within the range of physiological variation (please refer to chapter 2.1 in S.4.5.01-04).
The only two potential sources for nitrate are: a) The first manufacturing step where methanol solution 82% in nitric acid 1.3 M is used to dissolve the dried A-generator and the subsequent application of actinium-227 and daughters onto an anion exchange cartridge for separation of radium-223,and subsequent onto the first cation exchange cartridge. The resulting nitrate containing solution is going into waste. b) With the subsequent elution of radium-223 from this first cation exchange cartridge with nitric acid 1.3 M solution, radium-223 is passed via an actinide column onto a second cation exchange cartridge. Also, here the flowing-through nitrate containing solution goes to waste. The manufacturing process is robust and both, risk control and in-process monitoring, are in place. For in-process monitoring a semi-quantitative strip test for nitrate is applied during manufacturing to ensure consistently very low and stable results.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
The applicant proposes changes to the specifications of the raw material drinking water, 
resulting in different specifications for the same starting material (i.e., drinking water) across 
the three different manufacturers. It is requested that 3.2.S.2.3 for drinking water be updated 
to make it clear that the quality of drinking water at each site complies with EU requirements 
(reference is made to the Guideline on the quality of water for pharmaceutical use 
EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/496873/2018, which states: “ […] Potable Water is not covered 
by a pharmacopoeial monograph but must comply with the regulations on water intended for 
human consumption of a quality equivalent to that defined in Directive 98/83/EC or laid down 
by the competent authority”) or with the WHO requirements (reference is made to EudraLex 
The Rules Governing Medicinal Products in the European Union Volume 4 Good 
Manufacturing Practice Medicinal Products for Human and Veterinary Use Part II: Basic 
Requirements for Active Substances used as Starting Materials, which states “[…] 4.31 
Unless otherwise justified, process water should, at a minimum, meet World Health 
Organization (WHO) guidelines for drinking (potable) water quality”).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( CTD section):
In accordance with the EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/496873/2018 “Guideline on the quality of 
water for pharmaceutical use”, the grade of water used should take account of the nature and
intended use of the finished product and the stage at which the water is used. Neither for 
darolutamide drug substance nor the drug product (Nubeqa) there is a requirement for sterility 
or apyrogenicity. In the guideline it has been instructed that at least potable water must be used 
in the manufacture of the drug substance. Purified water is used in the final step 5.

Potable water used by Fermion Oy, Hanko Plant:
All process steps can be manufactured at Hanko Plant and the last three steps (step 3, step 4 and 
step 5) are solely manufactured by Fermion Oy, Hanko Plant. The quality of potable water in 
Finland must fulfil the decree of the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health of Finland relating 
to the quality and monitoring of water intended for human consumption (461/2000), and WHO 
Guideline for drinking water quality.

Potable water used by AMI Organics Limited:
The water used at Sachin and Ankleshwar plants is supplied by GIDC (Gujarat Industrial 
Development Corporation). The water conforms to the IS 10500:2012 Indian standards for 
potable water. The standard has been laid down by the competent authority. In addition the 
potable water is tested routinely by AMI according to the specification laid out in section 
3.2.S.2.3.

Ami Organics is not claiming WHO standard, but the applicant considers the potable water 
acceptable for its purpose based on EudraLex Volume 4 Good Manufacturing Practice 
Medicinal Products for Human and Veterinary Use, Part II: Basic Requirements for Active 
Substances used as Starting Materials, which states “[…] 4.31. Unless otherwise justified, 
process water should, at a minimum, meet World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for 
drinking (potable) water quality.”

The applicant considers the water quality used at Ami Organics limited as acceptable for the 
following reasons:
Potable water by Ami Organics Limited is only used in the first process steps 1 and 2. There 
are four isolations and three drying steps after the use of their potable water. It is not expected 
that any residues of water, used in steps 1 or 2, are carried over to the drug substance. A risk 
assessment has been carried out considering the stage the potable water is used in.
In the risk assessment it was acknowledged that potable water is a potential source for nitrites. 
The acceptance criteria for nitrites in the potable water has therefore been set to be NMT 0.007 
ppm and is routinely analyzed. Based on process knowledge, and with the specification for 
routine analysis of the potable water, the applicant is confident that the quality of water has no 
influence on the drug substance. Based on the test results, routine testing for specific parameters 
as well as the risk assessment the applicant considers an exemption from full testing of the 
water in accordance with WHO or Indian standards to be justified.

The potable water is tested routinely by AMI according to the specification laid out in section 
3.2.S.2.3.

Navin Fluorine International Limited:
Potable water by Navin Fluorine International Limited is used in the first process steps 1 and 2.
The water used at Navin Fluorine International Limited is municipal water (conforming to 
Indian standard IS 10500:2012) which has additionally been treated with chlorine followed by 
multi-grade filtration, activated carbon filtration, softener, ultra-filtration, RO and UV. After 
purification the water easily fulfills the requirement of at “least potable water”. The purification 
process has been validated and is monitored in line with general requirements for purified water, 
which are stricter than the requirements for potable water.
The specification set for routine testing of the potable (purified) water by Navine Fluroine 
International Limited has been included in the 3.2.S.2.3 section.

Conclusion:
The potable water quality, used by all manufacturers is considered acceptable for its purpose.

In line with EDQM rounding rules (https://faq.edqm.eu/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=1376855), 
the result is first rounded to the required number of decimal places before comparing to the 
specification. A result from 96.50% to 97.49% would be rounded to 97%. Therefore the lowest 
unrounded result to comply with the present end of shelf life specification of ≥ 97% would be 
96.50%, the lowest unrounded result to comply with the proposed new limit of ≥ 96.2% would be 
96.150%. 
Because of the previous rounding of the limit to  ≥ 97%, but the new proposed limit of ≥ 96.2% is 
stated to one decimal point, the largest possible difference between the old and the new limit would 
be rather 0.35%. But the shift would still be within the difference measured for the reference 
standard (see P.5.6.01, section 3.1). The same previous rounding of the limit to ≥ 97% also previously 
applied in the European Union and ≥ 96.2% is the currently approved limit (specification document 
P.5.1.02#022974830_01, which is the same as included in this application for Korea). 
(For other countries (for example Australia), which had previously required that the specification is 
stated with a decimal point (≥ 96.5%), the lowest compliant unrounded result was 96.450 and

In the pivotal VIEW 1 and VIEW 2 studies, no patients were administered with a higher dose

Therefore the only evidence contributed by these studies is that they showed no evidence of a 
dose response in safety outcomes.

method introduced in 2019 is 0.3% more sensitive to the high molecular weight (HMW) / aggregate 
species. Therefore, the corresponding shift of 0.3% is due to the analytical method only and the 
actual amount of HMW in Eylea 2mg is unchanged.  
 
Supporting data: 
 
For Eylea 2mg, the HMW specification limit continues to be supported by toxicology data and clinical 
data from the initial registration of Eylea 2 mg (as explained above).
Supporting toxicological data:

The limit (%aggregate) for the HMW species (≤ 3.8% as amended for SE-UPLC) continues to be 
supported by toxicology studies with higher doses and higher exposure to HMW species than in 
human patients. To support the initial registration of Eylea 2 mg, reference was made in P.5.6.01 
to the relevant toxicology study VGFT-TX-05011. With this response, this section in P.5.6.01 is 
further clarified.

In a 8-month pivotal IVT study in monkeys (Module 4.2.3.2, VGFT-TX-05011) conducted to support 
the marketing authorization of aflibercept 2 mg, aflibercept doses ranging from 0.5 to 4 mg/eye (in 
50 µL/eye) were administered bilaterally every 4 weeks for 9 doses in total, followed by a 5-month 
treatment free recovery period. Ocular findings were limited to non-adverse mild and transient 
ocular inflammation up to and including the high dose of 4 mg/eye. When normalized for the 
smaller vitreal volume in monkeys compared to humans (approximately 2 vs. 4 mL), the 4 mg/eye 
are expected to produce an initial vitreal concentration which is equivalent to that expected 
following an approximate 8 mg dose administered to a human eye. With an approximate high 
molecular weight species (HMWs) concentration of 1-1.5% the 8 mg dose corresponds to an initial 
HMWs dose of 0.08-0.12 mg/human eye, and further, to a HMWs concentration in aflibercept 2 mg 
(40 mg/mL) of 1.6-2.4 mg/mL (for 1% HMWs: 0.08 mg HMWs/50 µL injection volume =x/1000 µL; x 
= 1.6 mg HMWs/mL, for 1.5% HMWs: 2.4 mg HMWs/mL). This concentration is equivalent to a 
content of 4-6% HMWs (for 1% HMWs: 100%/40 mg/mL = x/1.6 mg/mL; x = 4%; for 1.4% HMWs: 
6%), which is covered by this 8-month pivotal IVT study in monkeys on aflibercept 2 mg.
Eylea 2 mg ongoing post-marketing pharmacovigilance surveillance data and analytical stability data 
continue to support the specification limits.
Supporting post-marketing pharmacovigilance surveillance data:
In addition, post-marketing pharmacovigilance data was evaluated from the time of initial 
submission until the end of 2024.
The safety profile for IOIs with Eylea 2 mg is continuously monitored. No significant change was 
seen in the rate of IOI in the period before and after the introduction of the SE-UPLC method (1.2 
cases per 10 000 injections and 1.0 case per 10 000 injections respectively).
Overall, no new safety concern potentially related to protein aggregate formation in terms of IOIs 
was observed from 2020 and onwards for Eylea 2 mg.
Supplemental toxicology data at a higher dose is now also available from study VGFT-TX-20170 made 
to support the registration of Eylea 8 mg. These toxicology data were generated specifically on 
aflibercept with a higher content of HMW species (6 and 10% HMW).


Supporting toxicological data (Eylea 8mg):
Supplemental toxicology data at a higher dose is now also available from study VGFT-TX-20170. 
While the study was performed to support the registration of Eylea 8 mg, reference is now also 
made in P.5.6.01 for Eylea 2 mg as explained below:
An additional study, intended to investigate the tolerability of high concentrations of HMWs to 
support the specification of aflibercept 8 mg, covers even higher HMWs – equivalent 
concentrations in humans. In this 3-month IVT toxicology study in monkeys utilizing the high 
concentration aflibercept formulation enriched with approximately 6% and 10% HMWs (Module 
4.2.3.2, VGFT-TX-20170), doses of 5.6 mg/eye (in 40 µL/eye) were administered bilaterally every 4 
weeks for a total of 4 doses. Consistent with findings noted in the study mentioned above, repeated 
IVT administration of 5.6 mg aflibercept per eye containing approximately 6 or 10% HMWs was 
well tolerated, with no adverse ocular inflammation evident. When normalized for the smaller 
vitreal volume in monkeys compared to humans (approximately half), the 5.6 mg/eye are expected 
to produce an initial vitreal concentration which is equivalent to that expected following an 
approximate 11.2 mg dose administered to a human eye. With a maximal HMWs content of 10% 
the 11.2 mg dose corresponds to an initial HMWs dose of 1.12 mg/human eye, and further, to a 
HMWs concentration in aflibercept 8 mg (114.3 mg/mL) of 16 mg/mL (1.12 mg HMWs/70 µL 
injection volume =x/1000 µL; x = 16 mg HMWs/mL). This concentration is equivalent to a content of 
14% HMWs (100%/114.3 mg/mL = x/16 mg/mL; x = 14%), which is covered by this 3-month IVT 
study in monkeys.
In conclusion, HMWs contents of up to 14% are covered by toxicological data and were well 
tolerated.
The positive clinical data from Eylea 8mg could also be considered to support the HMW limit for 
Eylea 2mg: 
While no material of with higher HMW was used during the 8mg clinical trials, the absolute amount 
of aggregate per 8mg injection, even considering only the 1.4-1.7% aggregate at release (equivalent 
112-136 µg HMW per 8mg injection) is already higher than the absolute amount of aggregate in the 
2mg injection when the specification limit of 3.8% (equivalent 76 µg HMW per 2mg injection) at the 
end of shelf life is considered.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Potency Testing Method for APIs and Formulations:
Regarding the shift from the current method to the gradient ratio method, please include 
explanations addressing the following points:
• 
Provide explanations from both perspectives: "Are there any technical reasons for 
adopting this method?" and "Have there been any regulatory changes?" Additionally, explain 
the background of adopting the current potency calculation method at that time (whether the 
gradient ratio method existed back then; if it did exist but was not adopted, include reasons for 
that decision). Explain comprehensively why this change is being made now, including both 
technical reasons for adoption and regulatory changes.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (CTD section):
The current assay was leveraged and developed from the Chromogenic assay used for 
Antihemophilic-FVIII on the then available Tecan automated assay system. It was established 
per the guidelines set forth by the 2002 European Pharmacopoeia.
Development of a slope ratio method was attempted at the time, however due to limitations in 
the equipment it was found to be not adequately reliable for samples for which the diluted 
analyte concentration differed from that of the diluted standard. For this reason, the linear 
regression method was chosen.
The technical reason for adopting the new gradient slope ratio method was to improve the 
precision and accuracy. In addition, both marketed products can be tested using a single script 
and a single validated spreadsheet. Additionally, the use of the Hamilton Heater Shaker allows 
critical reagents (CaCl2 and Substrate) and the reaction test plate to be maintained at 37°C ± 
2°C during the assay duration that in turn provides uniform measurements across the plate.
There have no regulatory changes to the Ph. Eur. potency method since the initial development 
of the potency method for Kovaltry in 2002., however, the optimized gradient slope ratio 
method aligns more closely with the compendial guidance.
Source:  Declaration-Justification of Specification Specific Activity
keywords: assay; analytical procedures; analytical method validation; pharmacopeia; justification of specification

Question/Consideration:
Question 4
Potency Testing Method for APIs and Formulations:
Regarding the shift from the current method to the gradient ratio method, please include 
explanations addressing the following points:
• 
Regarding technical reasons for adopting the gradient ratio method, while it has been 
mentioned that sample numbers can be reduced, include explanations if there are other 
advantages such as superiority in calculation methods themselves.
Furthermore, PMDA could not discern from the documents whether reducing sample numbers 
is due to differences in calculation methods or simply due to changes in equipment or 
procedures that allow avoiding unnecessary sampling. While reducing sample numbers is cited 
as an advantage, it could result in trade-offs such as decreased accuracy and precision; include 
a comprehensive explanation addressing this point.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4 (CTD section):
There is an advantage in the calculation for the potency. With the current method, 3 intermediate 
potency values are generated from the linear regression at each level of the tested concentration 
from which a mean value is reported. Any of the intermediate potency value in the current assay 
can generate an invalid reported result. With the gradient slope ratio method, as only one 
potency value is generated by comparing the slopes of the samples with that of the standard 
potential for an invalid reported result is minimized.
It is recognized that the number of samples averaged to create a batch potency value has the 
potential to affect the accuracy of the final reported result and this was evaluated in the method 
development. In the case of this assay replacement, with the increased precision of the 
optimized slope ratio assay, fewer test samples produce a result as accurate as the previous 
methods with more test samples. Intra and inter assay precision values were calculated from the 
comparability studies between the two methods. Using these precision values various testing 
scenarios (e.g. two samples on one test run, one sample for each of two test runs, two samples 
for each of three test runs, etc.) were evaluated to compare the accuracy of the final result to 
that of the existing methods. From this analysis it was determined that one sample, tested on 
each of two test runs provides comparable accuracy to that of the current testing (14 total 
samples for Kovaltry, tested in three test runs for each). The estimated variability of the mean 
(n=2) is lower than that of the current testing scheme for drug product with a comparable upper 
95% confidence interval on that variability.
Source:  Declaration-Justification of Specification Specific Activity

The samples and control are acceptable when the following criteria are met:
• Probability (p-value) Regression < 0.05
• Probability (p-value) Intersection ≥ 0.05
• Probability (p-value) Non-linearity ≥0.05
Probability non-linearity and probability intersection failure can be reassessed using the predetermined control residual error.
Ph. Eur 11.3 Chapter 5.3 Section 3.3.4 (Test of Validity) and Section 3.1.2 (slope Ratio) states that the assay results are said to be “statistically valid” if the outcome of the analysis of variance is as follows.
(i) The variation due to blanks in (hd + 1)-designs is not significant, i.e. the calculated probability is not smaller than 0.05. This indicates that the responses of the blanks do not significantly differ from the common intercept and the linear relationship is valid down to zero dose; A significant variation due to blanks indicates that the hypothesis of linearity is not valid near zero dose. If this is likely to be systematic rather than incidental for the type of assay, the (hd-design) is more appropriate. Any response to blanks should then be disregarded. In our slope ratio method, the hd design is used and zero dose is not used.
(ii) The variation due to intersection is not significant, i.e. the calculated probability is not less than 0.05. This indicates that condition 5B, Section 3.1 is satisfied.
“Condition 5B states that for any unknown preparation in the assay the straight line intersects the y-axis (at zero dose) at the same point as the straight line of the standard preparation (i.e. the response functions of all preparations in the assay must have the same intercept as the response function of the standard).”
(iii) In assays including at least 3 doses per preparation, the variation due to non-linearity is not significant, i.e. the calculated probability is not less than 0.05. This indicates that condition 4B, Section 3.1 is satisfied.
“Condition 4B states that the relationship between the dose and the response can be represented by a straight line for each preparation in the assay over the range of doses used.”
Acceptance criteria as indicated in the Table 4 above is also used in addition to the p-value validity testing.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1:
If it is an official method, there is an inconsistency with respect to the specifications 
T.02.28_01 Release Specification (page 14) to clarify the value of Q.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
The test “dissolution” is performed according to the harmonized method of USP 711 and 
Ph.Eur. 2.9.3 for immediate-release dosage forms. The dissolution is specified according to 
USP and Ph. Eur. acceptance criteria with Q=80 % of labeled claim of active substance after 
30 minutes.
The USP (United States Pharmacopeia) dissolution acceptance criteria are based on the 
amount of drug substance dissolved from a dosage form within a specific time frame. These 
criteria typically involve three stages (S1, S2, S3) with increasing numbers of units 
tested. The acceptance criteria are expressed as a percentage of the labeled amount of drug 
substance, denoted as "Q".
Three Stages:
The USP dissolution test proceeds through three stages:
S1: 6 units are tested. Acceptance criteria are usually Q+5% or greater.
S2: If S1 is not met, 6 more units are tested. The average of the combined S1 and S2 results 
must meet Q or greater.
S3: If S1 and S2 are not met, 6 more units are tested (total of 12). The average of the 
combined S1, S2, and S3 results must be Q or greater.

Consequently Q=80% resolves in (S1) as 6 single units with a min. average of 85%
For more information, please refer to USP 711

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Environmental risk assessment
Answer/Response:
Procedural, physical, and environmental practices are designed to prevent contamination.
Contamination control is achieved by: Area Environment, Heating, Ventilation and Air
Conditioning (HVAC) Design, Personnel, Workflow and Access Control, Gowning, Cleaning
and Sanitization, and Preventive Maintenance, Routine Environmental Monitoring, Inventory
Control, Product Change-Over, Product Labeling, Storage, and Identity Confirmation.

The raw materials used for manufacturing Damoctocog Alfa Pegol Drug Substance are not of
animal or human origin. Some animal or human origin materials were used in the early stage
of cell line development prior to accession cell banking (Table 2–1). However, these raw
materials were manufactured by processes that included treatment minimizing potential risk
of TSE transmission.

During early cell line development, the host cell passaging, transfection, and clone selection
were performed with culture media containing fetal bovine serum (FBS), human plasma
protein solution (HPPS), cholesterol and recombinant human insulin. These raw materials
were assessed for TSE risk and deemed to have minimal TSE risk according to the Note for
Guidance referenced above. In addition, FBS and cholesterol were certified to be free of TSE
transmitting agents via certification standards by the European Directorate for the Quality of
Medicines (EDQM). Prior to establishing the Accession Cell Bank, the cell line was adapted
to protein free media that did not contain animal derived components. No animal or human
derived materials were used in subsequent preparation of the Master Cell Bank and Working
Cell Bank.

Source:
