Bayer Response to Question 4 (CTD section P.5.1):
In April 2021 a new monograph 3021 for <Rivaroxaban tablets> became valid in the 
supplement 10.4 of the 10th edition of the European Pharmacopoeia.
Bayer AG is the originator of Rivaroxaban tablets; therefore, our former in-house test 
procedures and specification are also the origin of the Ph. Eur. Monograph 3021 
<Rivaroxaban tablets>. However, the specification and test procedure have been adapted to 
Ph. Eur. and are aligned now.
The identification tests “Identity A (Ph. Eur.) and Identity B (Ph. Eur.) are introduced as 
additional parameter to specification for Rivaroxaban tablets as required by the Ph. Eur. 
Monograph. These test parameters are already met with the former test “Identity (HPLC)” of 
current applied Bayer specification and test procedure for Rivaroxaban coated tablets. Test 
“Identity A (Ph. Eur)” is confirmed by the UV spectrum of the main peak in the HPLC 
chromatograms of the reference standard and the test item. The test “Identity B (Ph. Eur.)”is 
met by defining both main peak retention time and size in the HPLC chromatograms of the 
reference standard and the test item. If both results are met, the acceptance criteria are 
documented as “complies” in the certificate of analysis. By referencing in the technical
registration document T.02.02 (Test procedure) to Ph. Eur., an additional description of the 
acceptance criteria is not necessary from our perspective.

Question/Consideration:
Question 17
The results for water content, disintegration and hardness tests are reported, but the 
acceptance criterion is not stated. You are requested to include within the document 
specifications indicating that they correspond to a stability test and attach the respective 
analytical methodology. In addition, you must note the acceptance criterion for each test in 
the table presented in the stability study (evaluated parameters) and in the results tables, as a 
compliance with what is set out in the current RTCA Stability Studies.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 17 (CTD section P.3.3, P.5.6):
Average weight, friability, resistance to crushing and disintegration time is tested from the 
tablet cores during manufacturing as an in-process control in the tablet compression step. 
Loss on drying is tested from granules as in-process control (please refer to document T.08.04). 
None of these in-process quality attributes are critical quality attributes for the final drug 
product. It has been demonstrated that within the proposed in-process control range tablets 
meeting the quality criteria can be manufactured, thus the absence of these tests in release 
specification is considered justified.
The test parameters resistance to crushing and water content were investigated during 
pharmaceutical development. Water content was found to increase when tablets are stored 
without humidity control (25 °C/80 % RH in open containers). The increase in water content 
was accompanied by a decrease in tablets hardness. High temperatures (60 °C and 80 °C) 
decreased the water content which was also accompanied by a reduction in tablet hardness. 
However, the values observed for hardness during long-term stability testing remain 
sufficiently high to allow for tablet handling and shipping. The increased water content of the 
tablets did not affect the formation of degradation products or the dissolution behavior of the 
tablets as demonstrated in stress tests and long term stability studies.
It is concluded that the test parameters are not indicative of product quality. They are therefore 
not included in the specification or stability studies.  
Please also find the additionally the justification for not specified tests, such as water content, 
resistance to crushing and disintegration in the enclosed document T.02.18.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
In the cover letter, it is necessary to describe the method used for the “Sterility” test and provide data confirming the suitability of the method.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
We acknowledge the comments from the authority and providing below the test procedure for Sterility test and TRD for suitability of the method.
Source: P.5.3.922-01 Validation - Other Methods/ Iopromide solution for parenteral use (SH L00414A SH L00414B SH L00414C SH L00414G) (ULTRAVIST) (DocID#004448239/new)
We acknowledge the comments from the authority and providing below the test procedure for Sterility test:
Sterility test is performed according to harmonized pharmacopeial method (USP < 71>, PharmEur 2.6.1, JP 4.06)

Sterility Test Procedure for Ultravist 300:
Sterility (membrane filtration)
Principle of the method:
Membrane filtration using disposable elements (MILLIPORE Steritest system for two culture media). The sample solutions are filtered using the Steritest system. The membrane filter (mean pore size ≤ 0.45 μm) retains any microorganisms present. The membrane filter is covered with culture medium and the entire assembly is incubated. Turbidity is evidence of microbial growth and possibly of contamination of the sample solution.

Reagents:
- casein peptone + soybean peptone digest medium (CSB)
- thioglycolate medium
Consumables:
Merck (Millipore): Steritest™ Container Type TZHA

Test procedure:
Note:
Samples can be used directly for sterility test. No preparation necessary.
Conduct the test under aseptic conditions (laminar-flow bench). The composition of the culture media and buffer solutions meet the requirements of Ph.Eur. and USP. Likewise follow the USP and Ph.Eur. stipulations on preparatory tests to establish:
- the sterility of the culture media, solutions and apparatus employed
- the growth-promoting qualities of the culture media employed
- any antimicrobial activity of the test substance in the culture media

Conduct of the test:
The determination is conducted depending on the filling volume of the vessels.

Number of product samples for for testing for
5 ml solution for injection, ampoule 20 containers
10 ml solution for injection, vial 20 containers
20 ml solution for infusion, vial 20 containers
30 ml solution for infusion, vial 20 containers
50 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers
75 ml solution for infusion, 100 ml bottle 20 containers
100 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers
125 ml solution for infusion, 150-ml bottle 20 containers
150 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers
200 ml solution for infusion, 250-ml bottle 20 containers
500 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers
1000 ml solution for infusion, bottle 20 containers

For the extractable volumes of 125, 150 and 200 ml conduct the test in two runs with 10 containers each.
For the extractable volumes of 500 ml conduct the test in five runs with 4 containers each.
For the extractable volumes of 1000 ml conduct the test in ten runs with 2 containers each.

Distribute the contents of the relevant containers evenly between the two filter assemblies of the Steritest system, then filter (sample pool). The samples are transferred directly into the sterility test containers via injection needle. The maximum volume permitted through one membrane is 1000 ml. No rinsing fluid is used, since no antimicrobial properties of the product could be detected which would require rinsing of the membrane (see P.5.3.922#004448239.
Cover one membrane filter with 100 ml CSB and the other with 100 ml thioglycolate medium.
Incubation:
14 days at 20°C to 25°C (CSB)
14 days at 30°C to 35°C (thioglycolate medium)

Evaluation of initial test:
On every work day after incubation, examine the filter units for growth visible to the naked eye (turbidity).
The sterility requirement is met, if the culture media remain clear after being shaken for a moment.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Section 1.0.4 - Long term stability Report
For stability tests at accelerated storage condition for sterilized PFS (Tables 4-12 to 4-15 of 
“P.8.3.01_022980339_05 Stability Data.pdf”), please justify the out-of-specification result for 
the purity tests and test on isoaspartate content toward the end of the test (month 6 and/or 3). 
Please justify why 24 months of shelf life can be claimed.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.8.3):
Out-of-specification (OOS) results observed in the course of accelerated stability studies 
(25 ± 2 °C, 60 ± 5% relative humidity) performed for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/ml in 
prefilled syringe (PFS) are within expectation and in-line with the known degradation profile 
of Aflibercept drug product.
OOS results are known to occur after 3 and/or 6 months of storage for the tests “Purity by SE-
UPLC”, “Isoaspartate Content” and “Purity by reduced CE-SDS”. OOS results at the 
accelerated stability condition therefore do not reflect any adverse impact on the product 
quality. Instead, the purpose of those studies is to confirm that the degradation profile of 
Aflibercept at this storage condition is within expectation after changes in manufacturing, like 
e.g. the comparison between the drug product in vial and the drug product in PFS.
The available data confirms that the degradation profile is comparable for vial and PFS under 
accelerated condition. The OOS results at the accelerated stability condition do not correlate 
with a risk of not meeting the shelf-life specification acceptance criteria after 24 months at the 
recommended storage condition of 2-8 °C and it is not utilized to extrapolate the shelf life. 
Analytical comparability data demonstrates that the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/ml in vial 
and PFS are highly similar also in term of behavior during long term storage at 2-8 °C. 
Therefore, based on the 24 months stability data available for the vial, the same shelf life is 
justified for the PFS.
Note that the sterilized PFS batches in P.8.3.01-05 are currently under testing after 24 months 
and there is no indication that any batch will not meet the shelf-life specification acceptance 
criteria. We will provide the 24 months data once available.

syringe for intravitreous injection (#022980339; unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Section 1.1.0-P3 & 1.1.1 – item 40 - Elemental impurities
(i). Please clarify how the AET and concentration of elemental impurities in the migration and 
extraction studies are related to the “Threshold for Additional Controls” and “PDE” in 
3.2.P.5.5.01-01 and ICH Q3D.
(ii). In page 6 of 3.2.P.5.5.01-01, section 2.1 mentioned that “based on ICH Q3D a risk 
scoring describing the likelihood and amount of elemental impurities in the DP (with respect 
to permitted daily exposure (PDE) was established.”. Please clarify if the scoring is available 
for assessment. The purpose if for us to assess if the classes of elemental impurities, testing 
methods/studies and control are appropriate.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.P.5.5):
(i) The analytical evaluation threshold (AET) is always defined by using a safety threshold, 
and in these studies the safety concern threshold (SCT)/threshold of toxicological concern 
(TTC) of 1.5 µg/d for potentially genotoxic and mutagenic compounds has been applied. 
From that daily safety limit, study specific AET values have been derived as presented in 
P.2.4.06-01 and P.2.4.07-01.
SCT of 1.5 µg/d is lower than any of the element specific permitted daily exposure (PDE) 
values for parenteral route, the lowest PDE being 2 µg/d for Cd. Therefore, elemental 
impurities, as a part of all studied substances, are reported in extractable and leachable studies 
by using safety based AET , which is sufficiently low for all elemental impurities in relation 
to safety.
When extractable and leachable study results are evaluated in regard of toxicological safety, 
safety of potentially detected elemental impurities is assessed by using administration route 
related PDE limits for defining whether reported element may require some additional 
control.
Thresholds for additional controls (P.5.5.01-01) are theoretical limits related to the 
administration route specific PDE values and defining 30% of the respective PDE value as the 
limit for additional controls.
In summary, for reporting results from extractable and leachable studies the AET is used. 
Considering the toxicologic safety for elemental impurities, 30% of the respective PDE value 
is used as reference to determine whether additional analytical control is required. None of the 
elemental impurities requires additional analytical control for Aflibercept solution 
114.3 mg/ml in PFS.
(ii) Risk scoring mentioned in 3.2.P.5.5. in page 6 refers to ICH Q3D classification of 
elements to different risk classes 1, 2A, 2B, and 3, which then have different administration 
route dependent PDE values, please refer to Appendix 2 Established PDEs for Elemental 
Impurities - Table A.2.1: Permitted Daily Exposures for Elemental Impurities of the ICH
Q3D guideline (see attachment below). These ICH Q3D classes for elements are described in 
Table 2-2 in P.5.5.01-01.

Bayer confirms that the 40 mg finerenone formulation used in the bioequivalence study (Study No. 22292) is identical to the formulation used in the pivotal Phase 3 study (Study No. 20103) with only slight difference in the coating.

The qualitative and quantitative compositions of the tablet cores (uncoated tablets) are the same for the 40 mg finerenone film-coated tablets used in the pivotal Phase 3 study and the 40 mg finerenone film-coated tablets used in the bioequivalence study.

The film-coatings of the 40 mg finerenone formulation used in the pivotal Phase 3 study and the 40 mg finerenone formulation used in the bioequivalence study have the same qualitative composition but slight differences in the quantitative composition.

Question/Consideration:
Question 6
P2.2. Composition of the finished product: Please provide detailed information on the excipients and justify their selection.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 6 (P.2.2):
The applicant would like to inform that, generally, the matrix and coating chosen and established for Qlaira are also successfully used in other Bayer hormonal solid oral dosage forms. Qlaira has no sustained release properties, but is an instant release dosage form.
The functions of the excipients are generally overlapping while providing different focus properties.
Lactose monohydrate is a widely used filler in tablets with certain dry binding properties. These have to be supported by pregelatinized maize starch, which exhibits good dry binding properties (important for compression). Maize starch is utilized with similar intent, but brings along pronounced disintegrant properties.
Povidone 25 is used as binding agent in solution during fluid bed granulation. The readily produced granulate is mixed with magnesium stearate as a widely used lubricant supporting a good compression process of the final mixture.
Qlaira is coated with a Hypromellose coating that is interfused with Macrogol 6000 as a plasticizer increasing the coating’s strength. Titanium dioxide and yellow ferric oxide form the colouring system. Talc mainly served as a lubricant for the film tablets.
Please, refer to the table provided as Annex for further details.

Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section): 3.2.S.2.2 on materials on the manufacturing process

Regarding the replacement of -methyl pyrrolidone in step 3
The manufacturing description provided in S.2.2.02_022858359_04 describes the removal of NMP as following (underlined sentence): “Parts of N-methyl pyrrolidone are distilled off and replaced by fresh N-methyl pyrrolidone. 『602 kg』 triethyl orthoacetate and 『45.5 kg』 sulfuric acid 96% are added. The reaction mixture is stirred at 『100 °C』 for 『2 hours』 and afterwards cooled to 『52.5 °C』. After addition of water the suspension is cooled to 『20 °C』 and the suspension is filtered and washed with water.”
In the corresponding batch record in “EBR_Carboxy-TH-Naphthyridine Step 3&4 Batch size 2 packaging material page 46 of 468.pdf”, the addition of water is described on page 161.
The addition of N-methyl pyrrolidone is described on page 307. Please read the following terminology” Nach der ersten Destillation wird die abdestillierte NMP-Menge (ca. 600kg) im RA22RA001 aufgefüllt. Im Anchluß wird erneut eine Distillation durchgeführt.”
The filtering of the suspension is described on page 177 and 327. Please read the following terminology: “Druckfiltrieren MuLa nach BA26“ and “Die MuLa wird in den BA26 gedrückt”, respectively This terminology is quite technically and means that the supernatant of the liquid containing the solid Cyano-TH-naphthyridine crystals is removed. It should be noted that the supernatant is containing N-methyl pyrrolidone (beside other reaction components). Thus the description “Druckfiltrieren MuLa nach BA26“ inherently includes the information that this operation removes all reaction components from the crystallization process, including N-methyl pyrrolidone.

The addition of aqueous sodium acetate solution is described in pages 354 of GMP inspection document entiteled “EBR_Carboxy-TH-Naphthyridine Step 3&4 Batch size 2 packaging material page 46 of 468.pdf”

Question/Consideration: Please explain how the product accurately controls the injection volume of 0.07ml?
Answer/Response:
The Eylea 8mg PFS dosing system (finger flange and plunger rod) is designed to ensure accuracy for administration of an 8mg dose (equivalent to 70 µL) of Aflibercept,comprising a distance controlled priming and dose setting functionality to prevent under- and overdosing.
For a single dose of 0.07 mL, firstly, once the needle is affixed, the plunger rod is depressed to eliminate any surplus air and drug product. The enhanced finger flange design effectively restricts further movement of the plunger rod. Secondly, turn 90° rotation applied to the plunger rod, there is no predefined direction of the 90° rotation. Ready to dose when click occurs. The PFS is set ready for injection. Finally, after inserting the needle into the injection site, the dose is administered by pushing the plunger rod until it reaches a pre-defined hard stop, ensuring that this product accurately controls the injection volume of 0.07 mL.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Describe the rationale and justification for the change and explain it. When responding, also 
explain the justification of excluding fluoroethylcarbamate from the measurement target in the 
purity test of the drug product, even if the ethylchloroformate content in the raw material 
chloroformate is not controlled. Describe the rationale and justification for the change and 
explain it. When responding, also explain the justification of excluding fluoroethylcarbamate 
from the measurement target in the purity test of the drug product, even if the 
ethylchloroformate content in the raw material chloroformate is not controlled.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2
Fluoroethylcarbamate is not a new impurity and was initially covered under “any unspecified 
impurity” with an overall limit of 0.10% in the drug substance. After more batches have been 
produced and more experience has been gained, higher amounts or fluoroethylcarbamate have 
been observed not covered under the limit of “any unspecified impurities” in the drug 
substance anymore. A root cause analyses showed that the higher levels for the specification 
parameter “any unspecified impurity” are due to fluoroethylcarbamate that results from an 
impurity in the raw material methyl chloroformate, which cannot be tested before production 
at Bayer AG based on its extremely high toxicity. Therefore it cannot be excluded, that drug 
substance batches with higher fluoroethylcarbamate could be produced in future. As one
precautionary measure, in addition to future measures to detect enhanced Ethyl chloroformate 
content in the beginning of a campaign, the impurity Fluoroethylcarbamate, which shows no 
in silico alert, should be included in the API (micronized drug substance) specification in 
accordance with ICH Q3A as identified impurity with NMT 0.15%.

Regarding drug product, fluoroethylcarbamate is regarded as a by-product from drug 
substance but is no degradation product and does not result in any degradation products not 
specified already. As explained above, fluoroethylcarbamate is controlled at the drug 
substance level. Therefore, fluoroethylcarbamate needs to be listed as a by-product (impurity) 
in the Vericiguat DP (all dose strengths) test procedure (P.5.2.01) to avoid its quantification 
as an unspecified degradation product (max 0.2%). If not, DP batches may be reported as 
OOS (>0.2%), even though the API batch used for formulation met the approved 
specification.  In conclusion, since fluoroethylcarbamate is an unequivocal by-product of the 
synthesis instead of a degradant, the relevant test procedures are adapted accordingly.
keywords: any individual unspecified impurity; impurities DS; impurity limit for iso-B; DP specification; test procedure DP

the active ingredient declared photolabile.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 14 ( CTD section):
We acknowledge the agency’s comment and would like to clarify that a comprehensive stress 
testing study has been conducted on Testosterone enantate, covering all relevant stress 
conditions. The result clearly demonstrates that Testosterone enantate exhibits significant 
decomposition when exposed to light. Based on these findings, the drug substance is classified 
as photolabile and appropriate protective measures have been implemented. Specifically, the 
storage of the API is ensured in a hermetic container, protected from light and oxygen, under 
an inert gas atmosphere at 2-8°C, in line with the observed sensitivity. We have provided 
Stability data, including stress testing that includes Influence of light, which demonstrate the 
photolabile nature of the API. Therefore, we consider that the provided stress study fulfills the 
requirements for the photostability evaluation of the drug substance. It is already well 
established that the API is photolabile, which is also reported in the monograph, and for this 
reason the photostability studies have been performed for the API, as demonstrated in the 
provided TRD in Module 3, section 3.2.S.7.3.  It has been concluded that the API is light 
sensitive.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Module 3.2.2.3 applicant provided a report with results demonstrating that identification of RXM12 and RXM1J media feed by UPLC is specific, precise and robust but did not provide the results for RXM12 and RXM1J media feed identification by HPLC. Therefore, applicant is requested to comply with SAHPRA biological guideline (SAHPGL-PEM-BIO-05_v6) to provide comparative results demonstrating that the approved and proposed analytical procedures are equivalent.ext of Question in Bayer Body Text Full
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.2.3):
The Sponsor would like to clarify that both the HPLC and UPLC methods are used to confirm the identity of the feeds prior to inclusion in the aflibercept manufacturing process. These liquid chromatography methods were determined to be suitable for their intended use through method validation. Validation of the method ensures that the selected method can adequately identify the individual feeds. The proposed UPLC method was determined to be suitable for use through assay validation in accordance with ICH Q2 (results are summarized in S.2.3.12_022978999_01 (Regeneron validation report AV-SR-027120). While ICH only requires specificity for identification methods, further assessments were performed for the UPLC assay validation. The validation results demonstrate that the UPLC identity method is specific, precise, repeatable, and robust in the identification of RXM1J and RXM12 media feeds and suitable for use.
The current identification method uses HPLC parameters to reliably identify RXM12 or RXM1J media feed powder from other related amino acid media products. Because both RXM1J and RXM12 media feed contain similar amino acids, the specificity between the two media was assessed by comparing the peak area ratio of arginine/tyrosine (Arg/Tyr). To determine the method comparability between the HPLC and UPLC methods, the Arg/Tyr peak area ratio in RXM1J and RXM12 were compared between data generated using the UPLC method and the previously generated HPLC data. As part of the comparability study, 16 lots (eight lots of RXM1J and eight lots of RXM12) were tested using UPLC, and the peak area ratio of Arg/Tyr for both RXM1J and RXM12 was used to determine the method comparability between the HPLC and UPLC methods.
As shown in Table 1 the peak area ratio for Arg/Tyr for both RXM1J and RXM12 HPLC and UPLC are not comparable. This is because the current HPLC method uses a fluorescence (FLR) detector while the UPLC method uses a photodiode array (PDA) detector, as a result, the amino acid response between the two detectors is different. Therefore, the observed differences between the two methods can be attributed to the different principles of the two types of detection. FLR requires the excitation and emission from fluorescent molecules and PDA measures the absorption of ultraviolet light. When amino acids are analyzed using the FLR detectors they have different fluorescence yields when compared to the response from the PDA detector, therefore due to this difference, the ratio criteria set for the HPLC method cannot be translated to the UPLC method.
The results of the comparability study between HPLC and UPLC methods demonstrate that the Arg/Tyr peak area ratio for RXM1J and RXM12 media powder tested by UPLC is not comparable by absolute numbers to the results generated by HPLC. This is expected due to the different responses originating from the two different detector types. Additional evaluation was performed to determine the appropriate acceptance criteria to differentiate the two media using the UPLC method.
Assessment of the UPLC validation data, summarized in S.2.3.12_022978999_01 (Regeneron validation report AV-SR-027120, identified that the aspartic acid/glycine (Asp/Gly) peak area ratio can be used to differentiate between the two media. The Asp and Gly peaks were identified to be stable, well-resolved peaks and consistent in terms of peak height area and shape; therefore, the ratio between the two peaks was chosen to be used to differentiate between the two media feeds.
The assessment was performed using 169 runs of RXM1J and 179 runs of RXM12 media, the results are summarized in Figure 1 below. Based on this assessment the newly proposed criteria for the Asp/Gly peak area ratio for RXM12 is Asp/Gly: ≥ 3.0, and the peak area ratio for RXM1J is Asp/Gly:< 3.0. As shown in Figure 1, since the tolerance interval for RXM12 and RXM1J media do not overlap, the newly proposed criteria are suitable to distinguish between the two media feeds. Moreover, the difference between the upper tolerance intervals and lower tolerance intervals for the two media types and the two different amino acid ratios is larger for Asp/Gly (3.37 – 2.81 = 0.56) than for Arg/Tyr (2.43 – 2.06 = 0.37). This underscores the ability of the UPLC method to distinguish between the two media types, with the Asp/Gly ratio demonstrating a better ability to differentiate. This new criterion will replace the criteria listed in the current specification.
A summary of the identified acceptance criteria for the UPLC is presented in Table 2 on the next page.
Furthermore, testing using the UPLC instruments allows for increased speed, heightened resolution, and heightened sensitivity when compared to HPLC. These benefits aided in the selection of the UPLC method as a replacement for the HPLC method.
In conclusion, there is no impact to product quality with the introduction of the UPLC method proposed to replace the HPLC method for identification testing of RXM1J media feed. The UPLC method met all assay validation criteria for specificity, repeatability, precision, robustness and is therefore considered equivalent to the HPLC method for the identification of RXM1J. Consequently, the UPLC method is suitable for identity testing of the RXM1J media feed.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Recommended to provide:
- report on the revalidation of the manufacturing process of the finished product (data for 
2019 are presented). According to paragraph 146 of Appendix 3 of the Order of the Minister 
of Health of the Republic of Kazakhstan dated February 4, 2021 No. КР ДСМ-15 “On 
approval of good pharmaceutical practices”, processes and procedures are subject to periodic 
revalidation (repeated validation) to ensure that they remain suitable for achieving certain 
results;
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.3.5):
Bayer’s approach to validation and revalidation is in accordance with international guidelines 
e.g. EMA Guideline on Process Validation for Finished Products – Information and Data To 
Be Provided in Regulatory Submissions (November 2016) and the EU Annex 15: 
Qualification and Validation (October 2015) which outline the general principles and 
approaches for the appropriate elements of process validation for the manufacture of human 
drugs. These guidances align Process Validation activities with a product lifecycle concept as 
presented in the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) Guidance for Industry, Q8 
(R2) Pharmaceutical Development, Q9 Quality Risk Management, and Q10 Pharmaceutical 
Quality System. The lifecycle concept links product and process development, validation of 
the commercial manufacturing process, and maintenance of the process in a state of control 
during routine commercial production. Specifically, process validation confirms that the 
control strategy is adequate to the process design and the quality of the product. Subsequently, 
ongoing process verification confirms that the process remains in a state of control during 
commercial manufacture and supports the validated status of the product. Whereas only 
significant changes to the production process, including any changes to equipment or starting 
and packaging materials that may affect the quality of the product and (or) the consistency of 
the process, need to be re-validated.
The initial process validation and defined control strategy was completed in 2019. Since that 
time, no major changes have been implemented for the product as registered in Kazakhstan. 
The annual product review has confirmed periodically that the manufacturing process has 
reproducibly yielded finished product meeting the specified quality and in-process controls. 
Hence, the validated control strategy has continuously been verified to be adequate and still 
valid.
In summary, in line with the above Bayer would consider the requirements, as requested 
based “On approval of good pharmaceutical practices”, for processes and procedures to be 
subject to periodic revalidation (repeated validation) to ensure that they remain suitable for 
achieving certain results as fulfilled.

Please be informed that Microbial purity test is included in both Release Specifications and

and the method used. It is also included in the Test procedure section (P.5.2.01).
The medicinal product Angeliq does not demonstrate antimicrobial activity under the test

Please find the response below for Microbial Purity with the additional information which

Microbial purity:
The method for the microbiological purity is sufficiently described in the Ph. Eur. 2.6.12, 
USP <61> or JP 4.05 (harmonized method). The test for specified microorganisms are 
described in detail in Ph. Eur. 2.6.13, USP <62> or JP 4.05 (harmonized method) as well.
Procedure:
Weigh out not less than 10 g of the test product. Fill up with the appropriate amount of Casein 
soya bean digest broth (CSB) to obtain a 1:10 dilution (solution 1).
For TAMC prepare 2 petri dishes with each 1 mL of solution 1 and fill with 15-20 mL liquid 
Casein soya bean digest agar (CSA) (approx. 45°C). Incubate 3 – 5 days at 30 – 35°C. (Pour-
Plate Method of the Plate-Count method).
For TYMC prepare 2 petri dishes with each 1 mL of solution 1 and fill with 15-20 mL liquid 
Sabouraud-dextrose agar with chloramphenicol (approx. 45°C). Incubate 5 – 7 days at 20 – 
25°C. (Pour-Plate Method of the Plate-Count method).
For the test for absence of Escherichia coli, add 10 mL of solution 1 to 100 mL of Soya bean 
digest broth (CSB) to obtain solution 1.1. Incubate 18 – 24 h at 30 – 35°C. After incubation, 1 
mL of solution 1.1 is diluted in 100 mL MacConkey Broth and incubated 24 - 48 h at 42 -
44°C. After this incubation step, plate an aliquot on MacConkey agar and incubate 18 - 72 h 
at 30 – 35°C.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
The Justification of Specification for Identity Test  (HPLC)
Please provide the justification for the Specification for Identity Test  (HPLC-Amidotrizoic 
Acid) set within the defined scope (below bold line). 
“ The retention times of the amidotrizoic acid peak in the chromatograms of sample solution 
S and R2 must not differ from each other by more than ± 3%.”
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( CTD section):
The value of ±3% can be considered a general suitability criterion to ensure that the API 
Amidotrizoic acid retention times in the standard and sample are the same. This criterion is 
not specified in the validation, nor is it indicated in the analysis standard. It is an informative 
parameter and the limit is aligned with the acceptance criterion for intermediate precision, 
which is a CV of 3.0%, and is considered a best-case scenario.
Since for the proposed retention time of 2.5 min, the calculated CV% would be as follows:
• +3%: 2.58 min vs. 2.5 min à CV% = Dev Std / Average x 100 = 0.0566 / 2.54 x 100 = 
2.23 %  (< 3.0%)
• -3%: 2.43 min vs. 2.5 min à CV% = Dev Std / Average x 100 = 0.0495 / 2.465 x 100 = 
2.01 %  (< 3.0%)
*CV-Coefficient of variation
In summary, the justification would be that it is an internal criterion that is in accordance with 
the usual injection reproducibility in HPLC equipment.
Moreover according to USP general chapter <621> the deviations of relative retention time 
values measured for the test substance from the values obtained for the reference compound 
and mixture should not exceed the reliability estimates determined statistically from replicate 
assays of the reference compound. Also, relative retention times may be provided in 
monographs for informational purposes only, to aid in peak identification. There are no 
acceptance criteria applied to relative retention times.
Also, as per ICH Q2R1 Validation of Analytical Procedures guideline; for identification tests 
specificity parameter to be performed and it is covered in validation study of Assay for 
Amidotrizoic acid.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
The Justification of the calculation formula of Calcium Edetate Disodium
Please provide the detail elaboration for  variant used in calculation formula, in particular 
cupric sulfate : V2 = volume of cupric sulfate solution, 0.002M, consumed 
(in mL)
1 mL cupric sulfate solution, 0.002M corresponds to 0.7485 mg of sodium calcium edetate
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 ( CTD section):
Please find the more detailed information about the calculation formula is as follows:
1 ml of a 0.002 M cupric sulfate solution is equivalent to 0.7485 mg of sodium calcium 
edetate because they react in a 1:1 molar ratio, meaning the number of moles of cupric ions in 
the solution is equal to the number of moles of edetate in the complex, and the mass of 
copper(II) ions in the solution is directly proportional to the mass of edetate with which it 
reacts.
Step-by-step calculation:
1. Moles of cupric sulfate:
1 ml (0.001 L) of  0.002 M cupric sulfate solution contains  0.002 mol/L × 0.001 L = 
0.000002 moles of Cu(II).
2. Moles of sodium calcium edetate:
The reaction between cupric ions and EDTA is a 1:1 molar ratio, so 0.000002 moles of Cu(II) 
will react with 0.000002 moles of edetate.
3. Mass of sodium calcium edetate: 
• The molar mass of the sodium calcium edetate is 374.27 g/mol. 
• Mass = Moles × Molar Mass = 0.000002 moles × 374.27 g/mol = 0.0007485 g = 
0.7485 mg 
 
The supporting literature reference have been provided with this response. The most 
relevant information in these documents is highlighted in yellow.

Source:
Encyclopedia of Analytical Science • Third Edition • 2019, Chapter 
Titrimetry/Overview, pp. 111-2. Editors: Paul Worsfold, Alan Townshend, Colin F. 
Poole, Manuel Miró. (Relevant info about the complex formation and stoichiometry 
1:1).
Complexometric Determination of copper in the presence of other ions. Talanta, 1962, 
Vol. 9, pp. 769-74 (Additional information about the optimal pH and the use of a 
reducing agent in the complex formation).
keywords: calculation formula; Test Procedure; analytical procedures; standard solution; assay

Under ICH Q14, the omission of certain validation studies for multiple products that are 
considered "alike" can be permissible, provided that there is adequate justification based 
on scientific principles and the similarity of the molecules involved. The key concept here 
is bridging between similar molecules or formulations, which allows for the use of 
existing validation data when certain conditions are met. This can help avoid the 
redundancy of conducting full validation for each new product that is similar to an already 
validated product. 
 
Bridging studies in ICH Q14 for amidotrizoic acid containing different products  i.e. 
Gastrografin with and without star anise oil, Urografin 76% demonstrate that the method 
performance remains consistent across different products and also shows that the 
analytical method developed for a prior product i.e Gastrografin with star anise oil 
formulation or Urografin 76% can still be used effectively for the new product by 
comparing performance data (e.g., accuracy, precision, etc.).

Question/Consideration:
Regarding container closure integrity testing by dye ingress, you are asked to provide a summary of the study including the following information:
a. The number of samples tested
b. A summary of the dye ingress method
c. Confirmation that positive control samples (i.e. vials that have been intentionally compromised) were included in the study to verify that the test conditions were suitable, or that the dye ingress method has been suitably validated including positive controls.
Answer/Response:
During validation runs 375 samples were tested in total. All tested samples met the requirements. Additionally, 50 samples are tested annually as part of the stability studies regarding CCIT over the shelf life.

The Dye Ingress Method is a destructive probabilistic CCIT method that assesses container closure integrity (CCI) by immersing the test containers in a dye solution (Eosin Y, 1%) and simultaneously applying three cycles of differential pressure (30 min each alternating normal pressure and vacuum at 500 mbar). After the challenge is completed, the test samples’ outer surfaces are rinsed thoroughly under running water and the content is checked for dye ingress via visual examination under suitable illumination.

The dye ingress CCIT is performed according to valid standard operating procedures and methods that were validated following the same approach as for testing. Test units with injected dye solution (so called "positive samples"), are used to simulate leakage or damage to the primary packaging. All test units are immersed in a dye bath and subject to an underpressure cycle.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Based on the information provided why was tert-butanol not detected in the extractable study 
of the rubber stopper and detected in both the simulated and ongoing leachable studies? 
Further in the ongoing leachable study if the vial is stored in the upright orientation how is the 
tert-butanol leaching into the DP without direct contact?
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( S.2.4.):
Tert-butanol (CAS 75-65-0) was detected in the extractable study, but the concentration was 
just below the analytical evaluation threshold (AET) and therefore, it was not reported as an 
extractable compound. Then in the leachable simulation study tert-butanol (CAS 75-65-0) 
exceeded the AET, but was unexpected as it was not earlier reported in the extractable study 
(P.2.4.01_022988846_02).
When extractable study data was re-examined it was observed that tert-butanol was released 
during the extraction of the stopper with both pH 5 phosphate buffer and in the thermal 
extraction at 80 C, but the amounts were slightly below the AET of the extractable study. As 
a part of this leachable simulation study the vial stopper was cut into pieces and subjected to 
HS-GC-MS analyses for volatile compounds. The vial stopper was confirmed to be the source 
of tert-butanol with an estimated amount of approximately 7 – 10 µg/stopper.
At the initial stability study timepoint tert-butanol was detected with approximately 4.0 
µg/mL, which corresponds to 0.28 µg/eye and 0.56 µg/treatment. At the timepoint T6 the 
amount of tert-butanol was 9.0 µg/mL, which corresponds to 0.63 µg/eye and 1.26 
µg/treatment. Leachable analyses at the next timepoint T12 are on-going and when reported 
development in the amount of tert-butanol will be clarified then. Final confirmation of the 
amount of tert-butanol released in real time and under temperature storage conditions will be 
obtained when the leachable stability study will progress to the end of shelf-life.
Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL vials are stored upright at 2 – 8C vial stopper not having a 
direct contact with drug solution. Nevertheless, volatile leachable compounds are known to 
migrate from container closure systems into drug product although leachable compounds are 
not in direct contact with the drug solution. It is also known that storage temperature affects 
migration efficiency of volatile leachable compounds. When considering the released amount 
of tert-butanol (7 – 10 µg/stopper) in stopper material in relation to filling volume of the vial, 
which is 0.263 mL, the estimated theoretical maximum concentrations of tert-butanol in 
Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL are 27 – 38 µg/mL.
From that perspective available timepoint T6 results for tert-butanol are well in line with the 
theoretical maximum concentrations estimated above..

Source:  P.2.4.01-02 Pharmaceutical Development - Container Closure
System / Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial for intravitreous injection 
(Bayer AG, Berlin) (#022988846; unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 2  

Regarding the finished product specification, it is noted that the acceptance criteria of the 
sliding and static friction for this product (plastic PFS) is different from that stated in the 
specification of the glass PFS (HK-57330). 
Please justify the difference.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (CTD section 3.2.P.5.1 and 3.2.P.5.6):
Sliding Friction (also known as Gliding Force) refers to the force required to maintain 
continuous movement of the syringe plunger once initiated. Static Friction (also called 
Breakaway Force) is the force needed to overcome initial resistance and start the plunger’s 
movement from rest.
Measuring both static and sliding friction as part of the push-pull test method is critical for 
ensuring:
• 
Safe, smooth, and predictable syringe performance 
• 
Optimized material compatibility and lubrication strategy 
• 
Compliance with regulatory requirements governing functional device properties
The specifications for static and sliding friction differ between glass and plastic syringes due to 
inherent differences in:
• 
Material properties (rigidity, flexibility and elasticity) 
• 
Surface texture and adhesion characteristics 
• 
Manufacturing variability and tolerances
As outlined in P.5.6.01-01: Justification of Specification for Gadobutrol Solution 1 mol/L in 
Prefilled Plastic Syringe for Parenteral Use, the friction limits applied to plastic syringes were 
derived from experience with glass syringes.
However, plastic syringe barrels are inherently more flexible and less dimensionally rigid than 
glass, which increases variability in their interaction with the rubber plunger stopper. As a 
result, plastic syringes naturally exhibit higher and more variable friction forces, which justifies 
the application of broader acceptance criteria for both static and sliding friction values.  

Source:  

P.5.6.01-01 Justification of Specification for Gadobutrol Solution 1 mol/L in 
Prefilled Plastic Syringe for Parenteral Use (GADOVIST)(#DocID; 015878159_ 
new)

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
The viral clearance as presented cannot be evaluated due to insufficient description of the 
scale down process and incomplete or unclear viral clearance data. Provide all relevant 
parameters of the scale down process involved in the viral clearance study (ie. Column height, 
residence time, resin load etc.) and how they are representative of the production scale 
process or represent worst case. Provide a clear description of the viral clearance risk 
assessment and the calculations and justification for the calculations used to calculate the 
safety margin and theoretical RVLP exposure per maximum proposed dose.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (A.2):
A description and summary of the viral clearance studies are provided in 3.2.A.2.03, 
Virological Safety. The relevant parameters of the scale down process are described for the 
low pH hold of Protein A eluate, anion exchange chromatography (membrane adsorber), and 
filtration with Planova™ BioEX viral filter process steps (refer to 3.2.A.2.03 Table 3-4, Table 
3-6, and Table 3-8, respectively). Viral clearance by Protein A column chromatography 
process step was performed at production scale (2000 L, refer to Table 3-1). Additional 
details are in the study reports provided in 3.2.A.2.50, Study Reports of Virus Clearance 
Validation.

Each manufacturing process operation unit is representative of the production scale by 
proportionally scaling down while the critical operation parameters were kept consistent 
between the laboratory scale (the scaled-down test system) and the manufacturing scale. 
Accordingly, the results obtained by the scaled-down test system could be extrapolated to the 
manufacturing process at production scale. The suitability of each scaled-down test system 
was evaluated in the study by demonstrating acceptable recovery of the process intermediate 
and acceptable performance parameters, such as a chromatographic profile where applicable.  
All small scale viral clearance studies were performed using the worst-case scenarios of each 
step. For the low pH viral inactivation hold operation, the higher pH and lower incubation 
temperature values used for the scaled-down study were considered to cover the worst-case 
scenarios in the manufacturing process. For the anion exchange chromatography operation, 
the higher loading density, lower pH, and higher conductivity of the set range used for the 
scaled-down model were considered worst case scenarios. For the filtration with Planova™ 
BioEX viral filter operation, the higher filter loading density used for the scaled-down model 
was considered to cover the worst-case scenarios.

The viral clearance risk assessment includes an evaluation of the potential risk of virus 
contamination in BAY 3401016 production from the ERVLP present in the CHO cells that 
produce recombinant BAY 3401016 drug substance or from adventitious virus contaminants. 
The following measures are implemented to assess and mitigate the risk of virus 
contamination: determination of the level of CHO cell endogenous retrovirus particle in the 
unprocessed bulk; validation of sufficient virus clearance capacity achieved by the 
manufacturing process; evaluation of cell substrates and raw materials; monitoring and 
controlling of manufacturing environment. The viral clearance studies are designed and 
performed per guidance ICH Q5A. The removal of ERVLP (endogenous retrovirus-like 
particles) from the clarified harvest (i.e. the unprocessed bulk without the CHO cells) serves 
as a benchmark for retrovirus clearance capacity by the post-harvest purification process.

The calculation of estimated particles per dose follows ICH Q5A(R2) (Annex 4). The dose 
equivalent amount of ERVLP in the clarified harvest is estimated to be 9.51 log10 as described 
in 3.2.A.2.03 Table 4-1 (for convenience, Table 4-1 is reproduced below). The estimates in 
this table include worst case assumptions, including maximum daily dose. Determination of 
ERVLP concentration (6.79 log10 particles/mL) in the clarified harvest is described in 
3.2.A.2.50 Section 2.5 (Report ERVLP-24-02-3401016). The overall retrovirus clearance 
capacity, a summation of all demonstrated retroviral clearance results (≥ 18.72 ± 0.55 log10), 
provides ≥ 9.21 log10 (= 18.72 – 9.51) safety margin, which exceeds the 6.0 log10 general 
industry consensus safety margin described in ICH Q5A.

In summary, the lower value of Log10 Reduction Factor (LRF) is used as the worst case to 
determine virus clearance capacity for each operational step. The small-scale viral clearance 
studies conducted represent worst case scenario. Results from virus clearance validation 
studies with test articles of BAY 3401016 manufacturing intermediates have demonstrated 
that the process is highly effective and robust in virus inactivation and removal.

deletion of mass homogeneity IPC. The mixing process remains unchanged, only the 
homogeneity IPC test is proposed to be removed from the validated mixing process.
Bayer has manufactured Mirena batches for 30 years already and hence the mixing process is 
well established, and therefore proven to produce homogenous levonorgestrel-elastomer 
mixtures. In order to support the IPC deletion the actual mixing time (at least 40 minutes) 
applied on the product over the years was added and specified as an IPC to substitute the 
homogeneity test. Therefore, the proposed IPCs are only adapting to the actual conditions of 
the manufacturing process.
A process validation report P.3.5.01_02 in which the mixing time of min. 40 minutes has been 
observed and reported is provided to the competent Health Authority for review. In this 
validation study homogenous mixtures were achieved with the mixing time of 40 minutes.
Bayer Oy has performed mixing time study for Mirena regarding the mixing phase. 3 different 
final mixing times (20, 40 and 60 minutes) were tested. The mixture was homogenous already 
after mixing of 20 minutes. The situation did not alter significantly neither after mixing of 40 
minutes nor after mixing of 60 minutes. The average assay of 10 homogeneity samples was 
near to 50 % in all occasions, also RSD of the samples did not alter significantly.

Based on the mixing study and the overall long experience regarding the mixing step, it can 
be justified that mixing time of 40 minutes produces reproducibly and reliably homogenous 
mixtures for Mirena. Therefore, when using only the 40 minutes mixing time no maximum 
mixing time needs to be defined in the manufacturing batch record.

As a further assurance of the continuously homogenous mixtures achieved in the mixing step 
of Mirena data on recent 283 batches (manufactured between 03.01.2024 and 31.01.2025) of 
Mirena is provided. The data refers to average results of 4 IPC samples collected from these 
283 batches, which means that the data in graphs and histograms is based on 1132 blend 
samples in total.
The requirement for the average levonorgestrel concentration is 48 – 52 %, and the RSD of 4 
determinations must be ≤ 2 %. The average results of 283 batches fall between 47.9 and 50.8

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
The company was asked to confirm that positive control samples (i.e. vials that have been intentionally compromised) were included in the study to verify that the test conditions were suitable, or that the dye ingress method has been suitably validated including positive controls.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( 3.2.P.7):
The TGA’s request to incorporate deliberately compromised vials as a positive control in the Container Closure Integrity Testing (CCIT) method is acknowledged. While the CCIT test results presented to support this variation are based upon the method established in accordance with an earlier USP version <1207>, it is noted that current USP  <1207> is more specific with respect to the positive control expectations.
The Sponsor commits to completing and submitting the validation of the enhanced method, including deliberately compromised vials, within an agreed timeframe.
The proposal is to complete validation of the enhanced method for the Eylea 114.3mg/mL vial as part of a validation bracketing approach that will cover various combinations of drug products and container closure systems in different sizes and filling volumes.
Notwithstanding the commitment to undertake validation of the enhanced USP  <1207> method, the Sponsor considers that the CCIT results presented with this variation, in combination with the additional process validation data and manufacturing history illustrate the product is not at high risk of loss of integrity. The basis is as follows:
1. Sterility testing at multiple stability timepoints to highlight absence of contamination.
The sterility results obtained under the applied and already approved conditions for the current approved Catalent site provide evidence that the packaging system has performed as intended.
2. Scientific and Regulatory precedent – International guidance (e.g., ICH Q5C and USP <1207>) – supports the use of sterility testing or container closure integrity testing at the beginning and end of shelf life. While CCIT is preferred for long-term assurance, sterility testing is an established standard and validation of the enhanced CCIT method is planned.
3. Risk mitigation:
- Process controls in place to ensure container integrity (e.g. validated process – stopper, capping and checks)
- Historical data from Eylea vials from both 40mg/mL & 114.3mg/mL showing the closure system has a history of integrity
On this basis, it is proposed the current CCIT data and sterility results from stability studies provide reasonable assurance of product sterility during the whole life cycle. The Sponsor believes that this approach is scientifically justified and aligned with TGA expectations with provision that a re-validated CCIT method in accordance with the current USP <1207> is implemented within the proposed timeline. We respectfully request the TGA’s consideration of this variation with a post-approval commitment to complete validation of the CCIT method incorporating deliberately compromised vials as positive control, as per the Agency’s request.
Validation preparations are currently ongoing and will be implemented in Q4 2025.
Consequently, a protocol will be shared by Q4 2025, and a report will be presented in Q2 2026.
Dye Ingress method validation will be performed, as requested, demonstrating the method’s effectiveness by comparing negative and positive controls. Positive controls will have laser-drilled defects of different nominal leak sizes.
keywords: Container closure system; Sterility Testing; validation of test method; Process Validation and/or Evaluation; Validation Report

Question/Consideration:
Question 1:
Explain the mechanism by which fluoroethyl carbamate is generated from ethyl 
chloroformate.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.3.2.1):
Fluoroethyl carbamate is generated from Ethyl chloroformate, which is present as an impurity 
in Methyl chloroformate, through a reaction mechanism analogous to that of Fluoromethyl 
carbamate formation from methyl chloroformate during the synthesis of Vericiguat. The 
formation of Fluoroethyl carbamate occurs during step 3a of the Vericiguat manufacturing 
process, where Methyl chloroformate is used as a reagent to react with Fluorotrisamine forming 
Vericiguat.
The underlying reaction mechanism is as follows (Please refer to Figure. 1): The amino group 
at position 5 of the pyrimidine ring in Fluorotrisamine acts as a nucleophile and attacks the 
carbonyl carbon of methyl chloroformate. This nucleophilic attack is facilitated by the electron-
rich nature of the amino group. This attack leads to the formation of a tetrahedral intermediate 
where the carbonyl carbon of Methyl chloroformate is temporarily bonded to both the oxygen 
(original carbonyl oxygen) and the nitrogen (from Fluorotrisamine). The tetrahedral 
intermediate undergoes elimination of the chloride ion (a good leaving group) and a proton, 
resulting in the formation of a carbamate linkage between the methyl group from the Methyl 
chloroformate molecule and the amino group of Fluorotrisamine.
In case of Ethyl chloroformate as a reactant, the analogous reaction takes place under the 
formation of the impurity Fluoroethyl carbamate.
In summary, the reaction mechanisms for both Methyl chloroformate and Ethyl chloroformate 
are analogous, with both reactions occurring through the same pathway and exhibiting 
comparable reaction rates. This similarity underscores the potential for Fluoroethyl carbamate 
formation whenever Ethyl chloroformate is present as an impurity in the synthesis of 
Vericiguat.

Source:  S.3.2.01_4.0 Impurities / Vericiguat micronized drug substance (IQMS-
265350;unchanged). This document was previous identified as 
S.3.2.01_022990117-04. Please refer to declaration for documentation 
registration.
keywords: Characterization of impurities; Potential process impurities; Elucidation of Structure and other Characteristics; Impurities; synthesis

Question/Consideration:
Question 2:
Please explain why fluoroethyl carbamate (CTD 2.3.S, P. 6) was detected in excess of the 
specification limit (0.10%) in actual production, despite being less than 0.05% in the batch 
analysis submitted at the time of initial approval. If the ethyl chloroformate content in the raw 
material, methyl chloroformate, was higher in actual production than in the batch submitted at 
the time of initial approval, please show the actual measured values of ethyl chloroformate in 
each batch submitted at the time of initial approval and in the actual production batch.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (S.2.4.01, S.2.4.03, S.2.4.05, S.4.5.01):
Fluoroethyl carbamate is generated as an impurity in the presence of Ethyl chloroformate, as 
elucidated in the previously described reaction mechanism. During the process development 
phase, we identified this impurity and traced its origin. However, due to the consistently low 
concentrations observed - typically below 0.05% - we did not foresee any potential issues 
arising from its presence. Consequently, we did not include this impurity in the specification 
for Vericiguat. Development data confirmed that Fluoroethyl carbamate levels remained 
below 0.05%, and these findings were further verified during the first commercial campaign. 
As a result, any potential negative impact on product quality attributed to trace amounts of 
Ethyl chloroformate was deemed negligible. Therefore, Ethyl chloroformate was not included 
into the specification for the raw material, and Fluoroethyl carbamate was similarly not 
included in the API specifications (Please refer to “Discussion of critical steps”: S.2.4.01 and 
“Justification of specification”: S.4.5.01).

Ethyl Chloroformate content in Raw Materials
With respect to the ethyl chloroformate content in the raw material Methyl chloroformate, 
specific analytical data from the technical runs and the first commercial campaign are not 
available. At that time, Ethyl chloroformate was not listed on the Certificate of Analysis (CoA) 
provided by the manufacturer. It is pertinent to note that due to the extreme toxicity of Methyl 
chloroformate, conducting an incoming goods release test at Bayer’s QC laboratories is not 
feasible. Consequently, the release of this material is solely based on the CoAs provided by the 
manufacturer, in accordance with ICH Q7 7.32.

Based on the concentrations of Fluoroethyl carbamate determined in the first commercial 
batches (0.030 % ± 0.005 %), it can be concluded that the concentration of Ethyl chloroformate 
in the Methyl chloroformate at that time was less than 0.05 %.

In conclusion, although Fluoroethyl carbamate levels were initially assessed to be below 
0.05%, subsequent production batches have demonstrated elevated concentrations exceeding 
the specification limit of 0.10% (according to S.2.4.05). The lack of Ethyl chloroformate data 
in the initial approval CoA, coupled with its potential increase in later batches, may have 
contributed to this discrepancy.
Since the initial commercial campaign, no subsequent changes have been made to the 
manufacturing process or the analytical methods used for Vericiguat, crude and Vericiguat, 
intermediate stages. The root cause investigation carried out has once again confirmed that the 
formation of Fluoroethyl carbamate is only possible through a reaction with Ethyl 
chloroformate. Furthermore it was investigated how/if the impurity can be significantly reduced 
by e.g. changing the solvents /solvent ratios, washing volumes and crystallization conditions. 
None of these approaches were successful and therefore all attempts to elaborate a 
reprocessing/reworking procedure failed.
For this reason, the cause of the increased concentrations of Fluoroethyl carbamate found can 
only lie in a varying ingress of Ethyl chloroformate via the raw material Methyl chloroformate 
and/or a varying depletion factor for the impurity Fluoroethyl carbamate in routine production 
during the Vericiguat HCl salt formation followed by the downstream isolation and purification 
processes of Vericiguat.

The analytical results of recent Vericiguat batches, including the respective Ethyl 
chloroformate content, are detailed in response to question 4 (Please refer to Table. 2).

Question/Consideration:
Question 3:
Explain the justification for setting the control value of max. 0.10% for ethyl chloroformate 
content in methyl chloroformate. Show the actual measured values of ethyl chloroformate.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (S.2.3.02):
Methyl chloroformate is a fundamental chemical commodity produced annually on a multi-ton 
scale, serving a critical role in various chemical processes within the pharmaceutical and 
chemical industries. Recent experience in the synthesis of Vericiguat has demonstrated that the 
previous assumption - that Methyl chloroformate is devoid of significant traces of Ethyl 
chloroformate - is no longer valid. This necessitates the establishment of a dedicated 
specification limit for this potential impurity to ensure the high quality of Vericiguat (Please 
refer to Table 1).

Measured Values of Ethyl chloroformate
The following table presents the ethyl chloroformate content in recently delivered batches of 
Methyl chloroformate (MCF) raw material, as indicated by the Certificates of Analysis (CoAs) 
provided by the manufacturer.

Table 1: Batches of recently delivered Methyl chloroformate (MCF) raw material and the 
respective Ethyl chloroformate (ECF) content.

These data demonstrate a certain variability in the Ethyl chloroformate content in the 
production of the Methyl chloroformate (MCF) based on a limited numbers of batches. This 
variability may explain the varying concentrations of the impurity Fluoroethyl carbamate 
found in produced API batches to date.
As a commodity, Methyl chloroformate (MCF) is produced according to the needs of the world 
market. In this regards, traces of Ethyl chloroformate (ECF) are not relevant for the typical 
industrial use of MCF.
To ensure the lowest possible concentration of ECF, Bayer has discussed this issue intensively 
with the manufacturer. Based on the process capability analysis for the production of MCF, the 
manufacturer is willing to accept a specification limit of NMT 0.10 %, but not a lower limit as 
permanent compliance with this limit cannot be guaranteed.
Methyl chloroformate is a chemical substance with an extraordinarily high hazard potential and 
is therefore subject to various legal regulations on production, storage and use. For these 
reasons, manufacturers and end users are legally obliged to reduce stocks of this substance to 
an absolute minimum possible. Due to this regulation, the production of MCF is de facto a just-
in-time production with only small stocks. For this reason, targeted "lot picking" for the use of 
Methyl chloroformate batches with a very low Ethyl chloroformate content is not a realistic 
option.
Furthermore, a market survey has revealed that no other established manufacturer of MCF, 
apart from the current manufacturer, can consistently deliver MCF meeting the required quality 
standards with an Ethyl chloroformate content NMT 0.10 %. This reinforces the rationale for 
setting the control value at this level to ensure product integrity and compliance with high 
industry standards.
The specification of an Ethyl chloroformate (ECF) level of NMT 0.10 % will increase process 
safety and product quality of Vericiguat by preventing the use of MCF batches with an 
exceptionally high ECF content.
However, the definition of this specification limit for Ethyl chloroformate (ECF) does not fully 
ensure that the specification of NMT 0.10 % for the Fluoroethyl carbamate in the API can be 
complied with. On the other hand, if the ECF content are to be further reduced, there would be 
a significant risk that no suitable quantity of raw material would be available for the production 
of Vericiguat, as such quality is currently not securely available. This situation would ultimately 
lead to a disruption or even a complete inability to ensure market supply.

Question/Consideration:
Question 4:
Please provide the actual measured values of fluoroethyl carbamate in the vericiguat 
intermediate and the vericiguat micronized drug substance in lots where the ethyl 
chloroformate content in methyl chloroformate was controlled by max.0.10%. In addition, 
please explain again the necessity of expanding the specification limit to max.0.15% for 
fluoroethyl carbamate, despite changing the control of methyl chloroformate as raw material.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4 ( S.4.5.01):
A correlation analysis between the certified Ethyl chloroformate (ECF) content in Methyl 
chloroformate (MCF) and the detected levels of the impurity Fluoroethylcarbamate in 
Vericiguat intermediate and micronized drug substance reveals a moderate correlation between 
the three parameters (Please refer to Table 2). However, it is important to note that we do not 
have an extensive dataset for this correlation, as early batches did not present issues related to 
Fluoroethyl carbamate and thus, there was no need to  specify Ethyl chloroformate at that time.
The observed deviation from an expected 1:1 correlation may be attributed to several factors, 
including the precision of the analytical methods used for Ethyl chloroformate determination 
and a potential variability in depletion or enrichment factors during the downstream isolation 
and purification processes of Vericiguat.

Tab. 2: Actual measured values of Fluoroethyl carbamate in Vericiguat, intermediate and 
Vericiguat micronized drug substance produced from batches where the Ethyl chloroformate 
content in Methyl chloroformate was controlled by max. 0.10%.  
Level of quantitation (LoQ): 0.03 %

[Table 2 values as provided in the DOCUMENT]

Justification for Expanding the Specification Limit
An ingress of up to 0.10% Ethyl chloroformate is permissible based on the proposed 
specification for the raw material Methyl chloroformate (MCF) and the process capability given 
by the manufacturer of MCF.
Taking into account the correlations listed in Table 3, compliance with a specification of NMT 
0.10 % for Fluoroethyl carbamate cannot be consistently guaranteed even with an specification 
limit of 0.10 % for Ethyl chloroformate in Methyl chloroformate.
However, based on the historical data available to date for the Fluoroethyl carbamate content 
in Vericiguat, it can be stated that a specification limit of NMT 0.15 % Fluoroethyl carbamate 
can be safely adhered to.

Therefore, we are proposing an extension of the specification limit for the active pharmaceutical 
ingredient to include Fluoroethyl carbamate as a separate impurity item with a maximum 
specification limit of max. 0.15% in addition to limiting the impurity Ethyl chloroformate in the 
raw material Methyl chloroformate. The current overall manufacturing process performance 
does not allow for a Fluoroethyl carbamate content of NMT 0.10 % as currently specified. Not 
extending the specification limit would inevitably increase the risk of an disruption of market 
supply for a prolonged period of time due to out-of-specification results regarding this impurity 
because of
a) limited control of the ingress of Ethyl chloroformate via the raw material Methyl
chloroformate  
b) varying depletion factor for the impurity Fluoroethyl carbamate in routine production. 
c) inability to remove the impurity Fluoroethyl carbamate in the Vericiguat API by means
of reprocessing or reworking

and the long lead time to produce new Vericiguat starting from the defined starting materials.
The proposed revision of specification aligns with the qualification threshold requirements 
outlined in ICH Q3A and ensures a reliable and consistent supply of the Vericiguat drug 
substance to the market. Regarding the safety of our patients, the toxicological evaluation of 
Fluoroethyl carbamate did not result in an in silico alert, which was to be expected given its 
structural similarity to Vericiguat.

Even though we are applying for a broader specification, we are committed to making every 
effort to keep the concentration of the impurity Fluoroethyl carbamate as low as is reasonably 
possible. We also commit to revising the specification again once a sufficient number of 
additional batches have been produced and the manufacturing process can reliably produce 
batches with a low impurity profile.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1:
3.2.P.2.2.1 – Robustness test (initial Q8) and Instructions for Use: The suspensibility and 
re-suspensibility of the suspension were physically assessed by Swissmedic based on the kits' 
instructions for use (IFU). The EMA's observation on day 180 and the EMA's alternative 
proposal for preparing the suspension (see Module 1.7.2 - Response to LoOI Day 180 - 
Quality, page 9) are taken into account. The reference to 3.2.P.2.2 "Medicinal Products - 
Pharmaceutical Development - Additional Information - 0229992655 (Sequence 0049)" is 
also taken into account. Taking into account the EMA's discussions, the additional 
instructions in the instructions for use (IFU) do not fully mitigate the problem of lump 
formation when reconstituting the granules into a suspension. Despite following the modified 
IFU, Swissmedic observed lumps that could only be dispersed after a waiting time of 
approximately 20 to 30 minutes and after shaking the suspension again. Swissmedic therefore 
requests that the IFU be supplemented with a waiting period and proposes that the IFU be 
amended as follows.
a) 
The reconstitution of the granules into a suspension should be prepared xx minutes 
before the intended administration of the dose. Based on observations during the 
reconstitution of the granules into a suspension, a waiting time of 30 minutes (“xx”) is 
proposed, but the applicant may propose a different waiting time.
b) 
During preparation of the suspension according to the instructions for use, the bottle 
should be systematically turned upside down to check for the presence of any undispersed 
granule lumps, regardless of whether or not there are visible lumps.
c) 
Before administering the dose from the freshly prepared suspension, a waiting period 
of 20 to 30 minutes should be observed, followed by a further 60 seconds of shaking to ensure 
complete dispersion of any lumps that may have formed during reconstitution of the granules 
into the suspension.
Please submit an updated instruction manual.
As a follow-up to the CHMP Day 180 list of outstanding questions, we request you to provide 
the final assessment report and IFU as adopted by the EU regarding the anti-clumping 
measures.
Please indicate how the IFU used during clinical trials differed from the proposed commercial 
IFU and what specific instructions were given in case of clumping during reconstitution of the 
granules into a suspension.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.2.2.01 & STED.7.3.02):
The primary objective of Clinical Study 15681 (PATENT CHILD) was to evaluate the safety, 
tolerability, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacokinetics of the investigational medicinal 
product riociguat. For logistical reasons, the components of the study kit were provided 
separately during the trial.
The instructions for use (IFU) were derived in accordance with internal pharmaceutical 
development documentation. The IFU provided for the conduct of PATENT CHILD 
instructed to “shake the bottle for at least 1 minute by hand until a homogenous suspension is 
generated. All granulate granules should be suspended into the 200 mL drinking water. This 
will take at least 1 minute.” These instructions were intentionally concise and tailored to the 
clinical setting, differing significantly from the more comprehensive instructions developed 
for the commercial product.
During the development phase of the medicinal product, the reconstitution process was clearly 
defined and rigorously tested across multiple batches.
This included determining the duration of shaking required to achieve a homogenous 
suspension, free of clumps or sediment. As a result, the reconstitution instructions used in the 
clinical study did not include specific references to the potential occurrence of clumps or 
sediment, as these aspects had been thoroughly addressed and validated during product 
development. The commercial-use kit was developed in alignment with key regulatory and 
quality standards, including the EMA guideline “Guideline on quality documentation for 
medicinal products when used with a medical device” 
(EMA/CHMP/QWP/BWP/259165/2019) and ISO 14971 “Medical devices — Application of 
risk management to medical devices.” As part of the development process, multiple formative 
and one summative usability study (Please refer to the Human Factor Report STED.7.3.02) 
were conducted to evaluate the handling of the medical devices and the re-suspension process. 
This included assessment of the visibility of clumps or sediment within the suspension.
Throughout the iterative development, user feedback and risk mitigation strategies were 
systematically integrated into the creation of the IFU.
Compared to the instructions used during clinical studies, the IFU for the commercial product 
includes several enhancements: a more detailed step-by-step description of the preparation 
process and the addition of pictograms to visually support the instructions. These updates also 
emphasize the need to check the suspension for clumps and sediment, accompanied by 
appropriate cautionary guidance.
During the usability study, sediment was observed only in instances where the user 
completely forgot to shake the suspension. When the bottle was inverted to withdraw the 
suspension with the syringe, the presence of sediment became apparent. However, it dissolved 
immediately upon this action.

Bayer confirms its agreement to revise the IFU in accordance with the request from the health 
authority. The updated IFU for Switzerland, the IFU adopted by the EU and final EMA 
assessment report are shared together with this response.
