Question/Consideration:
Question 2:
3.2.P.8.3 (and 3.2.P.5.3) - Stress tests / mass balance (initial Q47): The cause of the gap in 
the mass balance was attributed to the differences in the absorption coefficient between the 
active ingredient riociguat and its unknown degradation products. By applying a correction 
factor (CF) of 1.5 for unknown degradation products (derived from the CF of 
dihydropurinone and 4-amino-6-hydroxy-riociguat), the gap in the mass balance could be 
closed, at least for the results of the forced degradation studies, i.e. the oxidation stress 
studies. On the other hand, when applied to the ICH stability batches, this correction factor 
does not explain the difference between the content analysis of riociguat and the sum of the 
degradation products. With reference to stability data 3.2.P.8.3, for example, batch KM6013G 
shows a F. has an assay value of 93.9% (OOS), while the sum of the degradation products is 
only 0.73%, with an initial assay value (T = 0 months) of 100.7%. In this case, it is clear that 
even the application of a CF of 1.5 for the determination of impurities (taking into account the 
sum of the impurities) does not explain the difference in content (6.8%). Please explain, 
taking into account the data from the ICH stability batches, why the analytical method can be 
considered suitable in this case. Alternatively, we ask you to submit a revised analytical 
method indicating stability, together with the validation documentation, within one year of the 
Swissmedic decision
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (P.8.3.01):
Bayer acknowledges that the reported out of specification (OoS) result at 60 months appears 
to indicate a mass balance issue from a preliminary perspective.
At the time of obtaining the OoS result, an investigation was performed. While a certain 
decrease in assay was expected in the drug product stored for a period of time significantly
longer than its proposed shelf life, the difference between 48 and 60 months appeared 
exceptionally high.
During investigation the initial OoS result was confirmed. However, a root cause could not be 
identified.
Upon Swiss Medic request for explanation of the apparent mass balance issue, it became 
evident that further stability samples (KM6013E, KM6013F and KM6013G) tested at the 
same time point with the same analytical setup showed comparable behavior: even though no 
further OoS results were obtained they rank lower in assay than expected from previous 
testing points even when taking Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) degradation into 
account. Due to this finding, a potential systematic error in the 60 months analytical testing 
cannot be excluded. Since this OoS value is the only event where mass balance is clearly not 
achieved, we do not consider the stability study to reveal a systematic mass balance deficit.
Considering the fact that the stability study in question was concluded in 2022, samples of the 
relevant batches are no longer available for verification of this hypothesis.
In our opinion, this finding is an isolated event as demonstrated by more recent and on-going 
stability studies performed at the commercial manufacturing site (Please refer to P.8.3.01). 
This data shows that no further gaps in mass balance have been found, which also speaks to 
the more stringent analytical performance monitoring during pre-commercial and into the 
commercial phase.
Bayer AG will continue to monitor the analytical method performance at the commercial 
manufacturing site and commit to re-evaluate the analytical method in case of further events 
relating to implausible results, especially in context of discrepancies in mass balance may 
appear.
In the event that the agency does not concur with Bayer’s current scientific rationale, and if 
our commitment to continue with further analytical monitoring at the commercial site does 
not fully meet your expectations, Bayer AG will proceed to revise the analytical method.
In this case within one year after approval, we are going to submit validation documentation 
demonstrating modifications or optimizations to the analytical method as necessary.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
No submission of data confirming that there is no impact on quality due to a -9% bias in the 
evaluation of comparative equivalence using changed test procedures in the potency test.
Submit data confirming that the -9% bias in the comparative exercise for potency test does
not impact quality and that the changed test procedures are valid.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
There is no impact to the product’s quality as a result of the -9% bias in the comparative 
exercise for potency test but there will be an adjustment made to the specific activity for the 
release of DS and DP to account for the relative bias between the proposed and approved 
potency methods.
The proposed method (slope ratio) had a negative 9% relative bias in potency measurement of 
DS samples compared to the approved method (linear regression), which leads to perceived 
shift in the potency attribute of the DS batches. Based on process performance it was evaluated 
that no adjustment was required for the potency specification acceptance criteria (release and 
shelf-life). However, to account for the relative bias of the optimized method for the potency 
measurement, the specification acceptance criteria (release and shelf-life) for specific activity 
are proposed changed. Both the release and shelf-life lower acceptance criteria are adjusted to 
reflect the negative 9% relative bias in potency measurement. Further the upper acceptance 
criteria (release and shelf-life) for Specific Activity are proposed removed as the Ph.Eur 
monograph for recombinant rFVIII requires only a lower limit for specific activity of NLT 
2000 IU/mg to control for potential decline in purity as specific activity is a measure of relative 
purity. Hence it is recommended to shift the lower DS and DP specification limits 
proportionally to the biases observed between the two assays for the respective sample types. 
This action does not adversely impact the product's quality but will ensure that comparable 
quality standards are maintained with respect to DS and DP specific activity when 
implementing the new potency method. Once batch data is collected using potency values 
obtained from the new method, an evaluation will be performed to assess the appropriateness 
of the bias-adjusted DS/DP specific activity specifications.

Question/Consideration: Justify the use of two methodologies (HPLC or uHPLC) for both the content and impurity tests.
Answer/Response:
Both methods are scientifically equivalent in terms of selectivity, accuracy, precision, and robustness. The choice between HPLC and uHPLC does not affect the validity of the results, as both techniques are fully validated against the same analytical parameters and acceptance criteria.
Laboratories may be equipped with either HPLC or uHPLC systems. Providing both methods ensures that the procedure is broadly applicable without limiting its execution to a specific type of instrument.
Both procedures generate the same outcomes for content and impurity testing. The system suitability criteria are identical, ensuring comparable chromatographic resolution and quantitative reliability.
Therefore, HPLC and uHPLC are interchangeable for this purpose, and the results obtained by either method are equivalent and acceptable.
Enclosed herewith signed declaration for the same.

Bayer Response to Question 1 (R.2.01):
To demonstrate in-use compatibility of the proposed Container Closure System (CCS) in 
combination with the diluent solution and finally rIFN, the new CCS was filled with 0.54% 
NaCl solution, stoppered, and subjected to a stress incubation at 40°C/75% relative humidity

Following incubation, syringes were used for reconstitution of rIFN as per leaflet instruction. 
Once rIFN had been reconstituted, the solution was drawn back into the syringe to maximize 
contact time between the CCS and rIFN. Syringes holding the reconstituted Drug Product

Question/Consideration:
(i). Please submit stability data once applicable and update the input for stability report accordingly (e.g. 18 months for duration for the time being).
(ii). Please clarify the lack of sterility tests for accelerated condition (whole planned duration – Table 4-12 to 4-15) and long term condition (initial to 12th months – Table 4-5 to 4-8).
(iii). Please clarify why there is no data for the first 2 time points (initial & 3rd months) for long term condition (Table 4-5 to 4-8).
(iv). Please clarify if the tests were conducted according to the test schedule in Table 2-5 as there is “NR” in so many timepoint for various tests (e.g. appearance, clarify, color, pH, particulate matter content, endotoxin and sterility).
(v). Please update the study start date to 01.10.2023 as far as only sterilized PFS is concerned.
Answer/Response:
(i) Updated stability data including 24 month long-term storge are provided in the sections P.8.1.01-06, P.8.3.01-7.0.
(ii) The sterility testing concept for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe (PFS) is compliant with ICH guidelines and provides adequate control over quality, safety and efficacy of the drug product.
ICH Q5C “Stability Testing of Biotechnological/Biological Products” states in section 5.4 “Other Product Characteristics”:
“Sterility testing or alternatives (e.g., container/closure integrity testing) should be performed at a minimum initially and at the end of the proposed shelf-life.”
Therefore, sterility testing is performed at release and at the end of the shelf-life for long-term stability studies, while it is not required at any timepoint before the current end of shelf-life of 24 months.
Sterility testing is not performed for accelerated studies, since the purpose of these studies is to investigate the degradation behavior of the product at this storage condition. The inclusion of sterility testing during accelerated stability is furthermore not considered to provide meaningful information since the commercial product will have a predefined maximum time out of refrigeration, which is in the order of magnitude of a few days only and covered by dedicated maximum TOR stability studies that include sterility testing (refer to P.8.3.11-6.0). A potential sterility out of specification result after 1, 3 or 6 months at 25 ± 2 °C, 60 ± 5% relative humidity could therefore not be transferred to a sterility issue at the real-time storage condition.
(iii) The manufacturing process of Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL PFS consists of two parts: (i) aseptic filling of formulated drug substance into syringes (bulk PFS) at Vetter Pharma and (ii) Labeling, Assembly, Blistering and Sterilization (LABS) of the outer surface of the syringe at the Bayer AG, Berlin, Germany (BAG). The LABS process can occur several months after the filling process.
The shelf life of Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL PFS starts with the time of filling and is controlled (see CTD sections P.5.6.01-01 and P.8.1.01-06). The time between the filling and LABS processing is already part of the overall shelf life and the total shelf life is not impacted by the date of LABS processing.
Resultantly and depending on the time difference between bulk PFS manufacturing (filling) and LABS process, data for several time points (e.g., 0, 3 and 6 months) can be missing for the sterilized batches as also explained in P.8.2.01-01.
(iv) It is confirmed that the long-term and accelerated stability studies are conducted in accordance with the schedule as provided in table 2-5 of P.8.3.01-7.0. This table only defines at which time points stability tests are performed and at which time points stability tests are not required as indicated with “--“, i.e., for accelerated studies all time points beyond the 6 months.
The individual tests that are performed for the long term and the accelerated study at each time point are defined in Table 3-1 and Table 3-2 in P.8.1.01-06. “NR” indicates that a test item is not required at a certain time point. The applicant defined this table based on the experience with the approved Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL in vial and PFS as well as the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial. Specification parameter that do not undergo any changes throughout the shelf life and are therefore not stability indicating, have been waived at certain time points. However, the full testing panel as per P.5.1.02-01 is conducted at least at the end of shelf life.
(v) As explained in the response to Question 1 (iii), the shelf life of the finished product starts with the filling of bulk syringes. The start date of the stability studies, however, is always set at 30 days after filling. This is to support the procedure applied at Bayer to set the expiration date of the finished product, which is usually the last date of a month two years (or the respective shelf life) after start of the shelf life. For Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in PFS this means that syringes which were filled on e.g. 01.10.2024 will have an expiration date of 30.10.2026 expressed as 10/2026 on the label and the secondary packaging.
To cover the maximum 30 days difference, the stability study start (T0) is set 30 days after the filling date of the PFS, meaning 30 days after the start of the shelf life. In total, the product will have 25 months of storage, while the stability study runs 24 months.
The most appropriate study start date of the finished product (PFS after LABS) presented in P.8.3.01-7.0 is therefore April 2023 (KT0KK7S, KT0KKC1 and KT0KKC3) or May 2023 (KT0KVBJ and KT0KVBJ-D), which is the study start date of the parent bulk PFS batches as shown in Table 2-1 of the aforementioned CTD section.
For Eylea solution for intravitreal injection in pre-filled syringe 114.3mg/ml in Hong Kong, shelf life calculation is in exact date, which means that syringes which were filled on e.g. 01.10.2024 will have an expiration date of 01.10.2026. The expiry date shown on outer secondary packaging consists of day-month-year (e.g. 01.10.2026). Exact date format presentation is subject to site’s setting.

Question/Consideration: Please justify the necessity of this amount of overfill.
Answer/Response:
The Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL prefilled syringe was designed to deliver a 70 μL dose. An overfill is required for a prefilled syringe to ensure that the intended dose can consistently be delivered.
Overfilling is required to compensate variations in fill volume that occur during the filling process and for the dead volume within the injection needle and prefilled syringe. The dead volume is the drug solution remaining in the syringe and needle after injection.
Resultantly, the target fill volume of 0.184 mL was set considering dose preparation, void volume in syringe and needle, and variance of the fill volume within qualified limits as also explained in P.2.4.02-01.
Overfill must also compensate additional losses of drug that are associated with priming of the injection system. During the priming process, the air bubble in the syringe must be expelled. With that also some droplets of drug are expelled.
Overall, the capability of the Aflibercept 114.3 mg/mL prefilled syringe to precisely deliver a dose of 70 µL is shown in the dose accuracy results from design verification study and presented in P.2.6.01-01.

Question/Consideration:
(i). Please upload justification of specification.
(ii). For release and shelf-life specifications, please clarify why there is no test(s) on the device functionality (e.g. break out/sustaining forces) versus that of the vial previously approved (HK68359).
(iii). For release and shelf-life specifications, please clarify why the limits on Particulate Matter Content differ from that of the vial previously approved (HK68359).
Answer/Response:
(i) Handled locally.
(ii) The Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe (PFS) drug device combination product is a disposable, prefilled syringe with customized finger flange and plunger rod for single, fixed dose delivery. The drug device combination product has an integrated dosing mechanism that provides the delivery of a preselected dose. Manual dose setting by the user (e.g., healthcare professional) is not possible in contrast to the already approved Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL PFS, where a dose line is applied.
In accordance with the design control processes applied to develop the PFS, priming and injection forces are defined as functional performance attributes for the drug device combination product and are tested following applicable sections of ISO11608-1 as part of the design verification (including end of shelf-life testing).
Those forces are equivalent to breakout/ sustain forces for a filled/stoppered bulk syringe. The priming and injection forces consider hydrodynamic and friction forces of the bulk PFS combined with the friction forces of the fully assembled Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL drug device combination product (including the customized finger flange and plunger rod).
As outlined in section P.3.3.01-01 the priming and injection forces are considered as In-Process Controls for the packaging process of the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL PFS with an acceptance criterion of ≤ 30 N. These IPC tests will be performed during routine commercial production.
In combination with the additional performance tests this ensures that the drug device combination functions as intended. Therefore, the applicant considers it appropriate that breakout/ sustain forces are not included in the drug product’s release and shelf-life specification.
(iii) As pointed out in section P.5.6.01-01, the applicant harmonized the test procedure and acceptance criteria for sub-visible particles of the Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL prefilled syringe with the approved Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL prefilled syringe. The limits of the 40 mg/mL prefilled syringe were defined based on available batch data and independently from the vial presentation when switching the sub-visible particles test of the PFS from Light-Obscuration (Method 1) to Microscopy (Method 2). Question/Consideration:
(i).The release specification mentioned that the test on sterility (Syringe in blister tray) follow in- house testing method but not Ph. Eur. 2.6.1 like the shelf-life spec. However, the COA provided mentioned following Ph. Eur. 2.6.1. Please explain the discrepancy.
(ii). Please explain why many steps of testing are on product after aseptic filling but not after blistering and outer surface sterilization?
Answer/Response:
(i) The standard method for testing the sterility (Syringe in blister tray) is the in-house method using bioindicators, which was also applied to the batch KT0S635 presented in the CoA. This method is therefore also reflected in the release specification in P.5.1.01-01 and in the testing procedure in P.5.2.01-01.
However, in case of deviations during the outer sterilization of the syringe in blister tray the method according to Ph. Eur. 2.6.1 can be applied to test the sterility. Both methods are suitable to show sterility of the finished product and are listed as alternatives in the CoA.
(ii) As already mentioned in the response to Question 1 (i), the labeling, assembly, blistering, and outer surface sterilization (LABS) process may occur several months after the filling process, whereas the shelf-life of the DP starts after the filling process. The bulk PFS batch size comprises approximately 60,000 syringes, while the sterilization batch size was validated between 3,200 and 12,800 PFS. Each bulk PFS batch (parent) will therefore yield several outer surface sterilized (daughter) batches. To accommodate this aspect, it is intended to register a release testing approach where all tests, which are not affected by the outer surface sterilization process, are tested on bulk PFS batches (parent batch) only, especially since release specification acceptance criteria were derived from testing of Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial batches shortly after manufacturing, while labeling, assembly, blistering and sterilization of PFS can occur several months after filling. Such a release testing approach was approved and successfully introduced for the Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL in prefilled syringe.
The results from the side-by-side analytical comparison of bulk and sterilized PFS batches, presented in P.5.6.01-01, demonstrate that the labeling, assembly, blistering and outer surface sterilization processes for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in prefilled syringe for intravitreous injection (PFS) that is performed at Bayer AG, Berlin do not have a meaningful impact on any of the purity and potency quality attributes tested.
The data confirm that release testing for purity and potency of Aflibercept PFS before the LABS processes is appropriate for batch release and representative also for the product after LABS. The release test matrix in Table 2-1 of P.5.6.01-01 is therefore appropriate for maintaining control over the quality of the final drug product, i.e. the blistered and sterilized PFS.

d. Please attach validation data for the process after the change.

critical step parameters listed in the flowchart (Figure 2-1) of S.2.2.02-03; please clarify and
correct this.

two consecutive batches before and after the change.

of PEG-Mal and the Damoctocog alfa pegol before and after the change. If there are trends in
the data, please provide statistical analysis results.
h. The previously attached FDA approval letter did not list the process change items for this
application. If this is to be used as reference for review, please provide it.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( CTD section):
a. NOF Corporation is qualified to supply Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) for rFVIII-N
production at the Bayer Berkeley site. NOF has built a new manufacturing line. These
modifications are expected to improve product quality and do not have any negative
impact on the final product.
1. Change the temperature for starting addition of hexane in second and after
crystallization process.
• Current temperature at starting of hexane addition is 25–35°C.
However, the crystal is precipitated at 30°C, thus there is a risk for
precipitation before addition of hexane. Therefore, NOF will
change the temperature at starting of hexane addition in second and
after crystallization to 32–35°C. This change narrows the
temperature range, therefore NOF considers that there is no impact
for the quality of the product.
2. Change of the incubation temperature for second or later crystallization
process.
• Current incubation temperature is controlled by setting jacket
temperature to 25°C. However, the stability of the product is not
optimal at higher temperatures over extended periods. Stability can
be improved by lowering the incubation temperature. Therefore,
NOF will change the incubation temperature for second and after
crystallization processes to 5–15°C. NOF has confirmed that this
temperature change does not affect the efficacy of removing N-
SMP, as shown below. This change improves the quality of the
product.

3. Addition of in-process test for residual N-SMP after third crystallization
process.
• To obtain the product with the same level of impurities, NOF will
perform in-process test for residual N-SMP after third
crystallization process. The criterion for residual N-SMP is no more
than 0.020 (1H-NMR integration value, equivalent to 1.0 mol%). If
the test result exceeds the criterion, a re-crystallization step is
performed, followed by another in-process test. If the subsequent
test passes, two additional crystallization steps are conducted before
proceeding to the next manufacturing stage. NOF has determined
that this change does not impact the quality of the product, as the
impurity level remains consistent with previous standards.
4. Change of the temperature for washing with hexane
• Following the crystallization process, the current incubation
temperature for washing with hexane is controlled by setting the
jacket temperature to 25°C. For the same reason as previously
stated regarding product stability, NOF will change the temperature
for hexane washing to a lower range of 5–15°C.
5. Change of the drying temperature
• Current drying temperature is room temperature (below 30°C). For
the same reason as 2., NOF will change the drying temperature to
5-15°C. If it is difficult to remove the solvent, the drying process
can be performed at 15-25°C for up to 24 hours. The total drying
time should be within 100 hours.
6. Addition of in-process test for residual solvent in the drying process
• The effectiveness of removing solvent would be changed at DDS
Plant (Line V). To check the level of residual solvent, NOF will
perform in-process test for residual solvent after drying process.
The criterion for residual solvent is 80 ppm each (hexane, ethyl
acetate, acetonitrile, and toluene).

Question/Consideration:
Question 15
15. 3.2.S.3.2. MUTAGENIC IMPURITIES. Considering the use of p-toluenesulfonic acid and
low molecular weight alcohols (ethanol and methanol) in the synthesis of API, discuss the
formation and control of alkyl derivatives of p-toluenesulfonic acid, substances known to
be mutagenic.
Answer/Response:
Ethyl and methyl p-toluenesulfonate (tosylate) are class 2 compounds according to the
classifications in ICH guideline M7. They are potential by-products from the condensation
reaction between p-toluenesulfonic acid and the respective alcohol, ethanol and methanol. P-
toluenesulfonic acid and ethanol are employed in synthesis step 2b of the manufacturing process
of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance and methanol may be present as a residual
solvent in the transiently isolated and dried product of step 2a, BAY 2927088 crude.
Yet, the risk of the formation of both ethyl and methyl p-toluenesulfonate in step 2b is
considered negligible, as the following factors in that step impose substantial barriers for any
such unwanted sulfonic acid esterification, which are well documented in a review from 2015
[D. Snodin, A. Teasdale, Org. Process Res. Dev. 2015, 19, 1465−1485].
• Equimolar amounts of p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate and BAY 2927088 crude
are combined to form a salt solution of the drug substance, thus hampering the acid’s
ability to protonate alcohols, as is a prerequisite for alkyl tosylate formation. Moreover,
a superstoichiometric amount of sodium hydroxide, employed to generate and
crystallize the drug substance in its free base form in the later part of the process
diminishes the chances for such side reactions even further.
• A large fraction of 24% (w/w) of the solvent mixture comprises water, sufficient even
in unbuffered systems to reportedly put sulfonic acid esterification almost entirely to a
halt.
• Due to its nature as a (pH-shift) recrystallization, step 2b lacks any prolonged holding
or reaction times and operates at mildly elevated temperatures, thus further reducing the
likelihood of any notable alkyl tosylate formation.
Despite the above considerations, in order to further safeguard the absence of ethyl and methyl
tosylate in the final drug substance, the fate and purge of ethyl tosylate was investigated by a
spiking experiment. Of 10% of ethyl tosylate (with respect to the mass of BAY 2927088 crude)
which were added at the beginning of step 2b, none was detected in isolated BAY 2927088
purified intermediate (at a limit of quantification of 0.02%). With that purge alone, even 41%
of ethyl tosylate, which would be the amount resulting from the esterification of the entire
amount of subjected p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate, would be purged to no more than
0.08% of ethyl tosylate in BAY 2927088 purified, which is already below the acceptable limit
of max. 0.10%, in line with ICH guideline S9.
As for methyl tosylate, the fact that its precursor methanol may solely be introduced in small
amounts into step 2b as a residual solvent in BAY 2927088 crude, as opposed to ethanol
employed as solvent, renders its formation even less likely than that of ethyl tosylate.
In conclusion, the absence of alkyl tosylates in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug
substance is secured within step 2b, as neither the formation, nor retention of alkyl tosylates are
expectable, based on applicable literature precedence and experimentation.

Source:  S.2.4.10-01/ Control of Critical Steps and Intermediates - Additional
Information/BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance/ S.2.4.10_IQMS-
400119_1.0/new
keywords: genotoxic impurities; risk assessment; residual solvents; controls of critical steps and intermediates; synthesis

of impurities (ICH guides Q3A, Q3C, Q3D, M7 and their updates)), containing the
documentation related to the qualification of the DS-Pyridone impurity.
Answer/Response:
We would like to clarify that, according to Informative Item 1 of the amendment subject 12224
in SOLICITA website and in the ‘Subject Consultation’ section of the ANVISA website:
‘Informational Item 1: This amendment refers to situations where the impurities to be qualified
are present only in the API. If impurities or degradation products are also found in the finished
product (DP), please submit a single document using subject code 12380. The 12224 protocol
is not required.

Since DS-Pyridone is present not only in the API but also in the DP, the 12224 protocol is not
required.

Additionally, we would like to clarify that Bayer has not submitted the amendment code 12380
for the DP because in accordance with RDC 964/2025 (which establishes the general
requirements for conducting Forced Degradation Studies on medicines containing synthetic and
semi-synthetic active pharmaceutical ingredients and defines the parameters for the
notification, identification and qualification of degradation products in these products):

Art. 19 states that ‘A degradation product may be considered qualified when it meets at least
one of the following conditions:
I - the degradation product is a significant metabolite identified during studies in humans or
animals.

Considering that DS-pyridone is a major metabolite, it falls within the limits for toxicological
qualification as stated in “S.4.5.01-02 - Justification of Specification and Skip Testing” and,
according to the “NDA 219972 – Sevabertinib (BAY 2927088) – 2.6.6 Toxicology Written
Summary” (presented on 12/May/2025, expedient nº 0637512250, during NDA submission):
“The major human metabolite M1, BAY 3306572 (DS-pyridone), is also the major metabolite
in the rat and cynomolgus monkey. M1 is produced at high levels in monkeys. The metabolite
was also quantified in the 13-week repeated dose toxicity studies and in the reproductive
toxicity studies in the rat.” Therefore, we can conclude that DS-pyridone complies with Art.
19, item I of RDC 964/2025, which, makes amendment 12380 inapplicable.

In conclusion, we respectfully request the reconsideration of your request to perform the
specific amendment “12224 - RDC 359/2020 - Evaluation of the impurity safety limit (ICH
guides Q3A, Q3C, Q3D, M7 and their updates)” to GESEF, as it is not applicable to the API –

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Comment 8 (S.3.2):
Bayer provides the below risk assessment for worst case exposure of Long R3 IGF-1 to 
patient safety.
The maximum amount of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) in the drug was determined to 
be 0.02 ng/mg. This corresponds to a maximum amount of 0.02 µg when applying a dose of 
925 mg BAY 3401016 which would result from the loading and maintenance dose together. 
Basal levels of IGF-1 in serum differ significantly depending on age. IGF-1 values in the 
range of 100 to 400 ng/mL are reported normal for healthy adult subjects (Zhu et al. 2017, 
Chanson et al. 2016, Sabbah et al. 2021). Given a mean blood volume of 5 L per person, the 
total amount of IGF-1 in the circulation is in the range of 500 to 2000 µg / individual. It can 
be excluded that an additional entry of 0.02 µg IGF-1 by administration of the worst case dose 
of 925 mg should have an unintended pharmacological or toxicological effect. In the study,
after the initial loading dose of 700 mg, weekly administrations of 225 mg BAY 3401016 are 
planned thus even lower additional entry amounts are expected.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
3.2.P.5.6 (section 7.2, LoQ3): Please note that the internal action limit/alert limit of 10 CFU/10 
mL is not identical to the 100 CFU/100 mL described in EMA guideline 
EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015. Please adapt the internal action/alert limit of 10 
CFU/10 mL to 100 CFU/100 mL.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.5.6):
We acknowledge the authority’s comments and providing below the more elaborated 
justification for internal action limit (alert limit):
According to EMA guideline on the sterilization EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP 850374/2015, 
chapter 4.1.1 "For aqueous solutions, the limits stated in Table 1 (100 CFU / 100 mL) are 
acceptable for active substances and drug product formulations without further justification. 
Other testing regimes and limits to control bioburden at the defined level should be justified." 
With your answer you refer to the fact that 10 CFU/10 mL is not identical to 100 CFU/100 mL 
because of the lower testing volume of 10 mL compared to 100 mL.
Herewith we provide this required justification by explaining the rationale behind our testing 
and limit regime and demonstrate equivalence in terms of quality, allaying your concerns:
• The registered limit of 10 CFU/mL (sample volume 2x10 mL) has been approved 
worldwide since 2008 and was established prior the implementation of 
EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015. It is in accordance with Pharm.Eur./USP/JP 
requirements for terminally sterilized products.
• With the establishment of the EMA guideline in 2019, a historical review of bioburden 
data of terminally sterilized aqueous solution has been performed from 2019 to 2022 to 
evaluate the status and registered limits. The evaluation confirmed that the production 
process is under control, and a reliable contamination control strategy is in place. A very 
low rate of microbial contamination was detected, showing no growth in the vast 
majority of cases and retrospectively complying with the limit value recommended by 
the EMA.
• The internal action limit (alert limit) was therefore adapted in 2023 to 10 CFU/10 mL 
to establish an equivalence to the recommended bioburden limit of 100 CFU/100mL.
• If the internal action limit is exceeded, an investigation according to the local deviation 
process is initiated, which includes a detailed root cause investigation and an evaluation 
of bioburden resistance.
• Bioburden results are trended, and out-of-expectation results are evaluated and would 
lead to CAPAs.
• The Drug product solution itself was shown to not be susceptible to growth of the 
majority of microorganisms (IQMS-184374).
• Terminal sterilization of aqueous solution is performed with a 12-log overkill 
sterilization process, which is regularly validated by biological indicators to ensure a 
SAL of 10-6 (independent of the initial bioburden). Under the currently submitted 
bioburden limits of 10 CFU/mL and internal action limit of 10 CFU/ 10mL a SAL of 
10-6 was always ensured.
• Historical and on-going stability data confirmed the quality and sterility of the drug 
solution.
• We understand that with increasing sampling volume the detection limit decreases, and 
a statistically more accurate quantitative statement is possible. However, the lower 
sampling amount can make an equivalent quality statement, especially given a uniform 
distribution of microorganisms in solution and a usual read out of <1 CFU/10mL which 
corresponds to <10 CFU/100mL and is therefore safe and credible tenfold below the 
limit of 100 CFU/100mL. Unexpected microbial growth is thus also detected 
statistically reliably.
• For small filling volumes (e.g. syringes, vials), it is disproportionate to test a larger 
sample quantity for an in-process bioburden test (100 ml equals 50 2R Vials) than for 
the release test for sterility (sample size according to pharmacopeial requirements).

The results from comparability studies between Regeneron Rensselaer, USA(Regeneron 
Pharmaceuticals – USA)  and Regeneron Raheen, Ireland for the manufacture of the drug 
substance intermediate (DSI) are provided in section S.2.6.01-02. in line with ICH Q5E 
(Biotechnological/biological products subject to changes in their manufacturing process).
Comparability of DSI from the two manufacturing sites was concluded based on evaluation of 
Raheen DSI batches 8088100085, 8088100088 and 8088100089 with regards to:

results from Regeneron Rensselaer DSI
• Release testing against release specifications, historical min-max values and 
predefined comparability limits derived from historic Regeneron Rensselaer DSI 
release results
• Long-term stability results compared against the specification
• Accelerated and stress stability results compared against direct comparator batches of

and 8085900003; stress study comparator: 8088100071, 8088100072 and 
8088100081)

comparability was established in the aforementioned CTD section in line with ICH Q5E

requirements based on in-process control results, FDS release data including extended 
characterization and stability results.

from the historical manufacturing performance in the current FDS manufacturing site.

related to biological activity and biochemical properties were evaluated against more 
stringent comparability limits.

Question/Consideration: You are requested to provide a detailed narrative description of the drug product manufacturing process (10 mg, 20 mg and 40 mg tablets and 3.4% granules) that includes equipment types and process parameters such as blend speed, blend time, spray rate, temperature, coating parameters, etc.
Answer/Response:
Please note that the additional information to narrative description of the drug product manufacturing process for the tablet formulations as well as for the granules are for information only. The submitted IMPD-Q information reflects the current development status and was also submitted and approved by Health Canada for the other pediatric studies conducted by Bayer Inc. namely FIONA study (19920, e258048, Control#258048) and FIONA-OLE study (20186, e283357, Control#283357).

In the following section the additional information to manufacturing process for the granules are presented.

Manufacturing process BAY 94-8862 granules 3.4%
The drug product BAY-94-8862 granules 3.4% for oral suspension is currently still in the development phase and the process has not yet been validated, therefore changes to the process equipment and parameters are still feasible.

Screening and Optional Milling of Citric Acid Anhydrous and Sodium Citrate
All excipients are pre-screened through a sieve (e.g. Russell Finex 22). The excipients are sieved through a 500 µm sieve (e.g. Russell Finex 22).

Manufacture of Granulation Liquid
Hypromellose 5 cP is dispersed in purified water in bulk. BAY 94-8862 micronized is dispersed in the hypromellose dispersion by homogenization with a high-performance disperser (e.g. IKA Ultraturrax T65).

Manufacture of Premix
The components mannitol, methyl parahydroxybenzoate, microcrystalline cellulose, carmellose sodium, sucralose and xanthan gum are sieved and then mixed in the fluid-bed granulator.

Granulation
The premix is granulated with the granulation liquid in the fluid-bed granulator (e.g. Diosna CAP150) . Afterwards, the granules are dried. The granules are sieved through a 800 µm sieve (e.g. Russell Finex 22).

Question/Consideration: It was noted that black specks were observed during the stability testing of the granules. Therefore, you are requested to explain this observation (root cause analysis), its impact on overall safety/quality of the granules and the corrective/preventive actions taken.
Answer/Response:
The black particles were detected during stability testing and analyzed by a particle lab, which concluded that the foreign particles observed were technically unavoidable particles (TUP) from the excipient microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) and carboxymethylcellulose. A supplier statement is attached to our response (see Module 3.2.P.8.3, Supplier statement to TUP dated Oct-2023). It provides a summary of the sources, formation and nature of TUP in various excipients and concludes that “low levels of visible particles can result from the excipient manufacturing, handling or packaging processes, which do not look like the rest of the batch but pose no risk to formulation and patient safety”.

On every occurrence of TUPs – either during manufacturing, release of a batch or during stability studies – the occurrence was documented including the size of the particles. There is the potential that TUPs will be determined in upcoming batches as well as they are unavoidable.

However, based on the information provided above it can be concluded that there is no impact on the overall safety/quality of the granules.

Source: Supplier statement to TUP dated Oct-2023
keywords: Stability data; stability testing; packaging material, root cause evaluation; QC testing; Impurities

Question/Consideration:
Please provide the batch analyses of the drug substance using starting materials from different 
resources. The respective sources of the starting materials used in the drug substance should 
be indicated in the batch analyses, and the impact of different sources of starting materials on 
the quality of the drug substance should be discussed.
Answer/Response:
Regarding the origin and fate of impurities from the four starting materials involved in the 
synthesis of the Finerenone drug substance  (i.e. methoxy nitrile aldehyde, 2-cyano ethyl 
acetoacetate, 4-amino-5-methylpyridone and triethyl orthoacetate) it should be noted that the 
design and the stoichiometry of the manufacturing of the drug substance does not allow a 
direct relationship between the batch data of a starting material into the drug substance.
Methyl acetoacetate is an impurity of the starting material methoxy nitrile aldehyde from 
supplier Saltigo. This impurity in the starting material generates on the subsequent step 2 
ethylpyridinone the impurity methoxy-TH-naphthyridinone.
Mixed methyl/ethyl orthoesters and trimethyl orthoacetate are impurities in the starting 
material triethyl orthoacetate from supplier Evonik. These impurities in the starting material 
generate on the subsequent step carboxy-TH-naphthyridine the impurity carboxy-methyl-TH-
naphthyridine.
In the final API, this impurity carboxy-methyl-TH-naphthyridine is converted to  
rac-methylamido-TH-naphtyhridine and is safely controlled via the specification limit of max. 
0.15%.
Except rac-methyl-amido-TH-naphtyhridine, it is not possible to detect any supplier specific 
impurities introduced with the starting materials. As this is confirmed by now about 100 
different batches of finerenone, we cannot see any pattern of impurities that would justify to 
include the source of the starting material in API batch analysis.
Please note that the fate and origin of all organic impurities in all four starting materials have 
been evaluated with the outcome, that they are not critical, which means that they do not have 
an effect on the purity of the final drug substance. Details of this assessment are described in 
the current approved technical registration documents S.2.6.01 and S.2.3.03.
Independent from the control strategy, the stoichiometry of the manufacturing process does 
not allow a correlation of the batch data from one batch of starting material with regard to the 
batch data of one batch of finerenone micronized drug substance. This means that in general 
more than one batch of starting material is used during the manufacturing of one batch of 
finerenone micronized drug substance. In other words, one batch of micronized drug 
substance is manufactured from multiple batches of the starting materials methoxy nitrile 
aldehyde, 2-cyano ethyl acetoacetate, 4-amino-5-methylpyridone and triethyl orthoacetate.

In addition, it should be noted that methoxy nitrile aldehyde is supplied by 5 suppliers,  
2-Cyano ethyl acetoacetate is supplied by 4 suppliers, 4-Amino-5-methylpyridone is supplied 
by 3 suppliers and triethyl orthoacetate is supplied by 2 suppliers, see also the current 
approved technical registration document “justification of starting material” S.2.3.03.
If the criticality of the purity profile of a starting material needs to be assessed based on the 
batch data of the final drug substance against the batch data of a starting material supplier, 
there would be 5 * 4 * 4 *2= 160 possible combinations, which is practically impossible to 
manufacture in a reasonable period of time.
Therefore, the applicant considers that the batch data for all starting materials presented in 
technical registration document S.2.3.10 and the batch data of finerenone micronized drug 
substance presented in technical registration document S.4.4.01 are a sufficient data base for 
the evaluation of the quality of finerenone micronized drug substance for the proposed 
registration of the additional drug substance manufacturing site BAYER AG, Bergkamen.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
In accordance with Decision of the EEC Council No. 151 “On Approval of the Guidelines for 
Drawing up a Regulatory Document on the Quality of a Medicinal Product”, submit a draft 
regulatory document on quality, which provides for control of the indicator “Acid and 
peroxide value” in accordance with the Ph. EAEU, 2.5.1.25 “Solutions”, or provide a 
reasoned justification for the lack thereof.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
Bayer wishes to clarify that the drug product submitted for registration is a soft gelatine 
capsule, categorized as a single-dose solid dosage form (immediate release solid dosage form) 
in accordance with ICH regulations and the Ph. EAEU guidelines. The specifications for the 
Elinzanetant 60 mg capsule comply with the requirements specified in General Chapter 
2.5.1.10 concerning dosage form capsules.
Furthermore, we would like to emphasize that the control parameters for “Acid value” and 
“Peroxide value” are not applicable to solid dosage forms, as these parameters pertain solely 
to solutions (liquid dosage forms), as detailed in Ph. EAEU 2.5.1.25 “Solutions.”
However, it is important to highlight that we are conducting testing for Acid Value and 
Peroxide Value specifically for the lipid capsule fill mass excipients. These excipients—
Caprylocaproyl macroglycerides, Glycerol monocaprylocaprate, Glycerol mono-oleate and 
Polysorbate 80—are prone to oxidation and hydrolysis. Therefore, the Acid Value and 
Peroxide Value tests have been included in accordance with the Ph. Eur./USP monograph 
specifications for these excipients.
When Elinzanetant capsule 60 mg is exposed to oxidative conditions, the specified 
degradation product  N-Oxide is formed. The release limit for the known degradation product 
Elinzanetant N-Oxide was set to max. 0.5%, the shelf life limit for Elinzanetant N-Oxide was 
set to max. 1.0% This impurity is monitored in the drug product accordingly and the 
specification limit is covered by available toxicological data.
The implementation of this control ensures provides a more meaningful assessment of product 
quality compared to the peroxide and acid value, as it provides a more precise and sensitive 
assessment of oxidative stability.
Moreover, all-rac-α-Tocopherol is included in the capsule fill mass as an antioxidant, in order 
to protect the formulation against potential oxidation. The data on the all-rac-α-Tocopherol 
evaluation are included in Pharmaceutical Development – Drug product section  P.2.2.01 
(section 2.2.1.4)
In summary, the rigorous control methods applied to the excipients, in conjunction with the 
inclusion of a high-quality antioxidant, ensure the superior quality of Elinzanetant capsules, as 
demonstrated by the supporting stability data.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1: 3.2.P.5.1 Specifications
Question 1 a:
You stated that Calcobutrol is added in a 0.1% mol/mol ratio with regard to the total
gadolinium (bound in gadoquatrane) in the final formulation to chelate potential free
gadolinium, forming the gadobutrol complex. From drug product perspective, the
gadobutrol complex can be treated as impurity and therefore, it should be included in the
drug product specifications with appropriate acceptance criterion. Provide justification
for the established limits based on data.
Answer/Response:
Bayer respectfully does not believe that considering gadobutrol as a drug product impurity is 
appropriate for the following reasons:
1. Calcobutrol is added as a scavenger to complex any amounts of free gadolinium.
Therefore there is a fixed upper limit to the amount of gadobutrol that can be formed 
in the drug product defined by the amount of calcobutrol   Higher amounts are not 
possible, and amounts of free gadolinium that would exceed the amount of available 
calcobutrol are unlikely and would be detected during release testing.  Gadobutrol  
should therefore not be considered a degradation product for purposes of specification 
setting.
2. The amount of gadobutrol present in the product is several orders of magnitude below
the amounts determined to be safe for use as a drug product in the approved product 
Gadavist.  Since the amount cannot increase above a fixed threshold, setting a 
specification for gadobutrol adds cost and complexity while not providing any 
additional level of control over safety.
Further details on our rationale for not setting a specification is provided below.
According to the guideline ICH Q6A, section 1.2 a specification “establishes the set of criteria 
to which a drug substance or drug product should conform to be considered acceptable for its 
intended use.” and that specification “...should focus on those characteristics found to be 
useful in ensuring the safety and efficacy of the drug substance and drug product”. Moreover, 
under section 2.4 Design And Development Consideration, ICH Q6A list several examples of 
when “It may be possible to propose excluding or replacing certain tests..” on the basis of 
experience and data accumulated during the development of a new drug product, e.g. 
“extractables from product containers where it has been reproducibly shown that either no 
extractables are found in the drug product or the levels meet accepted standards for safety;”.

The maximum amount of gadobutrol that can form is limited by the amount of calcobutrol in 
the formulation, which according to the specification may not exceed 0.235 mg/mL and which 
in turn limits gadobutrol to a maximum of 0.291 mg/mL (0.11% in terms of the nominal 
concentration of gadoquatrane in gadoquatrane solution). Gadobutrol being the active 
ingredient of Gadavist®, a contrast agent that has been approved and marketed in the United 
States for over a decade, is qualified in humans at much higher limits. As discussed in 
P.5.6.01 the human exposure to gadobutrol would be at least 2078-fold higher when using 
Gadavist® compared to the theoretically possible amount of gadobutrol in Gadoquatrane 
solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection. Therefore, the level of gadobutrol cannot exceed 
accepted standards and a specification would not contribute to ensuring safety or efficacy.
Moreover, there is a clear negative correlation between the amount of calcobutrol and 
gadobutrol, and a positive correlation between the formation of Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane 
and gadobutrol in the formulation as can be seen from Figure 2-1 and Table 2.4 in P.5.6.01 
and as shown by experiments involving multiple sterilization cycles to force the formation of 
gadobutrol from calcobutrol. Thus, implicitly gadobutrol is controlled by the lower limit of 
calcobutrol and by the upper limits for Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane Isomer 1 and 2.

Bayer believes that the conversion of calcobutrol to gadobutrol is a situation comparable to 
the conversion of the active form of an preservative or antioxidant agent to its inactive form in 
such formulations. For preservative or antioxidant agents it seems acceptable to ensure an 
effective concentration of the preservative agent or antioxidant only by monitoring their 
assay, as is done for calcobutrol, whereas it is not required to also track the reaction products 
of the preservative or antioxidant, as the use of such compounds is generally recognized as 
safe. As the conversion path for calcobutrol is fully understood and leads to gadobutrol, a 
compound with a known safety profile, for that human exposure will always be far below safe 
limits when administering Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection complying 
with the specifications that Bayer proposed. An additional specification of gadobutrol is not 
considered relevant to the quality, safety or efficacy of  Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol 
Gd/mL for injection as it should not be decisive for the acceptability of the product.

Source:  P.5.6.01_022992844-02 (IQMS-265606) Justification of
Specification/ Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection 
(unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 1b
In addition to the possible degradation product ‘Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane’, it appears
that there are 2 more possible degradation products, i.e., Di-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane and
Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane. Both degradation products should also be included in the
specifications with appropriate acceptance criteria. Provide justification for the
established limits based on data.
Answer/Response:
It is accurate to state that Di-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane and Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane are 
theoretical degradation products that would arise from the twofold or threefold loss of 
Gadolinium from the tetrameric complex, however the formation of relevant amounts of Di- 
and Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane in Gadoquatrane solution can be excluded for the following 
reasons:
• 
The formation of Di-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane and Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane from the 
tetrameric Gadoquatrane (Gd4L) only occurs under very harsh acidic conditions (e.g. pH 
1.2, 37°C, 5 weeks incubation) by proton assisted dissociation, and it follows a stepwise 
dissociation encompassing the following reactions:
Gd4L → Gd + Gd3L → 2 Gd + Gd2L → 3 Gd + GdL  
(reference 1) 
At physiological pH and temperature, the proton concentration is low, and accordingly the 
dissociation of Gd3+ ions from macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agents could be 
shown to be extremely slow. See reference 1 at the end of the page 6. 
 
• 
Compared to the physiological conditions (37°C, pH 7.4, 15 days) used in reference 1, 
temperatures occurring during bulk manufacturing are typically not much higher than 
37°C or of only short duration and pH not lower than 7.2. Only for a short duration during 
terminal sterilization is the product exposed to higher temperatures.
(P.2.3.01, P.3.3.01) 
• The value of the 4 complex formation constants of Gadoquatrane should be very 
similar and the log k of about 20-21 clearly illustrates that thermodynamically the 
equilibrium clearly lies on side of the gadolinium complex. This means that the 
propensity for the formation of desgadolinium complexes will decrease if Gd3L 
increases as the back reaction to Gd4L will become more important. 
(S.1.3.01, section 7) 
• The release and shelf-life specification require the pH of the solution to be between 
6.9 and 7.9. 
(P.5.1.01 / P.5.1.02) 
• Given the stepwise dissociation, the low propensity to dissociation and the large 
excess of Gadoquatrane (Gd4L), Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane (Gd3L ) can reasonably 
be expected to be the most abundant of the des-gadolinium compounds. The 
maximum amount of Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane Isomer 1 and Isomer 2 allowed by 
the specification is 0.40% (in sum). Assuming that the same percentage of Di-Des-Gd-
Gadoquatrane (Gd2L ) forms from Mono-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane (Gd3L), this would 
correspond to only 0.0016% (in terms of the API), which is much lower than the 
reporting threshold. The amount of Tri-Des-Gd-Gadoquatrane (GdL) would be 
0.000064%. This consideration confirms that these compounds are not expected to 
occur in Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection above the reporting 
threshold (0.05%).
1 
Gruendemann, Frenzel, Lohrke, Boyken, Jost, Berger, Ulbrich, Pietsch, Investigative 
Radiology 2025, DOI: 10.1097/RLI.0000000000001195

Question/Consideration:
Question 3: 3.2.P.8 Stability
In section 3.2.P.8 Stability, we could not find information regarding ‘Freeze-Thaw
Temperature Recycling Study’ for the proposed drug product Gadoquatrane solution 0.4
mmol Gd/mL for injection. We acknowledge that you performed ‘Stress’ study at various
temperature for a storage duration of one month but this is not the same as freeze-thaw
temperature recycling study. The drug product should be subjected to at least 3 freeze/thaw
cycles in all container configurations, especially the prefilled syringes. Samples should be
exposed to 3 thermal cycles with each cycle consisting of xx hours at xx negative Celsius,
then ramp up to xx Celsius, then xx hours ramp down to xx negative Celsius. The thermal
cycled and control samples should be evaluated for all parameters listed in the
specifications. Also, data should be collected throughout the studies rather than only 2 time
points (at the beginning of the first cycle and the end of the last cycle).
Answer/Response:
Bayer acknowledges the Agency’s comments on the freeze-thaw temperature recycling study. 
This study was performed for Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL in 2 ml vial. The   
results demonstrate that the stability profile of Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/ml is not 
altered, see P.8.3.04.
Bayer utilizes the same plastic prefilled syringes across its entire contrast agents portfolio. A 
Temperature Recycling Study was conducted with Gadavist (NDA 201277) packaged in 
plastic prefilled syringes (7.5 in 10 ml) at the following conditions : -18°C/+25 C/60% RH; 4 
cycles. No significant changes to the tested parameters were reported including those 
assessing the functionality of the plastic prefilled syringes namely, sliding and static friction.
Based on the chemical stability of Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL observed after the 
freeze-thaw temperature recycling study in the 2 ml vial presentation and results obtained 
with Gadavist packaged in plastic prefilled syringes, Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL 
is stable under freezing/thawing conditions in all dosage forms.

Question/Consideration:
Question 17
3.2.P.8.3 Stability Data
The ASEAN Guideline on Stability Study of Drug Product is applicable for products in 
Singapore which is in the ASEAN stability zone IVb condition of 30C/75%RH.
The general condition for long term stability testing condition of the drug product is therefore 
30C/75%RH, to demonstrate the complete stability profile of the drug product under this 
storage condition. For drug products packaged in semi-permeable containers, additional water 
loss studies at 30C/35%RH is required.
We note the pre-filled syringes is made from cycloolefin polymer material and is not 
completely impermeable to water vapour.
Please provide the long-term stability studies at 30C/75%RH and water loss studies at 
30C/35%RH for the pre-filled syringes presentation.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 17 (3.2.P.8.3 Stability Data):
Bayer confirms that the pre-filled syringes presentation is a semi-permeable container. Please 
find water loss studies at 30C/35%RH for the pre-filled syringes presentation enclosed 
(P.8.3.11).

Regarding long-term storage conditions we would like to make reference to ICH Q1A, 
chapter 2.2.7.3. Drug products packaged in semi-permeable containers which states the 
following for long term storage conditions for aqueous-based products packaged in semi-
permeable containers: 25°C ± 2°C/40% RH ± 5% RH or 30°C ± 2°C/35% RH ± 5% RH.
Furthermore, the guideline states “Alternative storage conditions can be used, if justified.”.
While recognizing that the ASEAN Guideline on Stability Study of Drug Product is 
applicable for products in Singapore which is in the ASEAN stability zone IVb condition of 
30C/75%RH, it is our understanding that also the ASEAN Guideline allows for “…other 
storage conditions … if justified…”.
Taking this into account we would like to ask you consider the justification for storage 
conditions for Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL in prefilled syringe for injection as an 
aqueous-based product packaged in semi-permeable containers which is provided in the 
following.
Justification for long-term study design:
Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL prefilled syringes is an aqueous solution. As 
opposed to other formulation types (e.g. tablets, granules, emulsions, etc.) contact with water 
or water vapor or small changes in water content are typically uncritical or not applicable for 
aqueous solutions, where the API and excipients are dissolved in water anyways, e.g. no 
change in degradation pathways or kinetics is expected.
Moreover, in a closed container, the water vapor in the headspace will be in equilibrium with 
the aqueous solution and a relative humidity of close to 100% RH can be assumed for the 
headspace volume. Independent from the outer humidity, the only risk is a change in the 
concentration of dissolved materials (e.g. API, excipients) due to water loss, that could result 
in changes of test attributes as assay gadoquatrane, osmolality or pH. Given the smaller 
gradient between inside and outside the syringe, the water loss will be much lower at 75%RH 
compared to 35%RH. Using 30°C/35%RH is therefore a worst case compared to 
30°C/75%RH. Bayer is convinced that deriving the stability profile of Gadoquatrane solution 
0.4 mmol Gd/mL at 30°C/35%RH is adequate to demonstrate stability of Gadoquatrane 
solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for climatic zone IVb conditions as well.
Moreover, Bayer commits to include Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL in prefilled 
syringe for injection into the ongoing stability program at 30°C/75%RH. Furthermore, the 
next batch manufactured of Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL 5 ml, 7.5. mL, 10 mL 
and 15 mL in prefilled syringe will be put on ongoing stability at 30°C/75%RH.

Question/Consideration:
CMC Question 2
Supplementary Request Reason: Insufficient information and evidence for the master cell bank (S.2.3)
Supplementary Request:  ① Submit detailed information on the manufacturer of the master cell bank. ② Submit detailed data on the establishment of monoclonality for the master cell bank.
HA Comment : additional explanation is needed regarding point . ② Photos of the equipment used and the series of processes are required. While the photo for day 0 is confirmed in figure 2-2, request submission of photos for the subsequent days as well.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (S.2.3):
Part 1:
The MCB (master cell bank) was manufactured at the Bayer HealthCare LLC site in Berkeley, CA, USA.

Part 2:
Transfectant cell pool (CLI-724629) was single cell cloned by using a single cell printer (Cytena, Freiburg, Germany) into 384WPs (well plates). The device can eliminate droplets which contain more than one cell using parameters such as roundness and shape of the cells to prevent the deposition of cell doublets (or multiple cells) into each well. To further enhance the monoclonality, the 384WPs were imaged with Cell Metric (refer to Figure 7) before and after the single cell deposition into these plates. The printing process of the single cell containing droplet (CLI-732458, see Figure 8) is captured by pictures before, during and after printing (refer to Figure 9, Figure 10, Figure 11). In order to ensure all cells are in the focal plane of the imager, the 384WPs are centrifuged right after the single cell deposition prior to imaging, and again in the following days (day 0, 1, 4 and 7, see below) to track the growth of single cells into colonies. Only the colonies derived from a single cell on day 0 plus the respective single cell printer nozzle pictures from Cytena showing single cell deposition were considered for the top clones. Question/Consideration:
Question 1
The proposed starting material, Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide is not considered 
to be acceptable. In line with ICH guideline Q11 (EMA/CHMP/ICH/425213/2011) critical 
steps such as major chemical transformations which introduce essential molecular structural 
fragments should be included within scope. The manufacturing process should therefore be 
described from further back in the synthesis. 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline and tert-butyl 2,4-
dioxopiperidine-1-carboxylate could be suitable starting materials. The appropriate sections of 
the dossier should be comprehensively revised in order to reflect this change. It should also be 
noted that if a new manufacturing site is subsequently required, a revised QP declaration should 
be provided.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.2):
During development of the control strategy, the synthesis route of the Starting Material Phenyl-
oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide as shown in S.2.3.04 Flow Chart of the Starting Material 
was carefully evaluated. In this evaluation, no critical steps, potentially affecting the drug 
substance quality, were identified in the synthesis route leading to the starting material. The 
proposed starting material is synthesized from the two precursor 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline 
and 
tert-butyl 
2,4-dioxopiperidine-1-carboxylate 
forming 
Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-
carbothioamide by custom synthesis. Within ICH Q11 it is clearly stated that chemicals made 
from custom synthesis can be proposed as starting material if the selection is justified in 
accordance with all general principles for the selection of the starting materials. In addition, 
“significant structural fragment” is defined within the guideline only to distinguish starting 
materials from reagents, solvents, or other raw materials but major chemical transformations 
are not explicitly mentioned as a limiting factor.
Therefore, Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide was selected as proposed starting 
material from custom synthesis as the properties and excellent quality of Phenyl-
oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide are in line with the criteria from the guidelines 
EMA/454576/2016 and ICH Q11 as follows:
The proposed starting material Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide forms a significant 
structural fragment of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance. The material is a 
stable solid with defined chemical properties and structure, of excellent quality and fully 
characterized. The limit for any unspecified impurities of 0.10% already represents drug 
substance specification quality. Except for the specified impurities, no further impurities are 
observed above the reporting threshold of 0.05%. The analytical method is fully validated and 
selective to monitor further potential impurities next to the specified impurities (see also 
S.2.3.05 Control of Materials - Starting Materials - Test Procedure / Phenyl-
oxodihydropyridine-carbothioamide chemical).
The starting material manufacturing process delivered consistent impurity profiles. The 
specified impurities in those batches are well understood and characterized. Fate & Purge 
studies clearly demonstrate that no specified impurities in the starting material or their 
derivatives are present in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance (see also S.2.3.03 
– Justification of the Starting Materials and S.2.6.11- Manufacturing Process - Additional 
Information).
In addition, the starting material will only be obtained from qualified suppliers who 
manufacture the regulatory starting material according to the documentation cited in S.2.3.04 
Flow Chart of the Starting Material.
To demonstrate the consistent quality, the batch data for Phenyl-oxodihydropyridine-

Question/Consideration:
Question 2b
Characterisation of Hydrate 1 Mod. A using variable relative humidity (RH) - XRPD is required 
in order to understand the behaviour of this nonstoichiometric hydrate under different moisture 
conditions.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to 2b:
In RH XRPD experiments, the behaviour of the crystalline lattice of Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
examined under different humidity conditions (0 – 90% RH sorption and desorption in 10% 
steps) at a constant temperature of 25°C. In the sorption experiment, the substance (Hydrate 1 
Mod. A, Batch BXR9J78) was initially dried at 0% humidity and was present as Mod. IV at 1%
RH. This modification was retained up to 20% RH and converted in the next step to Hydrate 1 
Mod. A. This crystal lattice then remained unchanged up to 90% RH. This effect was also 
observed in the desorption experiment: At 20% RH, Hydrate 1 Mod. A was converted to the 
anhydrous form Mod. IV. These experiments clearly demonstrate the behaviour of Hydrate 1 
Mod. A in a kinetic experimental design. It cannot be directly correlated with the results of the 
storage studies, as these are based on a thermodynamic approach.
The overlays of the XRPD pattern of the sorption and desorption RH XRPD measurements are 
presented in S.3.1.01_IQMS_408096_2.0 BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance 
(Additional Information on Polymorphism), see Figure 3-1 and 3-2.
keywords: stability study and pharmaceutical form; Stability data; stress conditions; Elucidation of Structure and other Characteristics; Stability Indicating Test

Question/Consideration:
Question 2c
The DVS results should be further discussed. It is noted that although the sorption and 
desorption events are to some extent reversible, these curves are not superimposable, suggesting 
that there may be a change in the structure during the process, such as a phase transition or a 
change in the way water is bound. The results should be discussed in conjunction with the X-
ray single crystallography and variable RH-XRPD results.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2c:
The RH XRPD results perfectly match the data from the DVS measurements, which gives us 
information on the change of water amount in and on the sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. 
A). Dynamic uptake (sorption) of water was observed between 0 and 10% RH, followed by a 
flatter curve up to 95% RH and a total water uptake of 4%. The desorption curve follows this 
curve in the opposite direction, not without exhibiting a slight hysteresis. This is due to the fact 
that even in a variable non-stoichiometric hydrate, intermolecular interactions must first be 
overcome to remove the water from the lattice. This process, as well as the formation of the 
crystal lattice of the metastable Mod. IV, slightly delays the kinetics of desorption compared to 
sorption (see Figure 2 below).
keywords: stability study and pharmaceutical form; Stability data; stress conditions; Elucidation of Structure and other Characteristics; Degradation Products

Question/Consideration:
Question 2d
The transitions observed in the DSC thermogram (Figure 5-2) should be discussed.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2d:
Another technique for investigating the behaviour of Hydrate 1 Mod. A upon loss of water is 
through thermoanalytical methods. In this case, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and 
Thermogravimetry (TGA) techniques were used. The thermogram of the DSC measurement 
(see below Figure 3) of sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. A) initially displays a broad 
endothermic signal, indicating water release. This observation is confirmed by the TGA 
measurement, which describes a corresponding mass loss. Unlike stoichiometric hydrates, this 
stage is somewhat gradual and continuous, clearly highlighting the non-stoichiometric character 
of the hydrate. After the water release, the sample fundamentally has the possibility to become 
amorphous or to convert into any of the crystal lattices of the anhydrous modifications, thereby 
slightly stabilizing the lattice. In this case, a further small endothermic process is observed at 
higher temperatures, followed by a similarly small exothermic process. This involves the 
melting and recrystallization of one of the formed anhydrous forms, followed by the melting 
process of Mod. I. Compared to the previously described techniques, the DSC measurement is 
energetically non-neutral for the applied sample and can thus significantly favour 
transformation processes, especially at higher temperatures. This leads to the observation of the 
melting point of Mod. I, while the kinetic experiments (RH XRPD and DVS) did not result in 
a transformation of Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I. (see Figure 3).

Question/Consideration:
Question 2g
X-ray single crystal structure analysis shows a 4/5 stoichiometry and demonstrates weak 
interactions between the water molecules and the crystal lattice. For this type of compounds, 
water loss (which can happen relatively easily) leads to an ‘empty space’ in the crystal structure 
which may result in reduced chemical or physical stability. An overarching discussion including 
the data already submitted in the dossier and the additional data requested, should be provided 
to conclude on the stability of Hydrate 1 Mod. A. The conversion to an anhydrous form or other 
stoichiometric/nonstoichiometric hydrates as consequence of changes in temperature and 
relative humidity should be discussed.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2g:
The described results from RH XRPD, DVS, DSC/TGA, and stability studies have shown that 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A tends to convert into the crystal lattices of the anhydrous modifications after 
complete water loss. The formation of other hydrates was not observed in these experiments.
For the transformation of Hydrate 1 Mod. A to other solid state forms, both a kinetic and a 
thermodynamic approach can be pursued. Whereas the kinetically driven experiments initially 
led to the most metastable anhydrous forms, the thermodynamic experiments resulted in the 
thermodynamically most stable anhydrous form.
In kinetically driven experiments such as RH XRPD and DVS, the overdried Hydrate 1 Mod. 
A preferably transforms into the metastable crystal lattices of Mod. IV and Mod. III. These, in 
turn, show a strong tendency to convert directly into Mod. I. This was shown within the 
framework of the polymorphism study.
The thermodynamically stable Mod. I is also directly formed when Hydrate 1 Mod. A 
undergoes a long drying phase.
Thus, if there is a conversion of Hydrate 1 Mod. A to another solid state form, it ultimately 
leads to Mod. I.
The transition from Hydrate I Mod. A to Mod. I in the drug product has been assessed not to 
impact safety and efficacy of the drug (please see response to Question 2h).
keywords: stability data DS; stability study and pharmaceutical form; Degradation Products; Stability Indicating Test; stress conditions

Question/Consideration:
Question 2h
It should be fully justified how the assumptions that complete conversion of Hydrate 1 Mod. A 
to anhydrous Mod. I. results in a faster absorption rate were verified in the context of the cited 
exposure-response model. It should be demonstrated that 100% quantitative conversion of the 
polymorph is correlated to no significant effect on the efficacy/safety profile. The approach to 
inclusion of a test for polymorphism should be revised as appropriate in line with ICH Q6A.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2h (S.7, P.2):
It is acknowledged that there was a partial transition from Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I observed 
over stability for some of the drug product batches. To understand the impact in vitro of this 
phase transition, dissolution data were compared between tablets manufactured with BAY 
2927088 Hydrate 1 Mod. A, and tablets manufactured with Mod. I. Results showed comparable 
or faster dissolution kinetics for tablets containing Mod. I (Refer to section 
P.2.2.10_265402_1.0 BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10 mg-Pharmaceutical Development - 
Additional Information submitted in the original application S/N 0000).
Following the ICH Q6A Decision Tree #4, a potential impact on safety or efficacy of the drug 
product was assessed in vivo. Since the rate of dissolution is a key determinant of the overall 
rate of absorption, faster dissolution of Mod. I from in vitro dissolution testing would result in 
a faster absorption rate in vivo. A reference to the in vivo study can be found in section 
2.7.2 Summary of Clinical Pharmacology (chapter 2.3) submitted in the original application 
S/N 0000.
For the assessment, pharmacokinetic (PK) data from participants in study 21607 were 
evaluated. The absorption rate constant for each participant was estimated using population PK. 
This assessment included usage of the liquid service formulation as well as tablets covering a 
range for 90% of patients from very fast [15/hour] to slower absorption kinetics [3.5/hour]. 
Based on the absorption half-life, complete absorption i.e. four times the absorption half-life, 
is estimated to occur within 11 minutes for the very fast and 48 minutes for the patients with 
the slower absorption kinetics.
Impact on safety was evaluated through the effect of the individual absorption rate constant on 
the exposure-response relationships for all grade diarrhoea, grade 3 diarrhoea, all grade rash 
and dose modifications due to any treatment emergent adverse events (TEAE). Impact on 
efficacy evaluated the objective response rate (ORR) and best tumour response (BTR).
As shown in Figures 2-4 (ORR), 2-7 (all grade diarrhoea), 2-10 (grade 3 diarrhoea), 2-12 (all 
grade rash) and 2-14 (dose modifications due to TEAEs) in section 2.7.2 Summary of Clinical 
Pharmacology, no statistically significant (p<0.01) effect of the individual absorption rate 
constant and most relevant safety and efficacy parameters was found. As a result, even 
participants with a >5 folder higher absorption rate, which could result from a higher dissolution 
rate in case of a complete change of the solid state of the drug substance in the 10 mg tablet, 
showed a similar safety and efficacy profile compared to participants with lower absorption rate 
constants.
In summary, product batches containing only Mod. I instead of Hydrate 1 Mod. A can show a 
faster rate of dissolution in vitro. However, the difference between the solid-state forms seen in 
vitro does not translate to a difference regarding safety and efficacy in vivo. In other words, 
safety and efficacy of the drug are not impacted even if, in an extreme scenario, a complete 
change of the solid-state form of the drug substance would occur. Based on that conclusion, it 
is not considered necessary to add a test for polymorphism to the control strategy of the drug 
product.
