Question/Consideration:
Question 9
The compounds that undergo reprocessing should be identified and justified with data. The 
reprocessing method should be clearly described and the criteria for deciding when re-
processing can be performed provided in 3.2.S.2.2, in line with the Guideline on the chemistry 
of active substances, EMA/454576/2016.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 9 ( S.2):
According to EMA/454576/2016 guideline: Reprocessing of intermediates or APIs that do not 
meet specifications can be acceptable if it is performed using established methods that are part 
of the manufacturing process. This includes methods such as crystallization, distillation, 
filtration, and other similar physical or chemical manipulations. If reprocessing is frequently 
employed for a significant number of batches, it should be formally included in the standard 
operating procedures for the manufacturing process.
Therefore, we have introduced the possibility of reprocessing the product at any step in our 
manufacturing description. The reprocessing method for step 1 comprises repetition of the 
crystallization procedure of that step, as described in the respective 3.2.S.2.2.02. The 
reprocessing method for step 2 consists of repetition of the entire part 2b of that step. For steps 
3 and 4, repetition of the entire process is intended as the reprocessing method of the respective 
step. In all steps of the manufacturing process of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance, the criterion for reprocessing of a manufactured batch is a lack of compliance with 
any specified test item. As of 2025, no batch of any step manufactured according to the 
manufacturing process described in 3.2.S.2.2. failed to comply with any specified test item. 
Therefore, no reprocessing has been conducted for the above-mentioned reason up to this point.

Question/Consideration:
1) Documentation of compliance with medical device legislation, medical device class and
relevant international standards according to risk level, regarding the possibility of 
applying “Container Closure Integrity” tests instead of sterility testing.
Answer/Response:
The maintenance of the sterile barrier integrity, and hence the sterility throughout the shelf 
life is demonstrated during stability testing by testing the integrity of the primary package. 
The integrity of the package is tested with bubble test and the seal strength of the package 
with strip test.
The substitution of Sterility test with Container closure integrity tests during the shelf-life is 
in accordance with the guidelines or principles of both FDA and EMA:
In Questions & Answers of EMA web pages (Quality of medicines questions and answers: 
Part 2 / Stability - Endotoxin testing and sterility testing at the end of shelf-life) the following 
is stated:
“Sterility is part of the shelf-life specification.
Sterility testing should be performed at least at the end of Shelf-life, but it can be replaced by 
testing of the container closure integrity. Depending on the nature of the container, 
intermittent integrity testing might be envisaged, independent of whether the sterility testing 
is replaced or not.”
https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory-overview/research-development/scientific-
guidelines/quality-medicines-qa-introduction/quality-medicines-questions-answers-part-2
This approach is approved by FDA as well in Guidance document “Container and Closure 
System Integrity Testing in Lieu of Sterility Testing as a Component of the Stability Protocol 
for Sterile Products”.
FDA guideline states for example the following:
“Alternatives to sterility testing as part of the stability protocol, such as replacing the sterility 
test with container and closure system integrity testing, might include any properly validated 
physical or chemical container and closure system integrity test (e.g., bubble tests, 
pressure/vacuum decay, dye penetration tests or seal force tests, etc.). Such tests may be more 
useful than sterility testing in demonstrating the potential for product contamination over the 
product’s shelf life or dating period.”
Guideline on quality documentation for medicinal products when used with a medical device, 
(EMA/CHMP/QWP/BWP/259165/2019) states in section 5.2. regarding stability, on P.8 
stability studies for the integral medicinal product: 
Tests for identified stability-indicating CQAs (e.g. microbial quality, sterility, container 
closure integrity, content/potency and purity) over the shelf-life and in-use period, as 
appropriate for the integral medicinal product in question. If necessary, appropriate and 
scientifically justified alternatives for sterility (such as container closure integrity testing) may 
be used.
According to Bayer Oy’s opinion the assessments given in FDA guideline acts as risk 
assessment for the replacement of the sterility test with an appropriate container and closure 
system integrity test in the stability and during shelf-life, when it states that:
“Sterility tests for the purpose of demonstrating continuing sterility have limitations, with 
respect to the method's reliability, accuracy, and the conclusions that may be derived from the 
results. Because of the limitations of sterility tests described below, sterility tests are not 
recommended as a component of a stability program for confirming the continued sterility 
throughout a product's shelf life”
and
“Sterility testing has scientific and practical limitations, which are well known. Some of these 
are:
1. Sterility tests will only detect viable microorganisms present at the time of the test;
2. Viable organisms present at the time of the test can only be detected if they are capable of 
growth in the specified culture media;
3. Sterility tests may be subject to potential interference due to adventitious microbial 
contamination introduced at the time of testing, resulting in false positive readings; and
4. Sterility tests are always destructive of the samples tested and do not offer the opportunity 
to reexamine the same samples in the event of either positive or negative findings.”
and
“Container closure integrity tests may be more useful than sterility testing in demonstrating 
the potential for product contamination over the product’s shelf life. The advantages of using 
such container and closure system integrity tests in lieu of sterility tests in the stability 
protocol for sterile products include:
1. Such alternate methods may detect a breach of the container and/or closure system prior to 
product contamination;
2. Some of the alternate methods used to evaluate container and closure integrity can conserve 
samples that may be used for other stability tests;
3. Alternative test methods may require less time than sterility test methods which require at 
least seven days incubation; and
4. The potential for false positive results may be reduced with some alternative test methods 
when compared to sterility tests.”
Based on the above Bayer Oy considers justified the replacement of the Sterility test with 
validated Container closure integrity tests during shelf-life/stability studies of Mirena, which 
is a combination product regulated as a medicinal product

Source:  
Mirena Turkey_Declaration on Steriity test during Shelf-life
keywords: Container closure system; Sterility Testing; Stability data; risk assessment; Shelf Life ＆ Storage Condition

Question/Consideration:
Addition of recommended impurity limits to batch release specifications, as per the United 
States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) ANDAs: Impurities in Drug Products, ICH 
Q6A/Q3B guidelines
Answer/Response:
ICH Q6A guideline states in chapter 3.2.2 New Drug Products that “When it has been 
conclusively demonstrated via appropriate analytical methodology, that the drug substance does 
not degrade in the specific formulation, and under the specific storage conditions proposed in 
the new drug application, degradation product testing may be reduced or eliminated upon 
approval by the regulatory authorities.” 
 
This is the case for Mirena. Mirena is an old product, and it has been demonstrated in numerous 
stability studies covering a period of 30 years that levonorgestrel drug substance does not 
degrade in the product.  Therefore, impurity testing for Mirena at release is redundant and needs 
not to be performed. Level of impurities does not tend to increase even during shelf-life of 36 
months. At the end of shelf-life impurities level is near to zero, as reported for example in 
stability report P.8.3.01_02 with 36 M stability data.

Source:  Mirena Turkey_Declaration on Impurity testing
keywords: impurities; Degradation Products; Release Specification; Stability data; Shelf Life

Question/Consideration:
To remove the “uniformity of dosage units” specifications from the shelf life specifications, 
long-term “uniformity of dosage units” trend data and statistical analyses must be presented 
showing that the specification in question has not changed during the shelf life.
Answer/Response:
Uniformity of dosage units is not stability indicating property of a drug product. Furthermore, 
levonorgestrel assay of Mirena does not tend to decrease during shelf-life, as levonorgestrel 
API is a very stable substance. Similarly, level of impurities does not tend to increase during 
shelf-life. At the end of 36 months’ shelf-life levonorgestrel assay is at the same level as at 
release with no trends to downwards, and impurities level is near to zero at the end of shelf-life, 
and at the preceding stability study time points as well (ref. Stability report P.8.3.01_02 with 
36 M stability data).
Furthermore, Mirena, as a long-acting contraceptive product to be used for 5 years. Due to this 
Mirena is not actually “a dosage unit” in meaning of Pharmacopoeia monographs describing 
Uniformity of dosage units -tests.  Drug core of Mirena containing ca. 52 mg of levonorgestrel 
acts as a drug reservoir for the whole 5 years’ use period. The exact amount of levonorgestrel, 
whether it’s 48, 50 or 53 milligrams, does not affect the release of levonorgestrel from the IUS 
in use significantly. The drug core  acts  as a “reservoir” which must contain adequate amount 
of API (47 – 57 mg) to ensure continuous release of the API at predicted, appropriate rate for 5 
years.
In case of drug reservoir type product as Mirena, the daily dose (i.e. ca. 20 µg levonorgestrel 
released in 24 h) is determined by the release rate test, not by Uniformity of dosage units -test. 
Release rate test, in turn, is performed at every time point during the stability studies up to end 
of shelf-life. Therefore, according to the opinion of Bayer Oy, determination of uniformity test 
during shelf-life of Mirena is redundant based on the product classification as a reservoir type 
long-acting drug product.
ICH Q6A does not require performance of Uniformity of dosage units test during shelf-life 
either as it is stated in the guideline that this test may be performed in-process; but the 
acceptance criteria should be included in the specification. This means that according to ICH 
Q6A it is not even necessary to perform uniformity testing in release tests separately, as it is 
possible to utilize the results of in-process control testing as part of the release results.

Source:  Mirena Turkey_Declaration on Uniformity of dosage units test
keywords: Content Uniformity; Stability data; Shelf Life; assay; Release Specification

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Your current specifications propose to replace the existing HPLC and UV/VIS identity tests 
with Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) as a single identification method. The proposed 
NIRS method may serve as one identification technique; however, you must retain or 
implement a second, fundamentally different analytical approach that provides independent 
confirmation of identity through a different analytical method.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.5):
The identification of Darolutamide drug product by NIRS spectroscopy contains two 
fundamentally separate identification models incorporated to the NIRS method.
The first is based on Euclidean distance of identification model, where specific threshold 
value (0.277) has been determined with verified samples (positive identification) by primary 
HPLC method (HPLC 1). The identification model was validated with 27 independent 
Darolutamide drug product tablets (on concentration range 60 – 140%) and one negative 
challenge sample. The sample mold is specific for Darolutamide drug product tablet size and 
negative challenge sample was selected as being the same size and form. In addition, the 
negative challenge sample contains three Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API), which 
have similar functional groups and structures as Darolutamide. All known samples (positive) 
had hit quality values below the set threshold value (0.277) of the identification model. The 
negative challenge test sample had hit quality value of 0.717, well above the set threshold 
value for Darolutamide, and failed the identity test. Based on positive identification of known 
samples it can be extrapolated that the identification model (Euclidean distance) would reject 
a sample that is free of the Darolutamide compound.
The second identification is based on Mahalanobis distance of assay model (PLS algorithm) 
where specific threshold value (1.0) has been determined with verified samples (assay values) 
by primary HPLC method (HPLC 1). Assay model was validated with known samples of 
Darolutamide drug product and all Mahalanobis distance results were below the set threshold 
value (1.0).
In summary, the identification with NIRS method is conducted in two steps. At first samples 
need to pass the identification by Euclidean distance threshold (identification model). Second 
step is identification of assay model by Mahalanobis distance. Samples need to pass 
identification of both identification model and assay model to be released.

Source:  P.5.1.01-04 Release Specification / Darolutamide film-coated tablet 0.3 g
(#IQMS-406804; amended)

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Your application proposes to reduce the testing frequency for degradation products and 
microbial purity from every batch at release to testing at least one in every ten batches (skip-
lot testing). However, you have not provided adequate scientific justification or supporting 
data to demonstrate that this reduced testing frequency is appropriate and will not compromise 
product quality or patient safety. Provide comprehensive historical batch data and justification 
to support your proposal for skip-lot testing.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (P.5):
Additional supporting data for reduced testing frequency for degradation product and 
microbial purity are provided in 3.2.P.5.6.02, Justification of Skip Testing. Historical data 
comprising 115 batches from Jan-2024 through Dec-2024 on degradation products and 
microbial purity are presented in Table 3-1 and Table 3-3, respectively. Additional batch 
analysis for every tenth batch (n=33) throughout the production history, excluding the year 
2024, on degradation products and microbial purity are presented in Table 3-2 and Table 3-4, 
respectively. Degradation products of the drug product, consisting of Keto-darolutamide, any 
unspecified degradation product, and sum of all degradation products, remain below limit-of-
quantitation in the batches analyzed. Microbial purity, consisting of Total aerobic microbial 
count, Total combined yeast/mould count, and Escherichia coli, also remain below limit-of-
quantitation in the batches analyzed.
The product has a very low water activity (Aw) which greatly assists in the prevention of 
microbiological proliferation and ensuring the quality of the product. Based on extensive 
experience, the manufacturing process is robust, consistently producing batches within the 
specifications, as demonstrated by the provided historical data. Furthermore, the product is 
very stable as proven by the various long-term, accelerated and stress condition stability 
studies.
Therefore, implementation of skip testing for degradation products and microbial purity, 
performed at release on every tenth batch, is considered justified for the Darolutamide film- 
coated tablet 0.3 g.

Question 2-4:
Please provide relevant assessment reports or study data to demonstrate whether the TA strategy
and LOV monitoring are comparable (or if one is superior). Explain the rationale for classifying
LOV as an IPC parameter while the TA strategy is evaluated as a non-IPC parameter. Assess
whether the revised process control strategy can effectively monitor the manufacturing process.

Answer/Response:
Bayer response to Q2-4:
Chromatography Lift-off Volume (LOV) has previously been classified as a general (non-
critical) quality attribute by the applicant (see present / approved 3.2.S.2.4.01). It is employed
for the Protein A, Cation Exchange, Anion Exchange, Hydrophobic Interaction and Size
Exclusion chromatography steps as a potential indication of chromatography performance and
to signal potential deterioration of a given column.
As a result of a review of the control strategy, the single IPC parameter (LOV) to monitor the
column performance will be replaced by a more comprehensive and robust transition analysis
(TA). TA in combination with chromatogram review will be used outside of the IPC program
as part of a holistic strategy to continuously monitor column performance as part of the
company quality system.
The following long-term evaluation was performed and concluded that TA is equivalent or
more effective at detecting column deterioration:
Along with lift-off volume (LOV) monitoring, transition analysis (TA) data were used to
analyze the aflibercept lots processed between 25Jan2013 and 31Dec2020 (1,151 lots).
Regeneron routinely evaluates TA data with respect to unit operation-specific historically
accepted limits for non-gaussian height equivalent of a theoretical plate (NGHETP) and
skewness. Historical TA data were assessed for excursions from these historically accepted
limits. LOV and TA excursions were further categorized according to Table 2-4-1 to directly
compare efficacy and robustness of TA and LOV. A representative example from every
excursion category is detailed below.
[Includes Tables 2-4-1 to 2-4-5 and narrative examples showing TA had fewer false positives and identified all instances of column deterioration found by LOV, plus additional cases; also lists orthogonal IPC controls.]
The TA strategy is evaluated as a non-IPC parameter as multiple IPCs are monitored to ensure
proper column performance.
Table 2-4-5 provide a summary of the current IPCs that ensure adequate column performance.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3-3:
Please specify the involved DP strength affected by the SE-UPLC limit adjustment. It is
recommended to summarize the retrospective and monitoring stability data of multiple batches
related to the affected DP strength. Analyze and explain the reasons for the decrease in the SE-
UPLC main peak and the increase in aggregates, and justify the rationale for widening SE-
UPLC specification limit.
Answer/Response:
Bayer response to Q3-3:
The SE-UPLC limit adjustment is only applicable to Eylea 2mg vial and PFS.
As mentioned in the change description, this change is made based on difference in testing
results between SE-HPLC and SE-UPLC due to methodological variations, no change of
current SE-UPLC method and change of product quality.
The shelf-life acceptance criteria for purity test of Eylea 2mg was initially set using SE-HPLC
data and supported by toxicological and clinical data, which was approved at the time of NDA.
Bayer applied method change from SE-HPLC to SE-UPLC in 2018, the acceptance criteria
were not changed based on the method equivalence shown in the initial method comparability
study containing a limited release data set from ten DP batches tested in parallel by SE-HPLC
and SE-UPLC. After analysis of a more comprehensive data set comprising reference standard
and 70 pairs of DP release and stability samples, measured in parallel with SE-HPLC and SE-
UPLC revealed a offset in the test results using different methods. The shelf-life acceptance
criteria shall be adjusted.
Retrospective Analysis of Reference Standard Data
Reference standard results obtained at Bayer with both methods over a longer period of time
(SE-HPLC: 2017 to 2020; SE-UPLC: 2018 to 2020) reveal a 90% confidence interval for the
average offset of 0.34-0.37% (testing on reference standard RSVITV-5) for % aggregate (Table
3-3–1). A visual comparison of the aggregate results is shown in Figure 3-3-1. The % main
peak results display the same absolute offset in inverse direction.
Retrospective Analysis of DP Release and Stability Data
DP release and stability samples, which were tested in parallel with both methods (n = 70 pairs)
reveal 90% confidence intervals for the average offset of 0.29 to 0.34% aggregate and -0.25 to
-0.30% main peak (see Table 3-3-2).
With this statistical analysis with more data either from RS or from DP, Bayer found this
method variability between SE-HPLC and SE-UPLC. Therefore, SE-UPLC method offset of
0.3% should be considered to shift the SEC-UPLC limits at end of shelf-life to keep the
consistency with previous established method based on clinical study.
Attachment 10-8: P.5.6.01_018234200_06
Representative Stability Data in the Past Years
With this response, Bayer provided 20 batches of DP stability data for purity by SE-UPLC since
2018 for review(See Table 3-3-3 to Table 3-3-10).  There is no change of the DP quality since
all real-time stability data for SE-UPLC purity can meet the current shelf-life specification(main
peak≥96.5%, aggregates≤3.5%). We propose to adjust shelf-life specification with new SE-
UPLC limit  (main peak≥96.2%, aggregates≤3.8%) to reflect the observed methodological
offset between SE-HPLC and SE-UPLC.
keywords: HPLC-method; DP specification; shelf life specification; stability data; justification of specification DP

Since the Normative Document does not contain a method for determination of microbiological 
purity, in order to enable the medicinal product to be tested by the laboratories of the Republic 
of Belarus, the cover letter should describe this method (presence/absence of antimicrobial 
activity, sample preparation procedure with indication of sample quantity and diluent for each 
dilution, brief description of the methods and inoculation conditions on culture media; in case 
of membrane filtration, the rinsing solution and its volume per membrane should be specified). 
When submitting subsequent variations to the registration dossier in the Reference Country, 
this method should be included in the Normative Document.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
Please be informed that Microbial purity test is included in both Release Specifications and 
Shelf-life specifications section (P.5.1.01 and P.5.1.02), along with the acceptance criterion 
and the method used. It is also included in the Test procedure section (P.5.2.01).
Microbial purity:
The method for the microbiological purity is sufficiently described in the Ph. Eur. 2.6.12, 
USP <61> or JP 4.05 (harmonized method). The test for specified microorganisms are 
described in detail in Ph. Eur. 2.6.13, USP <62> or JP 4.05 (harmonized method) as well.
Procedure:
Weigh out not less than 10 g of the test product. Fill up with the appropriate amount of Casein 
soya bean digest broth (CSB) to obtain a 1:10 dilution (solution 1).
For TAMC prepare 2 petri dishes with each 1 mL of solution 1 and fill with 15-20 mL liquid 
Casein soya bean digest agar (CSA) (approx. 45°C). Incubate 3 – 5 days at 30 – 35°C. (Pour-
Plate Method of the Plate-Count method).
For TYMC prepare 2 petri dishes with each 1 mL of solution 1 and fill with 15-20 mL liquid 
Sabouraud-dextrose agar with chloramphenicol (approx. 45°C). Incubate 5 – 7 days at 20 – 
25°C. (Pour-Plate Method of the Plate-Count method).
For the test for absence of Escherichia coli, add 10 mL of solution 1 to 100 mL of Soya bean 
digest broth (CSB) to obtain solution 1.1. Incubate 18 – 24 h at 30 – 35°C. After incubation, 1 
mL of solution 1.1 is diluted in 100 mL MacConkey Broth and incubated 24 - 48 h at 42 - 
44°C. After this incubation step, plate an aliquot on MacConkey agar and incubate 18 - 72 h 
at 30 – 35°C.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
It is communicated that the change of lot size is a modification to the manufacturing process 
that is outside the parameters of the initial validation of the manufacturing process, so this 
Commission cannot only be notified, in addition, for the granting of the Sanitary Registration, 
lots submitted to stability study of a size of 133,000 tablets were presented, that is, pilot lots, 
for the change that require 1,500,000 tablets if it is an increase greater than 10 times the size 
of the pilot lot.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.3.2):
Bayer acknowledges the request and would like to clarify any misunderstandings as follows:
With the initial marketing authorization dossier submitted April 14, 2021 the manufacturing 
site Orion Pharma, Espoo was approved on March 30, 2022 with a batch size of 309 kg 
corresponding to approx. 500,000 tablets (as documented in P.3.2.01-01 Batch formula dated 
2018-11-12). For the support of the marketing authorization application at that time a stability 
report with pilot batches in regard to tableting and coating were submitted. 
As indicated in the respective stability report by footnote a does the pilot character of the 
batch size only refer to the less critical tableting and coating steps.
Excerpt of Registration stability report P.8.3.01:
The main manufacturing steps, which include the high-shear wet granulation having a 
significant impact on the key quality attributes of the final product was done in the 
commercial scale of 300 kg (appr. 500,000 film-coated tablets). From this 300 kg commercial 
scale tableting mass 80 kg were used for tableting and coating of the respective primary 
stability batch (e.g. 1748671). This 80 kg tableting mass portion of the 300 kg commercial 
scale calculates to a theoretical number of 133,000 film-coated tablets (300 kg = 500,000; 80 
kg= 133,000). (please refer also to  Annex 1).
Excerpt Master batch record registration batch 1748671:

Additionally, following ICH guidelines a Post-Approval Stability Protocol and Stability 
Commitment (CTD section 3.2.P.8.2) to put the first three commercial batches with 500,000 
tablets on stability was submitted in course of the NDA evaluation process (P.8.2.01-02 
submitted with response to COFEPRIS Official communication 213300404K0011).
The real-time results of these commitment batches (e.g. 1860672) - along with the data 
requested in below Question 2 - have been included in a variation to increase the shelf life of 
Nubeqal from 24 months to 36 months. Furthermore, this stability report (P.8.3.01 Stability 
Data) already contained the results for the increased batch size of 1,500,000 tablets as the 
threefold increase (309 kg to 927 kg) is considered a minor change which classifies for 
immediate implementation due to a batch size increase less than 10 times. Based on these 
stability data provided (for summary refer to Annex 3), the shelf-life extension was approved 
by COEFEPRIS early this year on 27 Jun 2025.
Comparative bulk quantities used for primary stability and commercial batch:
Batch 1748671 (133,333 tbl)
Usage: Primary stability
Batch 1860672 (500,000 tbl)
Usage: Shelf-Life extension

The minor impact of a batch size increase from 500,000 to 1,500,00 tablets is further 
manifested through the fact that the increase of the batch size is achieved by simply repeating 
the manufacturing steps up to the granulation and screening three times in a row.

Excerpt P.3.3.01:
Manufacturing site   
Batch size [kg]  
Sub-lotting
Espoo
309   
no
927   
Steps 2.1 - 2.5 as three sub-lots
Step 2.9 as two sub-lots
[…]
2.1 Mixing ; 2.2 Granulating; 2.3 Wet Screening; 2.4 Drying; 2.5 Screening (Granules); […]; 
2.9 Film-coating

No change, e.g. to the amounts weighed in or any other parameter of manufacturing process 
steps mentioned above was introduced. The increased batch size is mirrored by the bigger 
tableting mass (3 x 300 kg = 900 kg). This approach has the benefit that the granulation step 
which contains defined Critical Process Parameters (CPPs) is unchanged. (please refer to 
document P.3.3.01, and Annex 3 .
In conclusion, the originally approved batch size was always 309 kg (500,000 film-coated 
tablets). The increase to 927 kg (1,500,000 film-coated tablets) with its unaltered 
manufacturing principle is clearly below a tenfold increase and hence considered as minor and 
therefore an immediate implementation is considered as justified. The currently available 
results of the stability program (P.8.3.01) is provided with this response.

Question/Consideration:
Question 8
and does not include the acceptance criteria for water , disintegration, and hardness tests (it 
will be resubmitted with a clarification letter).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 8 (CTD section P.3.3, P.5.6):
Average weight, friability, resistance to crushing and disintegration time is tested from the 
tablet cores during manufacturing as an in-process control in the tablet compression step. 
Loss on drying is tested from granules as in-process control (please refer to document T.08.04). 
None of these in-process quality attributes are critical quality attributes for the final drug 
product. It has been demonstrated that within the proposed in-process control range tablets 
meeting the quality criteria can be manufactured, thus the absence of these tests in release 
specification is considered justified.
The test parameters resistance to crushing and water content were investigated during 
pharmaceutical development. Water content was found to increase when tablets are stored 
without humidity control (25 °C/80 % RH in open containers). The increase in water content 
was accompanied by a decrease in tablets hardness. High temperatures (60 °C and 80 °C) 
decreased the water content which was also accompanied by a reduction in tablet hardness. 
However, the values observed for hardness during long-term stability testing remain 
sufficiently high to allow for tablet handling and shipping. The increased water content of the 
tablets did not affect the formation of degradation products or the dissolution behavior of the 
tablets as demonstrated in stress tests and long term stability studies.
It is concluded that the test parameters are not indicative of product quality. They are therefore 
not included in the specification or stability studies.  
Please also find the additionally the justification for not specified tests, such as water content, 
resistance to crushing and disintegration in the enclosed document T.02.18.

Question/Consideration: 3.2.S.3.2: According to ICH M7, chapter 9.2 actual and potential degradation products likely to be present in the final drug substance or drug product and where the structure is known should be evaluated for mutagenic potential. The results and a description of the (Q)SAR systems used in silico are to be presented, as well as supporting information to conclude on class 4 and 5 classifications. Please submit this information for all impurities listed on tables 2-1 to 2-4 and 4-2 in tabular form with links to supporting information and the respective reports.
Answer/Response:
Mutagenic impurities described in S.3.2.01 have been assessed using two different in silico methods: a rule-based system (DEREK Nexus, version 6.0.0) and a statistical system (Leadscope Model Applier, version: 2.4.1). Combining both approaches, the classification was concluded taking also into account potentially available experimental data for the structure itself or structurally related compounds stored in the toxicity database VITIC Nexus (version 2.6.1). In addition, experimental Ames Test data were generated and described in the Toxicology Written Summary 2.6.6. Overall results are described in S.3.2.01.
Furthermore, the underlying original report entitled NON GLP Report Version 1: Structure-based assessment of potentially mutagenic impurities, Study ID: T104685-4, Report ID: PH-41284 as well as Derek Nexus Report for fluorobisiminocarbamate from 26. January 2023 (DEREK Nexus, version 6.1.0) have been provided as well.
Based on above mentioned documents, for all impurities listed in tables 2-1 to 2-4 and 4-2 of S.3.2.01, the information justifying the classification of impurities from tables 2-1 to 2-4 and 4-2 are presented in the table below.

Tabular classification/justification provided for impurities from S.3.2.01:

Question/Consideration: Please assign a value to the Gd-GlyMe-DOTA impurity reference standard according to the mass balance method.
Answer/Response:
The assay value of the Gd-GlyMe-DOTA impurity reference standard has been determined by mass balance according to the following formula:
A (%) = 100.0 – I – W – free Gd

A = Assay Gd-GlyMe-DOTA, as is
I = Impurities, sum (%)
W = Water (%)
Free Gd = free gadolinium
keywords: Reference Standards or Materials; impurity B; assay; Impurities; calculation formula

Question/Consideration: The assay of impurity is low, please conﬁrm whether the assignment is accurate.
Answer/Response: The assay of the Gd-GlyMe-DOTA impurity reference standard is 93.6%. Further components in the reference standard are water (5.7%) and organic impurities (sum of organic impurities: 0.7%). The reference standard complies to the specification of the drug substance synthesis intermediate Gd-GlyMe-DOTA. The high water content of 5.7% is due to the hygroscopic nature of the complex. Additionally, high purity is achieved through the control of organic impurities using HPLC, as well as monitoring free Gd levels. This control strategy ensures that the compound can be reliably used as a reference standard.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1a.
a. Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(b)
Reason for Supplement: 3.2.S.1.3. General Characteristics and 3.2.S.3.1 
Structure and Other Characteristics
1) Submission of detailed results of structural analysis on the non-quantified
hydrate form of the drug substance is required.
2) Molecular formula and molecular weight should be presented based on the
hydrated form of the drug substance.
3) Solubility data for non-polar solvents have not been submitted.
4) XRPD detailed numerical data (2Θ) for verification of the drug substance has
not been submitted and insufficient explanation of results based on the 
hydrated state.
Supplement Requirement: Please submit additional materials regarding the general 
characteristics of the drug substance considering the above matters.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1a. ( S.3.1):
a.1)
The drug substance in its crystalline form, Hydrate 1 Mod. A, has been fully characterized by 
thermoanalytical, spectroscopic, and X-ray diffractometric data (see S 3.1.01 Structure 
Elucidation and other Characteristics). In addition, the special non-stoichiometric character 
of this hydrate was clearly demonstrated by an X-ray single-crystal structure based on one 
single crystal. In the X-ray single-crystal analysis, it can be seen that the water molecules are 
randomly arranged between the layers of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) 
molecules. The crystal packing including the water molecules is shown in the following 
figures.

In addition to the interactions between the API molecule and the water molecules, 
intermolecular hydrogen bonds also occur between the water molecules, which supports the 
nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.

These different types of intermolecular interactions explain why this crystal lattice can 
implement varying numbers of water molecules without the actual lattice structure changing. 
The correlation of XRPD data to the X-ray single-crystal structure was achieved by 
comparing the calculated X-ray powder diffraction pattern with the measured X-ray powder 
diffraction pattern of the various batches of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.

Bayer acknowledges the Agency’s request to specify the amount of (x) based on the water 
content 1-4% specified for the drug substance and to include the range in the Korean 
application form.
Based on the nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A with an undefined 
ratio of sevabertinib to water, a value for (x) cannot be specified.
The water content in the DS is ensured by the manufacturing process and is controlled by the 
DS specification (refer to Specification S.4.1.01). DS batches that do not comply with the 
specification will not be used to manufacture the drug product (DP). However, converting the 
acceptance criterion for water into a specified value for (x) in the structural formula would not 
be a correct representation of the DS physical structure.
The dose strength of the DP is based on the anhydrate form, specifying that each tablet 
contains 10 mg sevabertinib. The latter information is critical for ensuring the safety and 
efficacy of the drug, as it directly relates to correct dosing and is independent of the water 
content of the hydrate. In light of these considerations, Bayer proposes that no value or range 
should be specified for the water content (x) in the local application form.

a.2)
It is well-known that two kinds of hydrate formation exist[1]:
Stoichiometric hydrates have a crystal lattice based on an exact water content with a well-
defined mole ratio of water molecules and given API molecule.
Non-stoichiometric hydrates have a continuously variable composition (due to the water 
content) within a certain range without any significant changes in crystalline structure.
Hydrate 1 Mod. A belongs to the second class described above and thus exhibits variability in 
water content. This must be described by the following structural formula:
C24H25ClN4O5 · x H2O

The variable molar fraction of water in the crystal lattice of hydrate 1 Mod. A makes it 
impossible to name a molar mass based on the hydrated form. The molecular weight can only 
be provided for the anhydrous form.
In 2008 Newman, Reutzel-Edens and Zografi[2] described in their minireview the way to 
evaluate sorption data of a given pharmaceutical active ingredient by using the following 
flowchart.

By using these criteria and based on the given definitions, Sevabertinib Hydrate (BAY 
2927088 hydrate) can be described as a non-stoichiometric hydrate, because its crystalline 
lattice is able to include variable numbers of water molecules without changes in the observed 
XRPD pattern and consequentially the crystalline structure. Water content in the drug 
substance will be controlled with the specification of 1.0 to 4.0 %.

a.3)
We have determined the requested solubility data of the solvents Tetrahydrofuran and 
Isopropyl acetate.
Solubility for Tetrahydrofuran was found to be 41.579 g/l (after 3 hours at 25°C).
Solubility for Isopropyl acetate was found to be 2.695 g/l (after 3 hours at 25°C).
This information is included in S.1.3.01 General Information - General Properties.

a.4)
Detailed numerical data (2Θ) of all technically relevant XRPD patterns of the different 
crystalline forms is provided in S.3.1.01 Structure Elucidation and other Characteristics / 
Additional Information on Polymorphism.
In RH XRPD experiments, the behavior of the crystalline lattice of Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
examined under different humidity conditions (0 – 90% RH sorption and desorption in 10% 
steps) at a constant temperature of 25°C. In the sorption experiment, the substance (Hydrate 1 
Mod. A, Batch BXR9J78) was initially dried at 0% humidity and was present as Mod. IV at 
1% RH. This modification was retained up to 20% RH and converted in the next step to 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A. This crystal lattice then remained unchanged up to 90% RH. This effect 
was also observed in the desorption experiment: at 20% RH, Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
converted to the anhydrous form Mod. IV. These experiments clearly demonstrate the 
behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A in a kinetic experimental design. It cannot be directly 
correlated with the results of the storage studies, as these are based on a thermodynamic 
approach.

The RH XRPD results perfectly match the data from the DVS measurements, which gives us 
information on the change of water amount in and on the sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. 
A). Dynamic uptake (sorption) of water was observed between 0 and 10% RH, followed by a 
flatter curve up to 95% RH and a total water uptake of 4%. The desorption curve follows this 
curve in the opposite direction, not without exhibiting a slight hysteresis. This is due to the 
fact that even in a variable non-stoichiometric hydrate, intermolecular interactions must first 
be overcome to remove the water from the lattice. This process, as well as the formation of 
the crystal lattice of the metastable Mod. IV, slightly delays the kinetics of desorption 
compared to sorption.

Another technique for investigating the behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A upon loss of water are 
thermoanalytical methods. In this case, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and 
Thermogravimetry (TGA) techniques were used. The thermogram of the DSC measurement 
of sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. A) initially shows a broad endothermic signal, which 
indicates the release of water. This is confirmed by the TGA measurement, which describes a 
mass loss. Unlike stoichiometric hydrates, this stage is somewhat soft and continuous, clearly 
highlighting the non-stoichiometric character of the hydrate.

After the water release, the sample fundamentally has the possibility to become amorphous or 
to convert into any of the crystal lattices of the anhydrous modifications, thereby slightly 
stabilizing the lattice. In this case, a further small endothermic process is observed at higher 
temperatures, followed by a similarly small exothermic process. This involves the melting and 
recrystallization of one of the formed anhydrous forms, followed by the melting process of 
Mod. I.
Compared to the previously described techniques, the DSC measurement is energetically non-
neutral for the applied sample and can thus significantly favor transformation processes, 
especially at higher temperatures. This leads to the observation of the melting point of Mod. I, 
while the kinetic experiments (RH XRPD and DVS) did not result in a transformation of 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I.

In summary, all available data support the assignment of sevabertinib hydrate as a non-
stoichiometric hydrate.

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1b. ( S.2.2):
ICH Q7 states the following: “Introducing an intermediate or API, including one that does not 
conform to standards or specifications, back into the process and reprocessing by repeating a 
crystallization step or other appropriate chemical or physical manipulation steps (e.g., 
distillation, filtration, chromatography, milling) that are part of the established manufacturing 
process is generally considered acceptable. However, if such reprocessing is used for a 
majority of batches, such reprocessing should be included as part of the standard 
manufacturing process”.
Therefore, we have introduced the possibility of reprocessing in our manufacturing 
description. It is not a routine operation. Although the reprocessing procedures for 
intermediates and APIs do not need to be documented in the quality assessment application, 
we mention it in the manufacturing description for clarity reasons. In line with the local 
guidelines, the reprocessing records for production batches will be maintained by the 
manufacturer and will be available for submission upon request by the MFDS.
In all steps of the manufacturing process of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance, the criterion for reprocessing of a manufactured batch is a lack of compliance with 
any specified test item. As of 2025, no batch of any step manufactured according to the 
manufacturing process described in 3.2.S.2.2. failed to comply with any specified test item.
Therefore, no reprocessing has been conducted for the above-mentioned reason up until this 
point.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1e.
e. Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(b)
Reason for Supplement: 3.2.S.3.2. Impurities
1) Methods and detailed validation results used for mutagenicity verification have
not been submitted.
2) Basis for the calculation of the purge factor for mutagenic impurities has not
been submitted.
Supplement Requirement: Please submit additional materials regarding impurities considering 
the above matters.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1e. ( S.2; S.3; S.4):
e.1)
The control strategy for genotoxic impurities is in line with the ICH M7 guideline, which 
states that the Threshold of Toxicological Concern (TTC) concept is not directly applicable in 
the case of a drug substance and drug product intended for advanced cancer indications as 
defined in the scope of ICH S9, which is relevant for BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance. In this case, impurities are controlled at acceptable levels for non-mutagenic 
impurities. During development, the risk calculations of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized 
drug substance were based on an acceptable limit of max. 0.10%, as this is the identification 
threshold for organic impurities in the ICH Q3A impurity guideline.
Mutagenic organic impurity 3-Chloro-2-methoxyaniline is analyzed in BAY 2927088 hydrate 
micronized drug substance (active substance) and in BAY 2927088 purified intermediate 
(step 2a) using HPLC method described in S.4.2.01 Test procedure. Data for 3-Chloro-2-
methoxyaniline are presented in Table 34.
The Batch data (S.2.4.05 Batch Analyses for Intermediates and S.4.4.01 Batch Analyses) show 
that “Any unspecified impurity” and therefore 3-Chloro-2-methoxyaniline was < 0.05 % in 
BAY 2927088 purified intermediate and BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance.

e.2)
A spiking experiment demonstrated that a quantity of 5.0% of 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline 
added to step BAY 2927088 crude (2a) leads to a content of 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline of 
0.06% in isolated BAY 2927088 crude. Adding 5.0% of 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline to step 
BAY 2927088 purified (2b) leads to a content of 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline of <0.05% in 
isolated BAY 2927088 purified. Thus, steps BAY 2927088 crude and purified combined 
render an overall purge factor of at least 8100 (cf. S.2.4.01 Discussion and Control of Critical 
Steps). This would result in 3-chloro-2-methoxyaniline values significantly below 50 ppm in 
the final drug substance, assuming a worst case of 5.0% starting value in step BAY 2927088 crude.
Below, detailed purge factor calculations of relevant potential mutagenic impurities (PMIs) in 
the starting materials of the manufacturing process of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug 
substance are described.
For the calculation of purge factors, reactivity, solubility and volatility of the impurities are 
identified as physicochemical parameters that influence the removal of the specific impurity 
in the manufacturing process. Under the given process conditions these parameters are 
assessed to define the purge factors for each individual operation. Basis of the determination 
of purge factors is provided in Table 35, as described by A. Teasdale et al. [3]

The total purge factor is obtained by multiplication of the purge factors of each operation and 
step. The concentration of the respective impurity before purging (concentration at start) is 
estimated in a conservative way. Purge ratios are calculated by division of the obtained total 
purge factors by the total purge factor required to ensure an acceptable level of the respective 
impurity in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance, i.e. 1000 ppm = 0.10%, in line 
with ICH guideline S9. A purge ratio of at least 1000 is considered to provide “sufficient 
confidence that the level of the impurity in the drug substance will be below the acceptable 
limit such that no analytical testing is recommended for this impurity. [4]

[Response continues with specific purge factor/ratio calculations and explanatory text for 3-Chloro-2-methoxyaniline, 1-Chloro-3-isothiocyanato-2-methoxy-benzene, and 2-Chloropropane, including tables and footnotes.]

Question/Consideration: Please provide the original API GMP certificate for the drug substance manufacturer, Bayer AG (Max-Dohrn-Straße 8, 10589 Berlin, Germany), which includes the name of this drug substance. If the certificate is available for query on an official website and only a copy is submitted, a declaration stating that the copy is identical to the original must also be submitted.
Answer/Response:
To fully address the request in Question 5 and to definitively demonstrate the GMP compliance of the drug substance manufacturing site, Bayer AG (Max-Dohrn-Straße 8, 10589 Berlin, Germany), for the micronization step of Sevabertinib, we are providing a comprehensive documentation package.
We, Bayer AG, herewith confirm that the substance name (HER2 / mutEGFR Inhibitor) given in the GMP certificate of Bayer AG (Max-Dohrn-Straße 8, 10689 Berlin, Germany) dated 31.05.2024 is an alternate name for the same drug substance BAY 2927088 hydrate and INN Sevabertinib. Reason for non-inclusion of the INN on the GMP certificate for Bayer AG (Max-Dohrn-Straße 8, 10589 Berlin, Germany) is, that the INN was not yet available at the time of GMP issuance.
To provide an official and unequivocal bridge between this certificate and the substance’s INN, we are requesting an official statement from the competent German authority, the Landesamt für Gesundheit und Soziales Berlin (LAGeSo), State Office for Health and Social Affairs Berlin, to officially confirm that "HER2 / mutEGFR Inhibitor" and Sevabertinib (INN) are one and the same substance.
To further corroborate this, we provide the following supporting evidence:
- Site Master File (SMF) of Bayer AG, Berlin: Please also refer to Appendix 2 of the site master file Berlin (p.9), which shows that HER2 / mutEGFR Inhibitor is equal to BAY 2927088.
- GMP certificates from the sites in Unified Quality System: Bayer AG is the originator of Sevabertinib (BAY 2927088) hydrate micronized drug substance (DS). At present, Bayer is the sole DS manufacturer at its sites in Wuppertal, Bergkamen and Berlin, Germany, as stated in the S.2.1.01 Manufacturer(s) document. All Bayer functions that are responsible for commercial manufacturing of the DS, fall under the same quality management system and are part of the same legal entity. In other words, all sites belong to the Bayer Group and have common access to all quality-relevant data regarding the DS. At present, DS synthesis is performed by the Bayer AG, Wuppertal and DS batch release is performed by the Quality Unit at the Supply Center Bergkamen. The GMP certificate from the synthesis site Wuppertal states “Sevabertinib (mEGFR/Bay2927088)”, from release and storage site Bergkamen states “mutEGFR/Sevabertinib”, which shows that Sevabertinib is equal to BAY 2927088.
For transparency and future file maintenance, please be informed that the INN “Sevabertinib” is expected to be updated on the Berlin site’s GMP certificate following the next scheduled inspection in April 2026 and the availability of the new GMP certificate for Bayer AG (Max-Dohrn-Straße 8, 10589 Berlin, Germany) is expected in June 2026. We will proactively provide this updated certificate, as part of our product lifecycle management commitment.
We are confident that this comprehensive documentation package, led by the official statement from the German competent authority, fully satisfies the GMP compliance verification requirement for Sevabertinib and provides a clear, unbroken chain of evidence. We believe this allows for the continuation of the review process without delay.

Question/Consideration: Based on the drug substance manufacturing process, it is possible that alkyl sulfonate ester impurities could be formed. Please provide a relevant evaluation.
Answer/Response:
Relevant alkyl sulfonate ester impurities that may possibly be formed in the drug substance manufacturing process are ethyl and methyl p-toluenesulfonate (tosylate). They are class 2 compounds according to the classifications in ICH guideline M7. They are potential by-products from the condensation reaction between p-toluenesulfonic acid and the respective alcohol, ethanol and methanol. P-toluenesulfonic acid and ethanol are employed in synthesis step 2b of the manufacturing process of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance and methanol may be present as a residual solvent in the transiently isolated and dried product of step 2a, BAY 2927088 crude.
Yet, the risk of the formation of both ethyl and methyl p-toluenesulfonate in step 2b is considered negligible, as the following factors in that step impose substantial barriers for any such unwanted sulfonic acid esterification, which are well documented in a review from 2015.
• Equimolar amounts of p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate and BAY 2927088 crude are combined to form a salt solution of the drug substance, thus hampering the acid’s ability to protonate alcohols, as is a prerequisite for alkyl tosylate formation. Moreover, a superstoichiometric amount of sodium hydroxide, employed to generate and crystallize the drug substance in its free base form in the later part of the process diminishes the chances for such side reactions even further.
• A large fraction of 24% (w/w) of the solvent mixture comprises water, sufficient even in unbuffered systems to reportedly put sulfonic acid esterification almost entirely to a halt.
• Due to its nature as a (pH-shift) recrystallization, step 2b lacks any prolonged holding or reaction times and operates at mildly elevated temperatures, thus further reducing the likelihood of any notable alkyl tosylate formation.
Despite the above considerations, in order to further safeguard the absence of ethyl and methyl tosylate in the final drug substance, the fate and purge of ethyl tosylate was investigated by a spiking experiment. Of 10% of ethyl tosylate (with respect to the mass of BAY 2927088 crude) which were added at the beginning of step 2b, none was detected in isolated BAY 2927088 purified intermediate (at a limit of quantification of 0.02%). With that purge alone, even 41% of ethyl tosylate, which would be the amount resulting from the esterification of the entire amount of subjected p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate, would be purged to no more than 0.08% of ethyl tosylate in BAY 2927088 purified, which is already below the acceptable limit of max. 0.10%, in line with ICH guideline S9.
As for methyl tosylate, the fact that its precursor methanol may solely be introduced in small amounts into step 2b as a residual solvent in BAY 2927088 crude, as opposed to ethanol employed as solvent, renders its formation even less likely than that of ethyl tosylate.
In conclusion, the absence of alkyl tosylates in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance is secured within step 2b, as neither the formation, nor retention of alkyl tosylates are expectable, based on applicable literature precedence and experimentation.

1 D. Snodin, A. Teasdale, Org. Process Res. Dev. 2015, 19, 1465−1485.

Question/Consideration: According to the technical data description, the semi-finished products after post-blending are tableted in batches (sublot). This tableting step does not involve continuous material in-feed and out-feed and should not meet the definition of a continuous process. Please clarify.
Answer/Response: The manufacturing process for Sevabertinib tablets combines both batch and continuous operations. Key steps such as feeding the pre-blend, roller compaction granulation, post-blending, tableting, and coating are integrated, with granulation and tableting performed continuously. Granules are divided into sublots after roller compaction, which are then pneumatically transferred for post-blending with magnesium stearate to create ready-to-press sublots. These sublots are moved by gravity from the blender to the tablet press hopper, where the sublots are merged. When sufficiently ready to press blend is present in the tablet press hopper the tableting process starts and runs continuously for the whole batch. The addition of new sublots to the hopper during the tableting means that there is continuous flow of material to and from the tablet press.

Question/Consideration: Please provide an evaluation of the impact on product quality when there are deviations in the excipient composition ratio.
Answer/Response:
The manufacturing process starts by preparing the pre-blend in batch mode where the drug substance, microcrystalline cellulose, lactose monohydrate and crospovidone are weighed for the whole batch in the amounts described by the P.3.2.01 Batch Formula. Thus, the composition of the granules is the same for the whole batch and no deviations in excipient composition ratio is possible during dry granulation. Furthermore, only one excipient (magnesium stearate) is added in the post-blending step. The amount of dosed magnesium stearate is monitored by the control system (see Chapter 4.1.1.1 of P.2.3.01 Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process for details). In the case of deviations in the specified amount of magnesium stearate, the corresponding granulate / post-blending sublot is flagged as non-conforming product, diverted from the process and discarded. Finally, one single lot of coating suspension is prepared per tablet batch and used for the entire tablet batch. Also here, the total amount of applied coating suspension is monitored and controlled by the control system. If any deviations in the amount of applied coating occur, the corresponding coating sublot is flagged as non-conforming product, diverted from the process and discarded.
In conclusion, the composition of all conforming coated tablets within one batch is quantitatively the same. This approach assures that only product is declared as conforming product, if the composition complies with the indented specification.

Question/Consideration: Upon reviewing the dissolution method development data for this case, although it can distinguish finished product batches with oversized drug substance particles that lead to non-compliant quality, most tests show dissolution results close to 100% at the setting dissolution time point. It is recommended to evaluate and revise the current dissolution specification for the finished product to better control product quality.
Answer/Response:
Alongside feedback from Rapporteurs on the dissolution method's discriminatory power, the Applicant received comments from the FDA, which requested a change to using phosphate buffer pH 6.8 with 0.3% SDS at 50 rpm instead of 0.5% SDS.
To address the FDA’s request, the Applicant adapted the dissolution method by reducing the SDS concentration in the phosphate buffer pH 6.8 from 0.5% to 0.3% SDS, maintaining a paddle speed of 50 rpm. Comparative dissolution testing of the 10 mg tablet formulation demonstrated comparable dissolution profiles when using 0.3%, 0.4%, or 0.5% SDS (Figure 18), confirming that the reduction in SDS did not compromise dissolution performance or product release characteristics while offering better discriminatory power between formulations. Please refer to updated P.5.3.21 Method Development - Dissolution.
This new method is detailed in the updated P.5.2.02 Test Procedure – Dissolution. For updated validation results, please refer to P.5.3.02 Validation of Test for Dissolution.
Additionally, representative clinical and process validation batches from both batch manufacturing process and continuous manufacturing process demonstrated consistent and comparable dissolution profiles applying the adapted more discriminative dissolution method, which is in line with the comparative dissolution data acquired in ICH M9 media, see P.2.2.02 Pharmaceutical Development - Dissolution Profiles. Updated batch analyses data are provided in P.5.4.01 Batch Analyses.
To evaluate the discriminatory capabilities of the revised dissolution method, the Applicant conducted dissolution studies examining the influence of several variables: drug substance particle size distribution (DS PSD), disintegrant (crospovidone) level, compression force, and sieve mesh size employed for pre-blend sieving.
For DS PSD, the discriminatory capability of the new method was similar to the prior approach, reliably distinguishing between batches with different particle size distributions (Figure 19).
Regarding compression force, the new method showed slightly enhanced sensitivity: it could more distinctly resolve dissolution differences between tablets compressed at varying forces (Figure 20).
Most notably, for crospovidone (disintegrant) level, the new method afforded significantly improved discrimination. This was evidenced not only by improved detection of dissolution variations with less disintegrant levels (50% of target amount), but also by the clear separation observed in batches prepared with no disintegrant at all, which exhibited markedly different dissolution profiles compared to those containing the standard level of crospovidone (Figure 21).
The results demonstrated that, with respect to sieve mesh size, the new method provided superior discriminatory power, clearly differentiating batches prepared with varying mesh sizes—a distinction that was less apparent with the previous method. Notably, mesh sizes of 0.3 mm and 0.8 mm were found to be favorable, supporting optimal dissolution performance, whereas employing a 1.0 mm mesh or omitting sieving altogether led to dissolution results below 80% at the 30 minutes time point (Figure 22).

Question/Consideration: According to the description of the impurity analytical method, the storage temperature for the sample solution is 15-25°C, but the solution stability validation for this method was performed at 2-8°C. Please clarify and update the technical data.
Answer/Response:
The test procedure (P.5.2.01 Test Procedure) gives the default parameters for the chromatographic conditions. These include an auto sampler setting of room temperature (15 – 25 °C). Effectively speaking, this setting corresponds to no active temperature control of the autosampler.
The validation of the test method for degradation products (P.5.3.01 Validation of Test for Assay and Impurities) showed that the level of DS-Pyridone increases if the test solution is stored at room temperature for several days. Such an increase is not observed when the solution is stored at 2 – 8 °C.
This effect is only relevant for test solutions that are not measured on the day of preparation, meaning that they are prepared first and then tested several days later. This procedure is however not the routine (or default) procedure in any given QC laboratory. Preparation and testing of the solution on the same day does not require the autosampler to be set at 2 – 8 °C; not controlling the temperature has no effect on the level of DS-Pyridone. Therefore, the test procedure refers to room temperature as the default option.
The test procedure may be changed to include 2 – 8 °C at the default for the autosampler. However, any interruption of the temperature control and/or excursions > 8 °C would correspond to a deviation from the test procedure, although a quality impact is not expected.
Furthermore, standard autosampler units may not be able to maintain temperature robustly between 2 and 8 °C, depending on local conditions.
The definition of default parameters in the test procedure instead of specified parameters means that the given conditions are applicable for routine use, which is correct regarding the temperature of the autosampler. It is however possible to apply more stringent conditions (e.g. an autosampler setting of 10 °C) without deviating from the test procedure.
The information given in the P.5.3.01 document is considered sufficient to interpret the default parameters stated in the test procedure (P.5.2.01 Test Procedure). In case the test solution is not tested on the day of use, it must be stored at 2 – 8 °C. On the day of testing, the autosampler can be used without temperature control but may be set to lower temperature if there is any concern regarding the level of DS-Pyridone or any unspecified degradant.
A change in the current test procedure is not considered meaningful for the test purpose.
Source:  P.5.2.01_2.0 Test Procedure / BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10 mg (IQMS-264697_2.0; unchanged)
P.5.3.01_1.0 Validation of Test for Assay and Impurities / BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10 mg (IQMS-263677_1.0; unchanged)

Degradation products:
One system suitability test can be used for several series of sample solutions. A new system suitability test is necessary after 5 days, at the latest, after converting the setup to another method, repair of modules in the setup or conspicuities in the chromatography.

Dissolution:

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Following the previous point, in said document are not declared all the tests regarding the ones 
that are on the approved dossier (P.5.1.902-01 version 1.1). Clarify and correct, in case there 
was a change, you must submit a procedure to update the specifications.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (P.8.3):
We acknowledge the authority’s comment and providing here below the clarification regarding 
the same.
In general, according to “WHO Technical Report Series, No.1010, Annex 10, 2018: Stability 
testing of active pharmaceutical ingredients and finished pharmaceutical products, Appendix 1: 
Examples of testing parameters”, appearance, assay and degradation products should be 
evaluated for all dosage forms.
According to “ICH Q1A (R2)-Guideline: Stability testing of new drug substances and 
products”, stability studies should include testing of those attributes of the drug product that are 
susceptible to change during storage and are likely to influence quality, safety and/or efficacy.
Therefore, Identification testing is only part of initial testing because identity is not susceptible 
to change during storage.
Extractable volume is not considered a stability indicating parameter for hermetic containers, 
therefore vials and bottles testing is usually only included in initial testing and at the end of the 
shelf life. Additionally, extractable volume will be tested at least once a year. However, as the 
content of API would increase or decrease in case the extractable volume would change, this 
parameter is also monitored via the content of API.
Sterility and endotoxins are not conducted at every time point because according to WHO 
Technical Report Series, No.1010, Annex 10, 2018, Appendix 1 it is not expected that every 
test is performed at each time point.
A sterility failure or the presence of bacterial endotoxins is unlikely to occur in the course of 
the shelf-life as long as the container integrity is given. In contrast to physico-chemical 
parameters, sterility and endotoxins are not influenced or changed by storage conditions or over 
time. Therefore, the determination at the beginning of shelf-life is sufficient. Additionally, both 
parameters are tested once a year and at the end of the shelf-life because the end of a storage
period is considered as the worst case for the integrity of the container. The result of sterility 
(and endotoxins) complying to the specification at the end of shelf-life confirm that the 
container was integer and sterility was given during the whole shelf-life.
Hence, there should not be any concern regarding the tests declared in P.5.1.902-01 and P.8.3.

parenteral use (ULTRAVIST 370) (#DocID;IQMS-173951/ amended).
WHO Technical Report Series, No.1010, Annex 10, 2018: Stability testing of 
active pharmaceutical ingredients and finished pharmaceutical products.
ICH Q1A (R2)-Guideline: Stability testing of new drug substances and 
products.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
It is noted that you did not provide the mixing process parameters (e.g., percentage of 
equipment occupancy, mixing speed, and mixing time) for the compounding process. Since 
your proposed commercial scale batches range from 30 L to 2500 L, we recommend that you 
provide the established mixing process parameters in a tabulated format for each commercial 
scale, including the equipment capacity. Provide the process parameters used in the exhibit 
batches and the batches that have already been manufactured to support the process 
parameters. Update Sections 3.2.P.3.3 and 3.2.P.3.4 accordingly.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.2, 3.2.P.3):

We acknowledge your request for detailed mixing process parameters and would like to 
provide the following clarifications.
The manufacturing process for Gadoquatrane solution was developed and validated with an 
automated process control system (PCS). The mixing parameters are dynamically controlled 
throughout the manufacturing process by the qualified PCS program, which adjusts 
parameters in real time based on the actual batch size. This ensures a consistent and 
reproducible mixing process without the need for fixed parameter values.
The adequacy of the mixing process, including the mixing speed and energy input, is verified 
during manufacturing through the in-process control (IPC) parameter "clarity of the solution". 
A theoretically longer stirring time does not have a negative impact on the quality of the 
solution. This IPC ensures that the mixing process achieves the intended outcome and meets 
predefined quality standards.
The mixing process and its parameters were evaluated during process development and 
classified as non-critical (see P.2.3.01 section 6.5). The completeness of dissolution of the 
drug substance was found to be independent of these parameters.
Furthermore, the evaluation of the minimum stirring speed has been determined to be non-
critical based on the high solubility of Gadoquatrane in aqueous media, including both water 
and buffer solutions (see S.1.3.01).

In the following more details are provided regarding mixing time, mixing speed, mixing 
equipment, process validation, in-process control and process parameters used in the exhibit 
batches:
• Mixing time:
The mixing time is not limited by process parameters, it is only limited by Holding time 1. 
This was tested and confirmed in a mechanical stress study.

Gadoquatrane solution was subjected to continuous shaking at room temperature for seven 
days using a shaker in horizontal orientation (c). The analytical samples (duplicate 
measurements) were taken at the start (Start), after 4 days (T4 days) and 7 days (T7 days). 
The results are shown below in Table 1
Table 1: Analytical data for mechanical stress study
...
The data clearly shows that even after seven days of shaking, no change in the measured 
product quality data has occurred.

• Mixing speed and used equipment
The mixing speeds are predefined within the technical PCS and are dynamically adjusted 
in real time based on the actual mass present in the mixing vessel during preparation of 
the bulk solution. This automated adjustment ensures that the mixing process is optimized 
and tailored to the specific batch size, thereby maintaining process consistency and 
product quality.
The mixing equipment utilized in our manufacturing process includes both mobile and 
stationary mixers, which differ in size, geometry, and material composition. These 
differences are fully accounted during process design, ensuring that consistent and robust 
mixing performance is achieved across all equipment types. The technical settings 
programmed into the PCS ensure that a consistent energy input is applied across the entire 
batch size range. This guarantees uniform mixing performance, regardless of the batch 
size, and ensures process reproducibility. The mixing speeds are limited to a maximum of 
500 rpm. During bulk manufacturing, it is also necessary to temporarily reduce the stirring 
speed to 0 rpm, for example, to check the clarity of the solution. The actual stirring speed
is based on the linear relationship for each piece of equipment according to the following 
formula:
𝒏(𝒘) = 𝒏𝟐−𝒏𝟏
𝒘𝟐−𝒘𝟏
∗𝒘+ [𝒏𝟏−𝒏𝟐−𝒏𝟏
𝒘𝟐−𝒘𝟏
∗𝒘𝟏]
...
Comprehensive process validation has been conducted to confirm the robustness of the 
mixing process across the full range of proposed batch sizes (30 L to 2500 L). Validation 
studies included the minimum and maximum manufacturable batch sizes, along with their 
corresponding maximum mixing speeds. These studies demonstrated that the process is 
capable of delivering consistent and reproducible results across the entire batch size range.

• Process parameters used in the exhibit batches
A comprehensive overview of the established process parameters is provided in Table 2. 
These parameters demonstrate the robustness of the mixing process and its ability to 
consistently produce high-quality product across the defined batch size range.
Table 2: process parameters used in the exhibit batches
...

In conclusion, no quality-impacting effects were observed during development, justifying a 
control of the process solely within the GMP Quality Management System. Therefore, it is 
our understanding that an adjustment of Sections 3.2.P.3.3 and 3.2.P.3.4 to include specific 
mixing parameters is not appropriate, as the manufacturing process parameters are 
dynamically adjusted due to the linear relationship specific to each piece of equipment.

Process/ Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection (amended)

the drug CGMP regulations (21 CFR parts 210, 211) and with the device quality system (QS)

specified in part 4 from the other of these two sets of requirements. Alternatively, you may 
demonstrate compliance with both the drug CGMPs and QS regulation in their entirety (non-

Holding times of ≤ 42 days for the ready-to-press mixture and ≤ 30 days for the uncoated tablets
have now been included in section P.3.3. In order to support these holding times, results for weight
per sample, average weight, friability, breaking load, disintegration and dissolution have been
provided. The holding times should be further verified by data on assay and impurities to assure
that no degradation occurs during the holding time.
Answer/Response:
To further support the holding times included in P.3.3.01_IQMS-418931_3.0, data on assay and
degradation products was added into P.2.2.10_IQMS-262224_2.0. This data demonstrates that the
holding times have neither an effect on the stability of the tablet core nor on the quality of the film-
coated tablet. Assay and degradation were analysed on the one hand after the holding time of the
tablet core and on the other hand at release of the batch after passing holding times for the ready-
to-press blend and the tablet core. Assay was still at 100% and the sum of degradation products
below 0.05%. Hence, it can be confirmed that the quality of the product is not impaired by the
holding times during manufacturing.
keywords: holding time; in-process control; assay and impurities; Degradation Products; Manufacturing Process and Process Controls

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
In accordance with guideline CPMP/QWP/4359/03, method description and validation should 
be provided for all analytical methods used during leachables studies.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (P.2.4):
With the introduction of the bromobutyl stopper, extractables data was initially prepared in 
exaggerated conditions of 50 °C / 72 h and 60 °C / 1 h using strong organic solvents, aqueous 
buffer solutions and water as extractant (see Table 1-2, Module 3.2.P.2.4.06 #022985386 v01).
Based on those observations, and since the stability study for Magnevist in vials using the 
alternative bromobutyl closure system had not yet been initiated, a simulated leachables study 
with actual Magnevist bulk solution as an extractant, in similar exaggerated conditions of 50 
°C / 72 h and 85 °C / 1 h was conducted  to achieve further, more realistic data of true leachables, 
and to confirm the safety of the new stopper material. In the simulated leachables study, even 
with the highly exaggerated extraction conditions, no compounds exceeding the study 
analytical evaluation threshold (AET) were observed. The AET was calculated using the 
strictest recommended safety concern threshold (SCT)/threshold of toxicological concern 
(TTC) of daily lifelong exposure for mutagenic compounds (1.5 μg/day) for parenteral 
products. TTC of 1.5 µg/d combined with the use of analytical uncertainty factors resulted in 
very conservative AET reporting for simulated leachables in Magnevist, which is used for 
significantly less than lifelong treatment.
Since no toxicologically relevant simulated leachables were detected even with these strict 
boundary conditions, stopper material was considered safe to proceed with a real-time stability 
study, which is on-going. A leachables screening study after 36 months testing and at the end 
of shelf-life 60 months will be performed. This will further confirm the safety of the container 
closure system for Magnevist. If any leachable compounds indicating toxicological concern are 
observed, a method validation will be performed in case required for confirming the safety of 
container closure system.
Details of the screening methods applied in the simulated leachables study can be provided if 
considered further complement the shared information.
Source:  P.2.4.06-01 Extraction Studies / Gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 0.5
mol/L in vial for parenteral use(MAGNEVIST) (#022985386; unchanged)
