Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Finished Product and Excipient:
More clarification on the proposed variations in the specification sheet (Section 3.2.P.5.1) and 
Manufacturing process (removing of manual assembly)
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( P.5.1):
Applicant acknowledges the agency’s question and confirm that the release and Shelf-life 
specifications and the associated analytical procedures for the drug product Mirena, 
Intrauterine delivery system, 52 mg have been updated. These updates are deleting certain test 
parameters and limits. We affirm that these changes have been made in alignment with 
regulatory guideline and will not impact the quality, safety, or efficacy of the drug product 

Change of the specification of drug product (Deletion of test criteria and limits). 

Sum of all impurities: Deletion of specification parameter from release specification  

• The synthesis impurities that are not potential degradation products are controlled in LNG 
release testing and are therefore omitted from the drug product specifications. The 
potential known and unidentified LNG degradation products above ≥ 0.1% reporting
threshold are included in the proposed Shelf-life test and in the corresponding stability 
study test results.  
• Levonorgestrel is inherently stable. The long history of Mirena IUS has verified that LNG 
remains virtually unchanged in the product manufacture, and during the shelf-life. This is 
demonstrated by comparing results of five MIRENA IUS drug product stability batches 
with the results for corresponding drug substance batches in document “Justification of 
Specification”. The results for drug substance batches in accordance with the Ph. Eur. 
method indicate for Mirena IUS actual low amount of the potential degradation products, 
from which the synthesis related impurities are omitted. Even at the end of Shelf-life the 
level of degradation products is negligible. This outstanding stability of LNG justifies the 
non-inclusion of the impurity test into the release specification.  

Deletion of specification parameter Ethylene oxide and Ethylene chlorohydrin from shelf life 
specification 

• Only parameters which have relevance with regard to product quality during the Shelf-
life, and therefore tested in stability studies, are included in the shelf life specification.  
• According to ICH Topic Q 1 A (R2) Stability Testing of new Drug Substances and 
Products parameters of the drug product that are susceptible to change during storage and 
are likely to influence quality, safety, and/or efficacy should be included in stability 
studies.  
• Ethylene oxide (EO) which is used as a sterilization agent for sterilization of the product is 
removed from Mirena IUS during the process, and therefore it does not exist anymore in 
the finished IUS product. It will suffice to determine the EO residues at release only, as 
they can’t increase during storage, and therefore are not tested during the Shelf-
life. Ethylene chlorohydrin (ECH) is also originated from the EO sterilization process, and 
it is removed during the aeration step from the product similarly as EO.  

Deletion of specification parameter Sterility from Shelf-life specification
“Sterility” test parameter will be deleted from Shelf-Life Specification as redundant because 
sterility test was replaced already in 2014 with container closure integrity test in stability 
studies.
The maintenance of the sterile barrier integrity, and hence the sterility throughout the shelf 
life is demonstrated during stability testing by testing the integrity of the primary package. 
The integrity of the package is tested with bubble test and the seal strength of the package 
with strip test.

Change of release and shelf-life specifications and associated analytical procedure of the 
drug product (Tightening of specification limits and Addition of new acceptance criteria 
and quality levels). 

Identity:  
Current "Identity (TLC)" test which is performed in connection with current TLC purity test 
will be replaced with two new identification test methods to comply with ICH Topic Q6A 
guideline. First new test method will be "Identity (LC)" test which is performed in connection 
with revised assay test and uses liquid chromatography technology. Second new test method 
will be "Identity (IR)" test which uses Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy - attenuated 
total reflectance (FTIR-ATR) technology).  
New acceptance criteria will be implemented in Release Specification, accordingly. 
Identification test parameter will be deleted from Shelf-Life Specification as redundant. 

Assay of system and Uniformity of dosage units:  
Current "Assay of system" test method has been optimized and revalidated. Extraction phase 
has been revised and two alternative liquid chromatography instruments (HPLC and UPLC) 
can be used. Acceptance criterion for "Assay of system" will be tightened from 47 – 58 mg to 
47 – 57 mg in Release and Shelf-Life Specifications.  Current "Uniformity of content" 
procedure will be replaced with USP <905> and Ph. Eur. 2.9.40 harmonized "Uniformity of 
dosage units" procedure.  
Current "Uniformity of content" test parameter will be deleted and replaced with new 
"Uniformity of dosage units" test parameter with new acceptance criteria in Release 
Specification. Uniformity of content test parameter will be deleted from Shelf-Life 
Specification because it is adequate to report only "Assay of system" test result in stability 
studies. 

Release rate:  
Current 1-point in vitro release rate test method (test point: Day 15) in 1.0 % 2-
hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (2-HPBCD) dissolution medium will be replaced with new 3-
point in vitro release rate test method (test points: Day 2, 5 and 8) to comply with 
requirements of relevant guidelines ICH Topic Q6A, USP <724> and Ph. Eur. 2.9.3. New 3-
point release rate test method has been modified from the current 1-point 1.0 % 2- HPBCD 
release rate test method used for several years. Dissolution medium remains unchanged, two 
alternative liquid chromatography instruments (HPLC and UPLC) and two alternative water 
bath shakers (rotating and reciprocal) can be used. Current "Release rate during 24h" test 
parameter will be deleted and replaced with new "Release rate, day 2, day 5 and day 8" test 
parameters with new acceptance criteria in Release and Shelf-Life Specifications. 

Breaking force:  
Current breaking force test method has been slightly optimized by increasing the length of the 
removal thread from approx. 2.5 cm to approx. 5 cm. Acceptance criteria will be re-worded to
clarify that acceptance criteria are for individual results and not for average. Acceptance 
criterion for one individual result will be tightened from min. 9 N to min. 9.5 N in Release 
and Shelf-Life Specifications to comply with EN ISO 7439 standard. 

Loading of IUS:  
New specification parameter "Loading of IUS" with its corresponding test method will be

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1a (S.2):
Please note that both Mod. IV and THF form 3 can be excluded for production batches for the following reasons:
The crystallization process was optimized through an extensive series of experiments to produce only Hydrate 1 Mod. A.
The only risk is the presence of THF in this step. However, the formation of the THF forms is prevented by precise temperature control.
The proven acceptable range (PAR) for step 3 of the manufacturing process has been established as 37-47 °C (S.2.4.01 Discussion and Control of Critical Steps).
The effectiveness of this measure is also demonstrated by batch data. Tetrahydrofuran was routinely monitored in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance in the development and validation campaign batches, and only traces (<0.007%) were found in BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance. The quality attribute residual solvent tetrahydrofuran is classified as a CQA and is included in the specification of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance with a specification limit of 0.072% for an ICH class 2 solvents. The presence of THF form 3 in the drug substance can thus be completely excluded.
The XRPD patterns of THF form 3 and Hydrate 1 Mod. A are also distinctly different (please see figure 1). For convenience reflexes are highlighted in the figure 1 to underline the differences. The most characteristic reflexes are at 9.0, 11.5, 15.5, 18.6, 20,1 and 21.0 ° 2Theta.

Mod. IV was found to be the most metastable anhydrous form in the polymorphism study. It cannot be handled under ambient conditions and would spontaneously convert to either Hydrate 1 Mod. A under the crystallization conditions.
Furthermore, Hydrate 1 Mod. A and Mod. IV can be clearly distinguished by their XRPD patterns (please see figure 2). For convenience reflexes at 8.4, 11.8, 12.8, 15.4, 20.2, 27.3, and 31.1 ° 2Theta are highlighted in the figure 2 to underline the differences.

Based on the argument above, a validation of the XRPD method to also cover Mod. IV and THF form 3 is not required.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Documents regarding the Drug Substance that comply with Article 7(2)(b) of the regulation.
c.
Related Regulation: Article 7(2)(b)
Reason for Supplement: In Section 3.2.S.4.5 Justification of Specifications, the toxicology study results (4‑week repeated‑dose toxicity study in rats and 4‑week repeated‑dose toxicity study in monkeys) presented as the basis for establishing the specification for the optical isomer showed toxicity at all tested dose levels, and therefore a NOAEL could not be identified. Accordingly, please provide adequate supporting justification.
Supplement Requirement: Please submit adequate supporting justification for establishing the specification for the enantiomeric purity test.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1c (S.4):
The opposite enantiomer (distomer) of sevabertinib is a stereochemical impurity arising from the synthetic process and is controlled by a validated chiral assay. In accordance with ICH S9 and ICH Q3A(R2)/Q3B(R2), this impurity is qualified based on its presence at trace levels in the GLP rat and monkey toxicology batches. In those batches the opposite enantiomer was present above the proposed commercial specification, which specifies enantiomeric purity with acceptance criterion of min. 99.5% (S.4.1.01 Specification).
The ICH S9 guideline permits the use of development batches to qualify impurities in anticancer drugs. It acknowledges that additional specialized toxicology studies on trace stereochemical impurities are usually unnecessary if animals and patients have already been exposed and no specific toxicity related to those impurities has been observed.
In the 4-week GLP toxicology studies, no additional or unforeseen toxicities were identified when compared to the 13-week GLP studies. The 4-week studies utilized the wrong enantiomer in the study medication (at conc. up to 1%), whereas the 13-week studies employed a formulation that was almost entirely free of impurities from the wrong enantiomer.
The S9 paradigm anticipates certain toxicities at pharmacologically relevant exposures and does not require identification of a NOAEL. Given that sevabertinib is an anticancer agent developed under ICH S9 principles, where particular toxicities at all dose levels are expected and determination of a NOAEL may not be reasonable, the absence of a NOAEL does not preclude impurity qualification.
Animal exposure at the STD10 and HNSTD and extensive patient exposure at the recommended 20 mg twice-daily dose with a manageable safety profile support the acceptability of the proposed control strategy and specification for the opposite enantiomer.
Source: S.4.1.01 Specification / BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance (IQMS-263650_3.0; unchanged)

(Tranexamic acid) as well as surgery. No further details about the nature and location

composition or any changes in our raw materials supply” has caused the event. As per 
Bayer's Product Technical Complaint (PTC) assessment, no product quality defect was 
identified. Therefore, the reported medical events are not indicative of a quality deficit 
per se. According to WHO-UMC criteria, the relationship between the drug and the 
event is likely given the listedness of the adverse event.

4. Case Number: 2025A039164
This spontaneous, serious and non-medically confirmed case was reported in Russia. 
The case involves a 41-year-old female patient who experienced hypertension 
(serious, listed), bilateral deafness (serious, unlisted), and hypersensitivity (non-
serious, listed) after taking Qlaira. Dechallenge information was not provided. While 
hypertension and hypersensitivity are known potential side effects, bilateral deafness 
is not listed as an adverse effect of Qlaira. The reporter suspected a product issue as 
she had been taking Qlaira for a long time and never had hypersensitivity reaction 
before. No further assessment of the product quality could be made as no information 
about the package or sample was provided. According to WHO-UMC criteria, the 
relationship between the drug and the events hypertension and hypersensitivity is 
likely given the listedness of the adverse events. However, the relationship between 
deafness and Qlaira is uncertain due to lack of adequate information.

5. Case Number: 2025A109110
This spontaneous, serious, and non-medically confirmed case was reported in Russia. 
The case refers to a female patient of unknown age who experienced hallucinations 
(serious, unlisted) along with intermenstrual bleeding (non-serious, listed), lower 
abdominal pain (non-serious, listed), herpes virus infection (non-serious, unlisted), 
urinary calculus (non-serious, unlisted), and crying (non-serious, unlisted) after taking 
Qlaira for endometriosis (off-label use). The case was classified as serious due to the 
medically important nature of the hallucinations. The reporter noted improvement 
upon discontinuation of the drug. The events of hallucinations, herpes virus infection, 
urinary calculus, and crying are not listed adverse effects in the Qlaira label. Since the case is not medically confirmed, the occurrence of the reported events 
remains uncertain. Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are not known to reduce 
immunity; however, ongoing living conditions can affect human immunity, making 
individuals susceptible to opportunistic infections such as herpes virus infections. 
There is evidence that COCs can contribute to the formation of urinary calculus. 
Urinary stones typically develop over a longer period, and the duration of Qlaira 
exposure remains unknown in this case, preventing a clear association from being 
established. 
Although depression and mood changes are listed events in the Qlaira label, the crying 
and hallucinations in this patient appear to be sequelae of the severe abdominal pain 
due to endometriosis. The reporter speculated that there might be a product quality 
issue or simple intolerance. No product quality defect was identified by Bayer's 
Product Technical Complaint (PTC) assessment; therefore, the reported medical 
events are not indicative of a quality deficit per se. According to WHO-UMC criteria, 
the relationship between the drug and the listed events is likely; however, due to the 
course of the disease, the availability of limited information, and the presence of 
alternative explanations, the relationship between the drug and the unlisted events 
remains uncertain.
Overall assessment of serious cases:
In summary, above five spontaneous cases were reported by consumers in Russia. Four of these 
five cases are not medically confirmed. The PTC review of the cases where batch numbers were 
provided found no quality issues in Qlaira badges. All cases were categorized as serious, either 
due to the nature of the events, such as intermenstrual bleeding, CVA, surgery, hypertension, 
hallucinations, deafness or due to hospitalization. Most reported events are listed and expected 
with combined oral contraceptive (COC) use. However, most of the cases provided limited 
information necessary to assess causal associations, such as temporal association, dechallenge, 
and rechallenge data. The relationship between unlisted events, such as bilateral deafness in a 
patient with hypertension or hallucinations in a woman with endometriosis, is considered 
uncertain. Overall, the events do not raise significant product quality concerns in any of these 
reports, and individual analyses do not identify a new safety concern regarding the use of Qlaira 
for the licensed indication of use.

Non-Serious cases
In the SOC Product Issue cases (155), the total number of non-serious cases amounts to 150 
(97%), which includes 66 categorized as listed and 84 as unlisted. The majority of the non-
serious cases were reported by consumers in Russia, totaling 146 out of 150. Among the 66 
non-serious listed cases, 14 are medically confirmed (MC) and 52 are non-medically 
confirmed (NMC). These reports are categorized as listed cases because the reported adverse 
events (AEs) are included in the labeling of Qlaira.
Additionally, there are 84 non-serious cases categorized as unlisted. Within this group, 6 
cases are medically confirmed (MC), while 78 are non-medically confirmed (NMC). This 
breakdown indicates that the majority of the SOC "Product Issue" cases are non-serious, with 
a significant number of them being non-medically confirmed.
The six non-serious unlisted MC cases primarily report occurrences of irregular bleeding (n = 
4), abdominal pain (n = 2), breast pain (n = 1), blood pressure increased (n = 1), and chest 
pain (n = 1), all of which are considered listed events. These cases are categorized as unlisted 
due to women feeling unwell corresponding to PTs: Feeling abnormal, Malaise, Asthenia, etc, 
which are not listed events in the Qlaira label.
The 78 non-serious unlisted NMC consumer reports predominantly detail irregular bleeding 
(n = 47), abdominal pain (n = 25), breast pain (n = 14), blood pressure increased/fluctuation 
(n = 10), swelling/edema (n = 9), depressed mood/depression (n = 5), and chest 
pain/discomfort (n = 4), all of which are listed events. These cases were categorized as 
unlisted because they reported at least one unlisted event such as headache (n = 10), hot flush 
(n = 4), endometriosis (n = 4), or various other events (≤2) including feeling unwell, fatigue, 
malaise, asthenia, somnolence, irritability, vaginal discharge, bloating, allergic reaction, 
ovarian cyst, acne, arthralgia, rash, anxiety, aggression, dizziness, palpitations, tearfulness, 
etc. The four consumer reports mentioning occurrences of endometriosis (unlisted) alongside 
other listed events provided very limited information for causality assessment.

Overall assessment of non-serious cases:
In summary, the majority of the non-serious cases were reported by consumers in Russia, 
totaling 146 out of 150. Among these, only 20 cases were medically confirmed. The unlisted 
cases were categorized as unlisted because they reported at least one unlisted event. Most of 
the reported events in these unlisted cases are listed and might occur during the use of 
combined oral contraceptives (COCs). The reported unlisted events were primarily non-
specific symptoms, provided limited information for causality assessment, or had an 
alternative explanation of the event such as in the case of endometriosis.
The PTC review of the cases where the product was traceable found no quality issues with the 
Qlaira. Overall, the reported cases do not raise significant product quality concerns, and 
individual analyses do not identify any new safety concerns regarding the use of Qlaira for the 
licensed indication.

expressed suspicions of counterfeit products specifically, while the remaining 111 cases 
documented adverse events and requested confirmation of product quality.
Among the 151 Russian cases, batch numbers were obtained for 104 reports, with samples 
collected for three cases, and photographs provided for two. In 20 instances, when consumers 
were contacted for additional information, they indicated no ongoing concerns regarding the 
quality or authenticity of the product. A detailed analysis of the scenarios surrounding these 
product issue cases is presented here, with all cases and their respective abstracts submitted as 
CIOMS I output.

Based on a thorough PTC investigation involving batch documentation, historical data, and 
any applicable samples or photographs, the following conclusions were drawn:
• The reports primarily pertained to products with shared packaging layouts for 
Kazakhstan and Russia, featuring bilingual packaging. This situation contributed to a 
higher volume of requests for confirmation of product quality and authenticity from 
Russian consumers. Notably, the delivery of Qlaira registered within the Eurasian 
Economic Union (EAEU), which included Kazakh language packaging, commenced 
on August 27, 2024.
• On 03-Dec-2024 Bayer published a statement on the local company website to inform 
stakeholders about the shared labeling available in the market. The statement was 
additionally submitted to the Health Authority (HA) and published on the HA website 
on 13-Feb-2025. On May 21, 2025, new package mock-ups were approved that 
excluded the Kazakh language (Russian only). Following these measures, there was a 
significant decline in cases requesting confirmation of product quality and 
authenticity.
• All cases for which batch numbers, samples, or photographs were available were 
confirmed as genuine Bayer products. No quality defects were identified in Bayer 
product in any of the investigations conducted.
The remaining four cases originated from Brazil, Colombia, Germany, and the United 
Kingdom, with no commonalities in terms of batches or reported events. No quality defects 
were identified in any of these cases.

Germany: One case reported a bee found alongside a tablet in a blister pack. 
Photographic evidence showed an intact bee next to the blister, indicating that the 
insect was undamaged and too large to fit within the blister cavity. An investigation of 
batch documentation and historical data found no quality defects attributable to Bayer.

Brazil: A consumer reported intermenstrual bleeding and requested confirmation of 
product quality, claiming that some tablets appeared to contain hormones while others 
did not. It is important to note that Qlaira is a combined oral contraceptive that utilizes 
a sequential dosing schedule. Each blister consists of 26 hormone-containing tablets 
and 2 hormone-free tablets with five different colors. This might have caused
confusion for the patent. No sample was provided for analysis. Investigations into 
batch documentation and historical data did not confirm any quality defects.
Intermenstrual bleeding is a recognized adverse event associated with Qlaira/Natazia 
use, as listed in the Company Core Data Sheet (CCDS), and is not indicative of a 
consequence of a quality defect.

United Kingdom: A report indicated difficulties in accessing the product; however, 
no quality or technical issues were identified, and no further investigation was 
warranted.

Colombia: A report of an incomplete blister indicated that a tablet was missing. The 
sample was received by the responsible quality unit, revealing that the upper row was 
empty, but all other tablets were present and correctly configured within the blister. A 
review of batch records, historical data, and retain samples did not confirm any quality 
defects.

Overall Conclusion:
The high number (97%) of product issue cases reported from Russia can be attributed to 
consumer confusion stemming from the presence of the Kazakh language on the product 
label, alongside Russian. This bilingual labeling led users to associate any adverse events 
(AEs) with potential product quality issues, despite the fact that most reported AEs were 
listed events for Qlaira use, even in the absence of any actual product quality issues.
Bayer actively addressed these concerns, conducting thorough investigations into the 
traceable products. No genuine product quality issues were identified in these traceable 
products, and it is assumed that similar conclusions apply to the non-traceable products.
Following the removal of the Kazakh language from the Russian label, there has been a 
dramatic decrease in the number of product issue cases from Russia. This further supports the 
notion that the spike in reports was primarily driven by confusion related to bilingual labeling.
A detailed analysis of the product issue cases and the aforementioned scenario indicates that 
no new safety concerns have emerged and the benefit-risk ratio of Qlaira in its approved 
indications remains positive.

regarding the comparative assessment of the old and new analytical procedures. 
 
Comparative analytical results between the old and new test procedures have already been

approved specifications and the newly proposed specifications. These data demonstrate that 
the updated test procedure yields results consistent with the historical performance of the

specification and do not alter the analytical principle, detection mechanism, or scientific intent
of the test. The revised methods have undergone full method validation/verification, and the 
results confirm that the updated procedures meet all required performance characteristics—
including accuracy, precision, specificity, linearity, and robustness.

its intended purpose and performs at least equivalently to the previously approved procedure.

critical quality attributes. 
 
Additionally, a formal declaration outlining the differences between the old and new 
specifications has been provided to ensure full transparency regarding the scope of the 
change. 
 
Given that (1) comparative batch level results are already included in P.5.4.01, (2) full method 
validation/verification demonstrates equivalence, and (3) the manufacturing process remains 
unchanged, we trust that the submitted data adequately address the requirement for 
demonstrating the suitability and equivalence of the proposed analytical test procedure.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3.
Regarding the hydrate issue in the basic properties of the drug substance, it is recommended 
to provide detailed research data and diffractograms to prove that XH2O in the molecular 
formula of the drug substance is a non-stoichiometric variable hydrate (channel hydrate?), for 
example, can variable humidity XRPD diffractograms at different humidity levels be provided 
to demonstrate that change in moisture does not affect the crystal structure? Alternatively, as 
mentioned in the submission documentation: “single crystal X-ray structure analysis 
performed on a crystal from recrystallization batch OLB 270722-10a indicated a 
stoichiometry of 4/5 and demonstrated these weak interactions.” Please provide representative 
diffractograms and data. 
It is recommended to specify the upper and lower limits of X in the molecular formula in 
the instructions for use.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 ( S.3):
It is well-known that two kinds of hydrate formation exist: [1]
Stoichiometric hydrates have a crystal lattice based on an exact water content with a well-
defined mole ratio of water molecules and given API molecule.
Non-stoichiometric hydrates have a continuously variable composition (due to the water 
content) within a certain range without any significant changes in crystalline structure.

Hydrate 1 Mod. A belongs to the second class described above and thus exhibits variability in 
water content. This must be described by the following structural formula:
C24H25ClN4O5 · x H2O

In 2008 Newman, Reutzel-Edens and Zografi [2] described in their minireview the way to 
evaluate sorption data of a given pharmaceutical active ingredient by using the following 
flowchart (Figure 1):
References：
[1] J.-R. Authelin, Int. J. Pharm, 303, 2005, 37 – 53
[2] A. W. Newman, S. M. Reutzel-Edens, G. Zografi, J. Pharm. Sci., 97, 3, 2008, 1047 -
1059

Figure 1: Decision tree for hydrate characterization
By using these criteria and based on the given definitions, Sevabertinib Hydrate 
(BAY 2927088 hydrate) can be described as a non-stoichiometric hydrate, because its 
crystalline lattice is able to include variable numbers of water molecules without changes in 
the observed XRPD pattern and consequentially the crystalline structure. Water content in the 
drug substance will be controlled with the specification of 1.0 to 4.0 %.
The drug substance in its crystalline form, Hydrate 1 Mod. A, has been fully characterized by 
thermoanalytical, spectroscopic, and X-ray diffractometric data (see S 3.1.01 Structure 
Elucidation and other Characteristics). In addition, the special non-stoichiometric character
of this hydrate was clearly demonstrated by an X-ray single-crystal structure based on one 
single crystal. In the X-ray single-crystal analysis, it can be seen that the water molecules are 
randomly arranged between the layers of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) 
molecules. The crystal packing including the water molecules is shown in the following 
figures.
Figure 2: Crystal packing of Hydrate 1 Mod. A
In addition to the interactions between the API molecule and the water molecules, 
intermolecular hydrogen bonds also occur between the water molecules, which supports the 
nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.
Figure 3: Crystal packing of Hydrate 1 Mod. A – hydrogen bonds

These different types of intermolecular interactions explain why this crystal lattice can 
implement varying numbers of water molecules without the actual lattice structure changing. 
The correlation of XRPD data to the X-ray single-crystal structure was achieved by 
comparing the calculated X-ray powder diffraction pattern with the measured X-ray powder 
diffraction pattern of the various batches of Hydrate 1 Mod. A.
Figure 4: Overlay of calculated and measured XRPD of Hydrate 1 Mod. A

In RH XRPD experiments, the behavior of the crystalline lattice of Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
examined under different humidity conditions (0 – 90% RH sorption and desorption in 10% 
steps) at a constant temperature of 25°C. In the sorption experiment, the substance (Hydrate 1 
Mod. A, Batch BXR9J78) was initially dried at 0% humidity and was present as Mod. IV at 
1% RH. This modification was retained up to 20% RH and converted in the next step to 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A. This crystal lattice then remained unchanged up to 90% RH. This effect 
was also observed in the desorption experiment: at 20% RH, Hydrate 1 Mod. A was 
converted to the anhydrous form Mod. IV. These experiments clearly demonstrate the 
behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A in a kinetic experimental design. It cannot be directly 
correlated with the results of the storage studies, as these are based on a thermodynamic 
approach.
Figure 5: Overlay of XRPD patterns, RH XRPD Sorption
Figure 6: Overlay of XRPD patterns, RH XRPD Desorption

The RH XRPD results perfectly match the data from the DVS measurements, which gives us 
information on the change of water amount in and on the sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. 
A). Dynamic uptake (sorption) of water was observed between 0 and 10% RH, followed by a 
flatter curve up to 95% RH and a total water uptake of 4%. The desorption curve follows this 
curve in the opposite direction, not without exhibiting a slight hysteresis. This is due to the 
fact that even in a variable non-stoichiometric hydrate, intermolecular interactions must first 
be overcome to remove the water from the lattice. This process, as well as the formation of 
the crystal lattice of the metastable Mod. IV, slightly delays the kinetics of desorption 
compared to sorption.
Figure 7: DVS Isotherm Plot

Another technique for investigating the behavior of Hydrate 1 Mod. A upon loss of water is 
thermoanalytical methods. In this case, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and 
Thermogravimetry (TGA) techniques were used. The thermogram of the DSC measurement 
of sample BXR9J78 (Hydrate 1 Mod. A) initially shows a broad endothermic signal, which 
indicates the release of water. This is confirmed by the TGA measurement, which describes a 
mass loss. Unlike stoichiometric hydrates, this stage is somewhat soft and continuous, clearly 
highlighting the non-stoichiometric character of the hydrate.
After the water release, the sample fundamentally has the possibility to become amorphous or 
to convert into any of the crystal lattices of the anhydrous modifications, thereby slightly 
stabilizing the lattice. In this case, a further small endothermic process is observed at higher 
temperatures, followed by a similarly small exothermic process. This involves the melting and 
recrystallization of one of the formed anhydrous forms, followed by the melting process of 
Mod. I.
Compared to the previously described techniques, the DSC measurement is energetically non-
neutral for the applied sample and can thus significantly favor transformation processes, 
especially at higher temperatures. This leads to the observation of the melting point of Mod. I, 
while the kinetic experiments (RH XRPD and DVS) did not result in a transformation of 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I.
Figure 8: DSC and TGA thermogram of Hydrate 1 Mod. A

Batch data for sevabertinib hydrate with different water content and the corresponding 
XRPDs are shown in Table 1 and Figure 9 through to Figure 16. These data demonstrate that 
the water content can vary widely without a change in the crystalline lattice, supporting the 
assignment of sevabertinib hydrate as a non-stoichiometric hydrate. While the XRPD pattern 
in Figure 9 is consistent with the assignment of sevabertinib hydrate as hydrate 1 Mod. A, the 
diffractogram shows broader signals and a diminished signal-to-noise ratio as compared to the 
other figures. This is consistent with the non-stoichiometric hydrate nature of sevabertinib 
where the minimum amount of water leads to an emerging destabilization of the crystal 
lattice.
Table 1: Water amount of Sevabertinib Hydrate
(Figures 9–16: XRPD of Sevabertinib Hydrate Batches)

In summary, all available data support the assignment of sevabertinib hydrate as a non-
stoichiometric hydrate.

Based on the nonstoichiometric, variable character of Hydrate 1 Mod. A with an undefined 
ratio of sevabertinib to water, a value for (x) cannot be specified.
Water content (%) and the hydration number x represent fundamentally different concepts and 
physical dimensions. Water content determined by Karl Fischer titration is a mass‑based 
parameter (w/w%) that reflects the total amount of water present, including surface‑adsorbed 
water, pore water, and lattice‑associated water. In contrast, the hydration number x is a 
crystallographic concept describing the molar ratio (mol/mol) of structurally defined water 
molecules within the crystal lattice per mole of the drug substance.
As the lattice occupancy of water can vary with the environmental equilibrium state rather 
than remaining within a specification‑worthy interval, it is not only inappropriate to define a 
fixed hydration number x, but also scientifically unsound to provide a “range” for x.
Converting a mass‑based water content to a structural x value—fixed or ranged—does not 
accurately represent the crystal structure and may lead to conceptual misunderstanding.

Question/Consideration:
Question 4
Given the significant crystal transformation in the drug product, please further clarify:
(1) Why was Hydrate 1 Mod A selected as the form for commercial development, and why
were other forms such as the anhydrous form or more stable forms not chosen? Please 
provide specific solubility data of Modification I (Mod I) and Hydrate I Mod A under 
different pH conditions.
(2) Please provide the crystal form testing diffractogram at the end of shelf life for all
registration batches (DP), and attempt to analyze the overall trend of drug product 
polymorphic transformation from the perspective of CMC control.
(3) Please provide the formulation information of the liquid service formulation (LSF) used
in the study 21607 subject's pharmacokinetics data, specify the type and amount of 
excipients, whether the drug substance is completely dissolved, and specify the batch 
number and crystal form determination of the tablets used in the study (whether it is pure 
hydrate 1 crystal form A), which are used to demonstrate the bridgebility between crystal 
form 1 and target crystal form A.
Based on this, please further elaborate in detail why it can be concluded that the absorption 
rate of Mod I in vivo is necessarily higher, given its greater solubility and faster dissolution 
rate. The applicant’s in vivo bridging relies on the rationale that differences in the absorption 
rate affect safety and efficacy. In other words, is there a possibility that Mod I has a lower in 
vivo absorption rate? If so, how should this risk be assessed?
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4 ( S.1, P.2, P.5):
(1)
The selection of Hydrate 1 Mod. A as the solid state form to be developed was based on a 
holistic assessment of all data available at the time of decision. The solid state information 
came from an extensive externally conducted polymorphism screening. In this screening data 
evaluation did not identify any anhydrous forms. A large number of solvates with organic 
solvents was found in addition to four forms identified as non-stoichiometric hydrates. 
Solvates including organic solvents were excluded from further considerations. Because no 
anhydrous forms had been identified the selection of a suitable form was narrowed down to
the hydrates. As all hydrates were identified to be non-stoichiometric, manufacturing 
considerations were also included. We had already shown that we could manufacture Hydrate 
1 reproducibly. Thus, Hydrate 1, which is now called Hydrate 1 Mod. A, was selected as the 
solid state form for development.
Since it had been shown that BAY 2927088 shows a complicated solid state landscape, an in-
depth polymorphism study was initiated in-house. This led to the realization that four 
anhydrous forms of BAY 2927088 exist, three of which Mod. II, Mod. III and Mod. IV, are 
metastable. The fourth anhydrous form, Mod. I, was found to be identical with the form called 
Hydrate II in the external polymorphism screening. It had not been recognized in the initial 
investigation that it was an anhydrous form. Based on the in-house polymorphism study Mod. 
I is the thermodynamically stable anhydrous form. The in-house study also showed that 
Hydrate 1 exists in three different polymorphs: Hydrate 1 Mod. A, Hydrate 1 Mod. B and 
Hydrate 1 Mod. C. Of these Hydrate 1 Mod. A was shown to be the most suitable form. 
Hydrate 1 Mod. A is identical with the form called Hydrate 1 in the initial screening.
At the time when the results from the in-house polymorphism study became available, a 
process to manufacture Drug Substance in the form of Hydrate 1 Mod. A in commercial scale 
had been established. It had also been demonstrated that the solid state form did not change 
during DS stability. Also, Drug Product batches manufactured from this DS consistently 
contained Hydrate 1 Mod. A at time of release. The partial transition of this solid state form in 
the Drug Product to Mod. I became only apparent with the primary stability batches. The 
change in solid state form was assessed not to impact safety and efficacy of the Drug Product 
and has therefore no impact on the commercial product.
Solubility data for Hydrate 1 Mod. A and Mod. I are provided below.
The solubility of BAY 2927088 hydrate micronized drug substance was determined by 
stirring batch no. UNGG220 (hydrate 1 mod. A) in aqueous buffer solutions, to be tested in a 
thermostatically controlled water bath at 25 °C and 37 °C for 24 hours. The suspension was 
passed through a 0.45 µm membrane filter. The concentration was monitored by HPLC 
(method see S.4.2.01 “Test Procedure”). The solubility of BAY 2927088 Modification I was 
determined by stirring batch no. OLB 090724-7e (Modification I) in aqueous buffer solutions, 
to be tested in a thermostatically controlled water bath at 25 °C and 37 °C for 24 hours. The 
suspension was passed through a 0.45 µm membrane filter. The concentration was monitored 
by HPLC (method see S.4.2.01 “Test Procedure”).
The solubility in aqueous buffer solutions at different pH values of BAY 2927088 hydrate 
micronized are shown in Table 2 and Table 3 and for BAY 2927088 Modification I in Table 4 
and Table 5, respectively, below.

(2)
The crystal form testing diffractogram at the end of shelf life (batches MSAT230906 and 
KM60497) or the latest available pull point for all registration batches (DP) are summarized 
and provided as below:
(Table 6: Summary of stability batches and polymorphism testing results; Figures 17–36: XRPD overlays)

The observed transition from Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I in the tablets is a solid-solid phase 
transition that can be triggered by a wide range of events, e.g. temperature cycling, 
mechanical stress, humidity. While the overall direction of the transition is governed by 
thermodynamics, predicting the kinetics of the transformation is not possible. Deducing a 
trend of drug product polymorphic transformation would therefore be scientifically unsound. 
From the perspective of CMC control it is also not necessary as it has been demonstrated that 
even for a complete change from Hydrate 1 Mod. A to Mod. I, safety and efficacy of the drug 
product would not be impacted.

(3)
LSF 
Please find the composition of BAY 2927088 solution 0.5 % (also referred to as “LSF”) in the 
following table 7.
(Table 7: composition listing API and excipients with amounts)
For all clinical batches of the LSF the drug substance was completely dissolved, i.e. a clear 
solution was obtained (please see P.5.4.01_IQMS-435663_1.0_BAY 2927088 solution 0.5 % 
for oral use 201 (Clinical Batches). No change of this test item was observed in the stability 
studies.

Tablets
Only tablets containing Hydrate 1 Mod A, as determined at release of the DP by informative 
XRPD testing, were provided for distribution to use in study 21607. Please find the release 
test results, including the polymorphic form, for 20 mg tablets in tables 8 and 9 below.
Please find the release test results, including the polymorphic form, for 10 mg tablets in 
documents P.5.4.01_IQMS-261279_1.0_BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10 mg (Clinical 
Batches) and P.5.4.01_IQMS-263273_2.0_BAY 2927088 coated tablet 10 mg (Site 
Leverkusen), respectively.

(4)
In vitro permeability studies revealed sevabertinib to be highly permeable comparing 
permeability data with historic reference compounds (see Module 4.2.2.6, Report B002815). 
Taking into account the characteristics of sevabertinib regarding solubility in aqueous media 
and its high permeability in Caco-2-cells, the compound can be classified as BCS class 2 
according to the definition of the Biopharmaceutical Classification System [3]. For this class, 
oral absorption is predominantly controlled by dissolution under physiological conditions, 
because permeability is not rate‑limiting and the driving factor for systemic uptake is the 
availability of drug in solution in the gastrointestinal lumen [4].
A faster dissolution rate accelerates the rise of this concentration over time. Because intestinal 
absorption rate is proportional to luminal drug concentration, faster dissolution leads to earlier 
and higher intestinal concentrations, resulting in a faster onset of absorption and an increased 
absorption rate [4].
Based on these considerations, the higher solubility of Mod. I compared to Hydrate 1 Mod. A 
(see response to Question 4 (1) above) and the comparable or faster dissolution kinetics of 
tablets containing only Mod. I (see P.2.2.10_IQMS-265402_1.0_BAY 2927088 coated tablet 
10 mg), the possibility that Mod I has a lower in vivo absorption rate is considered very 
unlikely. A higher absorption rate may lead to higher and earlier maximum concentrations. 
Therefore, the potential impact of absorption rate on safety and efficacy was analyzed. The 
analyses demonstrated that absorption rate had no impact on safety or efficacy 
(Module 5.3.3.5, Report B003834).

Question/Consideration:
Question 5
Regarding commercial manufacturing batch size: It is recommended that the 
manufacturing batch size be fixed at 20 kg in the current manufacturing process 
information table. The batch size may be scaled up to 60 kg after accumulating more batch 
production data at post-approval stage.
The reasons are as follows:
(1) Step 1: Mixing, sieving, and mixing follow a batch production model. Therefore, the
batch size cannot typically be defined by production time as required for process 
validation of a continuous manufacturing model. Please clarify whether the same 
production equipment (whether a 200 L mixing equipment or mixing equipment of 
different volumes is used?) and the same process parameters (whether mixing speed and 
mixing time are the same?) are adopted for production at batch sizes of 20 kg, 30 kg, and 
60 kg?
(2) In accordance with the Process Validation Guidelines issued by CFDI in 2025,
prospective process validation shall be adopted for the first marketing application, and at 
least three consecutive successful batches of process validation should generally be 
performed under commercial-scale production conditions. If other validation batch 
numbers are to be used (e.g., if approval for 60 kg is sought, currently only one batch of 
validation data exists for 60 kg (based on the fact that Premix Step 1 is not a continuous 
manufacturing process and the process validation requirements for batch production are 
applied)), the rationality needs to be justified (e.g., in cases where advanced 
manufacturing technologies such as PAT are adopted, but such technologies were not 
actually used in Premix Step).
Given the currently limited overall development and production batches, it is recommended 
that the manufacturing process information table first fix the batch size at 20 kg, and 
supportive data be submitted to increase it to 60 kg at the post-marketing stage.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 5 ( P.2, P.3):
(1) Bayer acknowledges that the CFDI Guideline for Process Validation Inspection (April
2025), states that prospective process validation is the preferred method for initial process 
validation and that this validation should generally be carried out on a minimum of three 
consecutive batches. However, the validation strategy employed for the pre-blend and 
subsequent continuous manufacturing process was not designed to validate a single fixed 
batch size, but rather to validate a commercial batch size range of 20 to 60 kg (as amount 
of pre-blend) using a risk-based bracketing approach, consistent with the risk 
management principles of the CFDI Guideline and requirements of ICH Q13 Guideline.
The scientific basis for the bracketing approach was to produce representative batches for 
the intended batch size extremes, more specifically 20 to 60 kg. This approach is 
compliant to the “Process Validation for Multi-strength Products” procedure described in 
section 7.1 of CFDI Guideline. In our specific case, the variable process element is the 
batch size of the input material. All other process parameters were kept constant. The 
batch size is not solely defined by the manufacturing line run time at a defined mass flow
rate; our batch size definition also considers the amount of input material as described in 
section 2.2 of ICH Q13. Therefore, it is Bayer’s understanding that the process validation 
of BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated tablets was successfully conducted on 
three consecutive commercial-scale batches.
The validation batch configuration (refer to P.3.5.01) was as follows:
• Two consecutive batches at 20 kg  
• One consecutive batch at 60 kg
The blending process uses a 200 L or 400 L vessel for the first blending step and a 300 L 
vessel for the second blending step. The process parameters (blending speed and blending 
time) of both blending steps are kept constant for all clinical and validation batches 
produced on the continuous manufacturing line. In our approach, the quality attribute that 
is affected by the blending process is the blend uniformity. Thus, the validation was set-
up to demonstrate process robustness over the whole range of batch sizes (Table 10). The 
uniformity of the pre-blend was validated by using the two extremes of the batch size 
range (20 kg and 60 kg). A potential impact of both, vessel size and batch size is most 
suitably investigated by calculating the filling load, i.e. the batch size divided by the 
vessel size. Thus, the investigated ranges during process development and validation of 
the filling load range were:
• 0.10 kg/L - 0.15 kg/L for the first blending step 
• 0.07 kg/L - 0.20 kg/L for the second blending step.
The blending process parameters were kept identical for all produced validation
mentioned in section 5.1.1.3 of the CFDI Guideline for the manufacturing process.
As described in P.3.5.01, the homogeneity of all three pre-blends was analyzed during 
process validation, and the results for the three validation batches and one clinical batch 
are provided for reference in Table 11. These successful results at both extremes provide 
high degree of assurance that the process is robust for any batch size within the 20 - 60 kg 
range by maintaining the filling loads and process conditions for both blending steps.
In addition to blend uniformity measurement during validation, further evidence on batch 
homogeneity has been generated via content uniformity testing (CU) of coated tablets. 
CU of all coating sublots produced in the subsequent continuous manufacturing process 
during process validation was tested and met the specification. The Acceptance Value 
(AV) ranges were (see also Table 12 to Table 15, see also P.3.5.01):
• BXA9L5D 
  o 2.6–5.0 for coating sublots 
  o 2.7 for the release sample  
• BXA9L5E 
  o 1.8–5.4 for coating sublots 
  o 3.6 for the release sample 
• BXA9L5F 
  o 1.9–5.5 for coating sublots 
  o 2.5 for the release sample
These comparable results further support the suitability of the established pre-blend 
blending conditions across the 20–60 kg batch-size range and the corresponding filling 
degrees.
The results of the process validation study, the obtained process knowledge during 
process development and the overall control strategy of the manufacturing line show 
reliable evidence, that the established process conditions and controls during blending of 
the pre-blend are capable of producing BAY 2927088 (Sevabertinib) 10 mg coated 
tablets in the specified quality within the investigated pre-blend batch size range  of 
20 – 60 kg, i.e. a blending load of 0.07 – 0.20 kg/L.

(2) As described in Point (1), our validation approach used three consecutive batches with the
batch size range 20 - 60 kg defined by the pre-blend as input material for the continuous 
manufacturing line. This approach is considered compliant with the referenced Guideline for 
Process Validation from CFDI (Status April 2025), specifically section “4.1 Initial process 
validation”, “5.1 Traditional process validation” and “7.1 Process Validation for Multi-
strength Products”, as the rational for this approach was to demonstrate the blend uniformity 
for varying blender fill load extremes, which were comparable to those used for the clinical 
supply, while maintaining all other process parameters of the production process. The 
evidence collected with extensive blend homogeneity testing of the blend and content 
uniformity testing after continuous manufacturing is sufficient to justify our proposal to 
register a batch size range of 20 – 60 kg. Therefore, Bayer respectfully ask to maintain the 
proposed batch size range in the MPIT.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
The presence of polymorphic form II in the drug substance might have an impact on 
safety/efficacy of the drug product. Parameter polymorphism is therefore considered a critical 
attribute and should be kept in the specifications of the drug substance unless otherwise 
justified. The MAH is therefore asked to retain the parameter polymorphism in the 
specifications of the drug substance with the mention “must comply if tested” and to leave the 
information regarding laboratory responsible for XRPD testing as well as the description and 
validation of the analytical method.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.S.4):
We agree to the agency’s comment and therefore agree to keep polymorphism as a critical 
attribute of the drug substance. However, polymorphic form I is the thermodynamically stable 
form at ambient temperature and producing metastable polymorphic form II under the 
established process conditions is highly unlikely.  Based on the data provided with this 
variation in section 3.2.S.4.5, it was shown that in approximately 300 batches, manufactured 
in two years, the result for polymorphism was constantly polymorphic form I. Throughout the 
manufacturing history of darolutamide only polymorphic form I has been produced.
The test for polymorphism by X-ray analysis is kept in the specification as a periodic skip test 
of every twentieth batch. Please see below the documentation that has been amended in order 
to keep the dossier aligned.
We consider the proposed period of testing (every twentieth batch) sufficient considering the 
large number of batches already manufactured and the large number of batches which are 
manufactured annually.
For additional assurance of the polymorphic form, the identity test by IR will remain in the 
specification as a routine test for all manufactured batches. The spectra of Polymorphic form I 
and polymorphic form II are compared in Figure 1, and the match of the IR spectra is only 
64%. Polymorphic form II would not comply with the criteria that the spectrum of the sample 
must comply with that of the reference standard.

The following dossier sections have been amended for this response:
• 3.2.S.2.1 Manufacturer(s): testing site for polymorphism was included again (same 
site as previously)
• 3.2.S.2.4 Control of Critical Steps and Intermediates: Polymorphism is again classified 
as a critical quality attribute. A justification for the skip testing has been included.
• 3.2.S.2.6 Manufacturing Process Development: Polymorphic form has been added 
again in the list of critical quality attributes
• 3.2.S.4.1 Specification: Polymorphism has been included again in the specification 
with the following footnote: “Must comply if tested. Analysis is performed 
as periodic skip testing of every twentieth batch.”
• 3.2.S.4.2 Test Procedure: the test procedure for polymorphism has been re-introduced 
to the document (same wording as before). We have taken the opportunity to include 
an exemplary diffractogram of a more current batch.
• 3.2.S.4.4 Batch Analyses: inclusion of test for Polymorphism (with footnote regarding 
skip testing on every twentieth batch).
• 3.2.S.4.5 Justification of Specification and Skip Testing: Discussion of specification 
for Polymorphism has been moved from chapter 3 “Non-specified Test Items” to
chapter 2 “Discussion of Individual Tests and Limits”, and justification of skip testing 
has been introduced.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Considering that the concentration and homogeneity of the active substance are critical 
quality attributes of the product, please submit a complete process validation report under the 
new control scheme (ﬁnal mixing time), together with technical and statistical evidence 
demonstrating a direct relationship between the ﬁnal mixing time and the fulﬁllment of 
concentration and homogeneity requirements, a formal risk analysis that justiﬁes the removal 
of in-process analytical controls, and comparative historical data demonstrating that the 
proposed new parameter maintains the process under control and does not increase product 
variability.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
There is no actual change in the manufacturing process of Mirena in connection of the 
deletion of mass homogeneity IPC, mixing process itself remains unchanged. Furthermore, 
the IPCs, Concentration of levonorgestrel and Homogeneity, can’t be considered as two 
separate IPC tests, as they are both obtained and calculated from exactly the same blend 
analysis.
Bayer has manufactured Mirena batches for 30 years already and hence the mixing process is 
well established, and therefore proven to produce homogenous levonorgestrel-elastomer 
mixtures. In order to support the IPC deletion the actual mixing time (at least 40 minutes) 
applied on the product over the years was added and specified as an IPC to substitute the 
homogeneity test. Therefore, the proposed IPCs are only adapting to the actual conditions of 
the manufacturing process.
An updated process validation report P.3.5.01_02 in which the mixing time of min. 40 
minutes has been observed and reported is provided to the competent Health Authority for 
review. In this validation study homogenous mixtures were achieved with the mixing time of 
40 minutes.
As a further assurance of the continuously homogenous mixtures achieved in the mixing step 
of Mirena data on recent 283 batches (manufactured between 03.01.2024 and 31.01.2025) of 
Mirena is provided. The data refers to average results of 4 IPC samples collected from these 
283 batches, which means that the data in graphs and histograms is based on 1132 blend 
samples in total.
The requirement for the average levonorgestrel concentration is 48 – 52 %, and the RSD of 4 
determinations must be ≤ 2 %. The average results of 283 batches fall between 47.9 and 50.8 
%, with the average of all determinations as  49.4 %. Average of the calculated RSD values 
is 0.4 %. maximum observed RSD has been 1.6 %,
The data provided reliably verifies that mixing process of Mirena results into a homogenous 
mixture when mixed for 40 minutes. Therefore, Bayer considers deletion of the homogeneity 
IPC justified.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Regarding the request to remove from the shelf-life speciﬁcation the parameters “Ethylene 
oxide” and “Ethylene chlorohydrin,” indicating that such tests would be redundant, please 
consider the following: because the product is sterilized using ethylene oxide, and because 
ethylene oxide and ethylene chlorohydrin are potentially toxic residues whose evaluation is 
directly related to patient safety, submit consolidated historical data of ethylene oxide and 
ethylene chlorohydrin results in stability studies (real-time and accelerated), by batch, storage 
condition and sampling time point, including statistical analysis and trend evaluation and a 
technical justiﬁcation demonstrating that there is no risk of increase or secondary formation of 
residues during storage. Also provide a formal risk analysis that supports the removal of these
tests from the shelf-life speciﬁcation, taking into account the impact on patient safety. Provide 
conﬁrmation that residual levels consistently comply with the applicable toxicological limits 
throughout the approved shelf life.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( CTD section):
Both ethylene oxide  (EO) and ethylene chlorohydrin (ECH), which are the sterilization 
residue substances, are removed to acceptable level from the product in aeration process. The 
limits specified for EO and ECH at release, are 5 ppm and 10 ppm, respectively.
Determination of EO and ECH residues after the aeration step at release is sufficient to ensure 
the product quality and safety for the patient, especially in case of a drug product like Mirena, 
which will be used for several years, i.e. there will be no new exposure to EO and ECH 
encountered with administration of new medication intermittently.
ECH limit of Mirena, 10 ppm, is acceptable based on EMA guideline 
EMA/CHMP/CVMP/QWP/850374/2015 (Guideline on the sterilisation of the medicinal 
product, active substance, excipient and primary container), which specifies a limit of 50 ppm 
for ECH residues in drug products.
Regarding Ethylene oxide, guideline ICH M7(R2) (ASSESSMENT AND CONTROL OF DNA 
REACTIVE (MUTAGENIC) IMPURITIES IN PHARMACEUTICALS TO LIMIT POTENTIAL 
CARCINOGENIC RISK) states the following on maximum limit for daily intake of EO:
ICH M7 derives a limit for total human daily dose of Ethylene oxide as 21.3 µg/person/day.
A daily life-long intake of 21.3 µg ethylene oxide would correspond to a theoretical cancer 
risk of 10-5 and therefore be an acceptable intake when present as an impurity in a drug 
substance.
EO limit specified for Mirena at release is 5 ppm. All manufactured Mirena batches fulfill this 
requirement at release without exceptions. Furthermore, the EO and ECH concentrations in 
the product can only decrease during storage. Hence, testing at release only is adequate.  The 
average weight of an inserted Mirena IUS is 0.343 g. This means that the maximum EO 
amount in an IUS is ca. 1.7 µg. As the same Mirena IUS is used even for a period of 5 years, 
the maximum intake of EO during the 5 years period when using Mirena is this 1.7 µg.
Comparison of the Mirena’s maximum  intake with the values for maximum daily intake 
presented in ICH M7 clearly show that the determination of ethylene oxide, and also ethylene 
chlorohydrin residues, at release only for Mirena is appropriate and well justified. The EO and 
ECH residues in Mirena do not need to be determined during the shelf-life, and they do not 
pose a risk to the patient’s health.

Source:  P.5.1.01_07 Release Specification / Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery
system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#022984913; unchanged)

accelerated), with trend analyses demonstrating consistent behavior throughout the shelf life.

sterility test does not increase microbiological risk nor impact patient safety
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 ( CTD section):
The maintenance of the sterile barrier integrity, and hence the sterility throughout the shelf-
life is demonstrated during stability testing by testing the integrity of the primary package. 
The integrity of the package is tested with bubble test and the seal strength of the package 
with strip test.
The substitution of Sterility test with Container closure integrity tests during the shelf-
life is in accordance with the guidelines and principles of both FDA and EMA:
In Questions & Answers of EMA web pages (Quality of medicines questions and answers: 
Part 2 / Stability - Endotoxin testing and sterility testing at the end of shelf-life) the following 
is stated:
“Sterility is part of the shelf-life specification.
Sterility testing should be performed at least at the end of Shelf-life, but it can be replaced by 
testing of the container closure integrity. Depending on the nature of the container, 
intermittent integrity testing might be envisaged, independent of whether the sterility testing 
is replaced or not.”
https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory-overview/research-development/scientific-
guidelines/quality-medicines-qa-introduction/quality-medicines-questions-answers-part-2
This approach is approved by FDA as well in Guidance document “Container and Closure 
System Integrity Testing in Lieu of Sterility Testing as a Component of the Stability Protocol 
for Sterile Products”.
FDA guideline states for example the following:
“Alternatives to sterility testing as part of the stability protocol, such as replacing the sterility 
test with container and closure system integrity testing, might include any properly validated 
physical or chemical container and closure system integrity test (e.g., bubble tests, 
pressure/vacuum decay, dye penetration tests or seal force tests, etc.). Such tests may be more 
useful than sterility testing in demonstrating the potential for product contamination over the 
product’s shelf life or dating period.”
The proposed approach is in accordance with the relevant Health Authority Guidelines (EMA 
& FDA). Therefore, according to Bayer Oy’s opinion there is no need to additionally perform 
any risk assessments concerning the sterility test substitution for the testing during the Shelf-
life.

Source:  P.5.1.01_07 Release Specification / Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery
system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#022984913; unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 11
Please confirm the size of the artificial breaches used to generate positive controls for dye 
ingress testing of container closure systems, and justify these with reference to USP<1207> 
requirements.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 11:
Container closure integrity testing of the stability batches PQ0784 and PQ0786 was 
performed at approximately 3 months after manufacturing and at the end of the proposed shelf 
life of 36 months using an established methylene blue dye ingress method supported by an 
established method developed in 2013. The container closure system used in that study was 
identical to the system of the study batches.
The artificial challenges investigated during implementation were defined by the type and 
extent of manipulation rather than by a calibrated breach diameter. Samples were examined 
for each of the following conditions:
• 
Stoppers pierced 10, 20 or 30 times at the same location
• 
Stoppers pierced laterally at different locations
• 
Damaged aluminium caps
• 
Bottles without aluminium caps.

Testing involved immersion in a 20 g/L methylene blue solution under a relative vacuum of 
−270 mbar for 10 minutes, followed by a further 30 minutes of immersion at atmospheric 
pressure. Evaluation comprised visual inspection and UV–visible spectra recorded over 500–
900 nm, with assessment of the characteristic methylene blue absorption maximum at 
approximately 669 nm.
The unmodified, untreated samples, comprising 30 units of each of the two batches in 2013, 
showed no evidence of dye ingress. For the challenged samples, the spectroscopic results 
recorded a methylene blue peak following 30 punctures at the same location and following 
lateral puncturing of the stopper. These findings demonstrated detection of dye ingress under 
the respective challenge conditions.
The relevant USP reference for this approach is USP 〈1207.1〉, Section 4.5.2, “Type Defects”. 
This section describes qualitatively characterized primary packaging material defects and 
recognizes that assigning precise dimensions to such defects is generally not meaningful or 
feasible because of their irregularity and complexity. The puncture and closure-manipulation 
challenges used in the historical analysis are consistent with this qualitative approach. Their 
dimensions cannot be expressed retrospectively as a defined breach diameter in micrometers.
Furthermore, both visual and spectrophotometric evaluation are described for tracer liquid 
testing in USP 〈1207.2〉, Section 3.4. The positive spectroscopic findings provide evidence 
that the method could detect dye ingress associated with the specified puncture challenges. 
The reported visual sensitivity values of 0.04 µL per 10 mL describe dye detection sensitivity; 
they do not establish a minimum detectable leak size.
In summary, the analytical method employed qualitatively defined defect challenges 
supported by the type-defect concept described in USP 〈1207.1〉, rather than calibrated 
breaches of a specified diameter. Positive controls were not included alongside the samples 
during the subsequent stability testing of PQ0784 and PQ0786. The validation findings 
therefore support detection capability for the investigated challenge conditions but do not 
establish a numerical breach-size detection limit or provide concurrent positive-control 
verification for those individual stability test runs.
keywords: Container closure system; Shelf Life; Stability data; Validation of Analytical procedures; Stopper

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
It is known that capitalisation reduces readability of names for patients. As advised in 
the MHRA Guideline for the Naming of Medicinal Products and Braille Requirements 
for Name on Label, ‘the invented name should not comprise wholly of initial letters or 
code numbers’. It remains our recommendation for the proposed invented name 
‘HYRNUO’ to be amended to ‘Hyrnuo (i.e., use of capitalised 'H' and lower case 
'yrnuo') in order to improve readability. The labelling should be updated accordingly.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2
In order to conclude the procedure positively, Bayer has implemented MHRA’s request, and 
changed the appearance of the brand name from HYRNUO to Hyrnuo.
Bayer wish to respectfully note, however, that we do not agree that capital letters adversely 
affect readability for Hyrnuo. We acknowledge MHRA’s guidance on Naming of Medicinal 
Products and Braille Requirements for Name on Label, which states to avoid widespread use 
of words in all capitals particularly in blocks of text. Our understanding is that in this 
guidance, reference to ‘initial letters’ is understood to mean acronyms or abbreviations 
formed from the first (initial) letters of multiple words (e.g. HRT, SSRI), and does not 
preclude the use of capitals for a short, distinctive brand name.
However, we respect MHRA’s position that all capitals should not be used, and look forward 
to seeing the updated naming guidance that will clearly state this.

Question/Consideration:

Bayer Response to Question 6 ( CTD section):
Please note that Ethinylestradiol betadex clathrate is not a pharmacopeial substance. But, the 
starting materials, Ethinylestradiol and betadex, which together build the drug substance are 
described in monographs of Ph. Eur. Thus, the quality of Ethinylestradiol betadex clathrate is 
based on Ph. Eur. quality of the two compounds that form the clathrate. The proposed regulatory 
specification is considered adequate to control the quality of the drug substance.
Regarding Impurity H in Ethinylestradiol, please note that this is not a potential impurity in the 
Bayer AG manufacturing process of this substance, and, therefore, it is not namely included in 
the quality specification. Impurity H is evaluated by the test item “any unspecified impurity” 
with the acceptance criterion of max. 0.10% and herewith is even tighter than the original Ph. 
Eur. Specification. Impurities D and L are not specified impurities regarding Ph.Eur. These 
impurities are also evaluated by the test item “any unspecified impurity”.
The limits of detection and quantitation were determined according to the requirements of ICH 
Q2(R1) for all organic impurities for details see S.4.3.01 - Validation of Test for Assay and 
Impurities’. The LOD and LOQ determined for Ethinylestradiol serve as surrogate validation 
and therefore can be used for all other organic impurities as well. Specificity is given as all 
impurities are selectively separated.

Question/Consideration:
Question 10
Since Levomefolate calcium is known to be unstable, please provide discussion on why the step 
where levomefolate calcium is introduced into the granulator is not considered critical since 
loss of the active substance occurs at this stage.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 10 ( CTD section):
We have identified three critical process steps: granulation, tableting, and film-coating. The 
addition of Levomefolate calcium is an integral part of the granulation process and is therefore 
considered critical.
The loss of LMCA can be attributed to several factors, including adhesion of LMCA to the 
surfaces of production equipment, adsorption at the exhaust filters of the granulator, and the 
chemical instability of LMCA, which is exacerbated by temperature and humidity.
To mitigate these risks and prevent LMCA from being exposed to high temperatures and 
humidity, we ensure that it is mixed under the fluidized bed with a cold volumetric flow 
immediately after the granulation process is completed. Furthermore, to minimize sticking to 
the surfaces of the feeding system, LMCA is mixed with croscarmellose sodium. Additionally, 
magnesium stearate is added and mixed subsequently to effectively "flush" the feeding system, 
reducing the potential for loss of the active substance.
Additionally, all process steps are monitored through the IPC mentioned in P.3.3.02_IQMS-
145041_1.0 via the MBR, ensuring that any deviation from the validated process is immediately 
detected.

Question/Consideration:
Question 13
The use of 7% overage quantity of Levomefolate calcium justification is noted but not 
satisfactory. Levomefolate calcium is known to be unstable. Furthermore, levomefolate calcium 
partly remains in the feeding tubes to fluid bed granulator and on the fluidized bed granulator 
surface, please specify if the analytical method is suitable to ensure full potency of the finished 
drug and does not result in a super potent drug product.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 13 ( CTD section):
The vitamin Levomefolate calcium (LMCA) is used for the prevention of neuronal tube defects 
of newborn children. According to literature, a dose of 0.451 mg LMCA equivalent to 0.4 mg 
folic acid are the target amounts for the prevention of these defects. LMCA is known for its 
instability towards increased temperatures and adhesion to surfaces. In order to guarantee for 
correct dosage and statistically cover the worst case scenarios for physical and chemical losses, 
the overage was calculated as a sum of mean overall production loss (and standard deviation) 
during the manufacturing. A mean overall production loss during the manufacturing of LMCA 
tablets of 4.3% with a standard deviation of ± 2.5% was observed (see P.2.2.01_IQMS-
145030_3.0). Therefore, a 7% overage for manufacturing of LMCA containing coated tablets 
is justified.
Prior to setup of the overage, an extensive evaluation on the production loss of LMCA was 
performed (P.2.2.10_IQMS-176943_1.0). Physical loss (e.g., due to adhesion of material) as 
well as chemical loss (caused by degradation) were investigated at every process step. Based 
on this in-depth investigation, the overage of 7% for the production of LMCA-containing film-
coated products was determined and confirmed. The whole manufacturing process was 
inspected and the chemical loss (increase of by-products) for all manufacturing steps was 
determined. Furthermore the physical loss of LMCA due to adhesion of the material on 
equipment surfaces was determined for the first two steps (addition of LMCA and compression 
to tablets) and for the film coating process, respectively.
A chemical loss of 1.0% standard deviation of ± 0.3% was observed over the whole production 
process (P.2.2.10_IQMS-176943_1.0, Table 7). For a detailed discussion of the extent of 
degradation in the different production steps (P.2.2.10_IQMS-176943_1.0, chapter 5). The 
physical loss over the whole process was 3.3% with a standard deviation of ± 2.7%. The loss 
of LMCA is related to the following factors: adhesion of LMCA at surfaces of production 
equipment, adsorption at exhaust filters of granulator and chemical instability of LMCA 
(promoted by temperature and humidity).
Regarding the analytical method, the range determined within the linearity test covers 
concentrations from 0.1 to 130%. The investigations of the accuracy covers a range of up to
130% of levomefolate calcium. This means, the method is capable to quantify the exact amounts 
of levomefolate calcium within the drug product.

Ethinylestradiol + Levomefolate calcium coated tablet 3.0 mg + 0.03 mg + 
0.451 mg (#P.5.3.01_IQMS-145213_1.0; unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 14
Since Levomefolate calcium coated tablet acts as a placebo in this product, please include test 
for absence of the actives (Drospirenone and Ethinylestradiol) in the specifications for 
Levomefolate calcium coated tablet.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 14 ( CTD section):
The levomefolate calcium coated tablet is not registered as placebo because it is used for the 
prevention of neuronal tube defects of newborn children , it is generally considered as drug 
substance.
In the Supply Center Weimar (Weimar, Germany), GMP-processes and measurements are in 
place to minimize the risk of a possible cross-contamination. These take into account the 
following factors:
• 
Room and equipment design and usage,
• 
Personnel and material flow,
• 
Physical-chemical, pharmacological, and toxicological properties of the active 
substance(s),
• 
Manufacturing processes and product characteristics,
• 
Campaign concepts,
• 
Cleaning and cleaning verification processes,
• 
Sensitivity of analytical methods in relation to the established "Maximum Allowable 
Carry Over" (MACO).

This comprehensive evaluation highlights the importance of each factor in maintaining a safe 
and compliant manufacturing environment. The careful design and utilization of rooms and 
equipment ensure that the workflow minimizes the potential for contamination. Additionally, 
understanding the properties of the substances involved allows for tailored approaches to 
handling and processing, further mitigating risks.
Rigorous cleaning protocols and verification processes are in place to ensure that all equipment 
is thoroughly cleaned between uses, effectively reducing any possible residual contaminants.
The evaluation of the presence (and eventually the amount) of previous drug substances in the 
subsequent formulations (drug products or placebo) which may be relevant for patient safety is 
considered by cleaning validation. In adherence to current regulations, the manufacturing 
equipment used at our site undergoes defined cleaning procedures. These cleaning processes 
are validated, among others, regarding the residual amount of drug substance after cleaning 
which may be transferred in the following manufactured batch via the product contact surfaces. 
From an analytical perspective, the effectiveness of the cleaning procedures is evaluated by 
sampling predefined points of the manufacturing equipment (e.g., with adequate sampling 
procedures) and analyzing the samples regarding the residual amount of drug substance(s). The 
implemented procedure at the site for cleaning validation ensures that any possible carryover 
from precious drug substances in the subsequent formulation is below the defined maximal 
acceptable carryover (MACO) and therefore poses no risk for product quality or patient safety.
keywords: drug product specification; GMP inspection; Validation of the Manufacturing Process; QC testing; Risk Asessment
