Question/Consideration:
Question 1
(3.2.P.2.4) The information that you have provided to support the absence of leachables, in your 
proposed drug product, is not considered adequate.  You have provided a brief discussion 
regarding a simulated leachables study, however, you have not provided a justification for the 
simulated study as required by USP <1664> Assessment of Drug Product Leachables 
Associated with Pharmaceutical Packaging/Delivery Systems.  The following is therefore 
requested:
a) Confirm that the simulated leachables study was conducted using actual drug product
manufactured as per current manufacturing process.  Batch number(s) should be provided 
and should be consistent with the batch number(s) used in the extractables study.
b) Provide the results of a leachables study over the proposed storage conditions and proposed
shelf-life using the actual drug product solution, manufactured as per current process, placed 
on inverted orientation.
c) In the absence of real-time leachable study data, provide a scientific justification as to why
a simulated leachables study was conducted instead of a real-time assessment over the 
proposed storage conditions and shelf-life of the product.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
a) 
Bayer confirms that the simulated leachables study was conducted using PRIMOVIST, 
sodium gadoxetate solution 0.25 mol/L for parenteral use, batch number KT0K9TJ 
manufactured according to the current manufacturing process.
The sample was collected at the end of filling line into a separate glass container to avoid 
contact with the new bromobutyl rubber stopper material.
The stoppers used in the extractables and simulated leachables studies had all the same 
pretreatments as used in the current PRIMOVIST, sodium gadoxetate solution 0.25 mol/L 
for parenteral use filling process.
Stoppers from the same lots were used in both the extractables and simulated leachables 
studies.

b) Real-time leachable shelf-life data is currently not available, please refer to the response
provided under Question 1c that discusses the justification for using a simulated leachables 
study.

c) Based on Health Canada’s feedback from the GADOVIST 1.0 (Ctrl no. 294352) and
ULTRAVIST (Ctrl. No. 294064) reviews, Bayer had provided the additional information 
pre-emptively in the note to reviewer, which we have now also discussed below.
With the introduction of the bromobutyl stopper, extractables data was prepared in 
exaggerated conditions of 50°C / 72 h and 85°C / 1 h (see Module 3.2.P.2.4.06_IQMS- 
254544_1.0 Extractions Studies). The stability study for sodium gadoxetate solution 
0.25 mol/L in vials using the alternative bromobutyl closure system, had not yet been 
initiated. Therefore, a simulated leachables study using sodium gadoxetate solution 
0.25 mol/L as extractant, in exaggerated conditions of 50 °C / 72 h and 85 °C / 1 h was 
conducted to confirm the safety of the new stopper material.
In the simulated leachables study no simulated leachables exceeding the study analytical 
evaluation threshold (AETs) was observed.
For the new bromobutyl stoppers an extensive extractables study was initially performed 
using several different extraction media, at elevated temperatures as stated above, with 
relatively long extraction time. These conditions were chosen to reflect recommendations 
in USP <1663> monograph, and ISO 10993-18 and 10993-12. For the AETs, when feasible, 
higher Uncertainty Factors (UF) of 4 and 10, than the usual UF 2 were used to confirm that 
all extractables are measured. The analyses were performed using state-of-art mass 
spectroscopic instruments.
Extractions with 2-propanol as extractant, 50% EtOH/water were performed, and also with 
water. In pH 4 and pH 9.5 buffer solutions only a few extractables in low amounts were 
detected. These were mainly fatty acids like palmitoleic, palmitic and oleic acids that are 
relatively non-toxic and common in elastomers and plastics. In addition to the extractables 
study, Bayer decided to conduct a simulated leachables study. In the simulated leachables 
study, using similar exaggerated extraction conditions to the extractables study, no 
reportable compounds were found. It was therefore considered adequate proof of stopper 
material suitability and safety for its intended use as container closure system and therefore 
no formal leachables stability study was planned.
A real-time stability study is on-going and a leachables study after 36 months testing and 
also at the end of 60 months shelf-life will be performed as per the USP <1664> Assessment 
of Drug Product Leachables Associated with Pharmaceutical Packaging/Delivery Systems, 
to further confirm the safety of the material
Source:  P.2.4.06-01 Extraction Studies / Sodium gadoxetate solution 0.25 mol/L for
parenteral use (PRIMOVIST) (#022985400/IQMS-254544_1.0; unchanged)

Question 2
It is recommended to set an upper limit for specific activity to reflect consistency between 
batches.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
Bayer acknowledges the recommendation to implement an upper limit for specific activity, to 
address this concern a upper specification limit for ‘Total Protein’ has been implemented in 
Drug Product. The drug substance and drug product total protein specifications ensure 
production process continuity and batch-to-batch consistency. Since specific activity is 
calculated by dividing the potency result by the total protein result and both potency and total 
protein have two-sided specification limits (upper and lower), the upper limit of specific activity 
is indirectly controlled by the potency and total protein specifications.
The specification for total protein at the drug product level sufficiently addresses control of 
Specific Activity.

Question/Consideration: 2. Section 3.2.P.3.5: Subsequent to the OOS in stability studies, Revise the release specification to include a test and acceptance criteria for water content at NMT 5%.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2) ( CTD section):
Applicant acknowledges the agency’s question and would like to clarify that the water content is not a mandatory specification parameter for solid oral dosage forms (drug products) in accordance to ICH Q6A, “Test procedures and acceptance criteria for new drug substances and new drug products: chemical substances”. As per ICH Q6A, water content test is “important for drug substances in cases where the new drug substance is known to be hygroscopic or degraded by moisture or when the drug substance is known to be a stoichiometric hydrate”.
For the drug product, water content has only an indirect impact on quality. Water content or loss on drying, respectively is determined for all drug substances (refer to the drug substance specifications S.4.1.01).
Relative humidity is the target parameter at the end of the granulation step. It is included as an in-process control test for the final mixture, with an acceptance criterion of 45% ±10% (refer to section P.3.3.901). This ensure uniform humidity levels in the granulate for subsequent processing steps.
Additionally, during the film-coating process, a minimum exhaust air temperature of >40°C is maintained. This measure prevents any increase in the moisture content of the tablets. The corresponding exhaust air temperature limit is defined and controlled within the TRD section P.3.3.901 as part of the in-process controls.
Finally, the consistent quality of the finished drug product, which may be affected by humidity, is assured through direct evaluation of key quality attributes, including, assay, impurities, appearance, dissolution and microbial purity. These quality parameters are relevant for release and shelf-life testing.
Source:
P.3.3.901 01 - Manufacturing Process / Drospirenone + Estradiol coated tablet 2 mg + 1 mg (ANGELIQ 1/2) (P.3.3.901#004442085_01 / P.3.3.01_IQMS-150507_1.0; unchanged).

Question/Consideration:
4. Section 3.2.P.8.3: Please note that we have concerns on your proposed shelf life (of 36 months) for the product when packaged in PVC/aluminium blisters and ‘Stored at or below 30 °C’. The concern arises from the observed out of specification (OOS) results for dissolution tests for drospirenone and estradiol for batches no. 01603A, 01604B & 01605A at T24. Your OOS investigation attributed the OOS to the high relative humidity level (75% RH) that were used at that stability investigation. Please take note of the unique climatic conditions of our region: a greater part of the East African region has a ‘hot and humid climate’ (ICH Climatic zone IVB). In addition, the patients are often unable to store the product in controlled conditions of humidity. Please consider a combination of some or all the following, so as to address the above concern:-
a) Change of the container closure system from PVC-blister foil to a more moisture resistant container system, such as a high barrier blister foil (HBF) in a hermetic pouch, or ALU-ALU blisters.
b) Inclusion of desiccants to offer additional protection against the high moisture levels that are typical the Zone IVB climatic zone.
c) Revise of the storage statement in the SmPC and Secondary Pack to “Store at or below 30 °C, Protect from moisture”
d) Revision of the release specification and the shelf-life specifications for Zone IVB (30 °C/75% RH) to include a test and limit for water determination. The limit should be justified, with data on the effects of hydration or water absorption on the drug product (ICH Q6A).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4 ( CTD section):
Applicant acknowledges the agency’s question and would like to inform that, at the time of initial submission, the correct documents were not submitted.

Based on the observations during the initial ICH study section P.8.3.01 (IQMS-178805_4.0), the shelf life specification of Angeliq 1/2 was subsequently re-evaluated (refer to section P.5.1.02; IQMS-185390) and a new report for CZ IVb was compiled - P.8.3.01 (IQMS-178806_5.0). This report provides a detailed assessment of the dissolution behavior (refer to the dissolution-section in chapter 3.1 of IQMS-178806_5.0). The rationale for the updated specification can be found in the document ‘Justification of Specification’ P.5.6.01 (IQMS-178095).

Angeliq 1/2 is an established and globally marketed drug product with demonstrated quality throughout its shelf life. To ensure continued product quality, an on-going stability program is implemented in accordance with international guidelines such as EU-GMP and ICH Q1A(R2). The current on-going stability report for CZ IVb P.8.3.02 (IQMS-224104) contains data from batches manufactured within the last seven years. All evaluated batches comply with the shelf life specifications and support the approved shelf life of 36 months. Based on these data, the current packaging (PVC/aluminum blisters) is considered adequate to maintain product quality, and no changes to the packaging are deemed necessary.

In light of the above justification, we kindly request the heath authority to accept the proposed approach.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Regarding the genotoxic impurities report for the starting material (Gadolinium Oxide), it is stated that high-temperature calcination destroys organic materials. Please provide the following:
1- Analytical confirmation including (TOC, GC-MS screening, IR/elemental carbon analysis).
2- Impurity profile and Certificates of Analysis from the active substance manufacturer showing non-organic residues.
3- Scientific studies addressing the decomposition/oxidation of organic substances under these conditions (high-temperature calcination destroys organics).
4- to provide a detailed report on potential sources of organic impurities, including transport, packaging, raw materials, and processing aids.
5- to provide of a detailed nitrosamine risk assessment report from the active substance manufacturer (NDMA & NDEA).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
Please see the responses to each of the points above-included:

1.Analytical confirmation including (TOC, GC-MS screening, IR/elemental carbon analysis):
Calcination is a process of heating a substance under controlled temperature and in a controlled environment. The high temperature calcination method calcines gadolinium salts at high temperature to decompose and generate gadolinium oxide. Calcination is also an elevated-temperature treatment to burn off or decompose the organic materials, as well as to crystallize and densify the ceramic products.
Due to the reaction conditions during calcination organic residues are not expected since all organic impurities are destroyed during the heating. The completion of the conversion to Gadolinium Oxide is controlled by determination of Loss on Ignition (Specification for parameter LOI: ≤ 1.0 % w/w).
In addition to mechanistic considerations from the route of conversion, proof of purity and correct chemical composition has been determined from elemental analysis by Inductively Coupled Plasma - Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES) and Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) evidence showing that high-temperature calcination destroys organic materials. Reference is also made to corresponding dossier section 3.2.S.3.2 of manufacturer Treibacher Industrie AG.
The corresponding analytical methods are both validated, reference is made to dossier section 3.2.S.4.3 Validation of analytical procedures: 3.2.S.4.3.4 Validation of Analytical Procedure for Determination of Impurities by ICP-OES (Optical Emission Spectrometry) and 3.2.S.4.3.5 Validation of Analytical Procedure for Determination of Impurities by ICP-MS (Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry).

Furthermore, please find attached 3 analytical reports of TOC measurement as well as the summarized results in the table below.
Batch number / Int. sample number / Parameter / Unit / Result
A-77913/1 (Gadoliniumoxid, 2016GdO05; 164098/01): TOC % C < 0.50; TC % C < 0.50; TIC % C < 0.50
A-83793/1/1 (Gadoliniumoxid, 2017GdO03; 172269/01): TOC % C < 0.50; TC % C < 0.50; TIC % C < 0.50
A-68844/1 (Gadoliniumoxid, pharma calcinated 2015GdO03; 160400/01): TOC % C < 0.50; TC % C < 0.50; TIC % C < 0.50
TC = total carbon; TIC = Total inorganic carbon; TOC = total organic carbon
Thus, it can be concluded that Gadolinium Oxide does not contain any organic impurities.

2.Impurity profile and Certificates of Analysis from the active substance manufacturer showing non-organic residues:
Please see enclosed a CoA from Gadolinium Oxide manufacturer, Treibacher, with non-organic impurities tested. In addition to this kindly refers to section of the dossier 3.2..S.3.2 Impurities.

3.Scientific studies addressing the decomposition/oxidation of organic substances under these conditions (high-temperature calcination destroys organics).
Please see enclosed a scientific study as required. The publication describes precisely the conversion of gadolinium oxalate to gadolinium oxide. In addition to other relevant aspects, it shows that, at a temperature of 700 °C, analytical analyses reveal only Gd₂O₃ and no intermediate phases are detected.

4.To provide a detailed report on potential sources of organic impurities, including transport, packaging, raw materials, and processing aids.
As indicated and duly justified in the response to point 1) “it can be concluded that Gadolinium Oxide does not contain any organic impurities”. This is also confirmed with the data included in response to point 2). Besides this, kindly note that:
- The starting material for Gadolinium oxide is Gadolinium oxalate, with a purity of more than 99.79%.
- There are no solvents or processing aids used.
- Gadolinium oxide drug substance is a mineral compound obtained by precipitation/calcinations. These mineral compounds are characterized by a very high level of purity due to the isolation/purification process. The potential impurities are only other mineral elements, and more specifically those listed in the specification section M3.2.S.4.1 (here enclosed for your convenience)
- The packaging material as described in the corresponding dossier section 3.2.S.6. Container Closure System (here enclosed again for your convenience) is “PE bag made from 100 % low density polyethylene LDPE without additives” In compliance with the requirements of the Commission Regulation (EU) No 1282/2011 on plastic materials and articles intended to come into contact with food.
The polyethylene raw material complies with the requirements of the Ph. Eur. monographs for polyolefins (3.1.3) and polyethylene without additives for containers for parenteral use and ophthalmic preparations (3.1.4) and with requirements of USP, Title 21, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Parts 177.1520 – olefin polymers (c) (Item 2.2) and 178.2010 as promulgated by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
- Treibacher (Gadolinium Oxide manufacturer) own a GMP certification, here enclosed for your convenience.
For all the stated above, report on potential sources of organic impurities, including transport, packaging, raw materials, and processing aids is deemed not necessary as absence of organic impurities is sufficient justified with data, in addition to this, kindly note that this has been accepted in more than 50 countries worldwide. Please refer to the statement enclose.

5.To provide of a detailed nitrosamine risk assessment report from the active substance manufacturer (NDMA & NDEA).
Please note that BAYER is working on this requirement, however final report is not expected before August. It will be submitted as soon as available. Please find enclosed the Commitment letter.
In addition to this, please find enclosed the Nitrosamines’s declaration from Treibacher as manufacturer of Gadolinium Oxide.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Based on our review of the microbial challenge test data submitted for Gadoquatrane solution 
0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection, we note that while microbial growth inhibition is observed up 
to 6 hours after opening, the stasis criterion of ≤ 0.5 log10 change relative to initial values is 
consistently met across all test organisms and both batches with an adequate margin only up 
to 4 hours. In particular, at the 6-hour timepoint, Pseudomonas aeruginosa demonstrates 
increases at the upper limit of the stasis criterion, indicating borderline performance.
In view of the above, the proposed in-use microbiological protection claim of 6 hours is not 
sufficiently supported. The available data support a 4-hour in-use period for 20°C to 25°C.
Please revise the in-use claim accordingly and update the proposed product labels and 
package insert, to reflect a 4-hour in-use period after opening, where applicable.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.P.2.5):
We acknowledge the evaluation regarding microbiological attributes. The recommended 
holding time after first opening in P.2.5.01 has been revised to 4 hours and the proposed 
product label mock-ups and Product Information for Australia and Singapore have been 
revised accordingly.
However, we would like to refer to study data supporting a specific in-use claim with regards 
to Gadoquatrane administration in conjunction with an automatic injector which has been 
approved for multi-patient use, see P.8.3.06 Stability Data - In-use Stability. Based on the 
study data, Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection can be considered safe from 
a microbiological, physical and chemical perspective for multi-patient use for up to 24 hours.
Furthermore, a study with added microbial stress has been finalized recently (microbial 
ingress challenge study). The MEDRAD® MRXperion Multi Patient Kit was intentionally 
and independently inoculated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC 9027) and Escherichia 
coli (ATCC 8739). In conclusion, it was demonstrated that the automated multi-patient 
injection system, when used in accordance with its intended use and instructions for use, 
effectively prevents microbial ingress from gross contamination when administering 
gadoquatrane solution (0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection) and normal saline over a 24-hour use 
period across up to 24 patient procedures. An executive summary is provided, see“Summary 
Microbial Ingress Evaluation”, please note that the actual data is currently undergoing a 
formatting workflow. As such, the finalized data can be shared on request as soon as the 
formatting process is complete. Additionally, to reflect this information, the Product 
Information for Australia and Singapore has been updated.

We cannot accept the proposed parametric release by sterility for Bayer AG, Berlin, Germany 
as the updated GMP certificate does not explicitly name Gadoquatrane Solution for Injection 
for parametric release. This means the criteria for parametric release across all participating

prepared to update module 3 accordingly for all countries involved.
However,regarding the specific requirement that Gadoquatrane Solution for Injection be 
named explicitly on the GMP certificate, we would like to clarify that the GMP certificate for 
Bayer AG, Berlin indeed covers parametric release for all sterile products, which includes 
Gadoquatrane Solution for Injection. For your reference, we have provided a confirmation 
from Lageso supporting this coverage, see Confirmation Lageso Gadoquatrane.
We continue to propose maintaining parametric release, as additional clarification from 
Lageso has been provided. Moreover, parametric release is increasingly recognized as a state-
of-the-art method. As outlined in  P.5.6.01 according to USP <1222>, “parametric release is

with parametric release has been included in chapter 8, P.5.6.01.

upon request, and we will ensure it is provided before the end of the evaluation round on 19th

production for Access Countries is scheduled for June 2026, and a decision on parametric 
release is essential for planning.

Question/Consideration:
Question 8
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls 
or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this 
does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, 
the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure 
integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected 
in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.

Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and
detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.
c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method
reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or 
provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 8 (3.2.P.3.3):
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate 
package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product 
lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP 
Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product 
manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of 
critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI 
at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control 
strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for 
the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm 
conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s 
(Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure 
systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method 
description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a 
risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments 
are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging 
processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are 
mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI 
testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on 
GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during 
the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in 
P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for 
routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered 
an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility 
with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this 
purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate 
a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug 
product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, 
critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon 
continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see 
P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use 
as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, 
further supporting the presented data from P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining 
presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media 
portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• 
Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• 
Bottle 65/100 mL
• 
Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–
closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence 
of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of 
the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes 
vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap 
and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium 
is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum 
is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive 
helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation 
includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom

to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of 
the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual 
maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During 
maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 
1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with 
DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of 
measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass 
spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup 
e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard 
with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of 
the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive 
sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are 
confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability 
testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using 
metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as 
negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all 
values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal 
detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the 
containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each 
measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample 
populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process 
variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization 
prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This 
approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal 
stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from 
P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.

Question/Consideration:
Question 9
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug 
product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 
mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification 
limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance 
scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper 
limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and 
manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing 
function.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 9 (3.2.P.5.1):
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon 
available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived 
based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. 
As discussed in P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. 
Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of 
release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life 
specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process 
validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe 
each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The 
data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No 
significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 
99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations 
and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance 
bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The 
specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.4.01 and 
P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in 
the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A 
explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should 
necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.

In response to the deficiency letter received from MFDS (South Korea Health Authority), the safety and complaint database for Mirena batches TU0494V, TU04BVT, and TU04E20 was thoroughly reviewed.
No drug safety cases were identified for the batch numbers referenced in the MFDS enquiry. There is no evidence of patient impact related to these batches from a safety perspective.

Based on the complaint investigations, all fifteen (15) complaints are unconfirmed (alleged quality defect, issue). Degradation-, does not coincide with the criteria established in the documents: -T.02.28-01: 
Release Specification-, - T.02.01-01: Shelf-Life Specification- and -ANNEX TO STABILITY

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (CTD Section P.5.2, P.8):
Response to 1.
The tests are conducted in accordance with the European Pharmacopoeia. 
•

• 
Disintegration: according to Ph. Eur. 2.9.1, Methode A. 
•

Response to 2. 
 
In April 2021 a new monograph 3021 for <Rivaroxaban tablets> became valid in the 
supplement 10.4 of the 10th edition of the European Pharmacopoeia. 
Bayer AG is the originator of Rivaroxaban tablets; therefore, our former in-house test 
procedures and specification are also the origin of the Ph. Eur. Monograph 3021 
<Rivaroxaban tablets>. However, the specification and test procedure have been adapted to 
Ph. Eur. and are aligned now.
Please note that batches manufactured before 2023 were tested according to specification that 
was valid at that time of manufacturing and testing. This is also documented in TRD T.04.02, 
Table 2-4 under footnote a.

All batches manufactured starting from year 2023, were tested according to adapted 
specification to Ph.Eur., as documented in shelf life specification T.02.01 and release 
specification T.02.28, see footnote b. For batches manufactured after year 2023, acceptance 
criteria “Total impurities (Ph.Eur.) with limit of max. 0.3%” is applied according to Ph.Eur. 
monograph 3021. Before adaptation to Ph.Eur. (before 2023), specification item “sum of all 
degradation products with limit max 0.5%” was valid.
Impurities include known by-products of rivaroxaban synthesis, known degradation products 
as well as any unspecified impurities or degradants that are detectable by the HPLC method
for related substances. They include all impurities specified in Ph. Eur. <3021>. And they are 
now covered by specification item “Total impurities (Ph.Eur.).

We acknowledge the testing of elemental impurities in the drug substance with acceptance 
criteria for Class 1, 2A, and 2B elements as defined in ICH Q3D. However, the submission 
lacks adequate information regarding the analytical method used for this testing. Provide a 
complete description of the analytical method used for elemental impurities testing, including:

preparation and calibration procedures. Submit validation data for the analytical method 
demonstrating: Specificity/selectivity, Linearity and range, Accuracy (recovery studies),

introduce elemental impurities at levels of toxicological concern. Therefore, the data support 
that the drug substance is compliant with the ICH Q3D control strategy for elemental impurities 
and does not require routine testing. Thus, the analytical method validation is not required to 
be provided for the elemental impurities.

manufactured and released within the same integrated quality system.

“6.3        Shelf life

not used immediately, in-use storage times and conditions prior to use are the responsibility of 
the user and would normally not be longer than 24 hours at 2 to 8 °C, unless opening has taken 
place in controlled and validated aseptic conditions.”
Is justified by the corresponding in-use stability studies included in section P.8.1 “Stability 
Summary and Conclusion” as well as in section P.2.5 “Microbial Attributes”.
Please refer to 3.2.P.8.1.3 In-use stability (page 14) enclosed in the responses (also please see 
below the main information extracted for your reference). Note that revision 06 of the technical 
document [TRD - M3.2.P.8.1-06 (#010689023)] is included as data has been updated and 
additional information included.
“3.2.P.8.1.3 In-use stability
In-use testing was done according to the Note for Guidance CPMP/QWP/2934/99. Vials with 
a filling volume of 100 mL of batch PL1267 stored under controlled conditions were used for 
in-use stability testing over 72 hours. As 12 mL is the minimum dose recommended for single 
application (0.2 mL/kg body weight x 60 kg = 12 mL), 12 mL were taken from each vial with

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
It is observed that in item 5, “Data Table,” of the stability study, the results for the “Appearance” 
test are reported solely under the generic term “compliant.” This statement is inconsistent with 
the acceptance criteria established in the approved technical specifications and with the 
organoleptic nature of the test. In compliance with section 6.1.3 of NTS No. 182-
MINSA/DIGEMID-2022, the regulated entity must objectively describe the observed physical 
characteristics (shape, color, dimensions, etc.), avoiding ambiguous terms that do not allow for 
verification of the device's physical stability during its validity period.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 ( CTD section):
We acknowledge the observation regarding the use of the term “complies” in the stability study 
data table for the Appearance test. We would like to clarify that this reporting format is 
consistent with the global TRD profile of 8.3.02 document, which governs the structure and 
terminology used across all markets.
Under section 2.4 of the P.8.3.02_IQMS-220334_3., the complete stability testing 
specifications and parameters are provided, including a reference to P.5.2.01, where the detailed 
acceptance criteria for the Appearance evaluation are defined. For clarity, the acceptance 
criteria applied during stability testing are as follows:
• 
Formulation: intrauterine system with silver ring
• 
Color of drug reservoir: whitish or pale yellow
• 
Surface property: the system is essentially free of visual flaws
• 
Appearance (overall): conforms to the above characteristics as defined in P.5.2
Additionally, the stability table includes a specific footnote stating: “The result is reported as 
‘complies’ if all acceptance criteria of ‘Appearance’, ‘Formulation’, ‘Surface property’ and 
‘Color’ of the drug reservoir are met.” This ensures that the term “complies” is not used in an 
ambiguous manner but instead reflects the fulfillment of all predefined organoleptic and 
physical criteria.
Given that this is a harmonized global document, the reporting format is standardized across all 
regions to maintain consistency in regulatory submissions. Modifying the format for a single 
jurisdiction would compromise global alignment and is therefore not advisable.
We trust that the combination of the detailed specifications in section 2.4, the reference to 
P.5.2.01,and the explanatory footnote provides sufficient clarity to verify the physical stability 
of the product throughout its shelf life, even when the summarized result is presented as 
“complies.”

Source:  P.8.3.02_IQMS-220334_3.0_Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery system 13.5 mg /
Stability Data - On-going Studies (new)
keywords: Stability data; stability study and pharmaceutical form; drug product specification; justification of specification; Shelf Life

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
It is noted that the stability study submitted omits the Sterility test in the initial and final periods, 
failing to comply with the mandatory requirement stipulated in Table 4 of the Annex to 
Technical Health Standard No. 182-MINSA/DIGEMID-2022. This standard expressly requires 
that vaginal or intrauterine systems with IFA release demonstrate the absence of microbial 
growth throughout their useful life; therefore, the applicant must incorporate the corresponding 
results or, failing that, provide technical justification through scientific and reliable 
documentation for the omission of this test, which is critical for product safety.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 ( CTD section):
We acknowledge the comment regarding the absence of sterility testing at the initial and final 
stability time points. Sterility testing is not included in routine stability studies because it is a 
destructive test and does not allow re-testing of the same sample. For this reason, sterility testing 
is not considered an appropriate method to confirm ongoing sterility throughout shelf life.
Instead, sterility assurance is maintained through the validated primary packaging system, 
which is designed according to EN ISO 11607-1. To confirm that the packaging continues to 
protect the product over time, we perform container-closure integrity tests (sealed joint strength 
and package seal integrity) as part of the stability program. These tests directly evaluate whether 
the packaging remains intact and capable of maintaining sterility.
Sterility testing is performed for the primary stability batches and the first three 
production-scale batches to confirm sterility at the start of commercial manufacturing. Based 
on this approach, the omission of sterility testing at later stability time points is scientifically 
justified.

Source:  P.5.6.01_IQMS-196681_1.0_Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery system 19.5 mg
/Justification of Specification(s)
ISO 11607-1:2019(en), Packaging for terminally sterilized medical devices — Part 
1: Requirements for materials, sterile barrier systems and packaging systems

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Regarding the identified N-nitroso-meglumine, as of March 11, 2026, a revised Acceptable 
Intake (AI) limit for N-Nitroso-Meglumine is 100 ng/day has been published for this 
nitrosamine (Appendix 1 of Health Canada's Guidance on nitrosamine impurities in 
medications). You are reminded that the revision of the analytical procedure, and repeat 
confirmatory testing are expected (to meet this new limit) and if warranted, the update of the 
drug product specification by August 1 2028 is required as the change falls under the phase 3 
of the call for review. Please confirm and provide a commitment.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1
In response to the inquiry regarding N-Nitroso-Meglumine, Bayer Inc. (Bayer) acknowledges 
the revised Acceptable Intake (AI) limit of 100 ng/day as published on 11-Mar-2026.
As per Section 15 of the Guidance on nitrosamine impurities in medications effective 2025-
Aug-01, on 12-Mar-2026, Bayer shared with Health Canada the results of the confirmatory 
testing of the nitrosamine drug-substance related impurity N-Nitroso- Meglumine (referred to 
as NO-Meglumine) in the drug product Gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 0.5 mol/L for 
injection (MAGNEVIST), as well as the findings from an in-vivo mutagenicity mouse study 
of NO-Meglumine (see Module 1.0.4, MAGNEVIST Confirmatory Testing Results email 
dated 12-March-2026).
As subsequently requested by Health Canada on 26-March-2026, Bayer will be submitting the 
full transgenic rodent mutation assay study report at the end of May 2026 (see Module 1.0.3, 
Health Canada Email dated 26-March-2026).
Based on the outcome of Health Canada’s ongoing assessment, Bayer commits to revise the 
analytical procedure and update the drug product specification by 01-Aug-2028, as applicable.
For convenience, the information shared with Health Canada on 12-Mar-2026 is copied 
below.
1. Acceptable Intake Limit (AIL)
NO-meglumine is recognized by EMA and FDA as a Nitrosamine Drug Substance-Related 
Impurity (NDSRI) having a recommended Acceptable Intake limit of 100 ng/d based on the 
predicted Carcinogenic Potency Categorization Approach (CPCA) which is described as a 
conservative approach.
According to EMA “Appendix 1: Acceptable intakes (AI) established for N-nitrosamines” the 
limit was increased to 1500 ng/d for NO-meglumine based on the negative results of an 
Enhanced Ames Test in 2024. Bayer continued evaluation of NO-Meglumine by an in-vivo
mutagenicity study (MutaMouse study). The experimental results of this study became 
available in January 2026.
Based on the statistically significant and dose-dependent increase of mutation frequency in 
the liver of MutaMice N-Nitroso-meglumine was found to be genotoxic and potentially 
carcinogenic in mice at the levels tested. Consequently, and in accordance with the EMA 
Nitrosamine Q&A guidance (Question 10, updated in October 2025), the AI limit for NO-
Meglumine is established at 100 ng/day, derived using the Carcinogenic Potency 
Categorization Approach (CPCA).
The EMA Q&A guidance allows for the adaption of the Acceptance Intake Limit (AIL) 
according to the Less-than-Lifetime (LTL) approach (as outlined in ICH M7(R2)) for medicinal 
products with a treatment duration of up to 12 months by a factor of 13.3. This factor can be 
applied to the AI for an interim period of 3 years to enable CAPA implementation.
For contrast agents, administrations during lifetime are on an infrequent and occasional basis. 
The LTL approach with a (daily) treatment duration of up to 12 months implies n=365 
treatments during lifetime with a contrast agent as a conservative scenario. As this number is 
extremely high given actual usage, the derived LTL AI of 1330 ng/day can be regarded as safe 
for patients during lifetime.
Bayer submits that the LTL adjusted AI of 1330 ng/day represents a scientifically appropriate 
and general safety limit for NO-Meglumine in contrast agents, rather than limiting its 
application to an interim period of three years.

3. Toxicological evaluation
Administering the maximum daily dose of 30 ml for MAGNEVIST, the maximum amount of 
150 ng/d NO-Meglumine would be applied to a patient in one treatment with MAGNEVIST.
This amount is well below the LTL AIL of 1330 ng/day for NO-Meglumine.
4. Clinical Benefit-Risk Assessment
Based on the review of the literature data, no publications suggesting mutagenic or carcinogenic 
potential of MAGNEVIST were retrieved. As a general precautionary measure, healthcare 
professionals should weigh diagnostic benefits against potential risks and employ the minimum 
effective dose when contrast media are indicated.
5. Mitigation measures / Root cause evaluation
NO-Meglumine can be formed during the bulk manufacturing and/or sterilization process 
and/or storage.
The following activities are planned to evaluate the formation of NO-meglumine in 
Gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 0.5 mol/L for injection (MAGNEVIST):
• The nitrite level in relevant excipients will be determined to identify the main sources 
for nitrite. Following that, possibilities to reduce the introduction of nitrite will be 
evaluated.
• Further MAGNEVIST batches will be tested to evaluate a potential increase of NO-
Meglumine during shelf life.
6. Conclusion
Based on the currently available data, Bayer believes it is justified to establish an LTL 
acceptable limit at 1330 ng/day as a general safety limit for NO-Meglumine in Gadopentetate 
dimeglumine solution 0.5 mol/L for injection (MAGNEVIST) in compliance with EMA 
precautionary guideline, rather than limiting its application to an interim period of three years.
All available data indicate that tested MAGNEVIST batches comply with the updated limits 
for NO-Meglumine, with patient exposure significantly below the LTL AI limit. At present, we 
consider the benefit-risk profile of MAGNEVIST as not being impacted and it remains 
favorable.
Bayer has included a copy of the confirmatory testing outcome report, as well as the 
corresponding appendices in Module 3.2.P.5.5 Characterisation of Impurities (See References).

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
(3.2.P.2.4) The information that you have provided to support the absence of leachables, in your 
proposed drug product, is not considered adequate.  You have provided a brief discussion 
regarding a simulated leachables study, however, you have not provided a justification for the 
simulated study as required by USP <1664> Assessment of Drug Product Leachables 
Associated with Pharmaceutical Packaging/Delivery Systems.  The following is therefore 
requested:
a) Confirm that the simulated leachables study was conducted using actual drug product
manufactured as per current manufacturing process.  Batch number(s) should be 
provided and should be consistent with the batch number(s) used in the extractables 
study.
b) Provide the results of a leachables study over the proposed storage conditions and
proposed shelf-life using the actual drug product solution, manufactured as per current 
process, placed on inverted orientation.
c) In the absence of real-time leachable study data, provide a scientific justification as to
why a simulated leachables study was conducted instead of a real-time assessment over 
the proposed storage conditions and shelf-life of the product.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2
a) Bayer confirms that the simulated leachables study was conducted using MAGNEVIST,
gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 0.5 mol/L for parenteral use, batch number KT0J7VP 
manufactured according to the current manufacturing process.
The sample was collected at the end of filling line into a separate glass container to avoid 
contact with the new bromobutyl rubber stopper material.
The stoppers used in the extractables and simulated leachables studies had all the same 
pre-treatments as used in the current MAGNEVIST, gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 
0.5 mol/L for parenteral use filling process.
Stoppers from the same lots were used in both the extractables and simulated leachables 
studies.
b) Real-time leachable shelf-life data is currently not available, please refer to the response
provided under Question 2c that discusses the justification for using a simulated leachables 
study.
c) With the introduction of the bromobutyl stopper, extractables data was prepared in
exaggerated conditions of 50°C / 72 h and 85°C / 1 h (see Module 3.2.P.2.4.06_IQMS-
254392_1.0 Extraction Studies). The stability study for gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 
0.5 mol/L in vials using the alternative bromobutyl closure system, had not yet been 
initiated. Therefore, a simulated leachables study using gadopentetate dimeglumine solution 
0.5 mol/L as extractant, in exaggerated conditions of 50 °C / 72 h and 85 °C / 1 h was 
conducted to confirm the safety of the new stopper material.
In the simulated leachables study no simulated leachables exceeding the study analytical 
evaluation threshold (AETs) was observed.
For the new bromobutyl stoppers an extensive extractables study was initially performed 
using several different extraction media, at elevated temperatures as stated above, with 
relatively long extraction time. These conditions were chosen to reflect recommendations 
in USP <1663> monograph, and ISO 10993-18 and 10993-12. For the AETs, when feasible, 
higher Uncertainty Factors (UF) of 4 and 10, than the usual UF 2 were used to confirm that 
all extractables are measured. The analyses were performed using state-of-art mass 
spectroscopic instruments.
Extractions with 2-propanol as extractant, 50% EtOH/water were performed, and also with 
water. In pH 4 and pH 9.5 buffer solutions only a few extractables in low amounts were 
detected. These were mainly fatty acids like palmitoleic, palmitic and oleic acids that are 
relatively non-toxic and common in elastomers and plastics. In addition to the extractables 
study, Bayer decided to conduct a simulated leachables study.
In the simulated leachables study, using similar exaggerated extraction conditions to the 
extractables study, no reportable compounds were found. It was therefore considered 
adequate proof of stopper material suitability and safety for its intended use as container 
closure system and therefore no formal leachables stability study was planned.
A real-time stability study is on-going and a leachables study after 36 months testing and 
also at the end of 60 months shelf-life will be performed as per the USP <1664> Assessment 
of Drug Product Leachables Associated with Pharmaceutical Packaging/Delivery Systems, 
to further confirm the safety of the material.

Question/Consideration: CDE CMC reviewer Mr. Zhou Haohui asked for FDA and EMA HA questions and responses for Gadoquatrane injection.

(3.2.A.1)

Facilities:

Drug Product Specifications & Analytical Methods:

Further questions not applicable for China:

(3.2.P.5 / 3.2.R)

Parametric Release & Sterility Assurance:
Regulatory concerns addressed linkage between batch records and parametric release, as well as monitoring strategies (please note; parametric release is not applicable for China). The applicant clarified documentation and provided batch records.
Furthermore, questions regarding prefilled syringes (PFS) were answered.

Furthermore, please find below the executive Summary: Gadoquatrane solution o.4 mml Gd/mL for injection - EMA Questions and Applicant Responses (Module 3 Quality).
Drug Substance
(3.2.S.1.3)
Complex Stability:
The Rapporteur requested experimental determination of complexation constants and comparative discussion with established gadolinium agents. The Applicant explained that experimental determination was not feasible due to the molecule’s size and extremely slow dissociation kinetics. Instead, a DFT (density functional theory) -based computational approach was applied using monomeric model units representing the tetrameric structure. These calculations demonstrated that each subunit exhibits thermodynamic stability comparable to gadobutrol (log kGdL > 20).
In conclusion, the complex stability of each single gadoquatrane unit is very comparable with the complex stability of gadobutrol. The small variation in calculated complex stability between the two model units further indicates that the linker atoms, which connect the monomers in a tetramer unit, have little influence on the overall stability. Thus, the complex stability of the gadoquatrane tetramer is primarily driven by the sub-unit stability which is comparable to gadobutrol.
(3.2.S.2.2)
Manufacture - Process Description & Controls:
The Rapporteur requested clarification and improvement of the manufacturing process description. The Applicant clarified that sodium bromide addition is mandatory, described seeding as non-critical, and provided information regarding reprocessing and recovery. Critical process parameters were highlighted, and generation and use of gaseous, potable, and purified water was clarified.
(3.2.S.2.3)
Mutagenic Impurities in Starting Materials:
The Rapporteur requested clarification on control of mutagenic impurities. The Applicant applied an ICH M7 Option 4 approach supported by purge calculations, spiking studies, and analytical validation. The Applicant concludes that all mutagenic impurities are adequately controlled.
Cyclen Impurity Control:
The Rapporteur requested clarification regarding impurities in Cyclen. The Applicant demonstrated via QSAR system that Benzylethanolamine is non-mutagenic and provided batch data confirming its presence below reporting thresholds. For para-Toluenesulfonic acid (pTSA), absence was confirmed and supported by worst-case purge calculations and spiking studies.
Glypro Impurities and Specification:
The Rapporteur requested clarification on Glypro impurities. The Applicant confirmed Isopropyl tosylate classification (ICH M7 class 2), provided spiking and purge data, justified specification limits, demonstrated racemic synthesis, and confirmed that glycine is chemically manufactured without fermentation-related viral risk.
Gadolinium oxide:
The Rapporteur requested tighter control of elemental impurities. The Applicant provided improved analytical data (ICP-MS), demonstrated compliance with ICH Q3D Option 2, and supported the control strategy with purge studies. Further tightening was not considered necessary.
Neopentyltetramine (NPTA) hydrochloride Impurities:
The Rapporteur requests additional information for NPTA HCl on spiking studies to verify purge of 2-chloropropane and methyl/ethyl tosylates, discussion of isopropyl tosylate, assessment of pentaerythritol and benzylamine, and evaluation of p-toluenesulfonyl chloride and pTSA including possible downstream ethyl tosylate formation and any need for specification limits. The response adds commercial batch data, purge calculations, and dedicated spiking studies for these late-stage risks, expands the impurity discussion in the starting material justification and impurity sections, and concludes that the relevant impurity risks are adequately controlled to acceptable levels.

Raw Material Specifications:
The Rapporteur requested improved raw material specifications. The Applicant harmonized specifications regarding identity, assay, and impurity controls and clarified water system compliance with current regulations.

(3.2.S.2.4)
Control of Intermediates:
The Rapporteur requests tabulated presentation of in-process controls for each manufacturing step, tightening and clarification of selected intermediate specifications, clarification that Bis(Gd-GlyMe-DOTA) represents two regio-isomers, and additional characterisation data for intermediates. The response adds a dedicated IPC table, tightens and clarifies Glyptac and Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude specifications, updates the regio-isomer wording, and provides additional characterisation data for Glyptac and Gd-GlyMe-DOTA.
Analytical Methods and Supporting Data:
The question requested clarification on IPC methods, spiking and purge studies, batch data, analytical validation, the PDE for diisopropylethylamine, and control of 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene. In response, the applicant provided the requested supporting documentation, tabulated batch and spiking data, detailed purge justifications, a PDE rationale, and data confirming adequate control and purge of 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene
(3.2.S.2.6)
Manufacturing Process Development:
The Rapporteur requested clarification on the scale at which PARs (Proven Acceptable Ranges) were established. The Applicant clarified scale applicability and scale verification, based on development data, process understanding, and commercial manufacturing experience.
Impurities:
The question requested clarification on possible downstream formation of des-acetyl-Gadoquatrane-like impurities, batch data and method capability for class 2 impurities, and the justification for compound-specific mutagenic impurity limits. The applicant discussed purge and spiking data showing effective clearance of des-acetyl impurities, submitted additional analytical and batch data for the relevant class 2 impurities, and justified the proposed limits for class 1 and class 2 mutagenic impurities in accordance with ICH M7 and related guidance.
(3.2.S.3.1)
Structure Elucidation:
The Rapporteur questioned structural confirmation of diastereomer 2. The Applicant explained crystallographic limitations due to pseudo-symmetry, provided alternative NMR data using lanthanum analogues, and demonstrated lack of clinical relevance.
(3.2.S.3.2)
Residual solvents and elemental impurities - Method validation:
The question requested validation documents for methods used to determine residual solvents and elemental impurities. The applicant submitted the requested validation.

(3.2.S.4.1)
Drug Substance Specification:
The Rapporteur requested clarification of the applicability of the drug substance specification at the drug product manufacturing site, and tighter limits for water and diastereomers. The applicant confirms that only one 3.2.S.4 section is provided because the drug substance manufacturer’s control is the only testing which is performed. The specification and test methods are appropriate to ensure the necessary quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance to produce Gadoquatrane drug product in the required quality. No additional specification parameters or analytical methods are employed by the finished product manufacturer upon receipt of the drug substance. Furthermore, tighter limits for water and diastereomeric ratio supported by development data and batch history were included in the specification.
(3.2.S.4.2)
Drug Substance -Test Procedure - Endotoxin Testing:
The Rapporteur requested removal of non-harmonised USP references and clarification of the need for an alternative endotoxin method. The applicant removed inappropriate USP references, retained the recombinant cascade reagent method as a validated alternative to the established endotoxin method, and provided the scientific and regulatory rationale for its continued inclusion.
(3.2.S.4.3)
Drug Substance - Method validation:
The Rapporteur requested updates of validation documents: removal of the rCR validation, updated repeatability data for several analytical procedures, and accuracy data for Gd-GlyMe-DOTA in the impurity method. The applicant maintained the rCR validation with reference to the response to previous question and provided updated repeatability and accuracy data for the requested methods, including additional validation for Gd-GlyMe-DOTA. The response confirms that analytical procedures are fully validated for their intended purpose across the specification range.
(3.2.S.4.4)
Batch Analysis:
The question requested reporting of non-limit test results using LOD/LOQ terminology and clarification of differing specifications applied to earlier development batches. The applicant updated free gadolinium reporting to the method LOQ and clarified that clinical development batches were released against phase-appropriate specifications in place at the time, whereas preclinical batches were not subject to formal release specifications.

(3.2.S.4.5)
Justification of specification and skip testing:
The question requested further justification for omission of chiral purity testing, support for omission of a separate gadolinium assay, and revision of the microbial skip-testing approach. The applicant provided exemplary results for optical rotation data supporting the racemic nature of the intermediate and final drug substance, introduced and justified a formula-based gadolinium assay, and revised microbial skip testing to a fixed testing frequency supported by stability results.
(3.2.S.5)
Reference Standards and Characterization:
The question requested clarification on establishment and characterisation of reference standards, additional structural support for selected impurity standards, and identification of standards used for free gadolinium and residual solvent methods. The applicant described the internal approach to reference and working standards, clarified the naming and retest scheme, provided additional structural support for the requested impurity standards, and identified the purchased standards used for the free gadolinium and residual solvent methods.
(3.2.S.6)
Container Closure System:
The question requested demonstration of compliance of the primary packaging materials with the cited Ph. Eur. monographs and updated specifications and certificates. The applicant clarified that pharmacopoeial compliance is covered through supplier qualification, while routine incoming control is limited to identity and thickness, and referred to supplier declarations supporting compliance of the packaging materials.
(3.2.S.7.3)
Stability Data and Stability-Indicating Parameters:
The question requested clarification on the relevance of parameters in stability studies, updated free gadolinium reporting, description of storage conditions, interpretation of assay results under stress, and additional free gadolinium stress data. The applicant justified parameters in stability studies, provided updated free gadolinium reporting to the LOQ, clarified the storage instruction. Furthermore, supportive stress data is referenced confirming that the stability control strategy remains appropriate.

Drug Product

(3.2.P.1)
Composition Tables:
The Rapporteur requested clarification on the composition tables, particularly the use of “q.s.” for certain excipients and the expression of drug substance content in mmol. The applicant explained that hydrochloric acid and water for injection are used as process-adjustable components to achieve pH and osmolality specifications and therefore cannot be fixed quantitatively. Initial quantities are defined during manufacturing and adjusted as necessary. The applicant further clarified that mmol information for gadoquatrane and gadolinium is already included within the composition tables via footnotes. Overall, the approach is maintained in line with Quality-by-Design principles.
(3.2.P.2.1)
Pediatric Use of Excipients:
The Rapporteur requested confirmation that the excipient selection considered pediatric use. The Applicant confirmed that all excipients have well-established safety profiles, including pediatric populations, and that formulation development adhered to relevant EMA guidelines. Supporting justification was added to the pharmaceutical development section.
(3.2.P.2.2)
Stress Studies:
The Rapporteur requested detailed stress study results. The applicant provided full datasets covering mechanical stress, pH variation, and freeze-thaw conditions. Results demonstrate that no significant degradation or quality changes occur, confirming robustness of the formulation.
Physicochemical and Biological Properties:
The Rapporteur requested inclusion of relevant physicochemical and biological properties. The applicant provided data on density, viscosity, osmolality, pH, solubility, and water content. These parameters are linked to product performance and manufacturability and are controlled as part of the defined quality attributes.

Manufacturing Process and Filter Validation:
The Rapporteur requested additional validation data, including filter compatibility, holding time studies, and process parameters. The applicant submitted detailed data confirming compatibility, absence of adsorption, and adequate control of extractables/leachables. Process parameters such as mixing speed and temperature were demonstrated to be non-critical and controlled dynamically via process control systems.

Container Closure System for Paediatric Use:
The Rapporteur requested justification of container closure in relation to paediatric dosing. The applicant demonstrated that multiple presentations allow weight-based dosing, and use is restricted to trained healthcare professionals. Smaller presentations support paediatric use, and the risk of dosing error is considered minimal.
Extractables and Leachables:
The Rapporteur requested detailed method descriptions and toxicological evaluation. The applicant justified the use of screening methods based on threshold of toxicological concern (TTC) and provided toxicological risk assessments confirming no safety concern for detected compounds.

Batch Formula:
The Rapporteur identified inconsistencies in batch formula descriptions. The Applicant corrected the discrepancies and harmonized relevant sections.
(3.2.P.3.3)
Process Parameters:
The Rapporteur requested details on the defined process parameters and definition of critical process parameters. The Applicant demonstrated that parameters such as mixing time, speed, and temperature are non-critical and controlled via the GMP system, supported by development data demonstrating robustness.
(3.2.P.3.3)
Shelf-Life Determination:
The Rapporteur requested confirmation that shelf life is calculated according to guideline CPMP/QWP/072/96. The Applicant confirmed full compliance.

IPC Methods:
The Rapporteur requested references and validation status of IPC methods. IPC methods were clarified as either compendial or performed using qualified equipment. Validation requirements were justified accordingly.
Filter Compatibility:
The Rapporteur requested studies on solution compatibility and extractables from filters. The Applicant provided full filter compatibility and extractables/leachables data in updated documentation, demonstrating no impact on product quality.
(3.2.P.4)
Calcobutrol Specification:
The Rapporteur requested justification for omission of microbiological and endotoxin testing and clarification of solvent impurity limits. Question/Consideration:
Question 8
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls 
or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this 
does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, 
the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure 
integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected 
in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.

Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and
detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.
c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method
reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or 
provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate 
package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product 
lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP 
Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product 
manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of 
critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI 
at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control 
strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for 
the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm 
conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s 
(Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure 
systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method 
description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a 
risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments 
are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging 
processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are 
mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI 
testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on 
GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during 
the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in 
P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for 
routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered 
an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility 
with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this 
purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate 
a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug 
product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, 
critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon 
continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see 
P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use 
as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, 
further supporting the presented data from P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining 
presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media 
portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• 
Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• 
Bottle 65/100 mL
• 
Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–
closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence 
of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of 
the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes 
vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap 
and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium 
is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum 
is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive 
helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation 
includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom
to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of 
the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual 
maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During 
maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 
1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with 
DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of 
measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass 
spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup 
e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard 
with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of 
the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive 
sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are 
confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability 
testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using 
metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as 
negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all 
values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal 
detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the 
containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each 
measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample 
populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process 
variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization 
prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This 
approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal 
stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from 
P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.
