Question/Consideration:
Question 9
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug 
product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 
mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification 
limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance 
scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper 
limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and 
manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing 
function.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon 
available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived 
based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. 
As discussed in P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. 
Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of 
release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life 
specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process 
validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe 
each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The 
data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No 
significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 
99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations 
and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance 
bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The 
specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.4.01 and 
P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in 
the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A 
explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should 
necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.

Question/Consideration:
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.

Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.

c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s (Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, further supporting the presented data from P.2.4.02.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.

Question/Consideration:
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing function.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. As discussed in P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.4.01 and P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.

Question/Consideration:
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.

Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.
c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method reliability at the container level.

If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s (Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, further supporting the presented data from P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• Bottle 65/100 mL
• Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.

Question/Consideration:
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing function.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. As discussed in P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated P.5.1.01, P.5.1.02, P.5.4.01 and P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.

Question/Consideration:
The response indicates that the helium leak test was not validated and that no positive controls or method detection limits were established. While equipment calibration is described, this does not demonstrate method suitability at the container closure system level. Accordingly, the data are considered developmental only and are insufficient to confirm container closure integrity for the proposed product. Please note that validated analytical methods are expected in line with ICH Q2 and USP <1207>.
Please provide:
a. Validation data for the helium leak test, including precision, accuracy, and detection limits.
b. The positive control strategy employed and corresponding results.
c. A justification explaining how equipment calibration alone ensures method reliability at the container level.
If validation has not been performed, please commit to completing method validation or provide alternative container closure integrity data generated using a validated method.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge the request and would like to provide the subsequent explanations:
Holistic container closure integrity (CCI) concept:
A holistic CCI concept has been established to provide a robust data basis to demonstrate package integrity across all drug product–packaging combinations throughout the product lifecycle. This concept is consistent with the principles outlined in USP <1207> and EU-GMP Annex 1, which require a lifecycle-based approach integrating development, product manufacturing, and commercial product stability for the assurance of CCI and maintenance of critical quality attributes. The concept comprises complementary components addressing CCI at different lifecycle stages, thereby ensuring a scientifically justified and risk-based control strategy.
During the development phase, based on prior knowledge and established control strategies for the materials, a one-time verification of inherent package integrity is performed to confirm conformance to the defined maximum allowable leakage limit (MALL) of 6 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s (Kirsch et al., 1997; USP <1207>). This verification is conducted on empty container-closure systems using the highly sensitive and quantitative helium leak test method. A detailed method description is provided below.
During product manufacturing and commercial product stability, the holistic concept applies a risk-based approach in line with EU-GMP Annex 1 expectations. Dedicated risk assessments are performed to evaluate the potential impact of fill-and-finish operations, packaging processes, storage, and distribution on container closure integrity. Identified residual risks are mitigated, where feasible, through process optimization or addressed through appropriate CCI testing. For Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL, two mitigation actions were defined on GMP level:
• Regular packaging seal testing (for vials and bottles)
• Implementation of a product-specific CCI test method
As packaging seal testing, in alignment with USP <1207.3>, crimping quality is checked during the filling process. The test forms part of the parametric release strategy and is mentioned in 3.2.P.5.6.01.
The product-specific CCI test methods are in implementation as validated test method for routine manufacturing. In combination with routine visual inspection, these tests are considered an appropriate measure for confirming CCI. Test method selection was based on compatibility with the specific drug product–packaging combination. A dye ingress test was selected for this purpose and is intended to monitor and confirm CCI during routine manufacturing. To generate a statistically meaningful data basis for CCI after development, 10 consecutive batches per drug product packaging combination will be tested according to AQL (Special inspection level S-4, critical defect classification, normal sampling). If no failures occur, sampling is reduced, upon continued compliance, to a skip-lot approach.
The dye ingress test method has been successfully validated for several vial presentations, see 3.2.P.5.3.08. Validation activities demonstrated the suitability of the method for the intended use as a GMP control to CCI. During the validation activities, negative samples showed integrity, further supporting the presented data from 3.2.P.2.4.02.
We commit to complete the validation of the dye ingress CCIT method for the remaining presentations included in a bracketing concept, representative for the entire contrast media portfolio at manufacturing site Bayer AG Berlin, specifically:
• Vial formats 10/10 mL, 30 mL
• Bottle 65/100 mL
• Prefilled syringes 5/10 mL, 7.5/10 mL, 10 mL, 15/20 mL.

Detailed method description helium leak test:
Helium leak testing is performed as a format-specific qualification activity for container–closure systems (CCS) used for parenteral drug products. The study is conducted in the absence of drug product.
The method is based on the quantitative determination of helium flow across the interface of the respective CCS. Depending on the container format, the container closure system includes vial or bottle closures (incl. rubber stopper and crimp cap) or, for prefilled syringes, the tip cap and plunger stopper interface. Helium leak testing is performed in open mode, whereby helium is introduced into the closure-side compartment of the format specific format part while vacuum is applied to the opposing container-side compartment of the format specific format part to drive helium flow across the container closure interface. For vials and bottles, sample preparation includes the introduction of a defined opening (approximately 6 mm) at the container bottom to enable helium flow through the CCS. For prefilled syringes, preparation involves removal of the tip cap or plunger stopper respectively.
The helium leak detection system is subject to routine maintenance and calibration. Annual maintenance is performed by the equipment supplier following proprietary procedures. During maintenance, the system is calibrated using certified standards covering a leak rate range of 1.81 × 10⁻⁸ to 4.76 × 10⁻⁵ mbar·L/s, traceable to external certification in accordance with DIN EN ISO 20486:2018.
Instrument conditioning and system suitability testing are performed on each day of measurement. Conditioning is achieved by directly coupling the helium source to the mass spectrometer to verify the absence of background helium signals originating from the test setup e.g. tubing and seals. System suitability is subsequently confirmed using an internal standard with a defined leak rate of 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mbar·L/s and two certified external standards. One of the external standards represents a negative sample and the other external standard a positive sample, so that helium flow rates of either less than or greater than 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s are confirmed respectively. The applicant wants to emphasize, that with this system suitability testing, a certified negative and positive control was included in all measurements.
System performance and method reliability are additionally verified on format level using metallic master samples representing the respective container format. These samples serve as negative controls and are measured prior to a sample sequence. Acceptance is achieved if all values remain below 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s.
Following system suitability confirmation, prepared empty CCS samples are analysed. Signal detection is independent from the tested format. Format-specific format parts are used to fit the containers into the equipment. Tight fit is verified as system suitability test prior each measurement series, guaranteeing the absence of leaks between container and format parts.
CCS qualification includes, for vials and bottles, the evaluation of at least three sample populations, representing low, nominal, and high crimping forces to cover expected process variability during routine manufacturing. All samples are subjected to terminal sterilization prior to testing. For each condition, 30 units are tested in accordance with USP <382>. This approach is designed to challenge closure integrity under worst-case processing and thermal stress conditions, particularly regarding elastomeric components. Reported results from 3.2.P.2.4.02 are representing the worst-case scenario.

Question/Consideration:
Given that calcobutrol is added at a nominal concentration of 0.196 mg/mL in the drug product formulation and long-term stability data consistently show levels around ~0.12 mg/mL, please provide a data-driven justification for retaining the current upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL for release and shelf-life. In particular, clarify whether:
- 
Any batches (including development, validation, or worst-case drug substance scenarios) have demonstrated calcobutrol levels approaching the proposed upper limit, and
- 
A tighter upper limit could be established based on observed stability trends and manufacturing experience without compromising the intended complexing function.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge that the assessor requested a data-driven justification and based upon available data concluded that the upper specification limit of 0.235 mg/mL cannot be derived based on batch data only.
The theoretical concentration of calcobutrol based upon the batch formula is 0.196 mg/mL. As discussed in 3.2.P.5.6.01, during the manufacturing process, a decrease in calcobutrol occurs. Therefore, typically calcobutrol concentration will be lower than 0.196 mg/mL at time of release and during shelf-life. To derive an upper limit for the calcobutrol release and shelf-life specification based upon available data, batch results from the clinical phase and from process validation (altogether 13 batches of Gadoquatrane solution in vial, bottle or prefilled syringe each filled from one of 13 distinct bulk solution batches, see Table 1) were considered. The data set was assessed for normality using the Anderson-Darling test (p = 0.386). No significant deviation from normality was observed (α = 0.05). The upper tolerance bound with 99% coverage at the 99% confidence level was calculated assuming normality. Calculations and statistical analysis were performed using Minitab® 21.4.1. The calculated upper tolerance bound of 0.185 mg/mL is proposed as upper specification limit for calcobutrol content. The specifications have been updated accordingly, see updated 3.2.P.5.1.01, 3.2.P.5.1.02, 3.2.P.5.4.01 and 3.2.P.5.6.01.
However, we would like to confirm that calcobutrol is safe and effective when occurring in the formulation within the originally proposed specification range and mention that ICH Q6A explicitly recognizes that “The basis for the acceptance criteria at the time of filing should necessarily focus on safety and efficacy” due to a “limited amount of data”.

Question/Consideration: Please carefully review and check the contents of the JX spec, especially the operational details. If there are any operational details that should be paid attention, Bayer needs to communicate with NIFDC in advance.
Answer/Response:
The applicant has reviewed and checked the contents of the JX spec, we would like to clarify below aspects which are paid attention to [identified and communicated by LRAM].

(1) Regarding the pretreatment time for the determination of substances and their content, the preparation of the test solution mentions that “Transfer 5 tablets to a 500 mL volumetric flask, add about 400 mL of solvent, shake for at least 12 h”
In all likelihood, the practical performance is “overnight”, which is generally at least 12 h but can be as long as 16 h under normal working conditions. Hence, stating “at least 12 h” allows for the test solution to be shaken overnight, which typically saves time.

(2) Under dissolution, it mentions in Reference stock solution that Weigh accurately about 22.22 mg of asundexian reference standard.
22.22 mg is the target if a volume of 20 mL is prepared. Generally, the target concentration should be 1.11 mg/mL for the reference stock solution. Using a calibrated and qualified analytical balance in this range should be a basic requirement for any trained lab technician.

(3) Procedure under dissolution: Carry out the method for ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometry (European Pharmacopoeia 2.2.25) to measure the absorbance of the test solution and the reference solution separately at the wavelength of 263 nm and with a cuvette path length of 5 mm, and calculate the dissolution per tablet.
Difference comparison between JX and TRD
Items in dissolution test
JX spec / TRD
Procedure: Absorbance at single wavelength of 263nm is directly determined / Recording the absorbance of 200nm to 600nm and then absorbance at 263nm is used.
Baseline correction: None / At single wavelength 575nm or the average in the range of 550 nm to 600 nm, in which no absorbance of the drug substance occurs
Robust result in P.5.3 shows the result of with/without baseline correction does not cause significant deterioration on the listed statistical parameters.

Global team accepts that the calculation of dissolution amount is performed using single wavelength 263nm without baseline correction done.
Except for above contents, there are no other special operation details to be paid attention to for the experiment to be performed by NIFDC.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Please explain why when calculating Assay (on water-free and solvent-free basis) of 
Vericiguat, the benzene content is not deducted.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (S.4.2.01):
The reason for benzene of not being deducted in the calculation of vericiguat assay is that 
benzene is present at trace (ppm) level and foreign contaminant, and it does not contribute to 
the bulk mass.
Residual solvents present at quantifiable levels (e.g. ethanol, dimethyl acetate) are corrected 
in the assay calculation to account for their contribution to the bulk mass. Class 1 solvents 
such as benzene are present, if at all, at trace (ppm) levels and are controlled as impurities in 
accordance with ICH Q3C; therefore, they are not included in assay normalization.
Residual solvents are corrected in the assay calculation, as they contribute to the overall mass 
of the material. However, in accordance with ICH Q3C, benzene doesn’t contribute to the 
calculation below.

Source:  ICH Q3C
keywords: assay; residual solvents; Impurities

Question/Consideration: Please confirm if EMA/FDA has any concern regarding to " Gd metal complex bonds".
Answer/Response:
No concerns were raised by the FDA.
EMA requested experimental determination of complexation constants and comparative discussion with established gadolinium agents. The Applicant explained that experimental determination was not feasible due to the molecule’s size and extremely slow dissociation kinetics. Instead, a DFT (density functional theory) -based computational approach was applied using monomeric model units representing the tetrameric structure. These calculations demonstrated that each subunit exhibits thermodynamic stability comparable to gadobutrol (log kGdL > 20).
In conclusion, the complex stability of each single Gadoquatrane unit is very comparable with the complex stability of gadobutrol. The small variation in calculated complex stability between the two model units further indicates that the linker atoms, which connect the monomers in a tetramer unit, have little influence on the overall stability. Thus, the complex stability of the gadoquatrane tetramer is primarily driven by the sub-unit stability which is comparable to gadobutrol.
keywords: General Properties; Elucidation of Structure and other Characteristics; manufacturer; Characterisation of Impurities; risk assessment

Question/Consideration: Regarding the Control of critical steps, please explain why the acceptance criteria for the parameter “inlet air temperature” in “Film-coating” step has been changed to 70-90℃ and provide the justification for this setting.
Answer/Response:
The film-coating equipment implemented at Patheon Bourgoin is different from the film-coating equipment at Bayer Leverkusen. The different equipment scale and technical design require adapted processing parameters to achieve similar product temperature and drying conditions during film-coating. The film-coating equipment at Patheon Bourgoin requires a higher inlet air temperature (70-90°C) compared to Bayer Leverkusen (63-67°C) to achieve the same product temperature (50-60°C) during the film-coating process. By keeping the product temperature and thereby the drying conditions similar, it is ensured to obtain product with the same quality in both film-coating processes, as demonstrated via successful process validation (P.3.5.01).

The approved tighter acceptance criterion is aligned with the current requirements of the European Pharmacopoeia and reflects the applicant’s intention to comply with the pharmacopoeial standard.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
The manufacturing process of the drug substance involves:
o 
Recharging operations (e.g., addition of gadolinium oxide in Step 2b), and
o 
Selective operations (e.g., selective washing with toluene and water in Step 1a; 
selective dichloromethane post-treatment in Step 2a).
Please summarize the frequency of these operations in previous commercial batches and 
process validation batches, analyze the reasons, and minimize variability by fixing the process 
as much as possible.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.S.2):
IPC-controlled amount of gadolinium oxide added in step 2b.
In the manufacturing process of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude from Glyptac (Step 2a/b), the 
process sequence up to the gadolinium insertion step is comparatively long and involves 
multiple operations, including chemical conversions, extractions, and layer separations. In 
addition, the input Glyptac material contains isopropyl alcohol within the specified limit (max 
8.0%), which may contribute to minor variability in the effective input quantity.
Due to the process complexity and cumulative handling operations, there is a possibility for 
product losses during processing, which may influence the exact stoichiometric requirement 
of gadolinium oxide during the metal insertion step.
As the organic impurity (and chemical process intermediate) “free ligand” content in Gd-
GlyMe-DOTA is controlled by meeting the tightly defined limit of in-process control 4 (IPC-
4), precise gadolinium oxide recharging is considered beneficial for ensuring consistent 
product quality.
Accordingly, gadolinium oxide is added in controlled lots based on HPLC-monitored in-
process testing via IPC-4. In cases where additional recharges are required, the subsequent 
incremental addition of gadolinium oxide is progressively reduced, as defined in the master 
batch record, to avoid over-titration. In addition, the maximum cumulative quantity of 
gadolinium oxide that can be added to a batch is capped as specified in the manufacturing 
description (“sum of total gadolinium oxide portions added max. 0.22 kg per kg Glyptac 
intermediate”).
This IPC-controlled incremental addition strategy ensures effective control of free ligand 
content while simultaneously limiting excess gadolinium oxide addition.

IPC-controlled Toluene/water workup in step 1a:
In the manufacturing process of Glyptac intermediate from cyclen (DO3A Route), 3.7 molar 
equivalents of anhydrous sodium acetate with respect to cyclen are employed. Considering the 
relatively high quantity of sodium acetate used with respect to cyclen, trace amounts of the 
inorganic impurity sodium formate present in sodium acetate can lead to the formation of the 
impurity RRT 1.09 (N-Formyl-1,4-DO2A-Diester, as described in chapter 5.2.5.5 of 
S.2.6.01).
This process-related impurity is controlled by in-process control 1 (IPC-1) in the step 1a 
process.
RRT 1.09 content (HPLC; %Area): not more than 0.8%
Thus, the RRT 1.09 / N-Formyl-1,4-DO2A-Diester impurity can be effectively monitored, 
controlled and limited through the IPC-governed toluene/water workup procedure as 
described in S.2.2.02.
As a strategic justification, it is noted that out of 60 manufactured batches, 10 batches 
underwent the toluene/water work-up process thereby consistently ensuring that N-Formyl-
1,4-DO2A-Diester (RRT 1.09) impurity is limited to not more than 0.8%.

IPC-controlled DCM workup in step 2a:
In the manufacturing process of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude from Glyptac (Step 2a/b), in-
process control 2 (IPC-2) monitors the level of process-related organic impurities (for details 
refer to S.2.6.01, chapter 5.2.4.1) and triggers a work-up of the reaction mixture should levels 
of the impurities be elevated and the IPC goal is not met. Ultimately, this IPC controls the 
downstream levels of Bis(Gd-GlyMe-DOTA), a specified organic impurity on Gd-GlyMe-
DOTA intermediate.
In the Cyglyp route towards Glyptac intermediate (Step 1c/d), the possibility for formation of 
the Bis(Gd-GlyMe-DOTA)-related impurities is comparatively high. In this route, the reaction 
sequence starts with the reaction of glypro with cyclen, which contains four reactive amine 
functions. Therefore, the probability of overalkylation with glypro, leading to the formation of 
corresponding downstream bis-carboxylic acid impurities, is statistically higher when 
compared to the DO3A route (Step 1a/b): here, cyclen is first reacted with t-butyl 
bromoacetate to form DO3A-Triester, a species containing only one reactive amine function, 
that is set to be alkylated with glypro in the downstream process. Thus, the origin for Bis(Gd-
GlyMe-DOTA)-related impurities is limited as the required 2-fold glypro alkylation can only 
occur on traces of 1,7- and 1,4-DO2A-Diester impurities in DO3A-Triester (Details in 
S.2.6.01, chapter 5.2.5.4). For a comprehensive comparison demonstrating the equivalency of 
both routes to safely deliver gadoquatrane drug substance, refer to S.2.6.01, chapter 5.1.1.

The above-described circumstances are reflected in the application of the IPC-governed 
dichloromethane work-up during manufacturing: out of 118 batches manufactured using 
Glyptac stemming for the DO3A route as input material, only one batch required DCM work-
up based on IPC-2 results. In contrast, all 103 batches manufactured using Glyptac stemming 
from the Cyglyp route as input material were processed via the dichloromethane work-up, in 
order to control the impurity through a successfully passed IPC-2 after workup.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
The drying step uses a vacuum drying method with steam heating.
Please explain how the drying endpoint is determined.
Provide data demonstrating how consistency of polymorphic form and water content across 
batches is ensured (process robustness).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.S.2):
The final drying operation in presence of gaseous water is a process where a high jacket 
temperature (max. 95 °C) is employed to ensure an efficient ethanol-removal from the moist 
product. Only at sufficient inner temperature, gaseous water (carrier gas for more efficient 
ethanol-removal) is applied to the product isolated from crystallization and the pressure 
during gaseous water application is controlled to not exceed 75 mbar. This ensures no 
condensation of water during the drying operation is taking place. This procedure ensures 
efficient ethanol-removal to meet the specification of ethanol in the drug substance (max. 
0.5%), while residual water remains in the drug substance.
Batch data of Gadoquatrane drug substance for the test items water content and polymorphic 
form are provided in Table 2. Based on the established process, 31 batches have been 
produced so far. All batches comply to the specification limit for water in the drug substance  
(max. 21.0%). The polymorphic form has been monitored for each batch and was found to be 
Hydrate II, Hydrate III or a mixture of Hydrate II and III.

Table 2: Water content and polymorphic form of commercial Gadoquatrane drug 
substance batches.
...

It should be noted that based on ICH Q6A Decision Tree #4, a specification of the 
polymorphic form in Gadoquatrane drug substance can be omitted (refer to S.4.5.01). As 
briefly outlined in the following, it has been demonstrated that all polymorphic forms and also 
drug substance with different water loading is suited to produce Gadoquatrane drug product.
Gadoquatrane exists in three crystalline forms, Hydrate I, Hydrate II and Hydrate III, as 
well as an amorphous phase. According to DVS (dynamic vapor sorption), Hydrates I and II 
show a water uptake of approx. 17.3% (Hydrate I) and approx. 8.6% (Hydrate II) at 50% RH 
and 20 °C, while Hydrate III can take up to a maximum of ca. 8% water between 0 and 
approx. 20% RH at 20 °C. According to TGA, Hydrates I contains approx. 
19.5% water and Hydrate II approx. 13.0% water (measured by mass loss up to 250 °C) (refer 
to S.3.1.01).
To demonstrate that a sufficient solubility for all three hydrate forms of Gadoquatrane drug 
substance in the manufacturing of the drug product Gadoquatrane solution is given, the 
solubility in drug product placebo solution was determined. The target concentration of 
Gadoquatrane in Gadoquatrane solution is 257.9 mg/mL. The solubility of Gadoquatrane drug 
substance form Hydrate I, II and III in drug product placebo solution has 
been determined individually and has been found to be above 600 mg/mL for each hydrate 
form.
In the drug product manufacturing process Gadoquatrane drug substance is dissolved in 
an aqueous buffer solution to form the parenteral drug product. The correct assay of the 
drug product is ensured by utilizing a density control. Thus, the drug product
manufacturing process is robust and independent of potential variability in the water content 
and the hygroscopicity of the drug substance.
In conclusion, all three hydrate forms (Hydrate I, II and III) are equally suited to produce 
Gadoquatrane drug product. The water content of the drug substance has no impact on the 
manufacturability or the assay and quality of the drug product.

stability setup, each placed in fiber drums.
The results demonstrate that the drug substance is stable at long-term and accelerated 
conditions over the tested period; no significant change in any of the test parameters was 
observed to date. The results also confirm the equivalence of the two packaging options, as no 
differences between the two packaging setups were observed (refer to S.7.3.01).
Long-term stability data of three commercial scale batches for Gadoquatrane drug substance 
manufactured via the DO3A route at storage condition of 25 °C/60% RH are presented 
covering a storage period of 12 months.
Additionally, accelerated studies at 40 °C/75% RH are reported for these batches covering 
6 months of storage.
The stability profile is equivalent to the stability profile of the drug substance resulting from 
Cyglyp manufacturing process (refer to S.7.3.01).
Thus, the retest period as documented in S.7.1.02 is justified for material manufactured by 
either route and for both packaging options. For summary, see S.7.1.01.
The polymorphic form was monitored as informative test point in all of the stability studies 
mentioned above. The results are provided in S.7.3.11. The data show that the polymorphic 
form initially present does not change in the course of all stability studies presented.

(II) Drug Product
Question 1
Based on process validation batches and actual commercial production, further refine and 
standardize the manufacturing process description, including but not limited to:
o Solution preparation temperature, stirring speed, and time
o Filtration parameters and filter integrity acceptance criteria
o Cleaning/sterilization parameters for primary packaging materials and maximum holding
time
o Clarification that filters are single-use
o Pre-filling filter flushing procedures and discharged volume/quantity (if applicable)
o Filling temperature and speed
o Capping parameters
o Sterilization loading and probe placement
o Container closure integrity testing (CCIT) methods and strategies in commercial
production
o Process time limits and yields for all steps
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.P.3):
o Solution preparation temperature, stirring speed, and time
The manufacturing process for Gadoquatrane solution was developed and validated with an 
automated process control system (PCS). The mixing parameters are dynamically controlled 
throughout the manufacturing process by the qualified PCS program, which adjusts 
parameters in real time based on the actual batch size. This ensures a consistent and 
reproducible mixing process without the need for fixed parameter values.
The adequacy of the mixing process, including the mixing speed and energy input, is verified 
during manufacturing through the in-process control (IPC) parameter "clarity of the solution". 
A theoretically longer stirring time does not have a negative impact on the quality of the 
solution. This IPC ensures that the mixing process achieves the intended outcome and meets 
predefined quality standards.
The mixing process and its parameters were evaluated during process development and 
classified as non-critical (see P.2.3.01 section 6.5). The completeness of dissolution of the 
drug substance was found to be independent of these parameters.
Furthermore, the evaluation of the minimum stirring speed has been determined to be non-
critical based on the high solubility of gadoquatrane in aqueous media, including both water 
and buffer solutions (see S.1.3.01).
In the following more details are provided regarding mixing time, mixing speed and mixing 
equipment
Mixing time:
The mixing time is not limited by process parameters; it is only limited by Holding time 1. 
This was tested and confirmed in a mechanical stress study.
...
Mixing speed and equipment used:
...
Mixing temperature:
...
In conclusion, no quality-impacting effects were observed during development, justifying a 
control of the process solely within the GMP Quality Management System. Therefore, it is 
our understanding that an adjustment of Sections 3.2.P.3.3 and 3.2.P.3.4 to include specific 
mixing parameters is not appropriate, as the manufacturing process parameters are 
dynamically adjusted due to the linear relationship specific to each piece of equipment.


o Filtration parameters and filter integrity acceptance criteria
The solution is filtered through a membrane filter into a storage container prior to filling.
The forward flow test is used as the method for the filter integrity test of membrane filters 
used for the filtration of the product solution. Three different types of membrane filters can be 
used for the filtration of the product solution (nylon 66, polyethersulfone or 
polyvinylidenefluoride; all with a pore size of 0.2 µm (refer to P.3.3.01).
The acceptance criteria for the filter integrity test (forward flow test) are specific to the filter 
type used, therefore specified according to supplier requirements and carried out according to 
local standard operating procedures.


o Cleaning/sterilization parameters for primary packaging materials and maximum
holding time
As a continuous process vials are washed, sterilized and filled. The sterilization of the vials 
takes place within a hot air tunnel. This sterilization process has been validated to demonstrate 
≥ 3 log reduction of endotoxin levels (refer to P.3.5.01 and Question 3). Since the washing, 
sterilization and filling are a continuous process no holding time between the sterilization of 
the vials and the filling exists.
The stoppers are precured with the quality level of “ready-to-sterilize”. The stopper washing 
process has been validated by the manufacturer to demonstrate a ≥ 3 log reduction in 
endotoxin levels.  
Incoming goods control is performed for stoppers and all results showed an Endotoxin level 
below the limit of detection – thus confirming the quality certified by the supplier.


o Clarification that filters are single-use
The applicant hereby confirms that filters are single-use filters.


o Pre-filling filter flushing procedures and discharged volume/quantity (if applicable)
No minimum flush volume is deemed as necessary before using the filters for filtration of the 
product solution, as the volume for complete filter saturation are very low or non-existent. 
Adsorption effects are generally negligible for the filtration, as a much larger volume of the 
complete solution is stored in a storage tank in which a concentration compensation occurs. 
Furthermore, line-specific flushing volumes are handled by local GMP Quality Management 
systems.
Results of the filter validation are presented in P.2.2.10. This document includes the results of 
the performed studies with regard to particle release, adsorption behaviour, chemical 
compatibility, and extractables and leachables. These studies clearly demonstrate that no pre-
filling flushing procedures are required.

o Container closure integrity testing (CCIT) methods and strategies in commercial
production
The applicant would like to clarify that CCIT is performed as release test and is included in 
the release specification (P.5.1.01) accordingly.


o Process time limits and yields for all steps
As requested, holding time 1 and holding time 2 have been included in P.3.3.01. Holding 
Times were defined as ECs with “low risk” and reporting category “notification” according to 
ICH Q12. P.2.3.01 was updated to include the ECs and respective justifications of risk 
category.
The following holding times have been established (refer to P.2.3.01):
- Holding Time 1: from start of compounding until completion of bioburden reduction
filtration, 36 hours  
- Holding Time 2: start of bioburden reduction filtration until end of terminal sterilisation,
144 hours (6 days).
Yield information is not proposed for inclusion in section P.3.3.01, as it is not considered a 
product-specific critical process parameter or a critical quality attribute. Yield is monitored 
and assessed within the pharmaceutical quality system as part of routine manufacturing 
oversight and process performance evaluation. Product quality and process consistency are 
ensured through validated manufacturing steps, in-process controls, and finished product 
testing. In addition, yield data may be influenced by operational factors not directly related to 
product quality. Therefore, inclusion of yield information in the regulatory dossier is not 
considered necessary.

Question/Consideration:
Question 4
Current data indicate use of the dye ingress method for container closure integrity testing.
Please provide validation data for the finalized commercial CCIT method, including:
o 
Proper positive control samples
o 
Sensitivity evaluation
o 
Comparative study between dye ingress and microbial challenge methods
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4 (3.2.P.5):
The validation data of the dye ingress test applied for commercial production is provided in 
P.5.3.08 and includes positive control samples as well as a sensitivity evaluation. CCIT is 
performed as release test and is included in P.5.1.01 accordingly.
In addition, a microbial challenge test was conducted, refer to P.5.3.11.
The results of the microbial challenge test demonstrate that the detection rate varies 
depending on the respective container format when evaluated under intentionally challenged 
worst-case conditions. Sensitivity of the microbial challenge method with a detection rate of 
95% was a leakage aperture of 10 ± 1µm for the 2 ml vial format, 5 ± 1µm for the 10 ml vial 
format and 3 ± 1µm for the 15 ml vial format. In comparison, sensitivity of the dye ingress 
method was a leakage aperture of 3 ± 1µm (detection rate of 100%) for the 2 ml vial format, 
5 ± 1µm (detection rate of 95%)  for the 10 ml vial format and 5 ± 1µm (detection rate of 
100%) for the 15 ml vial format. With a detection rate of 90%, defects as small as 3 ± 1µm for 
the 15 ml vial format were also detected using dye ingress testing.
Based on the knowledge gained from container closure system (CCS) development and crimp 
process assessment, the Applicant deems dye ingress testing to be a suitable routine container 
closure integrity (CCI) test method for Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 mmol Gd/mL for injection, 
as it will detect packaging defects at an acceptable level of security. Hence, container closure 
integrity is appropriately assured and product quality and patient safety are maintained with 
respect to this critical quality attribute.

doc_name: VV-RFI-006159 - CMC Response - NDA REC 31736 - Gadoquatrane - CN
Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Gadoquatrane drug substance is a mixture of three diastereomers. The CMC reviewer is interested in understanding the scientific rationale behind classifying all three diastereomers as drug substance (DS). Specifically, they would like more information on which studies (PK/ in vivo comparison?) were conducted to support this classification and the guidelines those studies were based on.
Answer/Response:
Gadoquatrane is a mixture of three diastereomers, two of them are pairs of enantiomers, whereas one diastereomer is a meso compound.
All isomers of Gadoquatrane were characterized with regard to their relaxivity (in vitro), as well as their pharmacokinetic parameters in an animal study (rats). Both relaxivity and PK, revealed to be very similar for the three isomers.

It is the fundamental principle of a contrast agent to catalyze the relaxation of water molecules, by their coordination to the paramagnetic metal ion. A multi-purpose contrast agent molecule is not supposed to interact physiologically with e.g. membrane channels, enzymes, receptors, etc. In that sense, a contrast agent is not comparable to a e.g. highly selectively active molecule of a therapeutic drug.

The decision was taken to define all three isomers as “Gadoquatrane”, as all three isomers qualify equally as low-dosed contrast agent. Separation of isomers clearly is unnecessary, as it would not improve the quality of the contrast agent.

doc_name: VV-RFI-006164 - CMC Response - NDA Eylea 8mg vial - REC 30588 - UY
Question/Consideration:
Question 3.2
Specifications – expand justification for:
* Potency: Based on the results submitted, the selected potency specifications are considered 
quite broad.
* Particulate matter: Based on the data submitted for particles ≤ 10 µm, a specification of less 
than 2000 per container is not considered adequate. New specifications must be proposed and 
their selection justified.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3.2 (3.2.P.5.6):
Potency:
Potency by bioassay acceptance criteria are aligned between product stages based on the 
demonstrated poolability of the respective data sets and the understanding that potency is not 
meaningfully changed by the formulation, filling and finishing steps. Resultantly, the same 
acceptance criteria were defined for the drug product as is proposed for the formulated drug 
substance and as established for the drug substance intermediate (DSI) – refer to S.4.5.01-01 
and P.5.6.01-02. The DSI for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL is the same as used for the 
approved strength Aflibercept solution 40 mg/mL (EYLEA), where the registered DSI 
potency limit is 60 – 140%.
The proposed DP acceptance criterion of 60 – 140% of reference standard was also covered 
by using a tolerance interval approach (99% coverage, 95% confidence) on the DP data 
available at the time, which supported limits of approximately 66% to 146%, while also 
considering the inherently high variability of the cell-based bioassay.
Particulate Matter:
Particulate matter acceptance criteria are based on the applicable pharmacopeial requirements 
for subvisible particles. Ph. Eur. 2.9.19, Method 1 (light obscuration), states for solutions for 
injection in containers with a nominal content of less than 100 mL that the preparation 
complies if the average number of particles does not exceed 6000 per container for particles 
≥ 10 µm and 600 per container for particles ≥ 25 µm. The currently proposed specification of 
≤ 2000 particles/mL for particles ≥ 10 µm and ≤ 50 particles/mL for particles ≥ 25 µm is 
therefore substantially more stringent than the pharmacopeial acceptance criteria.
For Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in vial, the target fill volume is 0.263 mL per 
container. Accordingly, the proposed limits correspond to approximately 527 particles per 
container for particles ≥ 10 µm and approximately 14 particles per container for particles ≥ 25 
µm. Compared with the pharmacopeial limits per container, this represents an approximate 
tightening by a factor of 11 for particles ≥ 10 µm and 43 for particles ≥ 25 µm.
In addition, the currently available batch data set for Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL 
indicates that subvisible particle results are not normally distributed and therefore do not 
support establishment of a meaningfully tighter and statistically robust specification at this 
stage. On this basis, Bayer considers the proposed limits of ≤ 2000 particles/mL for particles 
≥  10 µm and ≤ 50 particles/mL for particles ≥ 25 µm to be appropriate and adequately 
justified for release and shelf life.
The same specification limits for Potency and Particulate Matter have been accepted by EMA.
Source:  P.5.6.01-02 Justification of Specification / Aflibercept solution 114.3 mg/mL in
vial for intravitreous injection (#022977777; unchanged)
S.4.5.01-01 Justification of Specification and Skip Testing / Aflibercept solution 
114.3 mg/mL (#022973002; unchanged)

a) For related substances test justify not performed at release as they were not mentioned
in release specifications and mentioned in shelf life specifications
b) Kindly justify the release limit of preservatives set as 80-110% not 90-110%
Answer/Response:
a) The applicant would like to clarify that according to ICH guideline Q6A, degradation product testing may be reduced or eliminated upon approval by the regulatory authorities when it has been conclusively demonstrated via an appropriate analytical methodology that the drug substance does not degrade in the specific formulation and under the proposed storage conditions.
The initial values of degradation products of nine Proviron 25 mg with parabens batches included in the ongoing stability study P.8.3.02, show an extremely low level of degradation products. All batches were tested according to test procedure P.5.2.01 and evaluated against the shelf-life specification P.5.1.02.

All initial test results are substantially below the approved shelf-life specification limits. Furthermore, the available ongoing stability data demonstrate that individual and total degradation products remain unchanged during storage at 30 °C/65% RH. All test results for all parameters comply with the specification limits and show no discernible trend during storage.
The data provide clear evidence of a robust and reproducible manufacturing process for Proviron 25 mg with parabens. The ongoing stability study P.8.3.02-7.0 confirms the known stability profile and the approved shelf-life of Mesterolone tablet 25 mg with parabens (PROVIRON) under storage conditions of 30 °C/65% RH. Given the consistently very low levels of individual and total degradation products and the absence of any discernible trend during storage, it is considered scientifically justified to omit degradation product testing at marketing release of Proviron 25 mg with parabens.
Source:  P.8.3.02_7.0 Stability Data - On-going Studies / Mesterolone tablet 25 mg with parabens (PROVIRON) (IQMS-204898; new)

b) The applicant would like to explain that this limit was originally implemented with regard to Eudralex 3AQ11a, which is no longer in force. Its successor is ICH Q6A, which no longer states requirements on preservative content testing. Question/Consideration: Provide justification for the yield and overall yield.
Answer/Response:
As can be seen in S.2.2.01 in a graphic overview, the gadoquatrane drug substance manufacturing process consists of many unit operation and many individual chemical reactions. Throughout the manufacturing process, several impurity purge mechanisms are incorporated to ensure compliance with the required quality attributes of intermediates and the final product. These impurity control measures are designed to remove organic and inorganic process-related impurities. While these operations are essential for achieving the desired product quality, they inherently contribute to material losses during e.g. work-up, isolation, and purification operations.
Therefore, the isolated yields observed during manufacturing are not solely a reflection of reaction conversion efficiency but also represent the combined impact of impurity rejection, work-up efficiency, isolation efficiency, and purification requirements.
In the table below, the stoichiometry-determining input materials for each step are listed. Typically, isolated yields reported in S.2.4.05 Batch Analyses for Intermediates are closer to the upper limits listed in the respective S.2.2.02. Nevertheless, due to the circumstances described above, in some cases isolated yields are lower, while still showing the required quality in regards to the target specification.
Furthermore, reaction completion is monitored by established in-process controls (IPCs, see table below) at specific manufacturing stages. These controls verify that the targeted conversion has been achieved prior to work-up and isolation. Consequently, variability in isolated yield is primarily attributable to recovery and purification effects rather than incomplete reaction conversion.

In this context, we want to bring a minor amendment of S.2.2.02 Gadoquatrane drug substance to your attention. We have provided an explanation note for the PAR of the drying temperature to align with internal requirements and to reduce ambiguity. The PAR-min value of the drying temperature of Gd-Glydonip (step 4a) has no impact on the quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance and thus, the lower PAR limit is only relevant for the jacket temperature.
Submitted: Add acetonitrile and water and stir for 3 h (2 – 24 h). Solids are isolated, washed with acetonitrile and dried under reduced pressure not exceeding a maximum internal temperature of 52 °C (40 – 70 °C). Gd-Glydonip is obtained.
Proposed: Add acetonitrile and water and stir for 3 h (1 – 24 h). Solids are isolated, washed with acetonitrile and dried under reduced pressure not exceeding a maximum internal temperature of 52 °C (40 – 70 °C) c. Gd-Glydonip is obtained.
c PAR-min refers to minimum required jacket temperature.

Question/Consideration: Submit data sufficient to confirm the stereochemical structure of partial stereoisomer 2.
Answer/Response:
It was attempted to elucidate the absolute configuration of Diastereomer 2 (D2) both by X-ray single crystal diffraction and microcrystal electron diffraction. Although single crystals could be obtained and subjected to the above-mentioned techniques, the absolute configuration of the molecules within the crystal structure could not be unequivocally determined by either of these techniques. Considering that D2 is in fact a racemate (a mixture of the enantiomers RRRS/SSSR; specific optical rotation for isolated D2: 0.073°), we believe that we failed to resolve the correct atomic connections due to the pseudo high symmetry of the Gadoquatrane D2 molecule. [...]
To overcome this potential route cause, it has been attempted to isolate one pure enantiomer of Gadoquatrane D2. Therefore, extensive chiral screenings have been conducted (including internal and external resources e.g. at Daicel). Even though different analytical techniques have been applied (reversed phase LC, normal phase LC and supercritical fluid chromatography) a sufficient separation for a preparative isolation of a pure D2 enantiomer could not be achieved, presumably due to the large size of the molecule.
For D2, all data provided in S.3.1.01, especially the high-resolution MS data and the comparison of isotopic patterns, leave no room for doubt regarding the molecular formula of D2, which corresponds to the molecular formula of Gadoquatrane. Even though LC-MS only proves the sum formula and not the absolute structure, further evidence for the structure of D2 is provided by optical rotation data. The optical rotation is close to zero for all produced Gadoquatrane batches, which would not be the case if D2 existed as an enriched mixture of one enantiomer.
[...] Finally, as outlined in S.3.1.01, section 4.2, the ratio of all three diastereomers meets the expected statistical distribution at the Gadoquatrane crude level of 3:4:1 (D1:D2:D3). [...] Therefore, the peak can be unambiguously assigned to D2, and the ratio matches the theoretically expected ratio from racemic synthesis.
From our perspective, the structure of D2 Gadoquatrane is undoubtedly supported by MS data, optical rotation, and the racemic route of synthesis. No other identity for the D2 peak, which constitutes around 50% of the peak area in Gadoquatrane and corresponds to the sum formula of Gadoquatrane, is conceivable. Although this may be considered partially indirect evidence (aside from MS), it should be acceptable for this specific type of molecule.
To further confirm the structure of D2 by NMR, the diamagnetic Lanthanum analogues La-D1, La-D2 and La-D3 [...] were prepared [...] and the resulting products investigated by NMR spectroscopy.
[...] Despite the significant signal overlap, it was possible to unambiguously assign some of the 1H and 13C signals in all three diastereomers but the high complexity of the molecule prevented the determination of the absolute or relative configuration of the stereocenters of the analogue La complexes. However, the consistent 2D 13C{1H]-NMR data (Figure 1) in combination with the data already presented (high resolution mass spectra, X-ray structural analysis of D1 and D3) further prove that isomer 2 is a diastereomer of isomers 1 and 3.

Source:  S.3.1.01_IQMS-262693_2.0 Structure Elucidation and other Characteristics/ Gadoquatrane drug substance (amended)

Question/Consideration: Clearly define the conditions for application of the rCR kinetic-chromogenic method in endotoxin testing.
Answer/Response:
In S.4.2.01 two equivalent, alternative test methods are described to determine the endotoxin content of the drug substance. The LAL kinetic-turbidimetric test method represents the method for quantifying endotoxins from gram-negative bacteria using amoebocyte lysate from the horseshoe crab (Limulus polyphemus or Tachypleus tridentatus). [...]
The rCR kinetic-chromogenic test method uses recombinant cascade reagent (containing recombinant Factor C, recombinant Factor B, and recombinant proclotting enzyme) as detection reagent. This test was fully validated and was shown to give equivalent results to the LAL kinetic-turbidimetric method (see S.4.3.07). As this test relies on a newly developed recombinant reagent with not many available suppliers, there is only little experience about the availability of the reagent and supply perspectives in the future. Therefore, both test alternatives have been included in S.4.2.01 as two totally equivalent and interchangeable options. The decision which method will be used in the testing lab is solely based on the availability of the respective reagent. As there is no quality impact on which test method is to be used, we consider it justified not to include a criterion in the dossier. The equivalency between both methods has been confirmed and either method can be appropriately controlled by following the operating procedures at the testing site.

Question/Consideration: Submit adequate supporting data for determination of the purity of the reference standards (gadoquatrane and Gd-GlyMe-DOTA).
Answer/Response:
The reference standards Gadoquatrane and Gd-GlyMe-DOTA are used as quantitative external calibration standards in the testing of assay and impurities as described in S.4.2.01. To determine the content of reference substances, the “assay as is” is calculated as defined in S.5.01 for gadoquatrane and S.5.03 for Gd-GlyMe-DOTA. The “assay as is” refers to the ratio of the respective compound [...] which may also contain organic and inorganic impurities, water and residual solvents.
Thus, the “assay as is” is calculated by the mass balance approach. From the theoretical value of 100 % all impurities that are determined in the reference substance in relevant amounts, are subtracted.
For gadoquatrane reference substance, the following formula applies: A (%) = 100 – I – E – W – Gd [...]
[...] For Gd-GlyMe-DOTA reference substance, the following formula applies: A (%) = 100.0 – I – W – free Gd [...]

Question/Consideration: Clarify the primary packaging material
Answer/Response:
The primary packaging material to be used for Gadoquatrane drug substance has to exhibit two properties: (1) Only polypropylene (PP) is in contact with the drug substance (2) The packaging material is hermetically sealed and non-permeable to humidity. These properties can be achieved by two packaging set-ups as described in S.6.01.
Set-up 1: The drug substance is first packed in a polypropylene (PP) bag. Then, this bag is placed in a polyethylene (PE) bag laminated with aluminum. The following packaging materials are used: Foil bag 100 µm PP (1030); Foil bag 12/12/75 µm PET/Al/PE (4189).
Set-up 2: The drug substance is packed in polypropylene (PP) bags which are laminated with aluminum [...] Foil bag 12/12/75 µm PET/Al/PP (5729).
[...] The description provided in S.6.02 describes the composition of Foil bag 12/12/75 µm PET/Al/PE (4189) used as outer bag in set-up 1 [...] However, in the set-up 1 described above, there is always an inner bag made of PP between the PE layer from the aluminum laminated PE bag and the drug substance.
Thus, in both packaging set-ups only PP is in contact with the drug substance. Both packaging set-ups have been tested in stability studies (see S.7.1.01) and have been found to be equivalent. Please be informed that abbreviations are used in S.7.1.01. “PP + Al/PE” refers to set-up 1, “Al/PP” refers to set-up 2.
keywords: Container closure system; Packaging supplier; Secondary packaging; Container Closure System; Stability data

Question/Consideration: Submission of documents demonstrating container closure integrity
Answer/Response:
Gadoquatrane drug substance is a non-sterile material. Due to its hygroscopic nature, aluminum laminated foil is used in the primary packaging set-up to prevent change in the moisture content of the drug substance. Set-up 1 or set-up 2 can be used [...] and in both set-ups a sealed aluminum-laminated foil is used as outer bag. This packaging concept ensures that the product is protected both from exposure to contamination and product loss as well as air and gas exchange.
In stability studies presented in S.7.1.01 it was shown that both packaging set-ups lead to a stable drug substance quality with no trends observed in any of the tested parameters. While this set-up is considered “hermetic container” in internal procedures, it is considered a “tight container” according to the definition of Korean pharmacopoeia. A clarifying remark is included in S.7.2.01.
Container closure integrity tests according to USP <1207> are only intended for sterile pharmaceutical drug products packaged in “hermetic containers” as per Korean pharmocopoeia and are therefore not carried out on the drug substance Gadoquatrane which is packaged in a “tight container”.
