Question/Consideration:
Question 1
According to the EMA guideline on the investigation of bioequivalence and ICH M9 full batch details on the test and reference product should be provided. The assayed content of the batches used should not differ more than 5%. CoAs of the batches used in the comparative dissolution studies could not be located and should be provided as well as the batch size and site of manufacturing of all batches used. Furthermore, it should be confirmed that the manufacturing process for the Valette G batches used in the dissolution studies is the same as the currently validated process described in the section 3.2.P.3.5 of the documents provided for this work sharing procedure. It should be discussed why under deviation from guideline (conditions for f2 calculation not fulfilled), the new formulation could be considered as similar without conducting a BE-study (e.g. alternative statistical evaluation such as bootstrapping as outlined in the ICH M9).
Answer/Response:
The applicant acknowledges the Agency’s question and provides the respective certificates of analysis of the batches used within the comparative dissolution studies (CDT; P.2.2.02_IQMS-255078_2.0 and P.2.2.02_IQMS-397168_1.0) under the section 3.2.P.2.2.10: Pharmaceutical development-Additional information.
Additionally, an overview of the requested batch details is given in Table 1.

Table 1: Details of batches used within the comparative dissolution studies
Valette: WEW9M8 (2023-07-26, Weimar GmbH & Co KG, 3.8 mio tablets, Assay DNG 98.9%, Assay EE 100.1%); WEW9M9 (2023-07-26, 3.8, 98.5%, 99.7%); WEX3R7 (2024-01-11, 3.8, 99.6%, 101.3%); WE11ET (2024-11-15, 3.8, 98.4%, 99.9%); WE13NN (2025-03-10, 3.8, 99.4%, 100.8%).
Valette G: WEX2B1 (2023-10-11, Weimar GmbH & Co KG, 3.0, 98.7%, 100.2%); WEX2B5 (2023-10-11, 3.0, 99.7%, 101.1%); WEX2BX (2023-10-11, 3.0, 98.8%, 100.7%).
DNG: Dienogest; EE: Ethinylestrdiol.
All batches used within the CDTs have comparable content of the drug substances, with values between 98.4% and 99.7% for dienogest (difference not more than 1.3%) and values between 99.7% and 101.3% for ethinylestradiol (difference not more than 1.6%). Therefore, the requirement of not more than 5% differences in assayed content is fulfilled for all batches.
Furthermore, the applicant confirms that all Valette G batches used were manufactured according to the validated manufacturing process described in P.3.5.01_IQMS-398670_1.0.
In accordance with ICH M9 comparative dissolution testing (CDT) was performed using biowaiver-conditions (P.2.2.02_IQMS-255078_2.0) and the QC-medium water (P.2.2.02_IQMS-397168_1.0).
Within the CDT using biowaiver conditions, at pH 6.8 four out of six batches show dissolution rates > 85% for both drug substances within 15 minutes. For the two batches with lower dissolution rates than 85% WEW9M8 (Valette) and WEX2B1 (Valette G) – f2-values were calculated. The obtained results of 65 for dienogest and 62 for Ethinylestradiol confirm the similarity of these two batches. Additionally the f2-calculations are backed-up by calculating the more robust version of f2-bootstrapped; the bootstrap-f2 values are 59.97 for dienogest and 58.16 for Ethinylestradiol. Therefore, also via bootstrapping, the equivalence of the two batches was confirmed.
Pharmacokinetic rationale is provided: ethinylestradiol is completely absorbed after oral administration; dienogest has oral bioavailability >90%. Dissolution at pH 1.2 shows >87% dissolved after 15 minutes, simulating stomach residence time; thus most drug leaves stomach dissolved and is immediately available for absorption. Differences at pH 6.8 are considered overdiscriminating and unlikely relevant in vivo; by 30 minutes dissolution is similar under all conditions. Therefore, the new formulation can be considered similar without conducting bioequivalence studies.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
The applicant should add the IPC Test for Blend Uniformity of the final mixture before compression. This is required because the manufacturing process is considered a non-standard process due to the very small amount of active substance ethinylestradiol, which is less than 2 % of the composition. The homogeneity of the active ingredient in the final mixture is therefore highly critical and should therefore be routinely controlled from batch to batch per IPC Blend Uniformity of mixture, regardless of whether this has been checked during process validation.
Answer/Response:
The applicant acknowledges the agency’s request.
The applicant argues the process can be considered standard for the manufacturer/site based on EMA process validation guidance factors (experience with similar product/process, development knowledge, and GMP compliance history). Valette G has been established at Supply Center Weimar for over 15 years with nearly 2000 batches produced. Content uniformity testing (CUT) results for the low-dose ethinylestradiol show mostly 90–110% with mean 101%; AV values were always below 13% (spec limit 15%) and 90% of AV below 6.2%. Only 6 batches needed stage 2 testing (Ph. Eur. 2.9.40). No OOS events in the last decade involved assay or CUT for either API. This demonstrates robustness.
A new validation study on three production-scale batches (P.3.5.01_IQMS-398670_1.0) includes statistical evaluation (section 4.5) supporting that blend uniformity can be adequately assessed through content uniformity testing; aligned with Garcia et al. (2014). Variance component analysis per ASTM E2810 yielded a positive outcome for Uniformity of Dosage Units, and showed between-sampling-point variance lower than within-sampling-point variance, indicating a stable process.
Critical steps (granulation, tableting, sugar-coating) are controlled via various IPCs; acceptance criteria are based on development and scale-up knowledge, and validated process leads to products meeting IPCs and release specs.
SCW has >30 years experience producing low-dose hormone products, including 43 different bulk products with API concentrations below 2%, supporting classification as standard process per EMA guidance.
They also note routine blend uniformity sampling could increase risk to bulk product by disrupting the closed container principle.
In summary, they request consideration that homogeneity is ensured via control strategies (critical steps, CUT) without adding routine IPC blend uniformity testing.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
No data on permeability were provided in section 3.2.P.2. As BCS class III drug substances are more susceptible to the effects of excipients on the in vivo absorption, permeability data for both drug substances should be provided and an assessment of the different excipients for their potential to affect in vivo absorption as outlined in ICH M9.
Answer/Response:
Permeability data were not presented separately in section 3.2.P.2 because the available human pharmacokinetic data already demonstrate rapid and extensive absorption of both active substances. Ethinylestradiol is completely absorbed after oral administration, and dienogest shows an absolute oral bioavailability of approximately 90%, with both substances reaching maximum plasma concentrations within about 1 to 2 hours. In addition, dissolution of both compounds is rapid, with more than 87% dissolved within 15 minutes at pH 1.2 (Table 5-1 of P.2.2.02_IQMS-255078_2.0). Taken together, these data do not indicate permeability-limited absorption and therefore do not support a relevant risk of excipient-driven in vivo absorption effects as described for BCS class III substances in ICH M9. The excipients used in the revised formulation are conventional immediate-release tablet excipients and are not expected to affect gastrointestinal permeability or the in vivo absorption of Ethinylestradiol and dienogest. Therefore, the formulation change is not considered to adversely affect bioavailability.

•

• 
Impurity control: Comments focused on radionuclidic purity controls and source-related impurity risks. 
• 
Specifications: Acceptance criteria were expected to be justified by impurity profile, process knowledge, analytical capability, stability, and safety. 
• 
Analytical methods: Method descriptions, qualification or validation status, and suitability for proposed limits were commented. 
• 
Radiochemical impurities: Comments addressed distinction between free actinium-225, labelled product-related species, and other radioactive impurities. 
• 
Supplier comparability: New sources were linked to comparability of quality attributes. 
• 
Lifecycle control: Stability data, risk-based verification, monitoring, and reassessment after changes were identified as relevant control elements.
Overall, the reviewed comments were focused on clarification and justification of the actinium-225 control strategy. They were not considered critical, did not result in authority non-acceptance of initial clinical trial applications or amendments.

Question/Consideration: For the two newly introduced actinium sources (SRX and PanTera), the levels of thorium-227 and bismuth identified during extended characterization are higher than those in the other six actinium sources. Please compare and analyze the potential impact on the radiolabeling performance.
Answer/Response:
For the PanTera batches Ac-2025-001 and Ac-2026-001, thorium-227 was below the limit of detection (<0.02%), and bismuth levels were comparable to the other actinium-225 sources.
For SpectronRx batches CPA210BH25A-G and CPA224IN25A-G, trace levels of thorium-227 were reported. These values may be overestimated due to analytical interference of thorium-227 with actinium-227 sharing the same mass. Thorium-227 cannot be directly produced by the SpectronRx irradiation process, and it is reasonable to attribute the detected traces to actinium-227. The reported trace levels (0.53 and 0.34 ng/MBq, respectively) are not considered relevant for radiolabeling performance. Bismuth levels in the SpectronRx batches were slightly higher than in the other actinium-225 sources, but they were still very low. Bayer has evaluated that bismuth levels up to 25 ng/MBq do not adversely affect radiolabeling.
Technical and process verification batches produced with actinium-225 from PanTera and SpectronRx showed comparable radiolabeling performance, confirmed by iTLC results for radiochemical purity.
Therefore, no adverse impact on radiolabeling performance is expected. Actinium-225 from both suppliers is considered suitable and qualified for the manufacture of BAY 3547926.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
The new validated method for PSD determination may be acceptable. However, it is not 
deemed acceptable to introduce a correction factor to align the D50 values obtained with the 
new equipment to the current specifications. Furthermore, the data obtained for D90 with the 
new method despite being comparable to the current method may still result in OOS results. 
The applicant should therefore re-establish the specification limits for PSD based on the 
results obtained with the new equipment, in accordance with ICH Q6A. Ideally, the 
specifications should be based on the results obtained for active substance used in clinical 
pivotal batches and tightened to reflect the 44 batches data.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (3.2.S.4):
Bayer acknowledges the request for setting a Malvern equipment specific specification for 
analysis of the particle size distribution. In accordance with ICH Q6A, the acceptance criteria 
should be based on the observed range of variation and should take into account the dissolution 
profiles of batches that showed acceptable performance in vivo.

The particle size distribution of the batches used during clinical trials had been measured using 
the legacy instrument (Beckman Coulter). It has been demonstrated during clinical 
development (as presented in section 3.2.P.5.6) that the requirement for the dissolution (Q = 
75% after 45 min) of Darolutamide 0.3 g film-coated tablets is met if the d50 does not exceed 
100µm, measured with the Beckman-Coulter instrument (d50 of clinical batches: 22 - 63 mm), 
therefore the upper specification limit was set to 100µm (measured with Beckman Coulter). For 
a more detailed justification of the specification limits for the Beckman-Coulter method, please 
refer to section S.4.5 Justification of Specification.
The drug substance batches used in the pivotal clinical trials are not available for reanalysis 
with the Malvern equipment, but the batches measured for the determination of the proposed 
new Malvern specification are in a similar range (measured with Beckman-Coulter) and can 
therefore be considered representative for the purposes of setting the Malvern specification 
limits.

For determining a representative specification for the Malvern instrument additional batches 
have been analysed, therefore instead of previously 44 batches, data from 199 batches (09/2025-
06/2026) were used to compare the results between both methods (Beckman Coulter and 
Malvern Mastersizer). The batches are representative of the current production and the 
corresponding drug product batches have met the release specification for dissolution. The 
particle size distribution data of these batches is presented in the updated section 3.2.S.4.3 
(Method comparison report).

A brief summary of the PSD d50 and d90 results of these 199 batches is presented (Table 1).
The Beckman Coulter PSD d50 results, together with the current upper and lower specification 
limits are presented in Figure 1, and the Malvern results for the same batches in Figure 2. It is 
observed that the Malvern results do not match to the specification limit initially set for the 
Beckman Coulter equipment.

The trend is similar for d90 values (Figures 3 and 4). Based on the larger amount of batches it 
is concluded that batches with finer particles are likely to be below the specification limit with 
the current specification, although they are in specification if analyzed with Beckman Coulter.

Consequently, a Malvern method specific specification is required.
When setting specification limits for the Malvern method it is clear that an average ± 3 sigma 
cannot be used due to typical variability of PSD results within production. Specification limits 
would be wider than justified by process capability.

Therefore, in the proposal for PSD d50 and d90 specifications the variability of the analytical 
method has been taken into account. According to validation requirements of the laser 
diffraction method (USP <429> and Ph.Eur 2.9.31) a variation of up to 10% for the d50 value 
and up to 15% for the d90 is acceptable. These values have been considered in the calculation 
of the lower and upper limits.

In addition, and in accordance with ICH Q6A, for the upper limit of the PSD d50 and d90 
specifications the known increase in PSD during stability studies should be considered. 
Darolutamide has shown an increase in both the PSD d50 and d90 values in stability studies. 
Estimation of maximum particle size increase during retest period in combination with the 
variability of the PSD method results in a conservative allowance of +25%. This estimation is 
taken into account for the upper PSD specification limit.

Based on calculations from 199 batches, the proposed Malvern Mastersizer specification limits 
are: d50 = 7–60 µm and d90 = 90–300 µm.

To demonstrate conservativeness, an example atypically coarse stability batch (2044048, 25°C/60%RH after 48 months) is discussed: Beckman Coulter D50 85 µm (within current spec) vs Malvern D50 73 µm (OOS against proposed Malvern spec); D90 Beckman 283 µm vs Malvern 278 µm.

Final proposal: keep Beckman Coulter specification unchanged (d50 15–100 µm; d90 140–350 µm) and introduce Malvern Mastersizer specification (d50 7–60 µm; d90 90–300 µm). Both methods are proposed as alternative methods in the specification during a transfer period until Malvern replaces Beckman Coulter at all relevant QC sites.

Sections S.4.1, S.4.2, S.4.4, and S.4.5 have been updated to reflect the change.

Regarding the submitted variation procedures under B.II.d.1.(z) IB and B.II.d.2.(z) IB, which relate to changes in the test method and specification requirements for the parameter “Release Rate”:
a) Provide justification for selecting variation type IB, considering that the proposed changes constitute substantial modifications that may have a significant impact on the product’s quality, safety, and efficacy
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4a)
Justification for Type IB Variation Classification
• There are no changes to product itself. Product Quality is not affected with the changes in the variations in question, as the drug product remains totally unchanged.
• Analytical refinement only: Change from 1-point to 3-point (Day 2, 5, 8) release-rate testing is an enhancement of the analytical method, not a modification of the product or its CQAs.
• Regulatory alignment: Update made to comply with ICH Q6A, USP <724>, and Ph. Eur. 2.9.3, which recommend multi-point release testing.
• Validated method: New method fully validated (accuracy, precision, linearity, specificity, robustness). Alternative instruments (HPLC/UPLC) and shakers (rotating/reciprocal) shown to be equivalent.
• Comparative batch data: Side-by-side testing confirms consistent release profiles and no change in batch-to-batch variability.
• No impact on product quality, safety, or efficacy: Formulation, manufacturing process, stability profile, and clinical performance remain unchanged.
• Strengthened control strategy: More granular release-rate monitoring improves regulatory compliance without introducing new risks.
• Regulatory basis for Type IB: EU Variations Guidelines classify analytical method updates without quality impact as Type IB, not Type II.

Question/Consideration: e) Provide appropriate justification confirming that the change in the release-rate specification criteria does not affect the active substance release profile. Provide justification for the absence of new bioequivalence data in accordance with the EMA Guideline on the Investigation of Bioequivalence (CPMP/QWP/EWP/1401/98 Rev. 1).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4e)
The proposed change to the release-rate specification criteria does not impact the active substance release profile of the product. The change reflects an update to the acceptance criteria only and does not involve any modification to the formulation, active substance, manufacturing process, release mechanism, or product design that could influence the release characteristics of the active substance.
In accordance with the EMA Guideline on the Investigation of Bioequivalence (CPMP/QWP/EWP/1401/98 Rev. 1), new bioequivalence studies are generally required when changes have the potential to affect the in vivo performance of the medicinal product. As the current variation does not introduce any changes to the manufacturing process, formulation composition, active substance characteristics, or other critical quality attributes impacting release behaviour, the active substance release profile remains unchanged. Therefore, no new bioequivalence data have been generated or are considered necessary to support this change.
The unchanged manufacturing process and product composition, together with the absence of any impact on the release profile, support the conclusion that the proposed specification update does not affect the product's in vivo performance and does not warrant additional bioequivalence studies.

Question/Consideration:
Question 4
OOS observed for submitted stability data.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 4:
Please note that Batch KM503L5 showed an out-of-specification (OOS) result for 
appearance/visible particles after 1 month of storage at 40 °C/75% RH. One particle was 
detected during testing. Investigation identified the visible particle as consisting mainly of 
aluminium, carbon, and oxygen. The likely root cause was the aluminium foil used during 
preparation of the vials prior to filling. This represents an isolated case within the stability 
studies for the alternate stopper. The other samples were examined, and any impact of the 
alternate stopper could be excluded.

In addition, 30 mL vial batch KM503JG showed an OOS result for extractable volume after 6 
months of storage at 40 °C/75% RH. Five of 10 vials did not comply with the minimum 
extractable volume specified. No abnormalities of the stopper or crimping were observed in
the affected vials. The vials were intact and tight; therefore, an impact of the alternate stopper 
could be excluded. A fill volume that was too low during filling is considered the most likely 
cause, since samples from the weight loss testing also showed insufficient masses. It can be 
assumed that the underdosing already occurred during production. A systematic error could be 
ruled out.
keywords: Stability data; Evaluation of Stability Data; Shelf Life; QC testing; in-process control

Question/Consideration:
Question 2-2:
[2] Provide the document cited as "CTD3.2.S.4.3.86 – Aflibercept drug substance 
(Bridging study report for Bioassay)" in section "5. Potency by Bioassay" in 
3.2.S.4.5.1-S4501_IQMS-176964_10.0) (p.15), and explain the equivalence of the 
bioassays between before and after the change. If this Bridging Study does not include 
the results of measurements of the same samples and comparison of the results using 
the test methods before and after the change, provide the results and explain the 
equivalence of the test methods between before and after the change. In addition, 
given the change in calculation formula stated in [1] above, explain how the 
equivalence of test methods is ensured between before and after the change.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2-2:
In accordance with your instructions, the reference material – Bridging study report for 
Bioassay (S.4.3.86_IQMS-391281_1.0_Aflibercept drug substance (v1.0)) – is 
provided as attachment 1.
The change from IC50 (TA unconstrained) / IC50 (RS unconstrained) to IC50 (RS 
constrained) / IC50 (TA constrained) was introduced as part of the optimization of the 
bioassay to improve assay robustness, throughput, and data interpretation.
As a result of the calculation of the old formula (IC50 (TA unconstrained) / IC50 (RS 
unconstrained)), test articles which exhibit lower IC50 values than the standard, (and 
thus are more potent than the standard) would yield RP values < 100%. Test articles 
less potent than the standard (and therefore, exhibiting higher IC50 values than the 
standard) would yield RP values > 100%.

By reversing the equation in the optimized method, the potency calculation aligns with 
the general practice of expressing potency relative to the reference standard and is 
intended to provide a more accurate and interpretable assessment of the test article's 
effectiveness compared to the reference standard. The difference in the calculation is 
taken into account by a recalculation to compare the potency values of the original 
method to the optimized method.
The optimized method uses a constrained 4-PL model and expresses potency relative 
to the reference standard. The impact of the calculation formula change was addressed 
within the bridging study through side-by-side comparison of lots tested using both 
methods and by reprocessing/recalculating data using both the original and optimized 
calculation approaches (please refer to S.4.3.86 section 3). Comparability was assessed 
by comparing unconstrained relative potency values generated by the original method 
with unconstrained relative potency values recalculated from the optimized method, 
thereby accounting for the effect of the calculation change.
Equivalence was demonstrated by pair-wise potency ratios and 90% confidence 
intervals, which met the predefined USP <1090> equivalence criterion for release and 
stability samples (please refer to S.4.3.86 section 4). The optimized method was also 
shown to detect potency changes under stability and stress conditions comparably to 
the original method. Therefore, the calculation change is scientifically justified, and 
the proposed optimized bioassay is considered equivalent to and suitable to replace the 
current original method.

391281; new)
S.4.5.01-10.0 Justification of Specification and Skip Testing / Aflibercept drug substance 
(IQMS-176964; unchanged)

Question/Consideration: The acceptance criteria of the CCIT by dye ingress test is indicated as “none of the tested samples shows a greenish colour” which is not consistent with the pink-red colour typically observed for aqueous Eosin 1% solution. Please confirm the dye used for the CCIT and rectify the discrepancy for 3.2.P.5.2, 3.2.P.5.3 and 3.2.P.5.6 accordingly, where applicable.
Answer/Response:
The dye used for the container closure integrity test (CCIT) by dye ingress is confirmed to be an aqueous Eosin Y 1% solution. However, the term “greenish colour” refers to the visual appearance used for assessment under the specified illumination conditions of the CCIT method, and not to the inherent appearance of the bulk dye solution under ordinary transmitted or ambient light. Eosin Y 1% is a xanthene dye and is fluorescent. While aqueous Eosin Y 1% solution appears pink-red under normal viewing conditions, under the method-specific inspection conditions used for this test, dye ingress upon excitation by visible light, the dye may emit fluorescence in the green region depending on the optical set up.
Therefore, while an aqueous Eosin Y 1% solution appears pink-red under ordinary transmitted or ambient light, small amounts of dye that have entered the product container may be detected as a greenish fluorescent signal under the halogen-light inspection conditions.
No revisions to 3.2.P.5.2, 3.2.P.5.3 and 3.2.P.5.6 are required.
keywords: Container closure system; analytical procedures; validation of test method; Validation of Analytical procedures; Justification of Specification

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
TRANSPORT QUALIFICATION: Submit the following information regarding transport 
qualification, in accordance with Article 14, § 5, of RDC 205/2017:
(a) characterization of the intended route for the product, from the first stage of DP to the final 
storage location in Brazil, with a description of the types of transport (air, sea, land), as well as 
storage time and locations, with estimated duration, delay margin, among other relevant 
information. Also, data regarding the evaluation of the temperature profile of the intended route, 
load configuration in the transport system;
(b) details of each of the systems used (active and/or passive system), location of the equipment 
responsible for monitoring the temperature, and other specificities;
(c) specification of the maximum duration for each of the systems used and qualified, including 
summer-winter cycle data (justification for summer cycle temperatures, existence of studies 
with extreme environmental conditions, temperature excursion data);
(d) clarification regarding the existence of worst-case studies for the transport of the medicine 
without temperature control (autonomy of the packaging/systems);
(e) if the company has a summary report of the operational qualification of the transport system 
for another country with characteristics similar to the system it intends to adopt for Brazil, the 
presentation of this data is also important.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1 (R.5):
(a)
The intended route for Hyrnuo™ (Sevabertinib) from the drug product manufacturing site in 
Leverkusen, Germany to Brazil includes the transport mode by sea and air including road.
Load configuration for the goods is shown for a palletized unit load with 1,200 x 800 x 1,048 
mm dimensions of 3 layers consisting of 8 filled shipper boxes, each 375 x 280 x 301 mm 
(Length x Width x Height) secured by stretch foil wrapping.

The company clarifies that based on the available Stability Data (P.8.3.01), including a 
thermal cycling study (-20 and 40 °C), Hyrnuo™ (Sevabertinib) does not require special 
storage conditions (please refer to P.8.1.01 Stability Summary and Conclusion; P.8.1.02 Shelf 
Life). Additionally, stress tests have been performed at up to 60 °C for 3 months (please refer 
to P.8.3.04). The results confirm that no special storage conditions are required.
Based on the presented stability data, Bayer defines a temperature range of 2-25 °C for the 
transportation, which is wider compared to the local label range (15-30 °C).
For air freight Bayer uses the transport shipping equipment EcoSafe++, supplied by 
manufacturer EcoCool, which is a passive pallet shipper with Expanded Polystyrene 
insulation material on all sides of the pallet, coated with reflective insulation foil on the 
outside. In order to maintain the intended temperature range of +2 to +25°C water-based 
coolants are covering the payload from all sides and on top of the pallet underneath the 
insulation material. EcoSafe++ is a reliable passive transport system that was implemented at 
Bayer in 2019, since then no deviations were reported in conjunction with its usage. With 
Ecosafe++ a passive protection is ensured but no temperature control, which might buffer all 
potential delays. The temperature is monitored during the complete period of transport 
including eventual delays, which therefore do not result in additional risks. The qualification 
of Ecosafe++ for the proposed temperature range 2-25 °C, is proposed in the Post Approval 
Commitment.
The assessment of GxP-relevant events is made by the local Quality responsible in Brazil and 
in case corrective  and / or preventive action is needed due to a deviation during the 
transportation, a deviation management process is in place.
Transportation in Brazil is covered by the local documents as presented in the document VAL-
02554 – REL QT PERIODICA TOCO FSL5A35 - 15°-25°C rev 04, VAL-05712 REV.02 QT 
PERIODICA - GJB4E39 CARRETA 15° to 25°C.pdf and VAL-05156 REV.04 QT PERIODICA – 
EXPRESS – ENU4I13 15° a 25°C.pdf).
The specific risk assessment from drug product manufacturing site to Brazil is dependent on 
the transport mode listed below:
Sea transportation:
Lane specific risk assessment is presented in R.5.02 - Attachment 2 (“Lane Specific Risk 
Assessment for Sea freight”) for a booked temperature range 2 - 25 °C. The standard 
temperature setting of ocean containers is +19°C, with an ambient chain from +2°C to +25°C. 
Transportation takes place in actively temperature-controlled reefer containers from 
Leverkusen to Hamburg in Germany via road transport and via ocean transport to Santos, SP 
in Brazil. This document also includes estimated storage and transport duration (768 h 
qualified in total) and temperature evaluations. Delays are covered with a 48h buffer and 
based on the World Bank Timeliness Index for Destination Country (Brazil is categorized as 
"Very good").

Air transportation:
Transport requirements for transportation from Leverkusen to DUS Düsseldorf International 
Airport in Germany by road is covered by the “Quality Assurance Agreement (QAA) for 
Transport Services” under Good Distribution Practices (GDP) between Bayer and the 4PL 
logistics service providers.
The logistics service provider is specialized in the provision of transport services for 
pharmaceutical products and has extensive knowledge of the applicable laws. Furthermore, 
the logistics service provider is qualified by Bayer for the applicable services before use.
From DUS Düsseldorf International Airport via AMS Amsterdam Airport Schiphol to GRU 
Guarulhos – Governador André Franco Montoro International Airport transportation takes 
place under 3P (time & temperature sensitive) air service level within the temperature range 
of 2 - 25°C. Temperature is monitored by means of data loggers during the complete 
transportation period. The risk assessment covers a transit time of 4 days and includes risks 
categorized as equal to or less than medium risk score. All possible risks and respective 
mitigation measures are provided in the R.5.02 - Attachment 1 (“Lane Specific Risk 
Assessment for Air freight” ) and Attachment 5 (“Ecosafe ++ Container – Climate Test”) 
comprising of a detailed risk assessment with relevant information such as climate data 
including expected temperature deviation for the transport mode by air in the passively 
temperature-controlled EcoSafe++ packaging. The qualification of Ecosafe++ for the 
proposed temperature range 2 - 25 °C, for air including road transportation will be submitted 
as proposed in the Post Approval Commitment.

Brazil road transportation:
Local transport qualification for the refrigerated vehicles had been performed considering the 
temperature range of 15 – 25°C. The tests were carried out "with cargo" because it is the 
condition that offers the greatest challenge to the refrigeration system, as it presents barriers to 
air circulation in the environment, being a worst-case condition (refer to: “VAL-02554 - REL 
QT PERIÓDICA - TOCO FSL5A35 - 15-25C rev 04”, “VAL-05156 REV.04 QT 
PERIÓDICA - EXPRESS - ENU4I13 15 à 25C” and “VAL-05712 REV.02 QT PERIÓDICA 
- GJB4E39 - CARRETA 15 à 25C”).

(b)
Bayer informs that qualified transport equipment is used for the temperature control. For air 
freight the passively temperature-controlled Ecosafe ++ solution including attached data 
logger per pallet and for ocean freight the actively temperature-controlled reefer containers 
with a minimum of one logger per container are used. For further details, please refer to 
R.5.02 - Attachment 5 (“Ecosafe ++ Container – Climate Test”) and Attachment 6 and 7 
(“Summer/Winter Mapping Qualification Protocol – Reefer Container”). The summary report 
of the air freight qualification will be submitted as proposed in the Post Approval 
Commitment.

On the road in Germany, transportation occurs in temperature-controlled trucks (2-25 °C) 
including continuous temperature monitoring with data logger physically attached to each 
pallet for air freight or to each container for sea freight.

(c)
For the sea freight the transport mode is considered sufficiently qualified (R.5.02 – 
Attachments 6 and 7 (“Summer/Winter Mapping Qualification Protocol – Reefer Container”))
Temperature specification including the environmental conditions on the lane are summarized 
in the R.5.02 Attachments 3 and Attachment 4 "Lane Profile Risk Assessments for air and sea 
freight".  Performance qualification for summer-winter cycle for air freight including road 
transportation will be provided as proposed in the Post Approval Commitment. Considering 
the company needs to wait for the weather conditions of the seasons to be qualified, the 
documents related to transport qualification can be provided until December 2028.

(d)
Hyrnuo™ (Sevabertinib) does not require any special storage conditions (cf. P.8.1.02 Shelf 
Life), and the temperature range -20 – 40 °C is covered by P.8.3.01 Stability Data. Worst-case 
scenarios for the transport without temperature control are covered by stress stability studies 
P.8.3.04 Stability Data - Stress Tests for storage or transportation at temperatures up to 60 °C 
for 3 months, which does not adversely affect the quality of the tablets.

(e)
All presented information represent the proposed transport situation for Brazil. Currently, 
there is no available summary report of the operational qualification of the transport system 
for another country with characteristics similar to the system intended for Brazil. However, 
Attachment 3 in the proposed Transport Qualification Protocol for the Post Approval 
Commitment (PAC), shows a Performance Qualification Report for another Bayer product for 
the lane Finland to Costa Rica by air freight with EcoSafe++. The monitored temperature (13-
24°C) in this report was well within the required temperature range 2-25°C.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
Section 1.0.8.1
For SDA 35A alcohol which contains 96% ethanol and 4% ethyl acetate, enter ethanol and 
ethyl acetate individually in the correct amount to replace “alcohol 18-32 % w/w”.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
The Applicant would like to clarify that SDA 35A alcohol (Specially Denatured Alcohol 
35A) is procured from an external supplier. It is a proprietary denatured alcohol mixture 
consisting of ethanol (96%) and ethyl acetate, which is added as a denaturant. The 
concentration of ethyl acetate may vary between batches within the range of 2.5–10% (w/w), 
as its inclusion renders the alcohol unsuitable for consumption. The exact composition of the 
proprietary mixture is confidential and is not available to the Applicant.

Furthermore, expressing ethanol and ethyl acetate individually as % (w/w) of the finished 
capsule does not accurately reflect the manufacturing process, the actual composition of the 
final product, or the potential patient exposure.

Ethanol and ethyl acetate are volatile solvents used solely as processing aids in the capsule 
printing ink formulation. During the printing and drying operations, these solvents undergo 
substantial evaporation due to their high volatility. Consequently, the composition of the bulk 
printing ink is not representative of the composition of the finished printed capsules. 
Reporting solvent concentrations as a percentage of the finished capsule may therefore be 
misleading, as it implies that the solvents remain present at levels corresponding to the ink 
formulation, which is not the case.

From a scientific and regulatory perspective, the relevant consideration is the residual solvent 
content in the finished product rather than the solvent composition of the printing ink. Since 
ethanol and ethyl acetate are not intended to be present in the final product and are expected 
to be largely removed during manufacture, expressing their levels as % (w/w) of the finished 
capsule does not provide a meaningful representation of actual patient exposure.

In view of the above, the Applicant respectfully requests that the excipient be retained in 
PRS2.0 information as “SDA 35A alcohol”.
keywords: Control of Materials; specification; residual solvents; excipient name; manufacturing description

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
3.2.S.4.1 Specification (name, manufacturer) (S)

a) Kindly justify the presence of (1,2-Dichloroethane) in the specifications while it isn't stated in residual solvents section of CEP.
b) Kindly justify the absence of impurity U, V, W and H from related substances although they are mentioned as specified in the in Ph.Eur monograph.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 ( CTD section)
Response a) The solvent 1,2 dichloroethane is used in a very early step in the synthesis of the levonorgestrel starting material D-Et-Trienol. 1,2-dichloroethane is not part of the registered synthesis for levonorgestrel and the limit not specified on the CEP. However, 1,2-dichloroethane is specified in the Bayer quality specification for Levonorgestrel for historical reasons and the test is performed with a validated analytical procedure which is included in the CEP documentation submitted to the EDQM and subject of the approval of the CEP for the drug substance levonorgestrel by the EDQM.
Response b) The impurities U, V, W and H are evaluated by the test item “any other impurity”. Their limits in the Bayer specification (0.10%) are even tighter than the Ph. Eur. limits (0.15% for H, V; 0.2% for U; 0.3% for W). Since the Bayer specification already imposes a more stringent control on unspecified impurities, there is no regulatory need to list them separately. P.4.3 and P.4.4 documents are not available because the excipient analytical methods and specifications were established as part of a legacy system prior to current CTD requirements.
Although formal validation reports and specification justification documents were not generated at that time, the methods have been used reliably for many years, supported by routine QC performance, system suitability checks, and historical batch data. The specifications are based on compendial standards, supplier requirements, and long-term manufacturing experience, and remain appropriate to ensure excipient quality. Bayer Oy has manufactured Jadelle drug product for 30 years with the same specifications in place for the excipients, resulting consistently in finished drug product fulfilling the product specifications. From that perspective the analytical methods for the excipients can be stated to be valid for their intended purpose. The most important excipients for Jadelle 2 x 75 mg implant are the core elastomer [Poly(dimethylsiloxane) elastomer excipient core] and the tubing [Poly(dimethylsiloxane) elastomer excipient tubing]. The tubing is produced at the facilities of the drug product manufacturer. The third excipient in the implant itself [Poly(dimethylsiloxane) elastomer excipient condensation curable] is used only as a stopper in the implant ends to prevent too fast release of levonorgestrel via open implant ends. Regarding all the excipients in the implant, the identification of the materials is the most important quality test, which is performed by Infrared spectrometry (IR) for all of them. Identification by IR spectrum is quite a trivial method based simply on comparison with the reference spectrum. This identity test is performed for all three excipients of the Jadelle implant. For the tubing, in addition to identification, correct dimensions are most important features for providing appropriate release of levonorgestrel from the implant. These dimensions are ensured with the validated tubing manufacturing process in which the dimensions are continuously measured. Regarding drug core, the levonorgestrel-elastomer rod, outer diameter of the rod fulfilling the in-process control limits ensures correct amount of levonorgestrel in the implant, and for its part appropriate release of levonorgestrel also. Tubing dimensions are, however, more important to guarantee appropriate release rate for drug substance. The analytical methods for the excipients are not fully validated to fulfil current guidelines, as the product is over 30 years old. The material identification can be, however, determined with certainty by the IR method. Release analyses performed on the Jadelle implant batches, in addition to the dimensions for the core rod and for the tubing ensured by validated manufacturing processes, will guarantee and verify that the finished drug product will consistently fulfil the Quality Specifications of Jadelle implant. Question/Consideration:
Question 9
3.2. P.5.1 Specification(s)
• Kindly justify the absence of sterility and endotoxins testes from shelf-life specifications.
• Kindly justify not including the related substances test in release specifications.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 9
The maintenance of the sterile barrier integrity, and hence the sterility throughout the shelf life is demonstrated during stability testing by testing the integrity of the primary package. The integrity of the package is tested with bubble test and the seal strength of the package with strip test.
The substitution of Sterility and Endotoxin test with Container closure integrity tests during the shelf-life is in accordance with the guidelines or principles of both FDA and EMA:
In Questions & Answers of EMA web pages (Quality of medicines questions and answers: Part 2 / Stability - Endotoxin testing and sterility testing at the end of shelf-life) the following is stated:
“Sterility is part of the shelf-life specification.
Sterility testing should be performed at least at the end of Shelf-life, but it can be replaced by testing of the container closure integrity. Depending on the nature of the container, intermittent integrity testing might be envisaged, independent of whether the sterility testing is replaced or not.”
https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory-overview/research-development/scientific-guidelines/quality-medicines-qa-introduction/quality-medicines-questions-answers-part-2
This approach is approved by FDA as well in Guidance document “Container and Closure System Integrity Testing in Lieu of Sterility Testing as a Component of the Stability Protocol for Sterile Products”.
FDA guideline states for example the following:
“Alternatives to sterility testing as part of the stability protocol, such as replacing the sterility test with container and closure system integrity testing, might include any properly validated physical or chemical container and closure system integrity test (e.g., bubble tests, pressure/vacuum decay, dye penetration tests or seal force tests, etc.). Such tests may be more useful than sterility testing in demonstrating the potential for product contamination over the product’s shelf life or dating period.”
FDA's Guidance-for-Industry_Container-and-Closure-System-Integrity-Testing-in-Lieu-of-Sterility-Testing in-the-Stability
Related Substance: Due to inherent stability of levonorgestrel, Impurity test parameters will be deleted from release Specification. The long history of the production has verified that levonorgestrel remains virtually unchanged in the manufacturing process of the drug product, and also during the stability studies. This is demonstrated by comparison of the results for six drug product stability batches to the corresponding drug substance batch results. Comparison table provided in P.5.6.01_02 Justification of Specification

Question/Consideration: CTD Sec. 3.2.S.4.5 identifies a 7% (downward) adjustment in Drug Substance IPC specific activity specification while CTD Sec. 3.2.P.5.6 identifies a 14% (downward) adjustment in the Drug Substance and Drug Product specific activity specification. Provide an evaluation that the proposed revisions result in final product that is inline with the approved process and FVIII potency method.
Answer/Response:
The Sponsor appreciates the clarification received from Health Canada on 29-July-20206 regarding the 14% (downward) adjustment only referring to the Drug Product specific activity specification (see Module 1.0.4, Comment 3 Clarification dated 29-Jul-2026). Potency specifications for DP are in alignment with Ph. Eur. <1643> which specifies that content must be 80-125% of stated content throughout product shelf life. Regarding specific activity, these specifications are shifted downwards in accordance with the downward shift in potency due to the change to the optimized assay. Ph. Eur. <1643> also prescribes minimum limits for the specific activity of NLT 2000 IU/mg which are met with the proposed specification of NLT 3010 IU/mg. Based on the improved reliability of the potency measurement under the optimized assay, it is preferred to maintain the specifications for potency to be in alignment with the Ph. Eur. and adjust the specific activity specification to account for the bias in measurement.

With the bias of the new method and adjustment of the specific activity specifications downwards at DP, batches produced by the new method can be expected to contain a higher amount of protein of the same quality in comparison to batches produced by the previous method (e.g. batches produced using the optimized method if tested by the current method would produce higher potency and specific activity results).
In the case of Kovaltry, the change from the current to the optimized chromogenic method is justified by the clinical experience. Clinical trials were initiated using a one-stage potency assay before shifting to a chromogenic assay mid-trial. When this change occurred a shift in potency values of 23% was observed with the chromogenic assay producing higher values. An assessment was performed with the conclusion that DP manufactured using the chromogenic values for targeting resulted in DP activity non-inferior to that of earlier clinical material manufactured using the one-stage method. The shift from this existing chromogenic assay to the optimized chromogenic with an observed bias of 7-14% at DP would move Kovaltry activity between the two methods performed during clinical.
keywords: DP specification; drug substance specification; justification of specification DP; analytical procedures; assay

Question/Consideration: Provide a justification for not calibrating FVIII-PF in-house reference standards against the WHO 9th FVIII International Standard to maintain IU unit declaration
Answer/Response: The current FVIII in-house reference standards were calibrated against WHO 8th IS (with a potency assigned value from NIBSC of 9.4 IU/mL) for both the current method S-000-BF-104 and the optimized slope-ratio potency method S-000-BF-134. This was the current standard at the time of assignment. Starting 2026, the stability for the current FVIII-PF in-house reference standard with the optimized slope-ratio potency method S-000-BF-134 is being performed against WHO 9th IS (with a potency assigned value from NIBSC of 9.5 IU/mL). Using the WHO 9th IS as the reference standard ensures that the in-house standard continues to meet the required acceptance range of 90–110% of its initial T=0 potency value (initially assigned against the WHO 8th IS). This approach maintains IU unit declaration alignment with prior assignments and a new calibration is not needed against the WHO 9th IS. Future working standards will be calibrated against the WHO IS in effect at the time of their qualification.
keywords: Reference Standards or Materials; assay; Validation of Analytical procedures; analytical procedures; QC testing

Question/Consideration: Provide the plan on qualifying the FVIII-PF in-house reference standards against the WHO 9th FVIII International Standard to maintain linkage to the latest WHO International unitage.
Answer/Response:
Bayer does not plan to re-assign the in-house reference standard against the current WHO 9th IS as the stability studies for the in-house standard bridge the potency values obtained for this in-house standard between the WHO 8th IS and WHO 9th IS.
The potency assignment of the in-house reference standard, originally qualified against the WHO 8th IS, has remained stable since its initial T=0 assignment using S-000-BF-134.
From 2026, stability monitoring with S-000-BF-134 is being performed against WHO 9th IS. Using the WHO 9th IS as the reference standard ensures that the in-house standard continues to meet the required acceptance range of 90–110% of its initial T=0 potency value (initially assigned against the WHO 8th IS). This approach maintains alignment with prior assignments while ensuring ongoing accuracy of the in-house standard under the current WHO IS. If the in-house standard value on stability against the WHO 9th IS is outside the limits, an impact assessment will be performed, and the in-house standard will be reassigned or replaced. This will confirm the continuity of potency assignment of the in-house potency standard between the previous and new IS.
keywords: Reference Standards or Materials; Stability data; stability testing; assay; QC testing

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Justify the following tests is mentioned in NODCAR approval although it is not mentioned in 
CTD section "3.2.P.5.1" Speciﬁcations
Dissolution
Answer/Response:
The dissolution test is not applicable to Mirena, as it is an intrauterine drug delivery system 
designed to release levonorgestrel continuously over an extended period following placement 
in the uterus. Unlike conventional oral solid dosage forms, where dissolution testing is used to 
evaluate drug release into solution, Mirena does not rely on dissolution as its drug release 
mechanism.
Therefore, the appropriate performance test for Mirena is the in vitro release rate test, which 
directly evaluates the rate of levonorgestrel release from the intrauterine system and is 
considered a more relevant indicator of product performance. Consequently, the release rate 
test is included in the product specification in lieu of a dissolution test.

Source:  P.5.1.01-7.0 Release Specification/ Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery
system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) / (#IQMS-254490/ 022984913; 
unchanged)
keywords: Dissolution Protocol; Release Specification; drug product specification; Specifications; dissolution

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Justify absence of sterility test in CTD section "3.2.P.5.1" shelf life Speciﬁcations
Answer/Response:
The maintenance of the sterile barrier integrity, and hence the sterility throughout the shelf
life is demonstrated during stability testing by testing the integrity of the primary package.
The integrity of the package is tested with bubble test and the seal strength of the 
package with strip test. The substitution of Sterility test with Container closure integrity tests 
during the shelf-life is in accordance with the guidelines or principles of both FDA and 
EMA:
In Questions & Answers of EMA web pages (Quality of medicines questions and answers: 
Part 2 / Stability - Endotoxin testing and sterility testing at the end of shelf-life) the following 
is stated:
“Sterility is part of the shelf-life specification.
Sterility testing should be performed at least at the end of Shelf-life, but it can be replaced by 
testing of the container closure integrity. Depending on the nature of the container, 
intermittent integrity testing might be envisaged, independent of whether the sterility testing 
is replaced or not.”
https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory-overview/research-development/scientific-
guidelines/quality-medicines-qa-introduction/quality-medicines-questions-answers-part-2
This approach is approved by FDA as well in Guidance document “Container and Closure 
System Integrity Testing in Lieu of Sterility Testing as a Component of the Stability Protocol 
for Sterile Products”.
FDA guideline states for example the following:
“Alternatives to sterility testing as part of the stability protocol, such as replacing the sterility 
test with container and closure system integrity testing, might include any properly validated 
physical or chemical container and closure system integrity test (e.g., bubble tests, 
pressure/vacuum decay, dye penetration tests or seal force tests, etc.). Such tests may be more 
useful than sterility testing in demonstrating the potential for product contamination over the 
product’s shelf life or dating period.”
Source:  P.5.1.02_07 Shelf Life Specification / Levonorgestrel intrauterine delivery
system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#IQMS-254491/ 022984914; 
unchanged)
P.5.6.01_02 Justification of Specification / Levonorgestrel intrauterine 
delivery system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#IQMS-187354/ 008081237; 
unchanged)
keywords: Sterility Testing; Container closure system; Shelf Life; Stability data; Justification of Specification

Question/Consideration:
Question 4
Justify regrading speciﬁcation of test for any individual impurity in NODCAR approval is 
(0.5%) although in CTD section "3.2.P.5.1" Speciﬁcations ( NMT 1%)
Answer/Response:
The acceptance limit for single impurity is based on the limit specified in ICH 
guideline Q3B(R2) “Impurities in new drug products” for a drug product 
with maximum daily dose below 1 mg. The acceptance limit for the sum of all impurities is 
based on the USP monograph on Levonorgestrel.
Ph. Eur. has published a compendial HPLC purity method for Levonorgestrel (LNG) 
drug substance, which is in use for LNG drug substance quality control (QC) at Bayer. The 
same Ph. Eur. purity method has been validated for use in Mirena IUS also.
The synthesis impurities that are not potential degradation products are controlled in 
LNG release testing and are therefore omitted from the drug product specifications. The 
potential known and unidentified LNG degradation products above ≥ 0.1% reporting 
threshold are included in the test results.
The current limit for the Sum of impurities 1.0 %, and at the same time the limit for the 
Individual impurity is added into the Mirena specification. According to opinion 
of Bayer Oy the proposed impurity limits are appropriate and well justified.

system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#IQMS-25449/ 022984914; 
unchanged)

delivery system 52 mg with inserter (MIRENA) (#IQMS-187354/ 008081237; 
unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 5
Justify regarding the following impurities which is mentioned in BP monograph of API 
(Levonorgestrel) is considered a degradation product impurities although it is not mentioned 
in CTD section "3.2.P.5.1" release & shelf life Speciﬁcations”
• Impurity H (6-Oxo-Levonorgestrel / Hydroxy variant): Formed as a direct 
consequence of structural oxidation at the allylic C-6 position when exposed to 
atmospheric oxygen or light. 
• Impurity M
Answer/Response:
The acceptance limit for the sum of all impurities is based on the USP monograph of 
Levonorgestrel. Ph.Eur has published compendial HPLC purity method, Related substances A 
in the 01/2014:0926 monograph and this method has been implemented for Levonorgestrel 
drug substance quality control (QC) testing. Therefore, also the drug product HPLC purity 
method applies the Ph. Eur. method. The extraction procedure and HPLC method has been 
validated for the drug product. The synthesis impurities that are not potential degradation 
products are controlled at levonorgestrel drug substance QC testing and are omitted in the 
drug product test results according to ICH Q3B guidance. The potential known and 
unidentified levonorgestrel degradation products above ≥ 0.1% reporting threshold are 
included in the test results.
The mentioned impurities H and M are mentioned and specified in validation document 
P.5.3.10_02 Validation of Test for Impurities. The validation document verifies that the 
impurities H and M are separated from other substances in the test and, hence, they can be 
identified and quantified, as well, in the impurity test performed on Mirena intrauterine 
delivery system. This means that also impurities H and M will be observed and taken into 
account in impurity calculations in stability analysis, if available in the analyzed batch.
Due to inherent stability of levonorgestrel, Impurity test parameters will be deleted from 
release Specification. The long history of the production has verified that levonorgestrel 
remains virtually unchanged in the manufacturing process of the drug product, and also 
during the stability studies. This is demonstrated by comparison of the results for five drug 
product stability batches to the corresponding drug substance batch results . Comparison table 
provided in P.5.6.01_02 Justification of Specification.
Justification for the non-inclusion of the impurity parameters into the release specification 
provided in CTD section P.5.6.01_IQMS-187354_2.0

Question/Consideration:
Question 6
If the request to increase the overage is caused by the primary packaging that leads to 
continuous loss of the active pharmaceutical ingredient, then the root cause must be addressed 
which is changing the primary packaging—rather than requesting an increase in the overage
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 6:
We acknowledge the Agency’s comment.  
 
The aim of the change was to identify in which process step and to what extent losses occur 
during the manufacture of Ventavis, which is filled into 1 mL glass ampoules. Therefore, the 
assay of iloprost has been analyzed by a staged sampling concept over the whole manufacturing 
process of the drug product Ventavis, including ampoule filling and sterilization. The study 
results clearly indicate that the primary packaging (glass ampoule) mainly contributes to the 
reduction of iloprost content in the drug product solution by around 3-4 %. An adsorptive effect 
of drug substance iloprost to glass surfaces could be verified. 
 
Furthermore there is no analytical information hinting at a degradation of the drug substance 
and it is no stability problem, because the values for the iloprost assay remained stable along 
the shelf life.  
 
As result of the Corrective action process a drug substance manufacturing overage of 3 % was 
defined and the relevant sections are updated according to the requirements of ICH guideline             
Q 8 (R2) Pharmaceutical Development (see P.2.2.01#008274184 vers. 02 (IQMS- 188062), 
P.3.2.01#008281943 vers. 04 (IQMS-187957). 
 
Manufacture of stability batches was carried out in production scale applying the defined

Question/Consideration:
Question 2(3)
Sub-batch manufacturing process: After the change of this product, the mixing and granulation steps are divided into two sub-batches. ① Please explain the necessity of adopting sub-batch production. ② Please evaluate the uniformity of the sub-batch process, including the consistency of material quantity and quality of input materials between sub-batches, the consistency of process parameters between sub-batches, the quality consistency of intermediate products in each step between sub-batches, the quality uniformity within sub-batches, and the intra-batch and inter-batch quality uniformity of the commercial batch after mixing. ③ Please clarify the criteria for mixing of sub-batches, which are recommended to include at least content uniformity, water content, powder properties, storage conditions and allowable storage time of intermediate products, and related substances should also be examined when necessary. At the same time, based on the product characteristics assessment, determine whether it is necessary to test the key quality indicators of the sub-batch before total mixing during commercial production and the testing frequency.
Answer/Response:
① The sub-batch manufacturing process was implemented for the granulation step due to reduced operating volume of the fluid-bed granulator at the Receiving Unit Delpharm site (approx. 50% of the operating volume of the equipment from the Sending Unit Bayer Leverkusen. Please refer to A.1.02) This approach enables the required commercial batch size to be produced while operating within the qualified capacity of the available equipment
②/③ As per valid master batch record, for both sub-batches the same material quality and quantity is used. The manufacturing of the sub-batches was conducted at the same pre-defined operating ranges during process validation (please refer to Validation Report Vericiguat and R.3.3.01. The sub-batches were combined after completion of the granulation and drying steps in accordance with the master batch record and confirmation that no deviation with potential impact on granule quality or blend homogeneity had occurred. During process validation, the overall mixing homogeneity (i.e., the homogeneity of the tableting mixture, sampled and tested from at least 10 different locations in the container) after the granulation process was tested, after combining the sub-batches and blending with the lubricant. The overall mixing homogeneity of three batches for each of the three strengths met the acceptable standard (RSD ≤ 5%). Loss on drying of the granules after the drying step in the granulation process was tested. The loss on drying of six sub-batches for each of the three strengths met the acceptable standard (1%–3%). The tablet content homogeneity in the tableting process (sampled and tested from at least 20 different time points) was tested. The content homogeneity of three batches for each of the three strengths met the acceptable standard (RSD ≤ 4.0%). Accordingly, the basis for combining the sub-batches was the use of the same material quality and quantity, manufacture within the same pre-defined operating ranges and compliance with the acceptance criterion for loss on drying after drying. The abovementioned results demonstrate that the sub-batch approach yielded consistent granules and did not adversely affect the homogeneity of the final tableting blend or the content uniformity of the tablets.
Ultimately, the process validation results (i.e., the quality tests according to the specification) and the results of the comparative dissolution study demonstrate the suitability of the manufacturing process at the RU.
For commercial manufacture, the validated process and in-process controls provide assurance that the sub-batches are suitable for combination. Based on the validation data, the process is considered adequately validated, and the combination of two final blend sub-batches into one tableting batch is justified and well controlled.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2(5)
This product is a small-dosage formulation. Since the sub-batch process is newly added to the process after the change, please designate mixing, granulation, and total mixing as key process steps, and formulate critical process parameters as appropriate.
Answer/Response:
In consideration of the relatively low drug loading, the granulation, tablet compress and coating among others were considered key process steps during the initial risk assessment according to FMEA. However, A number of process parameters that were originally rated as ‘high risk’(Risk Priority Number, RPN>9) were re-evaluated as ‘low risk’(RPM≤9) upon process understanding during development studies. According to the intermediate risk analysis only the film-coating step is identified as critical manufacturing process step, which has a significant impact on one CQA (appearance) of the final product. Please refer to detailed quality risk assessment and control strategy in section P.2.3.01_IQMS-227251_2.0_ Pharmaceutical Development - Manufacturing Process. Mixing, granulation, and total mixing process steps are described in detail in the manufacturing process description in section P.3.3, including the sequence of operations, equipment, and established operating conditions applied for commercial manufacture.
Since this change involved a manufacturing site transfer only as stated in the response to item 2(2), the formulation, manufacturing principle, sequence of unit operations, and overall control strategy remained unchanged. The scientific basis for the manufacturing process and process parameters had already been established during pharmaceutical development and is documented in section P.2.3.01. Therefore, no further CPP re-definition was considered necessary specifically for this site transfer.
In addition, the manufacturing process comprises fluid-bed granulation, in which the active substance is contained in the granulation suspension and sprayed onto a pre-blend. This manufacturing principle is designed to support uniform distribution of the active substance within the granules and the final tableting mixture. For the introduced sub-batch approach, both sub-batches were manufactured using the same material quality and quantity and within the same pre-defined operating ranges. The sub-batches were combined after completion of granulation and drying in accordance with the master batch record and confirmation that no deviation with potential impact on granule quality or blend homogeneity had occurred, as described in the response to item 2(3).
The adequacy of the established process controls for these key process steps was confirmed during process validation at the Receiving Unit Delpharm (please refer to Process Validation Report Vericiguat). In particular, loss on drying of all six sub-batches for each of the three strengths met the acceptance criterion (1%–3%), the overall mixing homogeneity of the final tableting mixture met the acceptance criterion (RSD ≤ 5.0%) for three batches of each of the three strengths, and the tablet content homogeneity during compression met the acceptance criterion (RSD ≤ 4.0%) for three batches of each of the three strengths. These results demonstrate that the sub-batch approach yielded consistent granules and did not adversely affect the homogeneity of the final tableting blend or the content uniformity of the tablets.
Accordingly, the existing established process parameters, operating ranges, and in-process controls were considered appropriate for the transferred manufacturing process at the Receiving Unit Delpharm.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
Quality Study and Specification: Please provide the inter-batch consistency data (f2) of the dissolution profiles of the self-manufactured formulation after the change; in the dissolution profile similarity study for this change, the filter used for the test sample in the standard medium is different from that specified under the dissolution item of the registered standard, please provide relevant study validation data.
Answer/Response:
In response to the request for inter-batch consistency data of the self-manufactured formulation after the change, an additional batch-to-batch dissolution profile similarity assessment was performed using the process validation (PV) batches manufactured at Delpharm Milano S.r.l. (DEL). Pairwise f₂ calculations were conducted for all DEL PV batches within each strength using the mean dissolution values obtained from the individual dissolution results.
For HCl/NaCl pH 1.2 and 0.01 N HCl pH 2, the DEL batches exhibited rapid dissolution, with mean dissolution values already exceeding 85% at the earliest sampling time point. Therefore, the f₂ calculations were performed using the early profile time points of 10, 15 and 20 minutes, as these time points provide the most discriminatory assessment of dissolution profile similarity, while later time points primarily reflect the dissolution plateau. This approach is consistent with the methodology applied in the submitted dissolution profile studies.
For acetate buffer pH 4.5 and phosphate buffer pH 6.8, where dissolution occurred more gradually and the complete profile remained discriminatory, all available sampling time points (10, 15, 20, 30, 45 and 60 minutes) were included in the f₂ calculations.
The calculated inter-batch f₂ values are summarized below:
Table 1: Summary of f2 values for 2.5 mg dose strength DEL PV batches M002, M003 and M004
[table content as provided in DOCUMENT]
Table 2: Summary of f2 values for 5 mg dose strength DEL PV batches M002, M003 and M004
[table content as provided in DOCUMENT]
Table 3: Summary of f2 values for 10 mg dose strength DEL PV batches M003, M004 and M005
[table content as provided in DOCUMENT]
All calculated inter-batch f2 ranged from 70.6 to 99.8 and were above the acceptance criterion of f2 ≥ 50. Therefore, the dissolution profiles of the DEL process validation batches are considered similar according to the accepted f₂ criterion, demonstrating satisfactory inter-batch consistency of the self-manufactured post-change product for all strengths and dissolution media evaluated.
The dissolution profile studies submitted in support of the site transfer were performed using the routine dissolution testing setup available at the respective laboratories. As described in the submitted dissolution profile reports (P.2.2.02), Bayer AG, Leverkusen (LEV), used an automated dissolution sampling system. As part of this equipment configuration, a Poroplast 10 µm in-line pre-filter is integrated into the sampling cannula. The function of this component is solely to prevent larger undissolved particles from entering the automated sampling lines and causing blockage of the sampling system during sample withdrawal. The Poroplast 10 µm filter is therefore an equipment-related pre-filter and not the analytical filtration step used for preparation of the test solution.
After withdrawal from the dissolution vessel, the samples were filtered through a regenerated cellulose (RC) 0.45 µm filter. Consequently, the analytical filtration step and preparation of the final test solution were performed using the RC 0.45 µm filter specified in the registered dissolution test procedure. The Poroplast 10 µm pre-filter neither replaces nor modifies the analytical filtration process defined in the registered method.
At Delpharm Milano S.r.l. (DEL), dissolution testing is performed using manual sample withdrawal followed by filtration through the same RC 0.45 µm filter specified in the registered analytical procedure. Therefore, despite the different sampling configurations, the final analytical test solution at both sites is prepared using the registered RC 0.45 µm filtration step.
Furthermore, the comparability of the dissolution testing approaches used at LEV and DEL was evaluated during analytical method transfer (P.5.3.55). In this study, dissolution testing was performed by both laboratories on identical representative samples, and all predefined acceptance criteria for dissolution testing were met, including requirements for mean dissolution results, variability, and recovery. The transfer study demonstrated equivalence of the dissolution results generated by the LEV and DEL laboratories and concluded that DEL is qualified to perform routine dissolution testing for Vericiguat coated tablets.
Therefore, the reference to the Poroplast 10 µm filter in the dissolution profile reports reflects only the configuration of the automated sampling equipment used at LEV. The analytical filtration step itself remained unchanged and was performed using the registered RC 0.45 µm filter. In addition, the analytical method transfer confirmed that the LEV automated sampling procedure and the DEL manual sampling procedure yield equivalent dissolution results. Consequently, the use of the Poroplast 10 µm pre-filter is not considered to affect the dissolution results and the dissolution testing performed in the submitted studies is considered fully consistent with the registered analytical methodology.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1B:
As a result of the changes proposed in this submission, your IPC reduces the depth of the quality control net during an early and potentially vulnerable stage of the process, the up-to-96-hour hold post-first filtration. What is your post-approval monitoring plan for this change? Please address what corrective action protocol would apply if a release conductivity result, while within specification, were unexpectedly elevated relative to historical data.
Answer/Response:
The Continued Process Verification (CPV) strategy for Water for Injection is defined in the established CPV Plan, Document No. CPVP-BJ/DK0001 for post monitoring plan for this change. The test for conductivity at release is part of the CPV program and will continue to be monitored in a 6-month interval.
At Vetter, CPV is an integral component of the overall control strategy throughout the product lifecycle and is executed within a mature Pharmaceutical Quality System aligned with FDA Process Validation Guidance, ICH Q10, ICH Q9, and applicable GMP requirements.
The objective of CPV is to provide ongoing assurance that a validated manufacturing process remains in a state of control during routine commercial production while supporting effective quality risk management, continuous process understanding, and continual improvement.
Consequently, potential process variability can be identified at an early stage, allowing for timely investigation, implementation of appropriate corrective and preventive actions (CAPAs), and proactive maintenance of a robust state of control.

According to CPV Plan, Document No. CPVP-BJ/DK0001, trend assessment is performed using e.g. run chart analyses to identify statistically significant or operationally relevant signals. A signal is considered present when atypical behavior is observed e.g. sustained increase/decrease, process shift, cyclic pattern, or unfavorable movement toward specification limits.
If no signal is detected, the dataset is classified as no trend, and no further action is required.
For detected signals, an initial assessment determines whether the observation can be explained by known and documented causes, such as existing investigations, production incidents, analytical events, or isolated one-time occurrences. Adequately explained signals are not considered trends and require no additional action.
When a signal is confirmed as a trend following interdisciplinary evaluation, additional investigations are initiated to identify potential root causes and contributing factors. Existing process knowledge, manufacturing data, analytical results, deviation records, change controls, and relevant quality system information are reviewed to support the assessment. Based on the outcome of the evaluation, appropriate actions may be implemented to mitigate identified risks and maintain the state of process control. Such actions can include the initiation of corrective and preventive actions (CAPAs).
The effectiveness of implemented actions is subsequently verified through ongoing monitoring and trend review activities to ensure that the observed behavior has been adequately addressed and that process performance remains acceptable. All evaluations, decisions, rationales, and resulting activities are documented in the CPV Monitoring Report.
A trend is considered closed only after objective evidence demonstrates that appropriate actions have been completed and that the process continues to operate in a controlled state.
Continued Process Verification (CPV) monitoring plan is attached for your reference.
