Question/Consideration:
Justification for skip-lot testing
The risk assessment confirms a risk for N-nitroso-oxacarboxylic acid, with levels 
potentially exceeding 7.5 ppm (10%AI) during the 36-month shelf life, although 
remaining below 22.5 ppm (30% AI). Please provide further justification for the 
proposed skip-lot testing strategy in accordance with the applicable EMA requirements. 
Please also clarify whether routine testing at the end of shelf life has been considered 
and, if not, provide the scientific and risk-based justification for not implementing 
routine testing.
Answer/Response:
The relevant section of the EMA guideline (EMA/409815/2020 Rev.23) is as follows:
When a nitrosamine is identified after Step 2 confirmatory testing, a limit will usually need to 
be included in the specifications of the finished product and the product must comply if tested. 
If the root cause has been identified in the finished product manufacturing process or storage, 
or nitrosamines have been detected in the finished product, but the actual source of 
contamination remains unclear, routine testing of the finished product is required by default.
The control point (finished product, API or an intermediate) for nitrosamines should be 
selected in such a way that it will give assurance of presence of the impurity below the 
acceptable limit based on acceptable intake (AI) in the finished product.

The outcome of the confirmatory tests for Xarelto granules for oral supsension is interpreted 
as follows, based on the above mentioned guidance:
• The main root cause is the formation of a low amount of oxacarboxylic acid 
(vulnerable amine) from rivaroxaban directly in the granulation liquid, prior to 
granulation, as indicated in section 8.1 of the P.5.5.07 document. The oxacarboxylic 
acid is the sole source of N-nitroso-oxacarboxylic acid. 
• The origin of the nitrosating agent is unclear, but nitrite is unlikely to be part of the 
nitrosation mechanism, as explained in section 8.2 of the P.5.5.07 document.  
• The mechanism only acts during product storage, since the DP manufacturing does 
not yield N-nitroso-oxacarboxylic acid, even though oxacarboxylic acid is present. 
The only open item is the nitrosating agent (one or more) that is part of the 
mechanism during storage; see also the response to Question 3 below. 
• The control point is the storage of the filled product, which means ongoing stability 
studies of market batches.

Therefore, the source and root cause are known, while the mechanism is at least partially 
known by effectively ruling out nitrite. Furthermore, N-nitroso-oxacarboxylic acid remains 
below 30% AI well beyond the end of the shelf-life (36 months). The control point (stability 
testing of FP) is clear. Therefore, most points that are needed to fulfill the EMA requirements 
are clear.
As indicated document P.5.5.07 (section 9), Bayer has implemented an internal routine 
stability test in Q1-Q2 2026. This action is taken specifically to monitor any potential future 
changes in the manufacturing process, to confirm that no increase > 30% AI occurs.
Skip lot testing of retain samples is only mentioned as a potential option, if no changes are 
made to the production process. Skip lot testing may in that case replace stability testing until 
the end of the shelf-life. The decision to apply skip lot testing is controlled by the GMP 
change management process and is only implemented based on a sound rationale.
This interpretation and course of action is considered to be consistent with the EMA 
guideline.

Source:  
P.5.5.07-03 Risk Asssessment on Nitrosamines / Rivaroxaban granules 
2 % for oral suspension (Site Leverkusen) (P.5.5.07_IQMS-256157; 
unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Mitigation measures
The risk assessment concludes that no clear mitigation measures have been identified to 
consistently reduce theformation of N-nitroso-oxacarboxylic acid. Please clarify whether 
additional mitigation options, such as the use of lowernitrite excipients, inert 
gas/nitrogen during filling, or other formulation/manufacturing modifications, have 
been evaluated. If not, please provide the scientific justification for concluding that no 
feasible mitigation measures are available.
Answer/Response:
Possible mitigation measures are discussed in section 8.3 of the P.5.5.07 document.
Any given nitrosation mechnanism requires three conditions:
• source of vulnerable amine(s) 
• source of nitrosating agents 
• favorable reaction conditions, typically an aqueous environment at low pH and 
elevated temperature
During granulation and subsequent drying, all three factors are present, if nitrite indeed serves 
as the nitrosating agent. The investigation of the granulation and drying steps however 
showed that nitrisation of oxacarboxylic acid does not take place. If nitrite is not part of a 
potential mechanism during granulation, it is very unlikely to act in any mechanism that 
occurs subsequently during storage of dried granules. As a result, changing any of the 
excipients to lower the amount of residual nitrite is not expected to have an impact on the 
level of N-nitroso-oxacarboxylic acid.
Likewise, gaseous NOx (nitrous oxides) are an unlikely source of nitrosating agents, since 
they are expected to be present, in particular during the drying stage. Hence, the same 
rationale applies to NOx as for nitrite. Furthermore, the manufacturing process and the 
container closure system (bottles with screw cap) cannot be meaningfully adapted to exclude 
or minimize NOx, e.g. by filling under an inert gas.
In document P.5.5.07, it is hypothesized that a combination of nitrosating agents are part of 
the mechanism, since such a case has been published; see Org. Process Res. Dev. (2025) 29 
(9): 2259–2264.https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.oprd.5c00182. This case however does not apply 
to Xarelto granules for oral supsension, in terms of practical mitigating actions. The reference 
is nevertheless included to indicate that Bayer has indeed looked at possible actions from an 
scientific perspective.
In summary, the potential sources of nitrosating agents (nitrite, NOx) were considered, but the 
available analytical data indicate that neither one is effective, even under conditions

(granulation, drying) that would favor nitrosation. Therefore, actions to reduce nitrite and/or 
NOx have no apparent benefit, based on available data.

Source:  
P.5.5.07-03 Risk Asssessment on Nitrosamines / Rivaroxaban granules 
2 % for oral suspension (Site Leverkusen) (P.5.5.07_IQMS-256157; 
unchanged)

Question 1
Provide a tabulated comparison of the differences between the US, EMA, and SFDA 
specifications. Clearly identify all changes and provide a scientific justification for each

Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1:

Bayer has reviewed the finished product specifications for Elinzanetant capsule 60 mg 
approved in the United States (US), European Union (EMA), and submitted for the Kingdom 
of Saudi Arabia (SFDA). A detailed comparison of the specification parameters, acceptance 
criteria, and analytical procedures is provided in Table 1.
The review demonstrated that the specifications are highly aligned across regions. The only 
substantive difference identified relates to the dissolution acceptance criterion. The originally 
approved US specification includes a dissolution requirement of Q = 80% at 30 minutes, 
while the currently submitted SFDA specification includes a requirement of Q = 80% at 20 
minutes. The currently approved EMA specification requires Q = 85% at 20 minutes.
Initially, a dissolution specification of Q = 80% after 30 minutes was submitted worldwide. 
Following health authority feedback received during the Canada ACCESS procedure, the 
proposed limit of Q = 80% after 30 minutes was not accepted and was tightened to Q = 80% 
after 20 minutes. This tightened specification formed the basis for the harmonized global 
dossier approach. This global specification will be submitted to FDA as annual report in 2026.
For the EU procedure, EMA referred to the applicable European guideline and requested 
establishment of a dissolution specification of Q = 85% after 20 minutes. Consequently, the 
EMA-approved dissolution specification differs from the initially proposed global 
specification and from the subsequently harmonized global specification of Q = 80% after 20 
minutes.
In response to the SFDA request, Bayer agrees to amend the Saudi Arabian finished product 
specification to make it identical to the EMA specification.

Question/Consideration:
Question 1:
With respect to Step 2, the upper limits for hydrogen pressure and drying time are set at “60 bar” and “24 hours,” respectively, at Bayer AG, Wuppertal, whereas they are set at “10 bar” and “96 hours,” respectively, at Patheon Austria GmbH & Co KG. Please explain the reasons for changing these manufacturing parameters and the justification for the changes, also taking into account that the proven acceptable ranges (PARs) presented in the document T.30.35#021885341_02 at the time of the NDA were 50–90 bar and not more than 43 hours, respectively.
Answer/Response:
The parameter of hydrogenation pressure was found during development at Bayer AG, Wuppertal (Wuppertal) that hydrogenation takes place already at 5 bar. During the transfer of the product to Patheon Austria GmbH & Co KG (Patheon), the hydrogenation pressure needed to be adjusted due to equipment related safety reasons, which allows a maximum pressure of 50 bar. Sufficient span to the upper limit must be ensured. The suitability of the newly established value of 10 bar was verified during a pilot campaign at Patheon Austria GmbH & Co KG, demonstrating no negative impact on intermediate product quality. In addition, two further pilot batches were successfully manufactured at 8 bar, demonstrating complete conversion and comparable product quality. The PAR report concludes that no practical differences in process performance or product quality were observed between the evaluated pressure conditions and that no remaining starting material was detected in the isolated product.

The process parameter of drying time needed to be improved during the transfer to meet the specification of water with max. 1% of the resulting Intermediate. Exceeding this limit would negatively impact the subsequent conversion of the intermediate to Vericiguat. Stability data from a stress test for Fluorotrisamin (6 months 90 °C) generated in the course of PAR parameter setting (Lab experiments) prove that prolongation of the drying time does not negatively impact the quality of the intermediate product. We observed only a very minor increase within well below the specification limit in the level of unspecified impurities (from 0.06 % to 0.25 % (Spec. 0.50 %) and sum of impurities from 1.2 % to 2.1 %. (Spec. 5.0 %). In addition, we confirmed that the stress testing at Patheon under the condition of 120°C for 4 days demonstrated no significant impact on the quality of intermediate. No significant change in assay was observed, with the content remaining at 98.0% compared to the initial value of 98.2%, and no critical increase in unknown impurities was detected, and all unknown impurities remained below 0.15% area.

Based on the above, the adjustment of the parameters to suit the equipment used at Patheon is considered justified.

Source:  S.2.2.02-02 Manufacturing Process – Description / Fluorotrisamine intermediate (Site Linz) (IQMS-265282; unchanged)

Question/Consideration:
Question 5:
Please explain the reasons and justification for setting the blending speed in the first step at “14 rpm,” the spray rate in the third step at “0.8 kg/min,” the inlet air temperature at “85°C,” and the inlet air temperature and rotation speed in the fifth step at “70°C” and 4–5 rpm, respectively, at Delpharm Milano S.r.l., which differ from those at Bayer AG, Leverkusen. In particular, with respect to the rotation speed in the fifth step, please also take into account that the drum rotation speed in the coating process was identified as a high-risk parameter at the NDA (P.2.3.01#020885644_01).
Answer/Response:
The process parameter differences between Bayer AG (Site Leverkusen) and Delpharm Milano S.r.l (Site Segrate) are attributed only to differences in the manufacturing equipment. The qualitative and quantitative composition, unit operation principles and commercial batch size remain unchanged. Where equipment capacity or geometry differs, the affected operating parameters were adapted to reproduce equivalent process conditions on the receiving-site equipment, for example comparable thermodynamic conditions or mechanical energy input. The suitability of these adjusted parameters has been demonstrated by the successful process validation at the receiving site (P.3.5.01).

The fluid-bed granulator at Site Segrate exhibits approx. 50% of the operating volume of the fluid-bed granulator at Leverkusen Site. Therefore, two granulation sublots were introduced for Site Segrate which is presented in the respective batch composition and manufacturing process description (refer to P.3.2.01 and P.3.3.01).

Since the preparation of the pre-mix is also performed in two sublots, each sublot contains half the mass compared to the sending-site. The blending speed of 14 rpm reflects the operating range of the container rotating mixer at the receiving-site and produces an equivalent, homogeneous pre-mix. Homogeneity of the ready-to-press mixture (blend uniformity) was confirmed during validation: the variation coefficient of the drug substance content was well within the acceptance criterion (max. 5%) for all validation batches and dose strengths.

In fluid-bed granulation, the spray rate was adjusted to 0.8 kg/min (compared to 1.6 kg/min in Leverkusen) correspondingly to the reduced mass per sublot, which maintains the same ratio of liquid addition rate to product mass. The equivalence of the resulting granule quality was confirmed during validation: loss on drying after drying was within the acceptance range (1–3%) for all sublots and batches and downstream tablet attributes (uniformity of mass, resistance to crushing, disintegration, friability) all met the in-process control limits.

The difference between the product temperature control at Leverkusen and the inlet air temperature of 85°C registered at Site Segrate in granulation reflects the equipment-specific control and instrumentation. The selected inlet air temperature is within the development range (PAR) established for commercial-scale granulation (60–120°C; P.2.3.01, page 89, Table 32, T.35.35_IQMS-232541_3.0), and its suitability was confirmed by granule in-process controls, tablet properties and validation results.

For coating, the difference between outlet air temperature control at Leverkusen and the inlet air temperature of 70°C at Site Segrate likewise reflects equipment-specific control and monitoring. The selected value is within the development range (PAR) for commercial-scale coating (70–115°C; P.2.3.01, page 89, Table 32, T.35.35_IQMS-232541_3.0).

The applicant acknowledges that drum rotation speed was identified as a high-risk process parameter in the NDA because it is relevant for tablet-bed movement and coating appearance. The receiving-site range of 4–5 rpm differs from the 6–7 rpm used at Leverkusen due to differences in coating drum geometry. Since equivalent tablet-bed movement cannot be inferred from numerical rotation speed alone, the Site Segrate range was selected as equipment-appropriate. The suitability of the coating parameters (inlet air temperature and drum rotation speed) was confirmed by process validation, including compliant AQL testing and finished-product appearance attributes for all validation batches and dose strengths.

The parameter adjustments at Delpharm Milano S.r.l. are necessary equipment adaptations that maintain equivalent process conditions. Process validation (P.3.5.01) confirms that the receiving-site process is fully robust and capable of consistently producing product of the required quality.

Question/Consideration:
Question 6:
Regarding the change to the identification test for the coating agent by infrared spectrophotometry, from the potassium bromide disk method to the ATR method, notified in the minor change notification dated 27 April 2026, please explain the validity of comparison with a reference spectrum, taking into account that, because it is difficult to establish a reference spectrum for the ATR method, the reference spectrum method should, in principle, not be used, as stated in the “Guidelines for Drafting the Nineteenth Edition of the Japanese Pharmacopoeia (Partial Revision)” (PSEHB/PED Notification No. 11 dated 18 April 2023).
Answer/Response:
Although the JP Drafting Guideline states that the reference spectrum method is generally not adopted for ATR measurements because establishment of a universally applicable ATR reference spectrum may be difficult, the use of a reference spectrum for Identification Test (1) is considered appropriate for Lacquer Orange:
The reference spectrum was established using a well-characterized reference material representative of the commercial Lacquer. The ATR spectra are acquired under predefined and controlled measurement conditions, including the specified instrumental settings, spectral resolution, and data processing parameters, thereby ensuring consistency and reproducibility of the measurements.
The suitability of the reference spectrum has been confirmed during routine conformity testing. ATR spectra obtained for the batches used for manufacturing commercial tablet batches demonstrated excellent agreement with the established reference spectrum. No significant differences were observed in the overall spectral profile, the fingerprint region, or the characteristic absorption of bands relevant for identification.
The characteristic absorption bands and the overall ATR spectral profile provide sufficient specificity for confirming the identity of Lacquer.
Based on the demonstrated reproducibility of the ATR measurements, the consistent agreement of the supplied batch spectra with the established reference spectrum during routine conformity testing, and the use of predefined measurement conditions, comparison with the reference spectrum provides a scientifically sound, specific, and reliable means of identification. Therefore, the use of the reference spectrum method for the Identification Test is considered appropriate and justified.
keywords: IR spectrum; identity test in DP specification; analytical procedures; pharmacopeia; test method

Question/Consideration:
Question 1
An explanation of the application of the LTL AI of 1330 ng/day for Dotagraf, including the 
justification for its use as a permanent limit, taking into account the current EMA 
recommendations.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 1:
Further batches have been tested and the test results are reported in the updated investigation 
report.
All available data indicate that tested DOTAGRAF batches comply with the updated limits for 
NO-Meglumine plus NO-DO3A, with patient exposure well below the LTL AI 
limit (1330ng/day).
Given the infrequent lifetime use of Dotagraf, application of an LTL-based limit is consistent 
with the principles of ICH M7 and provides a scientifically justified approach to patient risk 
assessment.
While certain batches exceed the CPCA-based AI of 100 ng/day, this value represents a highly 
conservative generic threshold designed for daily treatment regimens and does not reflect the 
product-specific exposure scenario applicable to Dotagraf.
Consequently, the LTL AI of 1330 ng/day is considered the most appropriate and clinically 
relevant limit for NO-Meglumine in Dotagraf.
Source:  Investigation report Update September 2026
keywords: Nitrosamine Risk Assessment; risk assessment; nitrosamine; Nitrosamine impurities; HA correspondence for Nitrosamine

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
A complete calculation of the maximum daily exposure for Dotagraf, including clarification of 
how the conclusion of an exposure level of <0.15 μg/day was derived from the result of <5 
ng/mL.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2:
We would like to provide the following clarification regarding the derivation of the maximum 
daily exposure to N-Nitroso-Meglumine, a potential impurity in Dotagraf.
The analytical method (Method A) applied in 2025 for the determination of N-Nitroso-
Meglumine in Dotagraf demonstrated a limit of quantification (LOQ) of 5 ng/mL. As  N-
Nitroso-Meglumine was not detected above this threshold in the tested batches, the residual 
concentration in the finished product is considered to be <5 ng/mL.

The maximum daily exposure was calculated using a conservative worst-case assumption that 
N-Nitroso-Meglumine is present at the LOQ (5 ng/mL) and applying the maximum 
recommended daily dose of 30 mL (derived from 0.6 mL/kg body weight × 50 kg body weight):
Maximum daily exposure = 5 ng/mL × 30 mL/day = 150 ng/day = 0.15 µg/day
As the actual concentration is below the LOQ, the true maximum daily exposure to N-Nitroso-
Meglumine is therefore <0.15 µg/day.
Following the reduction of the Acceptable Intake (AI) for N-Nitroso-Meglumine from 
1500 ng/day to 100 ng/day by the EMA in March 2026, a more sensitive analytical method 
(Method B) was developed in order to demonstrate compliance with the revised AI, as the LOQ 
of the 2025 method (corresponding to a worst-case exposure of 150 ng/day) was no longer 
sufficient for this purpose Method B was optimized to achieve a target LOQ of 30% AIL (30 
ng/d), i.e. 1.00 ng/mL in the sample solution.
Method B was successfully validated across the range of 1.00 ng/mL to 100 ng/mL (30 – 300 
% AIL) N-Nitroso-Meglumine, with selectivity/specificity, linearity, precision, and accuracy 
meeting the predefined acceptance criteria.
While achieving the regulatory target LOQ of 10% AIL (0.333 ng/mL in the sample solution) 
was not technically feasible for Method B due to inherent limitations, the achieved LOQ of 
30% AIL is considered acceptable, as the corresponding conservative worst-case maximum 
daily exposure (1.00 ng/mL × 30 mL/day = 30 ng/day) remains well below the revised AI of 
100 ng/day, thereby supporting the continued safety profile of Dotagraf with respect to N-
Nitroso-Meglumine.

Question/Consideration: Provide a risk assessment regarding the reduction of testing frequency for the "Degradation products" parameter in the ﬁnished medicinal product speciﬁcation.
Answer/Response:
The risk assessment supporting the proposed reduction in testing frequency for the Degradation products parameter is based on an evaluation of the available historical batch data, the demonstrated stability profile of the product, the robustness of the manufacturing process and the annual production volume.
As presented in document P.5.6.02, release results for 115 commercial batches manufactured between January and December 2024 were evaluated. For all batches, keto-darolutamide, any unspecified degradation product, and the sum of all degradation products remained at very low levels and well below the approved acceptance criteria. No indication of an adverse trend or increased degradation product formation was observed. Furthermore, the 2024 results are consistent with those obtained throughout the commercial production history since product launch in 2019.
The conclusions of the risk assessment have been further confirmed by subsequent commercial manufacturing experience in 2025 and 2026. Production volumes in 2025 and 2026 have remained comparable to those observed in 2024, and degradation product results have continued to demonstrate a profile consistent with the historical dataset, with no indication of an adverse trend or increased degradation product formation.
The assessment also considered the stability characteristics of Darolutamide film-coated tablet 0.3 g. The product has demonstrated a very stable profile in long-term, accelerated and stress stability studies. In addition, the manufacturing process has been shown through extensive commercial experience to be robust and capable of consistently producing batches that comply with the established specifications.
The proposed testing frequency was selected considering both the demonstrated low risk of degradation product formation and the current production volume. At the 2024 production volume of 115 batches, testing every tenth batch would result in approximately 11 to 12 batches being tested annually, providing regular surveillance across the manufacturing year while maintaining an appropriate level of quality oversight.
Based on the consistently compliant historical batch data, the demonstrated stability of the product and the proven robustness of the manufacturing process, the risk associated with reducing the release testing frequency for Degradation Products to every tenth manufactured batch is considered low. Therefore, the proposed skip-testing frequency is considered scientifically justified and appropriate for Darolutamide film-coated tablet 0.3 g.

Question/Consideration:
Question 3
If Sum of all impurities (LC) is deleted from the release specification, a justification/risk  
assessment demonstrating that this parameter is non-significant must be provided  (variation 
B.II.d.1.d/IB).
Answer/Response:
The deletion of the Sum of all impurities (LC) parameter from the release specification and 
the test procedure for impurities in Mirena IUS has been revised to include only 
levonorgestrel (LNG) related degradation products, not any more synthesis related impurities 
as the current test. This approach is in line with the EMA guideline CPMP/ICH/2738/99 (ICH 
Q3B). The guideline states: “impurities present in the drug substance need not be monitored 
or specified in the drug product specifications unless they are also degradation products”.
This new test is removed from Release Specifications, i.e. it will be included in the shelf life 
testing only. To support the change, the acceptance limit for the sum of the degradation 
products is tightened from NMT 2.0% to NMT 1.0%. The potential known and unidentified 
LNG degradation products above ≥ 0.1% reporting threshold are included in the test results.
Levonorgestrel is inherently stable. The long history of Mirena IUS has verified that 
LNG  remains virtually unchanged in the product manufacture, and during the shelf-life. This 
is demonstrated by comparing results of five MIRENA IUS drug product stability batches 
with the results for corresponding drug substance batches (P.5.6.01). The results for 
drug substance batches in accordance with the Ph. Eur. method indicate actual low amount of 
the degradation products for Mirena IUS as the synthesis related impurities need not to be 
included in the results. This is shown to be true for the drug product batches listed, as the 
maximum result for the Sum of degradation products is only 0.1 %.
The daily dose released from a Mirena IUS is ca. 20 μg. According to the EMA guideline 
CPMP/ICH/2738/99 the identification threshold for impurities in a drug product with a 
maximum daily dose of 1 mg is 1.0% or 5 μg Total Daily Intake (TDI), whichever is lower. 
The potential known and unidentified LNG degradation products above 0.1% reporting 
threshold are included in the specifications of Mirena. Calculated as daily intake an impurity 
at 0.1 % level in Mirena provides a daily intake of 0.02 μg only. The level of possible 
unspecified degradation products in Mirena are therefore far below the identification 
threshold of 5 μg TDI. Even the sum of all degradation products calculated as daily intake 
(1.0 % of 20 μg daily dose) is ca. 0.2 μg (TDI) only.
The stability report (P.8.3.01) covering the whole 36 months’ shelf-life period of Mirena 
additionally proves the good stability of the product. The level of degradation products in all 3 
batches in the report is at 0.0 % after the 36 months study period.
Based on the arguments above the non-inclusion of the Sum of all impurities test into the 
release specification of Mirena is well justified.

A statistical study confirming the sterility of the product throughout its shelf life must be 
provided (variation B.II.d.1.d/IB).
Answer/Response:
Integrity of the primary package acting as a sterile barrier for Mirena is a prerequisite for the 
maintenance of the product sterility. Hence the sterility of the product throughout the shelf life 
is demonstrated during stability testing by testing the integrity of the primary package. The 
integrity of the package is tested with bubble test and the seal strength of the package with 
strip test.
The substitution of Sterility test with Container closure integrity tests during the shelf-life is 
in accordance with the guidelines or principles of both FDA and EMA:
In Questions & Answers of EMA web pages (Quality of medicines questions and answers: 
Part 2 / Stability - Endotoxin testing and sterility testing at the end of shelf-life) the following 
is stated:
“Sterility is part of the shelf-life specification. Sterility testing should be performed at least at 
the end of Shelf-life, but it can be replaced by testing of the container closure integrity.
Depending on the nature of the container, intermittent integrity testing might be envisaged, 
independent of whether the sterility testing is replaced or not.”
https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory-overview/research-development/scientific-
guidelines/quality-medicines-qa-introduction/quality-medicines-questions-answers-part-2
This approach is approved by FDA as well in Guidance document “Container and Closure 
System Integrity Testing in Lieu of Sterility Testing as a Component of the Stability Protocol 
for Sterile Products”.
FDA guideline states for example the following:
“Alternatives to sterility testing as part of the stability protocol, such as replacing the sterility 
test with container and closure system integrity testing, might include any properly validated 
physical or chemical container and closure system integrity test (e.g., bubble tests, 
pressure/vacuum decay, dye penetration tests or seal force tests, etc.). Such tests may be more 
useful than sterility testing in demonstrating the potential for product contamination over the 
product’s shelf life or dating period.”

Question/Consideration: Please justify the absence of microbiological testing in the active substance specification in accordance with the decision tree described in ICH Q6A. Alternatively, please update the specification accordingly.
Answer/Response:
The Applicant Bayer would like to confirm that the drug substance is not prone to support microbial growth.
Additionally, the microbiological purity of vericiguat micronized, which was monitored during development and pilot productions (S.4.4.02_IQMS-230884_3.0_Vericiguat micronized drug substance), was found to be within the acceptance criteria of total aerobic microbial count (TAMC) max. 1000 CFU/g, total combined yeast/mold count (TYMC) max. 100 CFU/g, and Escherichia coli absence in 1 g, which is appropriate for the intended oral application of the drug product.
Furthermore, the drug substance is not hygroscopic, and the water content of the micronized material is low (specification NMT 0.5%), which results in low water activity and therefore does not support microbial growth.
Microbiological impurities could potentially be introduced via process water, which is only used in step 3b as an antisolvent during crystallization, and this water is routinely monitored in the manufacturing plant to ensure absence of biological contamination.
In addition, the crystals are washed with organic solvents such as ethanol and isopropyl acetate to effectively replace water, further reducing any residual risk.
Overall, this supports the conclusion that the risk for microbiological contamination in vericiguat micronized drug substance can be considered negligible and routine testing is therefore not necessary.
Explanation is also given in the Justification of Specification section S.4.5.01, in section 3- Not specified Test items, 3.1 -Microbial Purity.

Question/Consideration: 3.2.S.2.3 - AgNO3 precipitation method: The applicant proposes the replacement of the current compendial identification methods for aqueous hydrochloric acid and aqueous hydrobromic acid with precipitation using AgNO₃. The omission of the silver nitrate confirmation step removes the specific identification of bromide based on the formation and characteristic behavior of the precipitate, hence, the reduced procedure does not differentiate bromide from chloride or other halides that may give similar reactions with silver ions. Please justify why the lack of specificity in the determination of the halide is acceptable.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge that the proposed identification procedure, based on precipitation with AgNO₃, confirms the presence of halide ions but does not, when considered in isolation, unequivocally differentiate chloride from bromide or other halides. However, the AgNO₃ precipitation test is not used as a stand-alone control of material.
Aqueous hydrochloric acid and aqueous hydrobromic acid are well-established raw materials at Cambrex Profarmaco Milano S.r.l. and are routinely used in accordance with their approved specifications. Both materials are sourced from qualified suppliers operating within an approved supplier qualification program.
Differentiation between the two materials is ensured throughout the supply chain and upon receipt through dedicated product codes, material descriptions, and labelling of the containers.
Upon receipt at Cambrex Profarmaco Milano S.r.l., incoming material testing is performed to verify compliance with the supplier Certificate of Analysis (CoA), including confirmation of identity based on internal test method and assessment of quality attributes relevant to the intended process use. The internal identification test method applied at Cambrex Profarmaco Milano S.r.l. allows differentiation between hydrochloric acid and hydrobromic acid based on the characteristic appearance of the resulting precipitate (white precipitate for chloride and yellow precipitate for bromide).
The assay is not considered a halide-specific identification test. Nevertheless, the assay provides an additional material-specific quality attribute and, together with the controls described above, further reduces the likelihood of misidentification of the raw material.
Therefore, although the proposed AgNO₃ precipitation test has limited specificity when considered independently, the totality of controls in place, including supplier qualification, material labelling, incoming inspection, identity testing, and assay testing, the specifications are considered adequate to ensure the identity of aqueous hydrochloric acid and aqueous hydrobromic acid for their intended use. Accordingly, omission of the additional compendial confirmation step is not considered to introduce an unacceptable risk of material misidentification.

Question/Consideration: 3.2.S.2.3-Sodium bicarbonate: The omission of the barium hydroxide confirmation step removes the specific identification of the evolved gas as carbon dioxide. Therefore, the test appears to demonstrate gas evolution only and not unequivocally the presence of carbonate. Please explain why the modified procedure remains acceptable, knowing that different gas can evolve upon addition of acid on other substances.
Answer/Response:
We acknowledge that the proposed identification procedure does not include the additional barium hydroxide confirmation step for the evolved gas contained in the currently approved compendial procedure. However, the proposed identification procedure is not used as a stand-alone control of material.
Sodium bicarbonate is a well-established raw material at Cambrex Profarmaco Milano S.r.l. and is routinely used in accordance with its approved specification. The material is sourced from qualified suppliers operating within an approved supplier qualification program.
Differentiation form other materials is ensured throughout the supply chain and upon receipt through a dedicated product code, material description, and labelling of the containers. Upon receipt at Cambrex Profarmaco Milano S.r.l., incoming material testing is performed to verify compliance with the supplier Certificate of Analysis (CoA), including confirmation of identity and assessment of quality attributes relevant to the intended process use.
The identity test based on visual observation of gas evolution following acidification of an aqueous solution provides strong evidence for the presence of hydrogen carbonate. However, it is not specific and does not allow unequivocal differentiation from carbonate or other substances that evolve gas upon acidification, such as sulphites.
Additional treatment of the evolved gas with barium hydroxide solution may facilitate visualization of the gas reaction; however, this test likewise lacks specificity. Carbon dioxide forms a precipitate with barium hydroxide, but sulphur dioxide and, to a lesser extent, hydrogen sulphide may also produce precipitates under these conditions. Consequently, the test does not permit unequivocal differentiation between these gases and primarily serves to distinguish them from gases that are unlikely to form precipitates with barium hydroxide, such as oxygen or nitrogen.
Identity verification is not based solely on this reaction but is supported by additional test parameters, including appearance, pH, and assay. The assay of sodium bicarbonate is characteristic because it is performed on a defined quantity of material and is directly related to the molecular weight of the substance through acidimetric titration. Materials possessing substantially different molecular weights would therefore yield results outside the established acceptance criteria.
Based on these rationales, the identity testing as submitted, confirming the evolution of gas upon acidification without further differentiation, provides a high degree of assurance when evaluated in conjunction with the assay result, the supplier's CoA, the material labelling, and the established supplier qualification and incoming control processes. The assay provides an additional material-specific quality attribute and, together with the controls described above, significantly reduces the likelihood of misidentification of the raw material.
Based on the totality of controls in place, including supplier qualification, material labelling, incoming inspection, identity testing, and assay testing, the specification is considered adequate to ensure the identity of sodium bicarbonate for its intended use.

Question/Consideration: 3.2.S.2.3 NaOH: The applicant proposes the deletion of the sodium carbonate acceptance criterion for aqueous sodium hydroxide solution. Please justify why control of total alkali alone is sufficient and demonstrate that removal of the carbonate limit does not adversely affect process performance or drug substance quality.
Answer/Response:
Aqueous sodium hydroxide solution is an established raw material at Cambrex Profarmaco Milano S.r.l. and is routinely used in accordance with its approved specification. The material is procured from qualified suppliers operating under an approved supplier qualification program.
Upon receipt, incoming material testing is performed to verify consistency with the supplier's Certificate of Analysis (CoA) and compliance with predefined acceptance criteria, including attributes relevant to the intended manufacturing use.
It is acknowledged that aqueous sodium hydroxide solutions may absorb carbon dioxide from ambient air, resulting in the formation of bicarbonate and carbonate species. This process primarily occurs when the solution is exposed to a continuous supply of fresh air over extended periods. In properly closed containers, carbon dioxide uptake is inherently limited by the small amount of carbon dioxide present in the enclosed headspace. Consequently, the extent of carbonate formation during normal storage conditions is expected to be minimal.
At Cambrex Profarmaco Milano S.r.l., sodium hydroxide solution is stored and handled in closed high-density polyethylene (HDPE) containers with a nominal volume of approximately 1,000 L. These containers remain closed during transportation and storage, thereby minimizing contact with atmospheric air. Exposure to fresh air occurs only during manufacturing operations when ventilation is required for pressure equalization. Given the broad use of sodium hydroxide solution across manufacturing activities, inventory is managed according to First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principles and extended storage periods are not anticipated. Under these handling and storage conditions, the potential for significant carbonate formation is considered negligible.
Furthermore, in Step 4 of the synthesis, sodium hydroxide is employed to promote ester saponification, yielding the corresponding carboxylate intermediate. The reagent is charged at approximately 3.0 equivalents, representing a substantial stoichiometric excess. Any minor amount of carbonate potentially present would not adversely affect the reaction outcome. Additionally, carbonate species are removed during the subsequent acidic work-up and washing operations.
Based on the storage conditions, handling practices, and manufacturing process understanding, routine testing or specification limits for carbonate content in aqueous sodium hydroxide solution are not considered necessary. The current material specification is therefore considered adequate to ensure the suitability of the sodium hydroxide solution for its intended use in manufacturing.
keywords: Control of Materials; specifcation raw materials; in-process control; Specification; Drug Product

Question/Consideration: 3.2.S.2.2-Bayer Wuppertal: The applicant proposes a significant downscaling of the manufacturing process at Bayer AG Wuppertal. Please provide a scientific justification demonstrating that the proposed reduction in batch size does not adversely affect process performance, impurity profile, or critical quality attributes of the drug substance.
Answer/Response:
The proposed change concerns a reduction in the manufacturing batch size at Bayer AG, Wuppertal. The manufacturing process remains unchanged with respect to the synthetic route, starting materials, raw materials, reagents, solvents, process sequence, reaction conditions, isolation and drying operations, in-process controls, critical process parameters (CPPs), control strategy, analytical methods, and intermediate and drug substance specifications. Manufacturing will be performed in qualified equipment appropriate for the proposed reduced scale.
Acoramidis hydrochloride drug substance and its intermediates are manufactured using a well-characterized and validated process supported by extensive development, process characterization, and commercial manufacturing experience. A risk-based assessment was performed to evaluate the impact of the proposed batch-size reduction on process performance and product quality. Based on the established process knowledge and manufacturing experience, no new risks and no increased risks to critical process parameters (CPPs), impurity formation or purge, or critical quality attributes (CQAs) were identified in the assessment.
Manufacturing, validation, and comparative batch data generated at Bayer AG, Wuppertal are now available and demonstrate consistent process performance at the proposed manufacturing scale. The manufacturing process consistently met the established in-process acceptance criteria and quality requirements for the intermediates and the final drug substance.
Process validation has been successfully completed for all manufacturing steps at Bayer AG Wuppertal. All validation batches complied with the predefined acceptance criteria and demonstrated reproducible process performance. The resulting intermediates and drug substance met their respective specifications.
Comparative batch data from batches manufactured at the current and proposed reduced scales confirm the absence of any scale-related impact on the product quality profile. The data demonstrate that the relevant process indicators, yields, in-process control results, impurity levels, residual solvents contents, water content, particle-size distribution, assay values, and other applicable quality attributes remain within established acceptance criteria and show no adverse trend attributable to the reduced batch size. The impurity profile of the drug substance, including specified, unspecified, and total impurities, remains comparable to that of batches manufactured at the approved scale.
A summary of the comparative batch analyses for all intermediates and for the final drug substance is provided in TRD references S.2.4.05 and S.4.4.01. These data confirm that the proposed reduction in batch size does not adversely affect process performance, impurity profile, or the CQAs of Acoramidis hydrochloride drug substance and its intermediates.
Therefore, the available manufacturing, process validation, and comparative batch data demonstrate that the proposed reduction in batch size does not adversely affect process performance, impurity profile, or the critical quality attributes (CQAs) of Acoramidis hydrochloride drug substance.

Question/Consideration: 3.2.S.4.2-PSD method: The applicant proposes an alternative sample preparation procedure for determination of particle size distribution, including the introduction of sonication. Please provide a scientific justification demonstrating that the proposed method is equivalent to the currently approved PSD method and define the acceptance criteria that will be applied to establish comparability between both methods.
Answer/Response:
Method familiarization and development activities demonstrated that controlled sonication provides reproducible dispersion of the particles at the Bayer testing site while maintaining the same measurement principle and generating PSD results comparable to those obtained with the approved vortex-based sample preparation procedure. A risk assessment was conducted to evaluate any potential impact of the modified sample preparation procedure on the measurement principle and the resulting particle size distribution data. The assessment concluded that sonication disperses agglomerates formed during sample preparation and is not expected to alter the intrinsic particle size distribution.
These conclusions were further supported by validation and robustness studies and method comparability testing.
Method comparability between the currently approved vortex-based sample preparation procedure and the proposed sonication-based procedure was demonstrated by comparative testing of three representative batches at the current and proposed testing sites, Cambrex Charles City Inc. and Bayer AG Wuppertal, respectively. The generated particle size distribution data were evaluated against predefined acceptance criteria in accordance with Bayer's analytical transfer procedure taking into account Ph. Eur. chapter 2.9.31. For all tested batches, the obtained D50 results showed relative deviations well within the predefined acceptance criterion of ≤ 15% (Table 1). These data demonstrate comparable method performance and confirm that the introduction of sonication for sample preparation does not adversely impact the determination of particle size distribution.

Question/Consideration:
Question 2-2:
[2] Provide the document cited as "CTD3.2.S.4.3.86 – Aflibercept drug substance 
(Bridging study report for Bioassay)" in section "5. Potency by Bioassay" in 
3.2.S.4.5.1-S4501_IQMS-176964_10.0) (p.15), and explain the equivalence of the 
bioassays between before and after the change. If this Bridging Study does not include 
the results of measurements of the same samples and comparison of the results using 
the test methods before and after the change, provide the results and explain the 
equivalence of the test methods between before and after the change. In addition, 
given the change in calculation formula stated in [1] above, explain how the 
equivalence of test methods is ensured between before and after the change.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2-2:
In accordance with your instructions, the reference material – Bridging study report for 
Bioassay (S.4.3.86_IQMS-391281_1.0_Aflibercept drug substance (v1.0)) – is 
provided as attachment 1.
The change from IC50 (TA unconstrained) / IC50 (RS unconstrained) to IC50 (RS 
constrained) / IC50 (TA constrained) was introduced as part of the optimization of the 
bioassay to improve assay robustness, throughput, and data interpretation.
As a result of the calculation of the old formula (IC50 (TA unconstrained) / IC50 (RS 
unconstrained)), test articles which exhibit lower IC50 values than the standard, (and 
thus are more potent than the standard) would yield RP values < 100%. Test articles 
less potent than the standard (and therefore, exhibiting higher IC50 values than the 
standard) would yield RP values > 100%.
By reversing the equation in the optimized method, the potency calculation aligns with 
the general practice of expressing potency relative to the reference standard and is 
intended to provide a more accurate and interpretable assessment of the test article's 
effectiveness compared to the reference standard. The difference in the calculation is 
taken into account by a recalculation to compare the potency values of the original 
method to the optimized method.
The optimized method uses a constrained 4-PL model and expresses potency relative 
to the reference standard. The impact of the calculation formula change was addressed 
within the bridging study through side-by-side comparison of lots tested using both 
methods and by reprocessing/recalculating data using both the original and optimized 
calculation approaches (please refer to S.4.3.86 section 3). Comparability was assessed 
by comparing unconstrained relative potency values generated by the original method 
with unconstrained relative potency values recalculated from the optimized method, 
thereby accounting for the effect of the calculation change.
Equivalence was demonstrated by pair-wise potency ratios and 90% confidence 
intervals, which met the predefined USP <1090> equivalence criterion for release and 
stability samples (please refer to S.4.3.86 section 4). The optimized method was also 
shown to detect potency changes under stability and stress conditions comparably to 
the original method. Therefore, the calculation change is scientifically justified, and 
the proposed optimized bioassay is considered equivalent to and suitable to replace the 
current original method.

quality attributes even if they are varied in a broad range and thus, they can be omitted in the 
manufacturing process description. The respective process parameter understanding studies 
are added to S.2.6.01 including variation of amounts for the following solvents and reagents:
• Process step 4a: variation of amounts of acetonitrile and water used as work-up 
solvents (Subchapters of 5.1.5.1: “Input quantity acetonitrile for dilution after 
reaction” and “Input quantity water for dilution after reaction”)
• Process step 4a: variation of amount of acetonitrile used for washing isolated Gd-
Glydonip (Subchapter of 5.1.5.1: “Input quantity acetonitrile for washing of Gd-
Glydonip”)
• Process step 4b: variation of amount of water and aqueous sodium hydroxide within 
aqueous basic work-up (Subchapters of 5.1.5.2: “Quantity of water added for dilution 
before basic treatment” and “DoE on basic treatment”)
• Process step 4b: variation of amount of t-butyl methyl ether used for washing the 
neutralized aqueous phase (Subchapter of 5.1.5.2: “Washing quantities t-butyl methyl 
ether”)
• Process step 4b: variation of amounts of ethanol and acetone used for crystallization of 
gadoquatrane crude after defined distillation endpoint is reached (Subchapters of 
5.1.5.2: “Quantity ethanol added to distillation residue” and “Quantity acetone added 
to distillation residue”)
• Process step 4b: variation of amount of acetone used for washing isolated 
gadoquatrane crude (Subchapter of 5.1.5.2: “Quantity acetone used for washing”)
• Process step 4c (for the diafiltration-/ultrafiltration process, the introductory passage 
of chapter 5.1.5.3 in S.2.6.01 already contained the following information): Being a 
physical separation method of solubilized components as opposed to a chemical 
reaction, the key parameter relevant for quality of step 4c is the number of diafiltration 
cycles, as other parameters (variation of water used for gadoquatrane crude 
dissolution, temperature, membrane surface area) only influence the time one cycle 
takes, not the product quality
• Process step 4d: variation of amount of activated charcoal used before final 
crystallization of gadoquatrane drug substance (Subchapter of 5.1.5.4: “Quantity of 
activated charcoal”)
The results of those studies demonstrate that constancy of quality of gadoquatrane is ensured 
within a broad parameter range justifying not to define setpoints for those non-critical process 
parameters.
Although demonstrated that the washing amount of ethanol in the final step 4d has no impact 
on the quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance in a broad range, Bayer agrees to amend the 
manufacturing process description by adding the respective washing amount of ethanol to 
further ensure the constancy of quality. Consequently, a subchapter to 5.1.5.4 in S.2.6.01 
(“Quantity of ethanol used for washing”) is added well.
Considering the number of steps towards the drug substance and additional control of 
intermediates, washing amounts and solvent amounts required for simple dissolution 
procedures or pH adjustments used in earlier synthesis steps have no impact on the quality of 
Gadoquatrane drug substance and therefore are not included in the manufacturing process 
descriptions. Furthermore, several in-process controls (IPCs) are implemented in the early 
steps before the final intermediate (Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate) to monitor the degree of 
conversion and level of impurities fulfilling the requirements of Notification No. 0210001 by 
ensuring the constancy of quality by additional control measures:
Steps 1a+1b: 3 IPCs plus control of Glyptac intermediate based on appropriate release 
specification (S.2.4.03 Glyptac intermediate)
Steps 1c+1d: 3 IPCs plus control of Glyptac intermediate based on appropriate release 
specification (S.2.4.03 Glyptac intermediate)
Steps 2a+2b: 4 IPCs plus control of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude intermediate based on 
appropriate release specification (S.2.4.03 Gd-GlyMe-DOTA crude intermediate)
Step 3: 1 IPC plus control of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate based on appropriate release 
specification (S.2.4.03 Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate)
In conclusion, Bayer does not agree that the manufacturing process descriptions should 
provide more detailed information for process parameters which have no impact on the 
quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance but agrees to add washing amounts of ethanol used in 
the last synthesis step. Control of intermediates and in-process controls justify that such 
detailed process descriptions are generally not required for all manufacturing process steps.
The amount of ethanol used for washing the drug substance after final crystallization has been 
included in the manufacturing description (S.2.2.02 Manufacturing Process – Description / 
Gadoquatrane drug substance):

After change:
After stirring, the mixture is cooled to『20 °C』, solids are isolated by filtration and washed

In accordance with the instruction, we will adjust the description in the approval application 
form to clarify that either double or five times the weight of ethanol will be added to the

Question/Consideration:
Question 2
Reply to the following inquiries regarding there are two manufacturing methods for DO3A 
route (Step 1a, Step 1b) and Cyglyp route (Step 1c, Step 1d).
1. 
The equivalence/homogeneity of the drug substance obtained from DO3A and Cyglyp 
routes is explained based on the compliance with the control for the intermediates Glyptac 
and Gd-GlyMe-DOTA and the specifications for the drug substance obtained from both 
routes (S.2.6.01, chapter 5.1.1). Provide information on impurity profiles (e.g., 
chromatograms) including the related substances that were not specified in the control of 
intermediates and specifications of drug substance, and explain that the differences in 
manufacturing procedure do not affect the efficacy and safety.
2.

period for the drug substance produced by DO3A route based on the results of the stability 
studies, etc., of the drug substance produced by Cyglyp route.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 2 (3.2.S.2, 3.2.S.7):
Bayer confirms that the differences in manufacturing procedure do not affect efficacy and 
safety. The quality of Gadoquatrane drug substance remains consistent, regardless of whether 
it is produced via Cyglyp route or DO3A route. The drug product Gadoquatrane solution 0.4 
mmol Gd/mL for injection is unaffected, maintaining the same quality, efficacy and safety. 
Further details are provided below.
Response to Question Q2-1:
The synthesis of Gadoquatrane drug substance includes two different routes of synthesis 
towards the first intermediate Glyptac. Both synthesis routes (DO3A route and Cyglyp route) 
are compared in detail in section 5.1.1 of S.2.6.01. The comparison includes the organic and 
inorganic impurity profile, as well as solvents and potential mutagenic impurities in the 
intermediates Glyptac and Gd-GlyMe-DOTA and in the final drug substance. Based on this 
data it is shown that the drug substance produced via DO3A route or Cyglyp route is of equal 
quality.
An additional comparison of the non-specified impurities in intermediates and in the drug 
substance is requested and is therefore provided in the following.
Organic impurities in Gadoquatrane drug substance:
In Gadoquatrane drug substance the following impurities are relevant in both routes and are 
specified with individual limits: Gd-GlyMe-DOTA (refer to Question 11), Formyl-Tris-Gd-
GlyMe-DOTA Isomer 1, Methyl-Gadoquatrane Isomer 1 and 2 and Desmethyl-Gadoquatrane 
Isomer 1.
Besides those specified impurities no further impurities are detected in Gadoquatrane drug 
substance batches above reporting threshold (RT 0.03%). This is demonstrated by the batch 
data of Gadoquatrane drug substance in Table 1 (result for any unspecified impurity <0.03%) 
and by the chromatograms provided in Figure 1. Thus, there is no difference which has an 
impact on quality in the impurity profile of Gadoquatrane drug substance produced via either 
DO3A or Cyglyp route.
Further organic impurities which can be formed in the final chemical steps 4a to 4b are 
described in section 5.2 of S.2.6.01. None of the discussed impurities are route-specific. The 
potential impurities can occur in both routes of synthesis and are effectively purged, as 
discussed in detail in the respective section.

Gd-Me-DOTA can be formed in both routes of synthesis and are effectively purged towards

Triester in Glyptac and ... Gd-DO3A in Gd-GlyMe-DOTA. Control of

Question/Consideration:
Question 3:
Reply to the following inquiries regarding the control of raw materials.
1. 
Explain the principles of the test method for the following control.
• 
Step 2a Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Iron: 20ppm or less (visual inspection)
• 
Step 2a Sulfuric acid: Chloride: 10ppm or less (visual inspection)
• 
Step 4b Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Chlorine: 0.0004% or less (visual inspection) 
and Iron: 0.0001% or less (visual inspection)
2. 
Explain the acceptance criteria and the principle of the test method the following 
control.
• 
Step 4b t-butyl methyl ether, Step 4b/4d Denatured ethanol and Step 4b Acetone: 
Acidity or alkalinity: must comply (visual and titration)
• 
Step 4d Activated charcoal: Acidity or alkalinity: must comply (visual)
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 3 (3.2.S.2):
Response to Question 3-1.:
The method for all of these tests has been classified as “visual inspection”, as the final 
judgement of colorized or turbid solutions has to be done visually. Please find here the 
descriptions of the principle of the methods for the requested tests.
Step 2a Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Iron: 20 ppm or less (color reaction)
An aqueous dilution of the test substance is reacted with ammonium persulphate and 
potassium thiocyanate solution containing butanol. In parallel, the same reaction is carried out 
with a standard iron solution.
The test solution meets the requirement if the intensity of the color produced in the butanol 
layers (due to Fe(SCN)3) is less intense than that produced by standard iron solution (20 
ppm).
Step 2a Sulfuric acid: Chloride: 10 ppm or less (precipitation reaction)
An aqueous dilution of the test substance is treated with nitric acid and silver nitrate. In 
parallel, the same reaction is carried out with a standard chloride solution.
The turbidity in the sample solution, produced by precipitated AgCl, is less than in the 
reference solution.
Step 4b Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Chlorine: 0.0004% or less (color reaction)
An aqueous dilution of the test substance is treated with potassium iodide and starch solution.
Any blue coloration (due to iodine produced) must disappear when adding max. 0.2 mL 
sodium thiosulfate solution 0.01 M.
Step 4b Hydrochloric acid concentrated: Iron: 0.0001% or less (color reaction)
An aqueous dilution of the test substance is treated with citric acid monohydrate and 
thioglycolic acid. In parallel, the same reaction is carried out with a standard iron solution.
After 5 minutes the sample solution is max. as pink as the reference solution. The pink 
coloration is due to the ferric thioglycolate produced.
Accordingly we will modify the approval application form to clarify the principles of these 
testing methods. We will also make similar changes to the relevant sections of CTD 2.3.S.
Before change:
... (visual)
After change:
... (color reaction)/(precipitation reaction)
Response to Question 3-2.:
Step 4a Acetonitril, Step 4b t-butyl methyl ether, Step 4b/4d Denatured ethanol and Step 
4b Acetone: Acidity or alkalinity: must comply (neutral litmus paper and titration)
The test substance mixed with water is tested with red and blue litmus paper.
The litmus paper shows neutral reaction.
If the litmus test is weakly alkaline or acidic, carry out a titration.
Test for alkaline substances: 50 mL of the test substance is titrated to color change from blue 
to yellow against bromophenol blue indicator.
The volume of hydrochloric acid 0.1 mol/L consumed must not exceed 0.3 mL.
Test for acidic substances: 50 mL of the test substance is titrated to color change from 
colorless to pink against phenolphthalein indicator.
The volume of sodium hydroxide solution 0.1 mol/L consumed must not exceed 0.3 mL.
Step 4d Activated charcoal: Acidity or alkalinity: must comply (neutral litmus paper)
The test substance is heated in water. After cooling to room temperature, the suspension is 
filtered, the filtrate has to be neutral against litmus paper.
Accordingly we will modify the approval application form to clarify the principles of these 
testing methods. We will also make similar changes to the relevant sections of CTD 2.3.S.
In addition, we have standardized the descriptions for "acidity or alkalinity" ... and ... made corresponding adjustments.

Question/Consideration:
Question 5
Explain the justification of the reworking based on the experiences of reworking and the 
analytical results of the reworked lots for Step 2a, "If in-process control 2 is not met, a 
dichloromethane work-up is performed." If there is no cases of reprocessing so far, remove 
the description related to the reprocessing.
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 5 ( 3.2.S.2, 3.2.S.4 ):
For the first commercial scale production campaigns, the dichloromethane work-up in Step 2a 
was carried out for every batch produced as part of the regular process with the aim to ensure 
consistent quality control of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate obtained in Step 3. Batch 
analysis data of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate batches, which were manufactured with 
execution of the dichloromethane workup during Step 2a are shown in S.2.4.05_01 
(Manufacturing date in 2022: 37148971, 37148972, 37148973). Likewise, batch analysis data 
of Gadoquatrane drug substance obtained from Gd-GlyMe-DOTA batches, which were 
manufactured with execution of the dichloromethane workup during Step 2a are shown in 
S.4.4.01 (Manufacturing date in 2022: UN623TE, UN623TG, UN623TI)
With ongoing manufacturing experience and development of the DO3A route of synthesis, it 
was determined that the dichloromethane work-up is not always required to meet the 
specifications of the downstream impurity Bis(Gd-GlyMe-DOTA) (limit max. 0.2% on Gd-
GlyMe-DOTA intermediate). To exert control of this impurity during manufacturing, in-
process-control 2 will need to comply to levels of the respective precursor species (Bis-
carboxylic acids controlled as RRT 0.84) of not more than 0.3% in step 2a (a detailed 
discussion including the structure of the controlled species can be found in S.2.6.01).
Batch analysis data of Gd-GlyMe-DOTA intermediate batches, which were manufactured 
with no dichloromethane workup performed during Step 2a are shown in S.2.4.05 
(Manufacturing date in 2024: 37169824, 37169825, 37169826). Likewise, batch analysis data 
of Gadoquatrane drug substance obtained from Gd-GlyMe-DOTA batches, which were 
manufactured with no dichloromethane workup performed during Step 2a are shown in 
S.4.4.01 (Manufacturing date in 2024: UN62XIK, UN62XIM, UN62XK7).
The batches of drug substance produced in 2022 and 2024 showed no difference in impurity 
profile and all batches complied with the current specification. Based on the experience 
gained during routine production on commercial scale, retaining the in-process control-
governed dichloromethane workup in the manufacturing description of Step 2a as reworking 
is justified by the quality-based arguments.

Question/Consideration:
Question 9
Please answer the following questions regarding the identification test, IR.
1. 
The Guideline for Drafting the Japanese Pharmacopoeia states that, in principle, the 
reference spectrum method should not be used because it is difficult to set a reference 
spectrum with ATR method. Therefore, please consider deleting the method of comparing 
with a reference spectrum. If Bayer considers that it is possible to set a reference spectrum, 
please provide a justification.
2. 
In the answer to 1 above, when differences are found in comparison with spectrum of 
reference standard (not comply) and repeat the comparison between spectrum of the test 
sample and reference standard, please explain a justification with a rationale (Including a 
justification for dissolving the sample and gadoquatrane reference standard in water, 
evaporating to dryness, and using it as a measurement sample).
Answer/Response:
Bayer Response to Question 9 (3.2.S.4):
1. In test method S.4.2.01, identity testing by IR is described using the attenuated total 
reflection (ATR) method. A figure of the reference spectrum is shown. This reference 
spectrum was generated by measuring the qualified gadoquatrane reference substance after 
structure elucidation has been carried out and is electronically stored in the software. During 
release testing, a visual comparison of the reference spectrum and the sample spectrum is 
performed on an overlay generated in the software. Therefore, the reference spectrum and the 
sample spectrum are recorded on the same equipment in the same laboratory environment. 
Different samples lead to reproducible results during the period of the validity of the reference 
substance which comply to the reference spectrum shown in in S.4.2.01 for illustration 
purposes.
This procedure is covered by Ph. Eur. 2.2.24 “Absorption spectrophotometry, infrared”, 
where it is described that the spectrum of the reference standard may be recorded immediately 
or stored in a spectral library for future consultation. Also, JP general chapter 2.25 “Infrared 
Spectrophotometry” allows both options (3.1 “Identification by the use of a Reference 
Standard” and 3.2 “Identification by the use of a Reference Spectrum”) without limitation to a 
specific sample preparation method. Recent IR-spectrophotometer are capable of generating 
reproducible ATR spectra, so that the shown example reference spectrum in S.4.2.01 will 
remain valid for comparison throughout the lifecycle of the drug substance.
The confirmation of identity by IR testing follows a stepwise approach.
1. The gadoquatrane reference standard is qualified and IR spectrum is measured with
the IR device of the laboratory responsible for release testing. The spectrum is stored 
in the software.
2. IR spectra of the release batches are generated and compared with the spectrum of the
reference standard stored in the software. If both spectra comply to each other, the 
identity is confirmed.
3. If there is any ambiguity ... because of different
water loadings ... both ... are recrystallized in parallel ... obtained with the same water content and the same solid state form ... identity can be confirmed 
unambiguously.
This procedure was chosen to reduce the amount of reference standard to be used ... appropriate to use a reference spectrum for comparison first and only in case of ambiguity 
use direct comparison to the reference standard after recrystallization.
2. Gadoquatrane drug substance can exist in different polymorphic forms (Hydrate I, II, III 
and amorphous phase), with a wide range of water loadings (up to 21.0 %, see S.4.1.01) and is 
classified as very hygroscopic. Depending on the water content, slight differences in the IR 
spectrum might be observed ... By dissolving the substance and the reference standard in water and drying them 
under the same conditions, both sample and reference standard can be obtained with the same 
water content. When the measurement and comparison are repeated subsequently, identity can 
be confirmed unambiguously.
